3.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
3.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

3.q: A ward manager is introducing Making Every Contact Count (MECC) and explains the first level of intervention to her team. Which description matches a MECC Level 1 very brief intervention?
o: Oral discussion and negotiation with follow-up and possible referral for support
High-intensity specialist sessions over several weeks for people at high risk
An individual discussion lasting more than 30 minutes over one or more sessions
Giving information or signposting, taking from 30 seconds to a couple of minutes
3.w: NHS England, Making Every Contact Count consensus statement (2016): MECC uses day-to-day interactions to support positive changes to physical and mental health and wellbeing. Level 1 very brief intervention takes from 30 seconds to a couple of minutes and enables information giving or signposting; Level 2 brief intervention involves discussion, negotiation or encouragement.

n.0: This describes a MECC Level 2 brief intervention.
n.1: High-intensity interventions are delivered by specialist services, not as MECC very brief interventions.
n.2: This describes an extended brief intervention (NICE PH49), which is more intensive than Level 1.

3.q: Bridget, 58, is due to have her first red cell transfusion before surgery. She asks the nurse what she should know about it. According to NICE NG24, which information should the nurse include?
o: That she will be able to give blood herself once she has recovered
That she will no longer be eligible to donate blood after a transfusion
That she cannot refuse once the transfusion has been prescribed
That a transfusion has no risks if the bedside checks are completed
3.w: NICE NG24 rec 1.14.2: give verbal and written information on the reason for transfusion, risks and benefits, the process, alternatives, that the person is no longer eligible to donate blood, and encourage questions; document the discussion (1.14.3).

n.0: NG24 states people who have had a transfusion are no longer eligible to donate blood.
n.2: A person with capacity may refuse a transfusion; consent remains her decision.
n.3: Transfusion carries risks that must be explained even with correct checks.

3.q: A community nursing team wants to improve the written information given to people after a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Which approach best involves people who use the service in this improvement?
o: Adapt a leaflet that a neighbouring trust has used for several years
Co-design the information with people who have recently been diagnosed
Ask the diabetes consultant to approve the content before it is printed
Ask the team's nurses to agree the content at the next team meeting
3.w: P6.9 requires nurses to work with people, their families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies. Co-design with people who have lived experience of the service makes information relevant, accessible and person-centred (Code 2.1 work in partnership).

n.0: Borrowing another organisation's leaflet may help, but it does not involve local service users in the improvement.
n.2: Clinical approval checks accuracy but does not involve people who use the service.
n.3: Staff agreement alone excludes the people the information is for.

3.q: Gareth, a learning disability liaison nurse, is training outpatient staff on the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag. A nurse asks what the flag is. Which answer is correct?
o: A GP code showing that a person is on the learning disability register
A paper sticker placed on the front of the person's hospital notes
A national record of a person's reasonable adjustments, visible to services
A local alert that each trust designs for its own patient system
3.w: The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag (Information Standard DAPB4019) is a national record on the National Care Records Service of the adjustments a disabled person needs, so that health and adult social care services in England can see and meet them (NHS England).

n.0: The GP learning disability register is separate; the flag records specific adjustments for any disabled person.
n.1: A paper sticker is a local, non-shareable marker; the flag is digital and national.
n.3: The flag is a national standard, not a locally designed alert, so it can be seen across organisations.

3.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
3.q: Paul, 31, has a mild learning disability and lives in supported living. He tells his keyworker he has a girlfriend he met at college. A support worker says people like Paul 'shouldn't really be in relationships'. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Support it, as Paul has the same right to relationships as anyone else
Ask the GP to decide whether the relationship is in Paul's best interests
Discourage the relationship until his family have given their agreement
Allow the relationship with staff supervising all of their meetings
3.w: People with a learning disability have the same right to private and family life, including relationships, as everyone else (Article 8 HRA; UNCRPD Article 23). Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)), and staff should support Paul, including with accessible information about relationships and safety.

n.1: Best interests decisions apply only to people lacking capacity, and decisions about sexual relations cannot be made for a person under the MCA (s27).
n.2: An adult's relationships do not need family approval.
n.3: Blanket supervision is a disproportionate restriction without any identified risk.

3.q: At a retirement celebration on the ward, a nurse takes a team photograph. A patient sitting in a bay is visible in the background. The nurse wants to post it on her public social media account. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Post the photograph after blurring the patient's face
Post the photograph with no names or ward details
Post the photograph using strict privacy settings
Post a version without the patient, who has not consented
3.w: NMC social media guidance: do not post pictures of patients and people receiving care without their consent, regardless of whether you believe they could be identified. Code 5.1 and 20.10.

n.0: NMC guidance requires consent before posting images of patients, whether or not you believe they could be identified.
n.1: Removing names does not remove the need for the patient's consent to the image being shared.
n.2: Privacy settings do not replace consent and content can still be shared onward.

3.q: Peter, 52, has Down syndrome and diagnosed Alzheimer's dementia. He lives in a shared house and is becoming disorientated at night. Staff propose locking his bedroom door so he does not wander. What should the nurse advise?
o: Assess capacity and look at less restrictive options first
Lock the door at night, as this is the safest plan for Peter
Ask the GP for a sedative so that he sleeps through the night
Arrange an urgent move to a nursing home with locked doors
3.w: Locking Peter in is a significant restriction. Under the MCA 2005 his capacity must be assessed, any decision made in his best interests and less restrictive options considered first (night lights, signage, sensor alerts, waking staff) (MCA s1(6), s4).

n.1: Locking him in without a best interests process is unlawful restraint and could be a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: Sedation increases falls and aspiration risk and is chemical restraint.
n.3: A move is a major decision; less restrictive support in his home should be explored first.

3.q: Fred, 72, has crusting around both eyelids after a viral illness. You are asked to clean his eyes. Which technique is correct?
o: Use one swab for each eye, wiping back and forth across the lid
Use one swab for both eyes, wiping from outer to inner corner
Use a fresh swab for each eye, wiping from inner to outer corner
Use a dry cotton bud inside the lower lid to remove crusts
3.w: Eye care principles: use sterile saline and a separate swab for each eye, wiping once from the inner canthus outward, so that debris and infection are not carried into the tear duct or the other eye (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wiping back and forth reintroduces debris to the eye.
n.1: Sharing a swab and wiping inward risks cross-infection and moving debris into the tear duct.
n.3: Inserting a cotton bud inside the lid risks corneal injury.

3.q: The son of a patient on a medical ward is shouting at the nurses' station because he was not told his father had been moved to another bay. He is red-faced and pacing. What should the nurse, Bryony, do first?
o: Call security straight away so that he can be escorted off the ward
Tell him firmly that shouting is unacceptable and that he must lower his voice
Speak calmly, acknowledge his frustration and offer to talk somewhere quieter
Explain that the move happened because of bed pressures beyond her control
3.w: De-escalation uses a calm tone and non-threatening body language, acknowledges the person's feelings, and moves the conversation away from an audience, while keeping a safe distance and exit route (AnnexA.4.2.5 de-escalation strategies when dealing with conflict).

n.0: Security may be needed if there is a risk of violence, but there is no threat here and calling them first may escalate the situation.
n.1: Leading with a demand can escalate anger before his concern is acknowledged.
n.3: Explaining reasons before acknowledging his feelings can sound defensive and does not de-escalate.

3.q: Ms Douglas, 55, has capacity. Last year she made a valid advance decision refusing antibiotics for pneumonia. Today she tells the nurse she has changed her mind and would want antibiotics if she became unwell. She does not want to put this in writing. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep following the advance decision until it is replaced
Ask her to sign a written withdrawal before it can apply
Accept the withdrawal and document it in her records
Ask two witnesses to confirm her change of mind
3.w: MCA 2005 s24(3)-(4): a person may withdraw an advance decision at any time when they have capacity, and a withdrawal need not be in writing. The nurse should record it clearly and tell the team.

n.0: Her withdrawal takes effect now; the old decision does not continue until replaced.
n.1: Withdrawal does not need to be in writing, so a signature is not required.
n.3: There is no witness requirement for withdrawing an advance decision.

3.q: A student nurse asks Priti why she called the outreach team for a patient whose NEWS2 is 4, when the escalation chart only requires a ward review. Priti had noticed new subtle confusion. Which response best shows sound professional judgement?
o: Explain that her clinical concern justified the escalation
Explain that students should not question escalation decisions
Explain that the score required outreach review at that level
Explain that she prefers to escalate every patient to be safe
3.w: Proficiency P1.10: demonstrate resilience and emotional intelligence and explain the rationale for judgements and decisions. NEWS2 (RCP 2017): clinical concern can prompt escalation beyond the aggregate score; new confusion scores 3.

n.1: This shuts down learning; Code 9.4 requires her to support students' learning.
n.2: Under NEWS2 (RCP 2017) an aggregate of 4 calls for a ward-based response, urgent review by the ward medical team if one parameter scores 3, not outreach; her call rested on clinical concern.
n.3: Blanket escalation is not a reasoned judgement; P1.10 requires the rationale to be explained.

3.q: Noah, 31, has a moderate learning disability. ABC records show he grabs other people's drinks in the café. Each time, staff buy him his own drink to calm the situation. The episodes have increased from twice to eight times a week. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The café is too noisy and is causing sensory overload
Staff are giving him attention, which maintains the behaviour
He is thirsty because his fluid intake at home is too low
Buying a drink acts as a consequence that reinforces the grabbing
3.w: The behaviour reliably produces access to a tangible (his own drink), and its frequency has risen since this response began, showing the consequence is reinforcing it. Functional assessment looks at consequences that maintain behaviour (NICE NG11 1.5.9).

n.0: Nothing in the records points to noise as a trigger; the pattern fits access to a drink.
n.1: The consistent consequence is the drink itself; attention is not what changes after the behaviour.
n.2: Thirst could be checked, but it would not explain the rise linked to staff buying a drink each time.

3.q: After staff use a two-person hold to stop Kieran, 20, from hitting another resident, the learning disability nurse leads the response. Kieran has a moderate learning disability. Which action should follow once everyone is safe?
o: Ask the GP for regular sedation to prevent further incidents
Add the hold to Kieran's plan as the first response for the future
Move Kieran to another service so that the other resident is protected
Record the hold and hold a debrief with Kieran and with staff
3.w: NICE NG11 1.9.6: every restrictive intervention is recorded and followed by a debrief with the person (in an accessible way) and with staff, to support recovery and learn how to prevent recurrence; data feed into the reduction programme.

n.0: Regular sedation is chemical restraint and is not supported by NG11 or STOMP after one incident.
n.1: Restrictive interventions are a last resort; making the hold the first response increases restriction.
n.2: A placement move is a major decision that is not justified by a single incident and does not address the cause.

3.q: Mrs Adeyemi, 72, has capacity and a leg ulcer. When the nurse arrives to change the dressing she says firmly that she does not want it done today because she is tired. The dressing is not urgent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Change the dressing gently because it is in her best interests
Respect her decision, explore her reasons and record the refusal
Ask her daughter to persuade her to accept the dressing change
Assess her capacity because she is refusing recommended care
3.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment. Mrs Adeyemi has capacity, so her refusal is valid. The nurse should explore why, explain any consequences, offer another time and document the refusal.

n.0: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity (MCA s4); treating a capacitous person against her refusal is unlawful.
n.2: Using a relative to pressure her undermines the voluntariness of any later consent.
n.3: Refusing care is not evidence of incapacity; MCA s1(4) says an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity, and capacity is presumed.

3.q: Staff have used intensive interaction with Nell, 37, who has a profound learning disability, for three months. The team wants to know whether she is making progress. What is the best way to evaluate this?
o: Repeat her IQ assessment to measure cognitive change
Record observations of her eye contact and turn-taking over time
Ask Nell's family whether she seems happier than she was before
Count how many tasks she completes each day
3.w: Progress in intensive interaction is shown by changes in the fundamentals of communication (attention, eye contact, turn-taking, length of shared interaction), so regular recorded observations, sometimes with video, are used.

n.0: IQ testing does not measure the fundamentals of communication.
n.2: Family views help but are not a structured record of communication progress.
n.3: Task completion measures compliance, not communication.

3.q: Amira, 29, is admitted to a gynaecology ward. Her notes record a history of sexual assault. When the nurse reaches to hold her hand during an examination, Amira flinches. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop, ask whether touch is acceptable and explain each step first
Ask a colleague to hold her hand in place of the nurse
Continue gently, as touch is a recognised comforting technique
Stop all communication until the examination is finished
3.w: Annexe A 1.3: use appropriate non-verbal communication, including touch, eye contact and personal space. Code 1.1 and 4.2: treat with respect and gain consent before any action.

n.1: Changing who touches her does not address whether she wants touch at all.
n.2: Comforting touch is only therapeutic when welcome; her reaction shows it is not.
n.3: Withdrawing communication leaves her anxious and unsupported.

3.q: Ivan, a newly appointed nurse at an acute trust, is booked onto the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training on Learning Disability and Autism. A colleague asks why the training carries Oliver's name. Which explanation is accurate?
o: He was a man with a learning disability whose death at Winterbourne View prompted the national inquiry
He was a learning disability nurse who designed the first national training curriculum
He was an autistic man with a learning disability who campaigned for training in his twenties
He was an autistic teenager who died after being given an antipsychotic his family had opposed
3.w: Oliver McGowan was an autistic teenager with a mild learning disability, epilepsy and cerebral palsy who died in 2016 after a severe reaction to antipsychotic medication that he and his family had asked doctors not to give. His parents campaigned for mandatory training (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: Winterbourne View was an abuse scandal exposed in 2011; Oliver did not die there.
n.1: Oliver was a patient, not a nurse or curriculum designer.
n.2: Oliver died as a teenager in 2016; the campaign was led by his parents after his death.

3.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
3.q: Ahmed, 36, has a learning disability and is in supported living. His carer gave buccal midazolam 3 minutes ago for a seizure that had lasted 5 minutes, but he is still convulsing. His plan does not say otherwise. What should happen now?
o: Wait 20 minutes for the midazolam to take full effect
Put him in a cool bath to bring the seizure to an end
Give a second dose of midazolam straight away
Call 999 for emergency help
3.w: NICE NG217 7.1.7: if convulsive status epilepticus does not respond to the first dose of benzodiazepine, call emergency services in the community. A second dose is considered if the seizure has not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first (7.1.8).

n.0: Waiting 20 minutes without calling for help delays emergency treatment.
n.1: A bath is dangerous during a seizure because of drowning risk.
n.2: A second dose is considered only after 5 to 10 minutes; giving it at 3 minutes is too early.

3.q: Jas, a learning disability nurse, is writing a Social Story for Riley, 15, who is autistic and is having a blood test. Which sentence fits the Social Story approach best?
o: The nurse will put a band on my arm. It will feel tight for a short time.
If I do not keep still, the nurse will have to try again.
Most young people are brave and do not cry when they have blood taken.
The needle is tiny, so it will not hurt me when it goes in.
3.w: Social Stories use descriptive, accurate and reassuring sentences, often in the first person, that explain what will happen and how it may feel. They avoid threats, comparisons and false promises (Carol Gray).

n.1: This frames the story as a warning, which can increase anxiety.
n.2: Comparisons and pressure to be 'brave' are not descriptive and can cause shame.
n.3: Promising it will not hurt is inaccurate and can damage trust.

3.q: At 16:30 the laboratory phones the ward with a potassium result of 6.9 mmol/L for Mr Hayes, 74, who has chronic kidney disease. He feels 'a bit weak' but is otherwise as before. The doctor who requested the test has gone home. What should the nurse do?
o: Escalate to the on-call doctor now and document the result
Recheck his observations in 4 hours and escalate if they change
Record the result for the day team to review in the morning
Ask the laboratory to send the result to his GP for review
3.w: NMC proficiency P3.12 requires nurses to interpret results and act promptly, escalating when required. A potassium of 6.9 mmol/L is markedly raised and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, so the on-call doctor must be told now and the communication documented (Code 10).

n.1: Normal-looking observations do not exclude the risk of arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia.
n.2: Waiting until morning leaves a dangerous result untreated for hours.
n.3: The GP is not responsible for an inpatient's urgent results.

3.q: Liam, 26, has no learning disability. He tells his GP practice nurse that he struggles with social situations and has rigid routines, and asks whether he could be autistic. Which approach is in line with NICE CG142?
o: Use the AQ-10 and record a diagnosis of autism if he scores 6 or above
Request genetic testing before deciding whether to assess for autism
Consider the AQ-10 and offer full assessment if he scores 6 or above
Arrange an MRI brain scan to look for structural signs of autism
3.w: NICE CG142 1.2.3: for adults with possible autism who do not have a moderate or severe learning disability, consider the AQ-10; a score of 6 or above, or clinical suspicion, should lead to an offer of comprehensive assessment.

n.0: The AQ-10 is a screening tool; it identifies who needs a comprehensive assessment and does not make a diagnosis.
n.1: Genetic tests are not used routinely to diagnose autism.
n.3: CG142 advises against routine neuroimaging for diagnosing autism.

3.q: During a teaching session, a practice educator lists four sources a nurse might rely on when explaining informed consent: the Mental Capacity Act 2005, the Care Act 2014, the NMC Code and Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]. A student asks which of these is case law made by the courts. Which source should the educator identify?
o: The Mental Capacity Act 2005
The NMC Code, professional standards of practice
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]
The Care Act 2014
3.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 is a Supreme Court judgment, so it is common (case) law. The two Acts are statutes made by Parliament and the Code is a set of professional standards set by the regulator.

n.0: The MCA 2005 is primary legislation (statute) passed by Parliament, not case law.
n.1: The Code is the NMC's professional standards; it is a regulatory document, not a court decision.
n.3: The Care Act 2014 is statute; its safeguarding duties come from Parliament, not a court judgment.

3.q: Mrs Patel, 58, is two days after bowel surgery. Her NEWS2 is 4. On assessment the nurse notices her knees are mottled and her lips look slightly blue. How should these findings change the nurse's view of her risk?
o: Her NEWS2 of 4 shows low risk, so routine monitoring is enough
They are expected after surgery and do not change her risk
They should be rechecked once her NEWS2 rises to 5 or more
She may be at higher risk than her NEWS2 score suggests
3.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider a higher risk of severe illness or death from sepsis than NEWS2 suggests if the person has a mottled or ashen appearance or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue. These are signs of physical ill health (Annexe B 1.2.1) needing urgent escalation.

n.0: NG253 says these signs indicate higher risk than the score alone suggests.
n.1: Mottling and cyanosis are not normal post-operative findings.
n.2: Waiting for the score to rise delays escalation of signs that already indicate higher risk.

3.q: Ben, 35, has a moderate learning disability. ABC charts show he hits out on some days when asked to get dressed but not on others. Night staff notes show the incidents follow nights when he slept less than four hours. How should the nurse describe the poor sleep in the formulation?
o: A consequence that keeps the behaviour going
A trigger that immediately precedes the behaviour
A setting event that makes the behaviour more likely
The function the behaviour serves for Ben
3.w: Setting events are background conditions (poor sleep, pain, hunger, illness) that change how likely a trigger is to provoke the behaviour. NICE NG11 1.5.9 asks for setting events to be identified alongside triggers and maintaining consequences.

n.0: Consequences follow the behaviour; poor sleep comes before it.
n.1: The immediate trigger is the request to get dressed; poor sleep is a background condition, not the antecedent.
n.3: The function is what the behaviour achieves (for example escape); sleep loss influences likelihood but is not a function.

3.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
3.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

3.q: Winston, 69, has COPD with hypercapnia and is prescribed a salbutamol nebuliser. His target saturation is 88-92%. How should the nebuliser be driven?
o: By oxygen at 6-8 L/min for the whole nebulisation
By compressed air, with oxygen by nasal cannulae if needed
By oxygen at 2 L/min to reduce the risk of hypercapnia
By oxygen at 15 L/min through a reservoir mask
3.w: BTS oxygen guideline: in people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, nebulisers should be air-driven, with supplemental oxygen given by nasal cannulae to keep saturation at 88-92%.

n.0: Prolonged oxygen-driven nebulisation risks hypercapnia in this group.
n.2: 2 L/min is too low to nebulise the drug effectively.
n.3: A reservoir mask delivers high-concentration oxygen and is not a nebuliser driver.

3.q: Leo, 40, lives in supported living. His keyworker now shows him two shirts each morning and lets him pick, and helps him plan his own meals each week. Previously staff decided these for him. Which of O'Brien's accomplishments is being developed most directly?
o: Choice
Competence
Respect
Community presence
3.w: Choice is about people having control over everyday decisions and their own life. Offering options and supporting Leo to decide develops choice; other accomplishments may benefit, but choice is the direct focus.

n.1: Competence is about developing skills; the change here is about who makes the decisions.
n.2: Respect is about valued roles and reputation in the community.
n.3: Community presence is about using ordinary community places.

3.q: Kayla, 6, has a moderate learning disability and a diagnosis of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. A student nurse is sorting causes of learning disability by when they act. How should this cause be classified?
o: Chromosomal, because alcohol alters the number of chromosomes
Prenatal, because alcohol affects the developing brain in the womb
Perinatal, because the damage occurs around the time of birth
Postnatal, because the effects become apparent after birth
3.w: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder results from alcohol crossing the placenta and damaging the developing fetal brain, so it is a prenatal (environmental) cause of learning disability.

n.0: Alcohol is a teratogen; it does not change chromosome number as in trisomy 21.
n.2: Perinatal causes act around birth, such as hypoxic injury during labour; alcohol exposure acts during pregnancy.
n.3: Classification depends on when the brain injury happens, not when the effects are noticed.

3.q: Marta works as an NHS ward nurse and plans to start offering cosmetic injections at a private clinic at weekends. Her NHS employer's indemnity covers her NHS work. What does the Code require before she starts the private work?
o: Confirmation from the clinic that her NHS indemnity extends to it
An appropriate indemnity arrangement that covers the private practice
Written approval of the private work from her NHS ward manager
A note of the private work in her next revalidation application
3.w: Code 12.1: make sure you have an appropriate indemnity arrangement in place relevant to your scope of practice. Professional indemnity is also a revalidation declaration.

n.0: Her NHS indemnity covers NHS work; the clinic cannot extend it, so she needs separate appropriate cover.
n.2: Employer approval may be needed under her contract, but the Code requirement is indemnity cover relevant to her scope of practice.
n.3: Recording it later does not meet Code 12.1, which requires cover to be in place before she practises.

3.q: Mr Evans, 69, has expressive aphasia after a stroke. He understands speech but struggles to find words. Which approach best supports communication?
o: Finish his sentences for him to reduce his frustration
Use closed questions, picture boards and extra time
Ask his wife to answer all questions on his behalf
Speak more loudly and repeat each sentence twice
3.w: Annexe A 2.5: identify the need for and manage alternative communication techniques. Code 7.3: use a range of verbal and non-verbal methods.

n.0: Finishing sentences may misrepresent what he means and reduces his control.
n.2: He can understand and should be supported to communicate for himself.
n.3: His difficulty is expressing words, not hearing; volume does not help.

3.q: Colin, 49, is found on a hospital corridor floor. He is breathing normally but responds to pain only. There is no suggestion of injury. Help is on its way. How should he be positioned?
o: Sitting upright against the wall
In the lateral recovery position
Flat on his back with legs raised
Prone with his head to one side
3.w: RCUK first aid 2025: place a person with decreased responsiveness who does not meet the criteria for CPR in a lateral (side-lying) recovery position. Do not use it if breathing is agonal or there is trauma.

n.0: Sitting a person with reduced responsiveness upright risks airway compromise and falls.
n.2: Supine positioning risks airway obstruction from the tongue or vomit.
n.3: Prone positioning impedes airway assessment and breathing.

3.q: Joan, 74, has lower back pain after a fall at home and is being cared for on a frailty unit. Her care plan lists several pain-relieving interventions. Which of these is a non-pharmacological intervention?
o: A rectal paracetamol suppository
A topical lidocaine plaster
Patient-controlled analgesia pump
Repositioning using pillows
3.w: Non-pharmacological measures include repositioning, heat or cold where appropriate, distraction, relaxation, reassurance and explanation. NICE NG31 gives repositioning as an example (Annexe B 3.5).

n.0: A suppository is a route for giving a drug.
n.1: A lidocaine plaster delivers a drug and is pharmacological.
n.2: PCA delivers opioid medicine and is pharmacological.

3.q: Kenneth, 68, lives in England and asks the practice nurse what the NHS bowel cancer screening programme will offer him. He has no bowel symptoms. Which answer is accurate?
o: A home test kit every 2 years
A home test kit every year
A colonoscopy every 5 years
A one-off camera test at age 70
3.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): everyone aged 50 to 74 is offered a bowel cancer screening home test kit every 2 years; people aged 75 or over can ask for a kit every 2 years.

n.1: The bowel screening kit is sent every 2 years, not annually.
n.2: Colonoscopy is a diagnostic test offered after a positive screening result, not the routine screen.
n.3: The current programme offers a home test kit every 2 years from 50 to 74.

3.q: George, 80, lives in a care home and has been assessed as having capacity to make decisions about his medicines. He refuses his atorvastatin, saying he does not want it at his age. His daughter asks the nurse to crush it into his yoghurt without telling him. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange a best interests meeting about covert administration
Agree after the GP signs a covert administration form
Respect his refusal, record it and inform the prescriber
Agree, as the statin is in his long-term interests
3.w: Covert administration is used only for people who actively refuse medication and lack capacity, under an agreed plan (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21; NICE SC1). George has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (MCA 2005 s1(4): an unwise decision does not mean lack of capacity), documented and shared with the prescriber.

n.0: A best interests process applies to people who lack capacity; George has capacity.
n.1: A GP's signature cannot authorise covert administration to a person who has capacity.
n.3: Giving medicine covertly to a person with capacity is unlawful, whatever the benefit.

3.q: Joanne is the first health professional at a road traffic collision and is passing information to the ambulance control room using the M/ETHANE structure. What does the 'H' in M/ETHANE stand for?
o: Hospital
Head injuries
Hazards
Help needed
3.w: M/ETHANE (JESIP joint doctrine): Major incident declared or standby; Exact location; Type of incident; Hazards (present and potential); Access routes; Number of casualties; Emergency services present and required (P6.12).

n.0: The receiving hospital is decided by the ambulance service; it is not an M/ETHANE heading.
n.1: Injury types inform casualty numbers and severity but are not the 'H' heading.
n.3: Resources needed are reported under 'Emergency services', not 'H'.

3.q: Thomas, 71, has advanced lung cancer and full capacity. The registrar decides that CPR would not be in his interests and plans to complete a DNACPR form. The registrar tells the nurse they will not mention it to Thomas because 'it might upset him'. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Remind the registrar that Thomas should be consulted unless it would cause him harm
Ask Thomas's wife to decide whether he should be told about the decision
Accept the plan, as DNACPR decisions are a medical matter that need no discussion
Record the DNACPR now and plan to tell Thomas at next week's ward round
3.w: R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals NHS FT [2014] EWCA Civ 822: Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions, and there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Lord Dyson MR (para 54) said doctors should be wary of being too ready to exclude patients from the process on the grounds that their involvement is likely to distress them; a belief that discussion would cause distress is unlikely to be enough unless the distress is likely to cause harm (para 56).

n.1: Thomas has capacity; his wife cannot decide what he is told about his own care.
n.2: R (Tracey) [2014] held there is a presumption the patient will be consulted, and warned against excluding patients because the discussion may distress them.
n.3: Delaying the conversation until after the decision is recorded still breaches the duty to consult him first.

3.q: Rajesh, 52, is on day 3 of intravenous antibiotics through a forearm cannula. He reports pain at the site, and you see redness and swelling tracking along the vein. He still needs intravenous antibiotics. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply a warm compress and reassess the site at the end of the shift
Leave the cannula in place and record the findings in the care plan
Flush the cannula with 0.9% sodium chloride and continue if it is patent
Remove the cannula and arrange resiting at a different site
3.w: Pain, erythema and swelling at a cannula site indicate phlebitis on a visual infusion phlebitis assessment, which calls for removal of the device. As IV therapy is still needed, a new cannula is resited elsewhere using ANTT, and the findings are documented.

n.0: A compress may ease symptoms after removal, but delaying removal leaves an infected device in place.
n.1: Documentation is needed, but leaving the cannula in place does not manage the phlebitis.
n.2: Patency does not rule out phlebitis; continuing to use an inflamed site risks thrombophlebitis and bloodstream infection.

3.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
3.q: Marcus, 44, has a learning disability, lacks capacity to decide where to live and has no family. The local authority proposes a move. For which accommodation arrangement must an IMCA be instructed?
o: Likely 28 days or more in hospital, or 8 weeks or more in a care home
Any stay of more than 12 weeks in any type of accommodation
A stay of more than 6 months in a registered care home
A stay of more than 7 days in hospital or 4 weeks in a care home
3.w: MCA s38-39: an IMCA must be instructed when NHS or local authority-arranged accommodation in hospital is likely to exceed 28 days, or in a care home 8 weeks, for a person who lacks capacity and has no one appropriate to consult. MCA s38(3) and (9): an IMCA is not needed only where the stay is likely to be less than 28 days (hospital) or less than 8 weeks (care home).

n.1: There is no single 12-week threshold; hospital and care home periods differ.
n.2: The care home threshold is 8 weeks, not 6 months.
n.3: The thresholds are 28 days and 8 weeks, not 7 days and 4 weeks.

3.q: Mrs Anita Rao, 68, is admitted for elective surgery. She is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. Her 12-year-old grandson has come with her and offers to interpret. What should the admitting nurse do?
o: Record and flag her need for a BSL interpreter and arrange one to attend
Rely on lip reading by facing Mrs Rao and speaking slowly and clearly
Accept the grandson's offer, as Mrs Rao is comfortable with him interpreting
Use written notes for the admission, as she can read English well
3.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs arising from disability or sensory loss. A qualified BSL interpreter ensures accurate information and valid consent; children should not be used to interpret clinical information (Code 7.2; P7.9).

n.1: Lip reading is unreliable for complex clinical information and is not her preferred communication method.
n.2: A child interpreter may mistranslate clinical information and is placed in an inappropriate role, risking invalid consent.
n.3: Written English may not be fully accessible to a first-language BSL user, and the standard requires her preferred format.

3.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
3.q: Peter, 45, has a severe learning disability and is on a medical ward. His sister says, 'He's not himself, he's gone quiet and isn't humming like he usually does.' His NEWS2 score is 1. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck his observations at the next routine time
Reassure her that a NEWS2 of 1 is low risk
Act on her concern, reassess fully and escalate
Ask her to write her concerns down for the doctor
3.w: Family carers know the person's baseline and often notice 'soft signs' of deterioration before observations change. LeDeR and CIPOLD learning show that ignoring carer concern contributes to avoidable deaths; the nurse should reassess (full observations, ABCDE) and escalate, using Martha's Rule routes if needed.

n.0: Waiting for routine observations may miss early deterioration.
n.1: A low score does not override a credible concern from someone who knows his baseline.
n.3: Written concerns delay action; the nurse should act now.

3.q: Ama, 68, has dark brown skin and is cared for in bed after a stroke. Over her heel you find an area that feels warmer and firmer than the surrounding skin, with a slightly purplish tone. It does not blanch with diascopy. What should you do?
o: Apply a dressing and recheck the area at the weekly skin review
Massage the area to stimulate blood flow and recheck it at the next shift
Record it as normal skin pigmentation and continue the current care plan
Start prevention and recheck her skin at least every 2 hours
3.w: NICE CG179: in darker skin tones non-blanching erythema may appear as colour change or discolouration, and warmth and firmness are additional signs. If non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention (including heel offloading) and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until it resolves.

n.0: Weekly review is far too infrequent; CG179 sets at least 2-hourly checks until resolved.
n.1: Massage or rubbing is advised against in CG179.
n.2: Dismissing changes as pigmentation misses early pressure damage in darker skin.

3.q: Gordon, 74, is in a single room with a suspected respiratory infection and needs a chest X-ray. The radiology department cannot bring a portable machine today. He is stable and can tolerate a mask. How should the nurse arrange his transfer?
o: Postpone the X-ray until his infection status has been confirmed
Transfer him without a mask and clean the wheelchair once the journey is complete
Ask him to wear an FFP3 respirator during the transfer and X-ray
Ask him to wear a surgical mask if tolerated and inform radiology of his status
3.w: NIPCM ch 2.1: infectious patients are transferred only when clinically necessary, and should wear a surgical mask in communal areas during transfer if tolerated; the receiving department and transport staff must be made aware of the precautions needed.

n.0: The X-ray is clinically needed, and transfer with precautions is appropriate rather than delaying diagnosis.
n.1: Without a mask he exposes others in corridors and waiting areas; cleaning afterwards does not prevent that exposure.
n.2: FFP3 respirators filter incoming air and must not be worn by infectious patients.

3.q: A community nurse uses a PAS-ADD checklist with support staff caring for Olivia, 45, who has a learning disability. What is the purpose of this tool?
o: To measure Olivia's IQ and adaptive functioning
To diagnose a specific mental illness without a clinical assessment
To screen for possible mental health problems needing full assessment
To assess Olivia's capacity to consent to treatment
3.w: The PAS-ADD family of tools (Psychiatric Assessment Schedules for Adults with Developmental Disabilities) includes checklists completed by carers to screen for possible mental health problems, prompting referral for full assessment. They support, but do not replace, clinical diagnosis.

n.0: IQ and adaptive functioning are measured with different psychometric tools.
n.1: A screening checklist identifies possible problems; diagnosis requires clinical assessment.
n.3: Capacity is assessed under the MCA for a specific decision, not with a PAS-ADD checklist.

3.q: Ray, 58, smokes, drinks about 30 units a week and takes little exercise. He tells the nurse he wants to be healthier but feels overwhelmed by everything he 'should' change. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise him to stop smoking and drinking on the same day
Tell him to start with alcohol, as it carries the greatest risk
Give leaflets on all three topics and review him in six months
Ask which change he feels most motivated to tackle first
3.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) rec 8: tailor interventions by assessing the person's behaviour, capability, context and how motivated they are to change; if many behaviours need to change, assess which one or ones the person is most motivated to tackle. NMC Annexe A 2.7: assess motivation and capacity for behaviour change.

n.0: Tackling several behaviours at once when he feels overwhelmed may reduce his chance of success; PH49 asks which he is most motivated to change.
n.1: Choosing for him ignores his motivation; PH49 recommends assessing which behaviour he is most motivated to tackle.
n.2: Leaflets without a plan miss the chance to agree goals; PH49 recommends goals, action plans and planned review.

3.q: Kieran, 45, is shouting in a corridor after being told his discharge is delayed. He is pacing and red-faced but has not threatened anyone. Which approach is the best first step?
o: Call security to remove him from the ward straight away
Stand close and tell him firmly to lower his voice immediately
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and acknowledge his frustration
Walk away and leave him until he has calmed himself down
3.w: De-escalation (Annexe A 3.5; NICE NG10) is the first-line response to agitation: a calm, non-threatening stance at a safe distance, active listening and acknowledging feelings, offering choices and reducing stimulation. Restrictive options are a last resort.

n.0: Removal by security is restrictive and premature when de-escalation has not been tried.
n.1: Standing close and issuing commands can feel threatening and escalate the situation.
n.3: Leaving an agitated person unsupported misses the chance to de-escalate and to keep others safe.

3.q: Following a fall caused by a missed risk assessment, Mrs Doyle, 80, develops anxiety and disturbed sleep. The hospital is deciding whether this is prolonged psychological harm under the statutory duty of candour. Which threshold applies?
o: Psychological harm lasting at least 14 days in total over the admission
Psychological harm lasting at least 3 months after discharge
Psychological harm lasting, or likely to last, 28 continuous days or more
Psychological harm needing a referral to mental health services
3.w: Reg 20(7): prolonged psychological harm means psychological harm which a service user has experienced, or is likely to experience, for a continuous period of at least 28 days.

n.0: The regulation uses 28 continuous days, not 14 days.
n.1: The threshold is 28 continuous days, not three months.
n.3: Referral is not the legal test; the test is duration of at least 28 continuous days.

3.q: In a nursing home, the GP reviews Hilda, 88, by video call and decides to reduce her bisoprolol dose from tomorrow. The GP cannot visit to amend the medication administration record (MAR). Under RPS/RCN guidance, how should the change be communicated?
o: By a message passed on by Hilda's daughter after the call
By a secure electronic message from the GP, with records updated
By the nurse amending the MAR from her notes of the call
By a text message from the GP to the nurse's personal mobile phone
3.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20.2: if the prescriber cannot issue a new prescription or amend the chart, the changes are communicated by an appropriately secure electronic method and the patient's records are updated.

n.0: A relayed message from a relative is not a direction from the prescriber.
n.2: Without the prescriber's written or secure electronic confirmation, the nurse would be altering a prescription.
n.3: A personal phone is not a secure, auditable route for prescribing information.

3.q: Kyle, a staff nurse, notices that Bev, a healthcare assistant, has become quiet and withdrawn since a relative criticised her in front of colleagues. Bev's care remains of a good standard. What is the most appropriate way for Kyle to support and motivate her?
o: Give Bev lighter tasks for the next few shifts so that she can recover
Speak with Bev privately, acknowledge her good care and ask how she is
Report Bev's change in mood to the ward manager for a formal welfare review
Tell Bev that complaints are part of the job and she should not take it personally
3.w: Leaders guide, support and motivate others (P5.6) and the Code asks registrants to work cooperatively and support the staff they are responsible for (Code 8, 25.2). Specific recognition and a private, supportive conversation help restore confidence and show that her work is valued.

n.0: Changing her work without discussion may suggest a lack of confidence in her.
n.2: Escalating to a formal process before talking with her is disproportionate.
n.3: Dismissing her feelings is unsupportive and unlikely to restore motivation.

3.q: On a ward, an AED is attached to Kevin, 63, during CPR. The AED announces it is analysing the rhythm. What should the team do?
o: Stop compressions and ensure nobody touches him
Continue compressions during the rhythm analysis
Check his carotid pulse while it analyses
Give two rescue breaths while it analyses
3.w: RCUK 2025: follow AED prompts; nobody should touch the person during rhythm analysis, as movement interferes with analysis. Resume compressions immediately after the shock or no-shock prompt.

n.1: Compressions during analysis cause artefact and can delay or prevent a shock.
n.2: Pulse checks involve touching him and delay the AED's decision.
n.3: Breaths involve touching him and interfere with analysis.

3.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
3.q: Phil, 49, has Down syndrome and dementia. He is now sleeping most of the day, barely drinking and his breathing has changed. Care staff say this is 'just his dementia getting worse'. What should the nurse consider?
o: That he is depressed and needs an antidepressant
That Phil may be dying and needs assessment
That his dementia is progressing and his plan stays the same
That he is tired after a busy week
3.w: Increased sleep, reduced intake and changes in breathing may indicate the last days of life, or a reversible cause such as infection. Recognising possible dying allows assessment, review of reversible causes and planning for comfort (NICE NG31 principles; LeDeR learning on overshadowing).

n.0: Depression does not explain these physical changes.
n.2: Attributing all change to dementia risks missing dying or a treatable illness.
n.3: Tiredness does not explain reduced drinking and changed breathing.

3.q: Nadia, 34, has a screen-positive result from an NHS screening programme. She is anxious and asks the nurse what this result means. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: She may have the condition and will be offered tests to confirm it
She has the condition and will now start treatment straight away
The result is likely to be a false positive, so no action is needed
She should repeat the same screening test again in 5 years' time
3.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): a screen-positive (higher-risk) result means you may have the condition; you will be offered diagnostic tests to confirm whether you have it, then treatment, advice and support.

n.1: A screening test is not diagnostic; diagnostic tests are needed to confirm the condition first.
n.2: Screen-positive results lead to diagnostic tests; they cannot be assumed to be false.
n.3: A screen-positive result leads to diagnostic testing, not routine re-screening.

3.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Stanley, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
o: Twelve-lead ECG at rest
Lying and standing BP
Peak expiratory flow
Ankle brachial pressure index
3.w: NICE NG249: the multifactorial falls assessment includes lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension, alongside medication review, cognition, continence, vision, footwear, gait and balance.

n.0: An ECG may be needed in some people but is not the standard NG249 component listed.
n.2: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not falls risk.
n.3: ABPI assesses arterial supply before leg compression, not falls.

3.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
3.q: Sean, 34, has a severe learning disability and epilepsy. Over a month his seizures have increased. Staff find tablets in his bedding and he spits out his evening dose. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to increase his anti-seizure medicine dose
Give his tablets covertly in his food from tonight
Find out why he refuses and review the formulation with the prescriber
Record each refusal and keep offering the tablets at the usual times
3.w: Two-step reasoning: the seizure increase is likely due to missed doses, so the cause of refusal must be found (taste, tablet size, swallowing difficulty, side effects, timing) and a solution such as a liquid formulation agreed with the prescriber and pharmacist. Non-adherence is a modifiable SUDEP risk factor (NG217 10.1.2).

n.0: A higher dose will not help if he is not taking the tablets and may cause toxicity when he does.
n.1: Covert administration needs a capacity assessment, best interests decision and pharmacist advice first.
n.3: Simply recording leaves seizures and SUDEP risk unaddressed.

3.q: A charge nurse asks what a basic business case for funding two additional healthcare assistant posts should contain. Which content is most appropriate?
o: Last year's off-duty rotas to show how often extra shifts were filled
A list of the staff who support the request, with their signatures
The problem, the options considered, their costs and the expected benefits
Details of recent incidents including the patients' names and dates of birth
3.w: A business case explains why change is needed, the options (including doing nothing), costs, expected benefits to patients and the organisation, and how success will be measured (P7.12). Evidence should be anonymised to protect confidentiality (Code 5).

n.0: Past rotas may support part of the argument but are not the core content of a business case.
n.1: Support from colleagues does not show need, cost or benefit.
n.3: Identifiable patient information is not needed and would breach confidentiality; anonymised data should be used.

3.q: Isla, 2, developed as expected until about 12 months. Since then she has lost the few words she had, stopped using her hands to pick up toys, and now repeatedly wrings her hands. Her parents report episodes of breath-holding. Which condition is most likely?
o: Prader-Willi syndrome
Rett syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
Angelman syndrome
3.w: Rett syndrome (MECP2, almost exclusively girls) typically shows 6 to 18 months of apparently normal development followed by regression: loss of purposeful hand use with repetitive hand wringing, loss of speech and breathing irregularities (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.0: Prader-Willi presents with infant hypotonia and later hyperphagia, not regression.
n.2: Fragile X causes developmental delay and anxiety but not regression with loss of hand use.
n.3: Angelman syndrome causes severe speech impairment, ataxia and frequent laughter, but not a period of normal development followed by loss of hand use.

3.q: Ruby, 19, is restrained by trained staff after assaulting a nurse. She is taken to the floor face down. Which action is most important for the nurse coordinating the restraint?
o: Monitor her airway and breathing and move her off her front quickly
Hold her in the face-down position until rapid tranquillisation works
Apply weight across her back to keep her still until she is calm
Leave the room so that the restraining staff can work without distraction
3.w: NICE NG10: avoid taking a person to the floor; if prone restraint is needed, use it for as short a time as possible, avoid pressure on the chest, neck or abdomen, and have one staff member monitor airway, breathing and physical condition throughout.

n.1: Prolonged prone restraint increases the risk of positional asphyxia.
n.2: Pressure on the back or chest restricts breathing and has caused deaths in restraint.
n.3: A staff member must stay to monitor her airway and wellbeing throughout.

3.q: Dan, 24, has Prader-Willi syndrome and lives in supported living. He has taken food from housemates' cupboards and gained 6 kg in two months. Staff want to lock the kitchen. What must happen first?
o: Assess his capacity on food access and, if lacking, decide in his best interests
Lock the kitchen straight away, because hyperphagia justifies any food restriction
Lock the kitchen once his parents have agreed to it on his behalf
Leave the kitchen open and record his food choices as unwise decisions
3.w: Two steps: locking the kitchen restricts Dan and his housemates, so it needs a lawful basis. Assess his capacity for this decision (MCA s2-3); if he lacks it, make a best interests decision (s4) choosing the least restrictive option (s1(6)), and review it regularly.

n.1: Restrictions need a lawful basis and proportionality; a diagnosis does not authorise any restriction.
n.2: Parents cannot consent on behalf of an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.3: Calling his choices unwise assumes he has capacity, which has not been assessed, given the compulsive nature of hyperphagia.

3.q: A new community nursing team has been formed by merging two teams. In the first few weeks there are disagreements about who covers which visits and how handovers should run. What should the team leader, Fiona, do first?
o: Allocate the visits herself and ask the team to follow the new system
Meet the whole team to clarify roles and agree ways of working together
Wait for the team to settle, as early disagreement usually fades with time
Ask the two former team leaders to decide the arrangements between them
3.w: In newly formed groups, uncertainty about roles commonly causes conflict. Leaders help by bringing the team together to clarify roles and agree shared ways of working, which builds cohesion and safe handovers (P5.1 group dynamics; AnnexA.4.2.2 active listening to team concerns).

n.0: Imposing a system without involving the team misses their knowledge and may prolong conflict.
n.2: Leaving role confusion unresolved risks missed visits and unsafe handovers.
n.3: Delegating to the former leaders may entrench the two old teams rather than build one team.

3.q: A ward's budget is overspent. The manager explains that money spent on agency staff this year means the planned purchase of new pressure-relieving mattresses cannot go ahead. Which economic concept does this illustrate?
o: Value for money
Opportunity cost
Cost-effectiveness
Economies of scale
3.w: Opportunity cost is the benefit lost from the next best use of a resource when it is spent on something else. In a fixed budget, spending on one item means another cannot be funded (P7.3 principles of health economics and resource allocation).

n.0: Value for money describes how well spending achieves outcomes, not the forgone alternative.
n.2: Cost-effectiveness compares the costs and outcomes of alternatives; it is not the loss of the forgone option.
n.3: Economies of scale are lower unit costs from producing more; they are not shown here.

3.q: Mr Owusu, 81, says he 'came over funny' before his fall at home. The nurse needs to understand what happened. Which response best clarifies his account?
o: "So you fainted, then. How long were you unconscious?"
"What did 'came over funny' feel like for you?"
"Lots of older people feel funny. Let's move on."
"Did you trip on something on the floor?"
3.w: Annexe A 1.6: use clarification techniques; P1.11 communicate effectively with people at all stages of life. Code 7.4 keep misunderstanding to a minimum.

n.0: This assumes a faint and leads him to a particular answer.
n.2: This dismisses an important symptom and stops clarification.
n.3: This closed question narrows to one cause before his experience is understood.

3.q: During an intensive interaction session, Sasha, a support worker, holds up a ball and repeatedly asks Ryan, 32, who has a profound learning disability, 'What colour is this?' Ryan looks away. What feedback should the nurse give Sasha?
o: Ask more slowly and wait longer before repeating the question
Let Ryan lead, and respond to what he chooses to do
Offer Ryan a choice of two coloured balls to make it easier
Give Ryan praise each time he looks at the ball
3.w: Intensive interaction is led by the person, not by staff questions or tasks. Staff wait, observe and respond to what the person initiates, so the person experiences control and success.

n.0: Slowing the same question keeps the session staff-led and task-focused.
n.2: A choice of balls is still a staff-set task rather than following Ryan.
n.3: Rewarding attention to the ball keeps the agenda with staff.

3.q: Mrs Turner, 72, had a hip replacement two days ago. Her son tells the nurse at visiting time that his mother 'seems confused and is seeing things on the curtains', which started this afternoon. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the son to stay with her to settle her for the night
Note it and ask the night staff to see if it continues
Reassure the son that this is common after an anaesthetic
Assess her for delirium and record the reported change
3.w: NICE CG103 recs 1.3.1 and 1.5.1-1.5.2: recent changes or fluctuations (including hallucinations) may be reported by relatives and should prompt assessment with an appropriate tool; changes must be documented.

n.0: Family presence can help, but it does not replace assessment of a new change.
n.1: Deferring to night staff delays assessment of an acute change.
n.2: Dismissing a new change risks missing delirium and its cause.

3.q: Femi, 30, is autistic with a learning disability. The hospital learning disability team knows he needs the first appointment of the day, a quiet waiting area and his mother present, but these adjustments are recorded only in local notes. He is about to be referred to another trust. What should the liaison nurse do?
o: Record his adjustments on the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag
Add the adjustments to the trust's own electronic alert system
Telephone the other trust's clinic to explain the adjustments
Give Femi's mother a letter listing the adjustments to bring along
3.w: The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag (DAPB4019) records adjustments nationally so that every organisation providing NHS or publicly funded care can see them; providers in England had to implement it fully by 30 September 2026 (NHS England).

n.1: A local alert is not visible to the receiving trust, which is the gap here.
n.2: A phone call may help this once but leaves no lasting record for other services and future referrals.
n.3: A letter places the burden on his mother and may be lost; the duty to share sits with services.

3.q: Ahmed is a registered nurse on an acute medical ward who regularly cares for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Which Oliver McGowan training package is appropriate for his role?
o: Tier 3, the specialist module for consultant-level practitioners
Tier 2, the e-learning and a one-day face-to-face session
Tier 1, repeated each year in place of further training
Tier 1, the e-learning and one-hour online interactive session
3.w: Tier 2 capabilities are for health and social care staff who provide care and support to people with a learning disability or autistic people; the Tier 2 package is the 90-minute e-learning plus a one-day face-to-face session (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice).

n.0: Tier 3 capabilities are for highly autonomous professionals leading complex care; it is not a separate Oliver McGowan package for ward nurses.
n.2: Repeating Tier 1 does not provide the Tier 2 capabilities his role needs.
n.3: Tier 1 is for staff who need general awareness, such as reception staff, not those providing direct care.

3.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which abbreviation practice best supports safe record keeping when documenting medicines and care in the notes. Which approach should she follow?
o: Write terms in full unless the trust approves the abbreviation
Use abbreviations for drug names to save time in busy shifts
Use the abbreviations she learned during her training abroad
Use any abbreviation that colleagues on the ward understand
3.w: Code 10.4: records must be clearly written and not include unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation. Annexe A 1.8 accurate, clear, legible records.

n.1: Abbreviating drug names risks medication errors and breaches Code 10.4.
n.2: Abbreviations vary between countries and may not be understood here.
n.3: Local shorthand may be misread by others; Code 10.4 says no unnecessary abbreviations.

3.q: Ama is due to revalidate next month. Her CPD log shows 35 hours: 18 hours at a study day and team workshops, and 17 hours reading journal articles on her own. What is the position on her CPD requirement?
o: She needs five more hours of any type of CPD
She needs two more hours of participatory learning
She needs fifteen more hours of participatory learning
She meets it, as she has 35 hours in total
3.w: NMC revalidation CPD requirement (updated 08/09/2021): 35 hours of CPD in three years, of which at least 20 must include participatory learning. 20 - 18 = 2 participatory hours still needed.

n.0: Her total of 35 is already met; the shortfall is in participatory hours, not overall hours.
n.2: She needs 20 participatory hours in total; with 18 already logged, the gap is two hours.
n.3: The total is met, but at least 20 of the 35 hours must be participatory; she has 18.

3.q: Gwen, 70, is in the last days of life with metastatic cancer and new bone pain. She has not taken opioids before. The team agree to start subcutaneous morphine for symptom control, and the nurse is planning her care. Which approach to dosing is recommended?
o: Wait until her pain is severe before giving the first dose of morphine
Start with the lowest effective dose and titrate to her symptoms
Start at the top of the prescribed range so that she is comfortable quickly
Give a loading dose by intramuscular injection, then change to subcutaneous
3.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.7 and 1.5.8: for people starting treatment who have not previously had medicines for symptom management, start with the lowest effective dose and titrate as clinically indicated, reassessing symptoms at least daily.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.11 asks for pain to be managed promptly and effectively once identified.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.7 recommends starting with the lowest effective dose for people not previously given symptom-control medicines.
n.3: Intramuscular injections should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.5.5).

3.q: Mr Hughes, 70, tells Ama, a Black staff nurse, that he does not want 'someone like her' looking after him. Ama is upset. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse in charge?
o: Reassign Ama quietly to avoid any further conflict
Challenge the remark, support Ama and report the incident
Ask Ama to carry on and to disregard the remark
Tell Mr Hughes he must leave the ward for his behaviour
3.w: Code 3.4: challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour; Code 20.2: treat people fairly without discrimination, bullying or harassment. Proficiency P1.4: understand and challenge discriminatory behaviour; report through local policy.

n.0: Reassigning without challenge colludes with the discrimination; Code 3.4 and 20.2 require it to be challenged.
n.2: This leaves the racist behaviour unchallenged and fails to support the colleague.
n.3: Withdrawing care is disproportionate; the behaviour should be challenged while care continues safely.

3.q: Deborah, 46, received IM adrenaline 500 micrograms for anaphylaxis 5 minutes ago. She remains wheezy with BP 84/52 mmHg. What should happen next?
o: Wait a further 15 minutes before repeating adrenaline
Give chlorphenamine IV and wait for it to take effect
Sit her upright with her legs lowered to ease breathing
Give a second IM adrenaline dose and an IV crystalloid bolus
3.w: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and give an IV crystalloid bolus (adults 500-1,000 mL) for circulatory problems, with high-flow oxygen and monitoring.

n.0: RCUK advises a repeat dose after 5 minutes, not 15.
n.1: Antihistamines are not used to treat ABC problems in anaphylaxis.
n.2: With hypotension she should lie flat with or without legs raised; sitting with legs down worsens circulation.

3.q: A learning disability nurse is teaching staff about restraint under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 for adults who lack capacity. Which statement correctly describes when restraint is lawful under s6?
o: When it is needed to make the person follow the daily routine
When it is in the person's best interests and the family have agreed
When it prevents harm to the person and is proportionate to that harm
When it is written in the care plan and signed by the manager
3.w: MCA 2005 s6: restraint is permitted only if the person taking action reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to the person who lacks capacity, and the act is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. It must also be in the person's best interests (s5).

n.0: Securing compliance with a routine is not prevention of harm and does not meet s6.
n.1: Family agreement is not the legal test; s6 requires necessity to prevent harm and proportionality.
n.3: Documentation is good practice, but a signed plan does not make a disproportionate restraint lawful.

3.q: Eric, 72, has a new ileostomy. He is preparing for discharge and asks how to fit his appliance. Which advice is correct?
o: Clean the skin with alcohol wipes before each change
Cut the flange well larger than the stoma to avoid rubbing
Measure the stoma and cut the flange slightly larger than it
Leave the appliance on for a week to protect the skin
3.w: The aperture should be cut just larger than the measured stoma (usually 2-3 mm) so that effluent does not contact the skin, re-measuring as post-operative swelling settles. Ileostomy output is corrosive, so a close fit protects skin (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: Alcohol dries and stings the skin; warm water is used.
n.1: A large gap exposes skin to corrosive effluent and causes excoriation.
n.3: Ileostomy appliances are emptied and changed regularly, not left for a week.

3.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
3.q: Jacob, 48, has a profound learning disability, dysphagia and reflux. He spends most of the day in a reclined wheelchair and is often semi-reclined for meals because staff find it easier. Which change would most reduce his risk of aspiration pneumonia?
o: Sit him upright for meals and afterwards, as his postural plan sets out
Move his main meal to late evening so that he can rest afterwards
Ask the GP to increase his antipsychotic to calm him at mealtimes
Offer thin drinks so that swallowing takes less effort for him
3.w: Reclined positions during and after eating increase aspiration risk, especially with dysphagia and reflux. Upright positioning in line with his 24-hour postural care plan protects his airway (LeDeR pneumonia report; NHS England RightCare aspiration pneumonia scenario).

n.1: Lying down soon after a large evening meal increases reflux and aspiration risk.
n.2: Sedating medicine impairs swallowing and airway protection and raises aspiration risk.
n.3: Thin drinks move faster and are harder to control, increasing aspiration risk if his plan specifies thickened fluids.

3.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
3.q: Nina, 44, has a moderate learning disability and capacity to decide about CPR. Her consultant believes CPR would be unlikely to succeed. Nina says she wants CPR. What should happen?
o: Ask her mother to decide instead of Nina
Record that Nina lacks capacity because she disagrees
Record DNACPR now and discuss it with her at a later review
Explain sensitively why CPR may not work and involve Nina
3.w: Patients with capacity must be involved in discussions about DNACPR; the clinician explains the reasons in an accessible way. A patient cannot demand treatment that will not work, but should be informed unless it would cause physical or psychological harm (Tracey v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014]; Resuscitation Council UK/BMA/RCN guidance).

n.0: Nina has capacity, so her mother cannot decide for her.
n.1: Disagreement with clinicians is not evidence of lack of capacity (MCA s1(4)).
n.2: Under Tracey, a patient with capacity should be involved when the decision is made unless discussion would cause harm; delaying the discussion is not lawful.

3.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
3.q: Ola, 26, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to admission for urgent treatment. The ward team concludes that his care will amount to a deprivation of liberty that must start today. How can this be authorised under DoLS?
o: Wait for a standard authorisation before applying any restrictions
Ask the Court of Protection for an emergency order before admission
The hospital gives an urgent authorisation and requests a standard one
Hold him under section 5(2) of the Mental Health Act until a decision
3.w: Under MCA Schedule A1, the managing authority (the hospital or care home) can give itself an urgent authorisation, lasting up to 7 days (extendable by 7 days by the supervisory body), when it requests a standard authorisation from the local authority.

n.0: Waiting would mean either delaying urgent treatment or depriving him of liberty without authority.
n.1: DoLS provide the urgent authorisation route in hospitals; a court order is not the first step.
n.3: Section 5(2) is a holding power for informal inpatients with mental disorder needing MHA assessment, not for authorising physical treatment.

3.q: Mrs Harper, 58, is choosing between two treatment options for her knee. She asks the nurse what she would do. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to decide by tomorrow morning
Tell her which of the two options the nurse would personally choose
Advise her to follow whatever the consultant recommends
Explore what matters to her and each option's risks and benefits
3.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire [2015] UKSC 11: patients must be made aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions; P4.2 shared decision making.

n.0: Written information alone, with a deadline, does not support shared decision making.
n.1: Personal preference replaces her own values and undermines shared decision making.
n.2: This removes her from the decision instead of supporting an informed choice.

3.q: Maureen, 66, started ramipril for hypertension 6 weeks ago. She tells the community nurse she has had a persistent tickly dry cough since, with no fever or breathlessness. Her chest is clear. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain dry cough is a known ramipril effect and arrange a review
Advise buying a cough suppressant from the pharmacy and continue
Explain the cough is likely viral and should settle in 2 weeks
Advise her to stop the ramipril straight away and see her GP
3.w: A persistent dry cough is a recognised adverse effect of ACE inhibitors such as ramipril (P4.5, supporting people with their medication). The prescriber should review, as an alternative such as an angiotensin II receptor blocker may be considered. Stopping without review leaves blood pressure untreated.

n.1: A cough suppressant masks a drug-induced cause without a medication review.
n.2: The timing and features point to an ACE inhibitor effect, not a viral illness.
n.3: Stopping an antihypertensive without review risks uncontrolled blood pressure.

3.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
3.q: Joy, 52, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about a hysterectomy. Her only regular contact is Sue, a paid support worker who has known her for 15 years. The surgeon asks whether Sue can be consulted instead of an IMCA. What is the correct answer?
o: No, so the decision has to be referred to the Court of Protection
Yes, because Sue knows Joy's wishes better than anyone else
Yes, because Sue has known Joy for more than five years
No, paid carers are not appropriate to consult; instruct an IMCA
3.w: MCA s37-38: an IMCA is required where there is no one other than a person engaged in providing care or treatment for payment whom it would be appropriate to consult. Sue's views should still be sought in the best interests process, but she cannot replace the IMCA.

n.0: An IMCA, not a court application, is the statutory safeguard here.
n.1: Sue's knowledge is valuable and should inform the decision, but it does not remove the need for an IMCA.
n.2: Length of paid relationship does not change the statutory exclusion of paid carers.

3.q: Before giving the first dose of oral amoxicillin to Stanley, 67, the nurse notices he is wearing a red allergy wristband labelled 'penicillin'. The allergy section of his drug chart is blank and the prescriber has gone home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose with an antihistamine to cover any possible reaction
Withhold it, clarify the allergy with Stanley and contact a prescriber
Give the dose, as the drug chart has no allergy recorded
Give half the dose and observe Stanley closely for any reaction
3.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 requires the person administering to check allergies or previous adverse drug reactions, and to raise ambiguities with the prescriber or pharmacy without delay. Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so the dose is withheld, the reaction history clarified, the chart updated and an alternative sought.

n.0: An antihistamine would not prevent anaphylaxis and the nurse cannot add a medicine.
n.2: The wristband is a warning that must be resolved; a blank chart is an omission, not evidence of no allergy.
n.3: Altering the prescribed dose is not within the nurse's role, and any dose risks anaphylaxis.

3.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
3.q: Katie, 17, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to her care at a residential college, where the team agrees the arrangements need authorising as a deprivation of liberty. Her parents say they are happy to consent. What is the correct approach?
o: Ask the local authority for a standard DoLS authorisation
Rely on her parents' consent, as she is under 18
Apply to the Court of Protection, as DoLS apply from age 18
Use section 2 of the Mental Health Act to authorise the arrangements
3.w: DoLS apply from 18. For 16 and 17 year olds who lack capacity, a deprivation of liberty must be authorised by the court (Court of Protection). The Supreme Court in Re D [2019] UKSC 42 held that parents cannot consent to the deprivation of liberty of a 16 or 17 year old.

n.0: Standard DoLS authorisations are for people aged 18 and over.
n.1: Parents cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for a 16 or 17 year old (Re D 2019).
n.3: Section 2 is for assessment of mental disorder in hospital, not authorising care at a college.

3.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation attempt on a medical ward, Sofia, the nurse in charge, arranges a short team debrief once the immediate tasks are complete. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: Identify which member of staff made an error so that it can be dealt with formally
Reflect together on what went well and what could improve, and support staff
