Complete the incident report and the statutory notification to the regulator
Decide as a team what information the family should and should not be given
3.w: Team reflection and debriefing support staff wellbeing and turn experience into learning for future practice (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; Code 8 work cooperatively; human factors and just culture principles).

n.0: A debrief is a supportive learning discussion, not a disciplinary process; a blame focus discourages openness.
n.2: Reporting is a separate governance step and is not the purpose of a team debrief.
n.3: Communication with the family is guided by candour and the person's wishes, not by a team agreement to withhold information.

3.q: Raymond, 82, has a DNACPR decision recorded after a discussion with him. Overnight he develops a temperature of 39.1°C, a heart rate of 118 and new confusion, giving a NEWS2 of 7. A colleague says there is 'no point escalating because he is DNACPR'. What should the nurse do?
o: Phone his family first to ask whether he should be treated for infection
Withhold escalation because the DNACPR shows he is not for active treatment
Escalate urgently for sepsis review, as the DNACPR decision covers CPR
Start the end of life care plan, as the DNACPR shows he is now dying
3.w: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BMA, RCUK, RCN, 3rd edition): a decision not to attempt CPR applies only to CPR and not to any other treatment. A NEWS2 of 7 needs an emergency response (RCP 2017) and possible sepsis is managed under NICE NG253 (2025).

n.0: Raymond's deterioration needs urgent escalation now; his family do not decide his treatment and delay risks harm.
n.1: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other appropriate treatment continues (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
n.3: A DNACPR decision does not mean a person is dying; recognising dying is a separate assessment (NICE NG31).

3.q: Ms Ford, 50, is due to have surgery this afternoon. She is restless, keeps asking the same questions and says she cannot stop thinking she will not wake up. Her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate initial nursing intervention?
o: Give her a leaflet about the operation and leave her to rest
Ask the anaesthetist to prescribe a sedative premedication
Tell her that modern anaesthetics are very safe and move on
Sit with her, explore her fears and explain what will happen
3.w: NMC proficiency P4.8 requires nurses to initiate interventions for common symptoms including anxiety. Listening, exploring specific fears and giving clear information are first-line, person-centred interventions for pre-operative anxiety.

n.0: A leaflet without discussion leaves her specific fears unexplored.
n.1: Medication may be considered later, but non-drug measures come first for anxiety with normal observations.
n.2: Brief reassurance without exploring her fears does not address her anxiety.

3.q: According to NICE CG32, which finding indicates that an adult is malnourished?
o: BMI under 18.5 kg/m²
BMI between 20 and 25 kg/m²
Unintentional weight loss of 3% in 6 months
Eating normally for the past 5 days
3.w: NICE CG32 defines malnutrition as BMI under 18.5 kg/m²; or unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3-6 months; or BMI under 20 kg/m² with unintentional weight loss over 5% in 3-6 months.

n.1: BMI 20-25 is within the healthy range.
n.2: 3% weight loss is below the CG32 thresholds.
n.3: Normal intake is not a malnutrition criterion.

3.q: Kofi, 20, scored 67 on an IQ test taken during a stressful college assessment. He works part-time, travels alone by bus, cooks for himself and manages his own money. His tutor asks the nurse whether Kofi has a learning disability. What is the best response?
o: Refer him for genetic testing to identify the cause of his learning disability
The definition also needs impaired social functioning, which is not evident
Yes, because a score below 70 confirms a mild learning disability
Repeat the IQ test, because a second score below 70 would confirm it
3.w: Two steps: the definition needs impaired intelligence AND impaired social (adaptive) functioning starting before adulthood. Kofi's daily living skills show no significant impairment of social functioning, so a single IQ score cannot establish a learning disability; adaptive functioning matters as much as IQ.

n.0: Genetic testing does not decide whether the definition is met, and on these facts social functioning is not impaired.
n.2: An IQ score alone does not define a learning disability; adaptive functioning must also be impaired.
n.3: Repeating the test still ignores the adaptive functioning limb, which on these facts is not impaired.

3.q: A nurse is admitting four people to an acute medical unit. Using the risk factors in NICE CG103, which person is at increased risk of developing delirium and should be observed for it?
o: Mr Green, 45, admitted for a planned endoscopy
Mrs Young, 78, admitted with a urinary infection
Ms Black, 30, admitted with a simple ankle fracture
Mr White, 52, admitted for blood pressure review
3.w: NICE CG103 (updated 2023) lists risk factors including age 65 or over, past or present cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture and severe illness. Mrs Young is 78, so she should be observed at least daily for indicators of delirium.

n.0: At 45 and admitted for a planned procedure, Mr Green has none of the CG103 risk factors described.
n.2: An ankle fracture is not a CG103 risk factor; current hip fracture is.
n.3: At 52 with no listed risk factor, Mr White is not identified as at risk by CG103.

3.q: A support worker asks Ola, a learning disability nurse, what the 'fundamentals of communication' are that intensive interaction aims to develop. Which group of skills should Ola describe?
o: Eye contact, turn-taking and enjoying being with another person
Following instructions, sitting still and finishing set tasks
Reading, writing and using symbols to make everyday choices
Using signs, gestures and photographs to request items
3.w: The fundamentals of communication include giving attention, eye contact, facial expression, turn-taking, and enjoying being with another person; these come before language (intensive interaction literature, Hewett and Nind).

n.1: Compliance skills are not the fundamentals of communication.
n.2: Literacy and symbols are later skills built on the fundamentals.
n.3: These are specific communication systems, not the underlying fundamentals.

3.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
3.q: Ruth, 41, has a learning disability and needs a double-length appointment and an easy read explanation for a hospital procedure. The clinic manager asks whether Ruth's care provider should pay the extra cost. What is the correct answer?
o: No, a disabled person cannot be required to pay for a reasonable adjustment
Yes, if the cost goes beyond what the clinic normally spends per patient
No, the extra cost should be shared equally between the clinic and the provider
Yes, as the adjustment benefits Ruth personally rather than the clinic
3.w: Equality Act 2010 s20(7): a person who is subject to the duty is not entitled to require a disabled person to pay the costs of complying with the duty. The NHS service bears the cost of reasonable adjustments.

n.1: There is no threshold above which the disabled person must pay.
n.2: Passing part of the cost to Ruth's provider still charges her for the adjustment.
n.3: The duty falls on the service provider, which must meet the cost.

3.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
3.q: In a supported living service, staff are asked what 'soft signs' of deterioration might look like in Lena, 33, who has a profound learning disability and no speech. Which example best fits?
o: A new oxygen saturation of 88% on air
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
A systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg
Eating less and sleeping more than usual
3.w: Soft signs are subtle changes from the person's baseline (eating, drinking, sleeping, mobility, mood, behaviour) that may precede changes in vital signs. Recognising them depends on knowing the person's usual presentation.

n.0: Saturation of 88% on air is a measured abnormality, not a soft sign.
n.1: A respiratory rate of 30 is a hard, measured sign that scores highly on NEWS2.
n.2: Systolic BP of 85 is a measured red-flag sign, not a soft sign.

3.q: Kayla, 30, had a psychosocial assessment in an emergency department after self-harm and is discharged home. The team remains concerned about her safety. According to NICE NG225, within what time should initial aftercare be provided?
o: Within 14 days, at a routine outpatient clinic
Within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment
Within 7 days of the psychosocial assessment
Within 24 hours of arriving at the department
3.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.10.2: if there are ongoing safety concerns after self-harm, the responsible team should provide initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment.

n.0: A routine 14-day appointment is far later than NG225 recommends when safety concerns persist.
n.2: 7 days is longer than the 48-hour aftercare window in NG225.
n.3: The timing runs from the psychosocial assessment, and the interval is 48 hours.

3.q: Mr Pearce, 67, has capacity and peripheral vascular disease. After a full explanation of the risks, he declines a recommended below-knee amputation, saying he would rather take his chances. The team thinks this is an unwise choice. Which principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies most directly?
o: Making an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity
Any act done for a person must be in their best interests
The less restrictive option must be considered first
All practicable steps must be taken to help the person decide
3.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Mr Pearce has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (Code 2.5).

n.1: Best interests (s1(5)) applies to acts for people who lack capacity; Mr Pearce has capacity.
n.2: The less restrictive principle (s1(6)) applies when acting for someone who lacks capacity.
n.3: Supporting decision-making (s1(3)) has already been met by the full explanation; the issue now is respecting an unwise choice.

3.q: Nadia is redressing a deep cavity wound on the sacrum of Ruth, 80. She is wearing non-sterile gloves and using ANTT, but realises she will need to touch the wound bed with her fingers to place the packing. What should she do?
o: Change to sterile gloves, as the Key-Site will be touched directly
Moisten the non-sterile gloves with sterile saline before packing
Rub alcohol handrub onto the gloves before touching the wound
Continue with the non-sterile gloves, as she cleaned her hands first
3.w: Under ANTT, if a Key-Site or Key-Part must be touched directly, sterile gloves are needed so that the hands do not contaminate it (a Surgical-ANTT approach). NIPCM ch 1.4 also requires sterile gloves for contact with a sterile site or body cavity.

n.1: Saline does not sterilise gloves; the gloves would still contaminate the wound bed.
n.2: Gloves are not decontaminated with handrub, and this does not make them sterile.
n.3: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable when Key-Sites are not touched; here she must touch the wound bed directly.

3.q: A caller to a surgical ward says she is the daughter of Mrs Green, 70, who had surgery today, and asks how the operation went. The nurse cannot confirm who the caller is. What should the nurse do?
o: Check Mrs Green's wishes and agreed contacts before sharing anything
Give a brief update, as the caller knows the patient's name
Ask the caller to confirm Mrs Green's date of birth, then answer
Confirm the operation went well but give no further details
3.w: Code 5.1 requires respect for a person's right to privacy, and 5.2 that people know how and why their information is shared. The nurse should establish whether Mrs Green consents to information being given to this caller (for example agreed contacts or a password).

n.1: Knowing a patient's name does not show the caller has a right to her information.
n.2: A date of birth is easily known by others and does not establish Mrs Green's consent.
n.3: Confirming the outcome is still disclosure of confidential information without consent.

3.q: Wendy, a registered nurse on a general medical ward, is told to care for a patient receiving non-invasive ventilation who has been moved from the respiratory unit. She has had no training in non-invasive ventilation. What should Wendy do?
o: Decline to be on the ward until a nurse with the right training is found
Accept the patient and ask the respiratory team for help if problems arise
Tell the nurse in charge she lacks the competence and escalate the concern now
Accept the patient after reading the trust's policy on non-invasive ventilation
3.w: Code 13: recognise and work within the limits of your competence, and (13.3) ask for help from a suitably qualified professional for anything beyond it. Code 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to provide care outside your scope. Skill mix is part of safe staffing (P6.2); the gap must be escalated so a competent nurse or support is provided.

n.0: Leaving the ward abandons her other patients; the right response is to raise and escalate the concern while continuing other care.
n.1: Accepting care she cannot provide safely puts the patient at risk until something goes wrong.
n.3: Reading a policy does not provide the training and competence needed for this care.

3.q: Jordan, 29, has a learning disability and has just had his annual health check. The practice nurse found raised blood pressure and that he has not seen a dentist for three years. Where should the agreed actions be recorded so Jordan and his supporters can follow them?
o: In his hospital passport held by the ward
In a behaviour support plan written by the team
In a health action plan agreed with Jordan
In a care and support plan from the local authority
3.w: Actions from the annual health check are written into a health action plan, which sets out what will be done, by whom and when, in a format the person can use (NHS.uk, Annual health checks).

n.0: A hospital passport tells hospital staff about the person on admission; it is not where annual health check actions are tracked.
n.1: A behaviour support plan addresses behaviour that challenges, not general health actions such as blood pressure and dental care.
n.3: A Care Act care and support plan covers social care needs; health actions belong in the health action plan.

3.q: Mr Kapoor, 67, has capacity and has told Hayley, his nurse, that he does not want the proposed amputation and would prefer palliative wound care. On the ward round the surgeon starts to describe the operation date without asking his views. What should Hayley do?
o: Say that Mr Kapoor has shared views about the operation and invite him to explain them
Record Mr Kapoor's wishes in his nursing notes once the ward round has finished
Wait until after the ward round and then ask Mr Kapoor whether he has changed his mind
Tell the surgeon that Mr Kapoor has asked her to cancel the operation on his behalf
3.w: Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice is heard in decisions about their care (AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4 act as an advocate for the vulnerable; Code 2.5 respect the right to refuse treatment). Inviting Mr Kapoor to speak supports his autonomy without speaking over him (MCA 2005 s1 principles).

n.1: Recording his wishes is necessary but does not ensure they are heard in the decision being made now.
n.2: Waiting allows a decision to be made without him; he has already expressed his wishes.
n.3: Hayley should not overstate or speak for him when he can speak for himself.

3.q: Ben, a staff nurse on a respiratory ward, has developed red, cracked skin across the backs of both hands after several weeks of frequent hand hygiene. He asks his ward manager for advice. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Use soap and water instead of handrub for routine care until his hands heal
Seek occupational health advice and use his own emollient regularly, including on breaks
Apply hand cream from the communal tub in the staff room after each patient contact
Wear non-sterile gloves for routine care tasks so his skin is protected
3.w: NIPCM ch 1.2 skin care: dry hands thoroughly, use an emollient hand cream regularly (for example during breaks and off duty), do not use communal tubs, and staff with skin problems should seek advice from occupational health or their GP. Damaged skin harbours organisms and may need further intervention or reporting.

n.0: Alcohol handrub is recommended for routine hand hygiene and is generally less drying than repeated soap and water.
n.2: NIPCM advises against communal tubs of hand cream because they can become contaminated.
n.3: Gloves are not recommended where no body fluid exposure is anticipated; overuse increases infection risk and does not replace hand hygiene.

3.q: Ellie, 17, has profound and multiple learning disabilities and cerebral palsy and receives gastrostomy feeds. Staff report that she grimaces and coughs when laid flat after feeds, and she has had three chest infections this year. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Hip displacement causing pain on repositioning
Absence seizures triggered by the feeding routine
Gastro-oesophageal reflux with risk of aspiration
Constipation causing abdominal pain after feeds
3.w: Reflux is common in cerebral palsy and PMLD. Distress and coughing when lying flat after feeds, with recurrent chest infections, suggest reflux with aspiration, which needs escalation, upright positioning and review of feeding (LeDeR pneumonia risk factors include reflux and postural problems).

n.0: Hip pain would link to movement, not specifically to lying flat after feeds with coughing.
n.1: Seizures do not explain the link with lying flat, coughing and chest infections.
n.3: Constipation is common but does not explain coughing when flat and recurrent chest infections.

3.q: Two nurses are at the bedside to start a red cell transfusion for Edith, 73, who is alert and orientated. Which method of patient identification meets the BSH standard for positive patient identification?
o: Ask 'Are you Edith Morris?' and then check her wristband details
Ask her to state her name and date of birth, then match wristband and unit
Check her wristband against the unit label and the bed-end name card
Confirm her identity with her daughter, then check the unit label
3.w: BSH guideline on administration of blood components (2017): positive patient identification at every stage, asking the patient to state full name and date of birth where able, and checking these against the identification band and the component label, using a structured bedside checklist (SHOT recommendation).

n.0: A closed question invites a confused or hard-of-hearing person to agree to the wrong name.
n.2: Bed-end cards are unreliable, and Edith can state her own details.
n.3: Relatives may be used when a patient cannot respond; Edith is alert and should identify herself.

4.q: A nurse on a postnatal ward is explaining immunity to a new mother. She says her baby is born with some protection against measles because of antibodies the mother made. Which type of immunity is this?
o: Population immunity from high vaccine coverage in the community
Active immunity produced by the baby's own immune system
Innate immunity from the baby's skin and mucous membranes
Passive immunity from antibodies that crossed the placenta
4.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): passive immunity is protection from antibodies transferred from immune individuals, most commonly across the placenta; it is temporary, commonly lasting a few weeks or months, and is more effective against some infections (for example tetanus and measles) than others.

n.0: Population immunity reduces exposure; it is not antibody protection inside the baby.
n.1: The baby did not make these antibodies; they were transferred from the mother, which is passive immunity.
n.2: Innate immunity is non-specific; measles-specific antibodies from the mother are passive acquired immunity.

4.q: Hassan, 54, is prescribed 7.5 mg of an intramuscular medicine. The ampoule contains 10 mg in 2 mL. The nurse works out the volume to draw up and a colleague is available. What volume is needed, and what should happen before administration?
o: 1.5 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
2.67 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
0.75 mL, then give it straight away as the colleague is busy
3.75 mL, then record the calculation in the notes and give it
4.w: Volume = (dose required / stock strength) x stock volume = (7.5 / 10) x 2 = 1.5 mL. RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 says any calculations needed are double checked, where practicable, by a second person.

n.1: 2.67 mL inverts the fraction (10 / 7.5 x 2); a check would catch it, but the volume is wrong.
n.2: 0.75 mL omits multiplying by the 2 mL volume, and skipping an available second check is unsafe.
n.3: 3.75 mL comes from dividing the dose by the stock volume (7.5 / 2) instead of using the formula, and no second check is made.

4.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
4.q: Keith, 58, has a severe learning disability and has been assessed as lacking capacity to decide about chemotherapy for bowel cancer. He has no family or friends, and lives in a care home where paid staff have supported him for years. What should happen?
o: Consult the care home manager, who can act as his advocate for this decision
Let the oncology team make the decision, as there is no family to involve in it
Apply for a deputy to be appointed before any treatment decision
Instruct an IMCA, as this is serious treatment and no one is appropriate to consult
4.w: MCA 2005 s37: an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate must be instructed when serious medical treatment is proposed by the NHS for a person who lacks capacity and there is no one, other than paid carers, whom it would be appropriate to consult.

n.0: Paid care staff are not 'appropriate to consult' for IMCA purposes, so they cannot replace an IMCA.
n.1: A best interests decision without family still requires an IMCA for serious medical treatment.
n.2: A deputy is not needed; the IMCA route is the statutory safeguard and a deputy application would cause delay.

4.q: An outpatient manager tells Dev, a learning disability liaison nurse, 'We make adjustments when a patient asks for them.' Dev explains the duty that applies to service providers such as NHS trusts under the Equality Act 2010. Which statement is correct?
o: The duty is anticipatory, so services must plan adjustments in advance
The duty applies to physical features such as ramps and toilets
The duty starts when a disabled person or carer asks for an adjustment
The duty applies once a learning disability diagnosis is confirmed
4.w: For service providers the reasonable adjustment duty is anticipatory: services must think ahead about what disabled people generally may need and plan adjustments before anyone asks (Equality Act 2010 s20 and Sch 2).

n.1: Physical features are one of three requirements; the duty also covers practices and auxiliary aids.
n.2: Waiting for a request puts the burden on disabled people; the provider duty is anticipatory.
n.3: The duty protects disabled people generally and does not depend on a confirmed diagnosis before planning starts.

4.q: Mr Burke, 64, has capacity and is waiting for biopsy results. His wife asks the nurse to make sure he is not told if it is cancer, as 'it would destroy him'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer the decision to the consultant to settle with his wife
Tell her that her request is unlawful and end the conversation there
Explore her worries and explain he will be asked what he wants to know
Agree, and record her request on the front of the notes
4.w: Code 2.4 respect the level of involvement a person wants; Code 5.5 share with the person the information they want or need to know. Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations.

n.0: The decision about what he is told rests with him, not with his wife and the consultant.
n.1: This dismisses her distress; her worries need exploring with compassion.
n.3: He has capacity; withholding his diagnosis at another's request breaches his right to information.

4.q: Ellen, 81, has a NEWS2 of 1. Her son tells you she is 'not right' and much quieter than usual. You find she is newly confused but otherwise unchanged. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Rescore NEWS2 with 3 for new confusion and escalate to a doctor
Wait for her next scheduled observations before deciding
Explain that confusion is common in older people in hospital
Document her son's concern and continue 4-6 hourly observations
4.w: New confusion scores 3 in the consciousness parameter (ACVPU 'C', RCP NEWS2 2017). Her score becomes 4 with a single red parameter, which needs at least hourly monitoring and medical review. Family concerns are a valid trigger under Martha's Rule.

n.1: Waiting delays recognition of a new red-score parameter.
n.2: New confusion is a marker of deterioration, such as sepsis or delirium, and must not be normalised.
n.3: Documenting without rescoring misses a single-parameter 3, which needs hourly observations and medical review.

4.q: A school nurse is teaching staff about adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), using the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh ACE study. Which experience is counted as an ACE in that study?
o: Living with a household member who served a prison sentence
Being born early and spending time in a neonatal unit
Moving house and changing school during the primary years
Having a parent who regularly worked night shifts
4.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): the nine ACEs were verbal, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up in a household with parental separation, domestic violence, mental illness, alcohol abuse, drug use or incarceration.

n.1: Prematurity is not one of the nine ACEs measured.
n.2: Moving house is not one of the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh study.
n.3: Parental shift work is not one of the nine ACEs measured.

4.q: A patient's family was told in person, with an apology, about a notifiable safety incident on the day it was identified. Under regulation 20, what must the provider do next?
o: Follow it with a written notification and keep a copy
Arrange a further meeting within 28 days to repeat the apology
Report the incident to the NMC for each nurse involved
Wait for the investigation to finish before any further contact
4.w: Reg 20(3)-(4): notification must be given in person, include an apology and be followed by a written notification; the provider must keep a copy and written records.

n.1: Reg 20 requires a written notification after the in-person one; a repeat meeting is not the specified step.
n.2: Reg 20 is about notifying the relevant person; NMC referral relates to fitness to practise concerns, not candour steps.
n.3: The written notification follows the in-person notification and gives what is known so far; it does not wait for the investigation to finish.

4.q: Mr Bello, 30, gave verbal consent for a urinary catheter to be inserted. Partway through, he becomes distressed and says, 'Stop, I don't want this any more.' The nurse is concerned that his bladder is still full. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the procedure, then discuss his concerns and the options
Finish quickly because stopping now would cause more discomfort
Continue, because consent was obtained before the procedure began
Pause, then restart once a colleague is present to reassure him
4.w: Consent is ongoing and a person with capacity may withdraw it at any point (Code 2.5 and 4.2). The nurse should stop, explore his worries, explain the risks of not proceeding and agree a plan with him, then document the discussion.

n.1: Completing a procedure after consent is withdrawn is treatment without consent, however brief.
n.2: Earlier consent does not continue once it has been withdrawn by a person with capacity.
n.3: Restarting without fresh consent overrides his refusal; a colleague's presence does not supply consent.

4.q: Leon, 40, has a severe learning disability and lives in a residential home. Over three weeks he has stopped dressing himself, a skill he has had for years, and spends more time in bed. What should the nurse do first?
o: Compare with his recorded baseline and look for a physical or mental health cause
Increase his support plan so that staff dress him fully each morning
Record that his skills are declining because of his severe learning disability
Refer him straight to the memory service for a dementia assessment
4.w: A new loss of skills is a change from baseline, not part of a stable learning disability. The first step is to establish the change against his baseline and look for treatable causes such as pain, infection, constipation, hypothyroidism, sensory loss or depression, avoiding diagnostic overshadowing.

n.1: Doing tasks for Leon may be needed short term but does not find the cause of the change.
n.2: Attributing new decline to the learning disability is diagnostic overshadowing.
n.3: Dementia is a possibility, but physical and mental health causes should be assessed first.

4.q: Maeve, 79, has dementia and lacks capacity. When she had capacity she made a written, signed and witnessed advance decision refusing antipsychotic medication. The team confirms it is valid and applicable. She is now refusing a newly prescribed antipsychotic. Her family ask for it to be given covertly. What applies?
o: Respect the advance decision and do not give the antipsychotic
Give it covertly, as a best interests meeting overrides the advance decision
Give it covertly until a court decides on the advance decision
Give it covertly if her family and the GP both agree
4.w: Under the MCA 2005 ss24-26, a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment has the same effect as a capacitous refusal and binds professionals. Best interests decisions cannot override it, so the antipsychotic cannot be given, covertly or otherwise.

n.1: A best interests decision cannot override a valid and applicable advance decision.
n.2: Treatment may be given to prevent serious deterioration while a court decides on validity, but here validity is confirmed.
n.3: Family and GP agreement does not override a binding advance refusal.

4.q: Two weeks after discharge from an acute mental health unit, a former patient messages Sam, his named nurse, asking to meet for coffee to say thank you. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Meet in a public place as the patient has been discharged
Accept if the patient's care coordinator agrees to it
Decline the invitation and keep contact professional
Meet once with a colleague present to say goodbye
4.w: Code 20.5-20.6: do not take advantage of vulnerability; stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past.

n.0: Code 20.6 boundaries extend to people who have been in your care in the past.
n.1: Another professional's agreement does not change the boundary set by Code 20.6.
n.3: A social meeting, even accompanied, blurs the professional relationship with a former patient.

4.q: A community learning disability team is deciding who would benefit most from intensive interaction. For which person is the approach most suitable?
o: Maya, 34, with a mild learning disability who reads easy read well
Callum, 28, with a profound learning disability and very limited communication
Sean, 45, who has dementia after many years of fluent speech
Lena, 19, with a moderate learning disability who uses Makaton fluently
4.w: Intensive interaction is used with people at early stages of communication development, such as people with profound and multiple learning disabilities and some autistic people with limited communication.

n.0: Maya already communicates through reading and speech; she does not need early communication fundamentals.
n.2: Sean's needs relate to dementia; he already has established communication.
n.3: Lena is a fluent Makaton user and already has a working communication system.

4.q: Eric, 72, has a new ileostomy. He is preparing for discharge and asks how to fit his appliance. Which advice is correct?
o: Clean the skin with alcohol wipes before each change
Cut the flange well larger than the stoma to avoid rubbing
Measure the stoma and cut the flange slightly larger than it
Leave the appliance on for a week to protect the skin
4.w: The aperture should be cut just larger than the measured stoma (usually 2-3 mm) so that effluent does not contact the skin, re-measuring as post-operative swelling settles. Ileostomy output is corrosive, so a close fit protects skin (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: Alcohol dries and stings the skin; warm water is used.
n.1: A large gap exposes skin to corrosive effluent and causes excoriation.
n.3: Ileostomy appliances are emptied and changed regularly, not left for a week.

4.q: Hazel, 77, is incontinent of urine. On her buttocks you find diffuse, shiny red areas with superficial skin loss, not over a bony prominence, with no evidence of pressure. How should this be classified?
o: As a category 1 pressure ulcer
As moisture-associated skin damage
As a category 2 pressure ulcer
As an unstageable pressure ulcer
4.w: NHS Improvement (2018): damage caused by moisture alone is a moisture lesion (moisture-associated skin damage), not a pressure ulcer. Where pressure and moisture combine, it is classed as a pressure ulcer. CG179 advises barrier preparations for moisture lesions.

n.0: A category 1 ulcer is non-blanching erythema of intact skin caused by pressure.
n.2: A category 2 ulcer needs pressure or shear as a cause; here there is moisture alone.
n.3: Unstageable is the international label for full-thickness loss hidden by slough or eschar (recorded as Category 3 under the NWCSP 2024 tool in England); Hazel's damage is superficial and caused by moisture.

4.q: Olivia, 23, has a learning disability and is anxious about her admission. During a ward round several staff discuss her care at the bedside using medical terms, talking over her. Which action best role-models person-centred care?
o: Continue the round and explain the plan to her carer afterwards
Speak to her directly in plain language and include her in the discussion
Give her a leaflet about her condition after the ward round finishes
Ask the team to discuss her care at the nurses' station instead
4.w: P4.1 asks nurses to role-model person-centred care. Code 2.1-2.3 and 7.1-7.3: work in partnership, encourage people to be involved in decisions, and use terms people can understand, making reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: Talking to her carer instead excludes her from decisions about her own care.
n.2: A leaflet afterwards does not involve her in the discussion and may not be accessible.
n.3: Moving the discussion away removes her from decisions that concern her.

4.q: Callum, a district nurse, mentions that his car has broken down. The son of a patient he visits offers to lend him £500 to repair it until payday. What should Callum do?
o: Accept the loan and declare it to his manager
Decline the loan and keep the relationship professional
Accept the loan and repay it in full on payday
Accept a smaller amount as a gift in place of a loan
4.w: Code 21.2: never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them. Code 21.3 requires honesty and integrity in financial dealings.

n.0: Declaring it does not make it acceptable; loans from people close to patients are prohibited by Code 21.2.
n.2: Code 21.2 says never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them, even if repaid.
n.3: A cash gift of this kind is not trivial and breaches Code 21.1.

4.q: A nurse joining a residential home notices that all residents are got up and dressed by 6 am to suit staff rotas, toileted at fixed times regardless of need, and given meals in the same order every day. Residents' preferences are not recorded. Which type of abuse does this most suggest?
o: Neglect and acts of omission
Organisational abuse
Psychological abuse
Physical abuse
4.w: Organisational abuse (Care Act statutory guidance para 14.17) includes poor care practice within an institution or service, for example rigid routines that serve the organisation rather than the people in its care.

n.0: Fixed toileting may neglect individual needs, but para 14.17 places neglect and poor practice arising from an institution's structure, policies and routines under organisational abuse.
n.2: Psychological abuse involves emotional harm such as threats or humiliation by an individual; the problem described is a system of care.
n.3: No physical harm or force is described.

4.q: Laura, a staff nurse, has worried for several weeks that the night skill mix on her ward is unsafe, with frequent missed observations. She has not yet raised it with anyone. According to NMC guidance, who should she raise it with first?
o: The NMC, so that it can investigate the ward's safety
The trust chief executive, as the person accountable for staffing
The Care Quality Commission, as the regulator for the ward
Her line manager, verbally or in writing, keeping a record
4.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: stage 1 line manager (verbally or in writing, keep a record); stage 2 designated person; stage 3 higher level; stage 4 regulator or helpline. Code 16.1.

n.0: The NMC regulates individual professionals; this is a system concern for the line manager first.
n.1: A higher level in the organisation is stage 3, after the line manager and designated person.
n.2: Going to a regulator is stage 4 of the NMC guidance, used if internal routes fail or are unsuitable.

4.q: Ravi, 55, is a day after a hernia repair. He is anxious and says he 'cannot catch his breath'. RR 26, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 128/80, alert, temperature 37.2°C. You have called for help. Which action best reflects the ABCDE approach?
o: Start oxygen, then continue to C and D while reassessing his breathing
Complete C, D and E fully before deciding whether he needs oxygen
Reassure him that anxiety is common after surgery and observe hourly
Wait for the doctor to examine him before giving any treatment
4.w: ABCDE treats each life-threatening problem as it is found and then reassesses. Hypoxaemia (93% with RR 26) is a B problem: start oxygen to a target of 94-98% (BTS; NG253 rec 1.10.1), then continue through C, D and E, re-evaluating after each intervention.

n.1: Completing the rest of the assessment first delays treatment of a breathing problem already identified.
n.2: Attributing tachypnoea and low saturation to anxiety risks missing a pulmonary embolism or other serious cause.
n.3: Nurses start initial treatment within competence while help arrives; waiting delays care (Code 15).

4.q: Mohammed, 58, has been taking regular codeine for back pain for a week. Which side effect should the nurse ask about and plan to prevent?
o: Constipation
Diarrhoea
Hypertension
Insomnia
4.w: Opioids, including codeine, commonly cause constipation, so bowel habit should be assessed and a laxative considered with regular opioid use (P4.5, P4.15). Other effects include nausea, drowsiness and respiratory depression.

n.1: Opioids slow gut motility rather than causing diarrhoea.
n.2: Opioids do not typically raise blood pressure.
n.3: Opioids more commonly cause drowsiness than insomnia.

4.q: A new community nursing team has been formed by merging two teams. In the first few weeks there are disagreements about who covers which visits and how handovers should run. What should the team leader, Fiona, do first?
o: Allocate the visits herself and ask the team to follow the new system
Meet the whole team to clarify roles and agree ways of working together
Wait for the team to settle, as early disagreement usually fades with time
Ask the two former team leaders to decide the arrangements between them
4.w: In newly formed groups, uncertainty about roles commonly causes conflict. Leaders help by bringing the team together to clarify roles and agree shared ways of working, which builds cohesion and safe handovers (P5.1 group dynamics; AnnexA.4.2.2 active listening to team concerns).

n.0: Imposing a system without involving the team misses their knowledge and may prolong conflict.
n.2: Leaving role confusion unresolved risks missed visits and unsafe handovers.
n.3: Delegating to the former leaders may entrench the two old teams rather than build one team.

4.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is concerned that a planned reduction in local district nursing posts will affect housebound patients. He wants to use his professional knowledge to influence the decision. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Refuse to accept new referrals until the reduction in posts is withdrawn
Share named patients' stories with a local newspaper to raise awareness
Write to his MP with anonymised evidence about the impact on care
Tell his patients during home visits that they should vote against the council
4.w: Political awareness and influence are part of the nurse's role (P7.13; P5.12). Engaging with elected representatives using anonymised evidence is legitimate, while the Code requires confidentiality (Code 5) and that personal political views are not expressed inappropriately to people in his care (Code 20.7).

n.0: Refusing referrals puts patients at risk and is not a professional way to influence policy.
n.1: Sharing identifiable patient information breaches confidentiality (Code 5).
n.3: Expressing personal political views to patients during care breaches Code 20.7.

4.q: Clive, 80, had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) that was still active when he died on a cardiology ward. The registered nurse has verified his expected death. Which action relating to the device is the nurse's responsibility?
o: Instigate deactivation and tell the mortuary or funeral director about the device
Record the device in the notes, as no further action is needed after death
Ask his family to inform the funeral director that a device is present
Remove the device before Clive is transferred to the mortuary
4.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the RN must instigate the process for deactivation of an implantable cardiac defibrillator where applicable, and must notify the funeral director or mortuary of any infections, radioactive implants, implantable devices and whether an ICD is still active.

n.1: An active ICD remains a hazard to people handling the body, so deactivation must be arranged.
n.2: Notifying the mortuary or funeral director is the verifying nurse's responsibility, not the family's.
n.3: Ward nurses do not remove implanted devices; the RN instigates deactivation and passes on the information.

4.q: Mrs Lowe, 88, who has dementia, seems not to respond during the nurse's admission assessment. Her daughter mentions she normally wears hearing aids, which are in her bag. What should the nurse do first?
o: Complete the assessment by asking her daughter the questions
Refer her to audiology for a review of her hearing
Record that she is unable to answer the assessment questions
Check the hearing aids are working and help her put them in
4.w: Annexe A 2.4: support and manage the use of personal communication aids. Code 7.2: take reasonable steps to meet people's communication needs.

n.0: Her daughter can contribute, but Mrs Lowe should first be helped to take part herself.
n.1: A referral may be useful later, but her own aids should be fitted now.
n.2: Recording her as unable to communicate before fitting her aids would be inaccurate.

4.q: Toby, 7, has a severe learning disability, uses no words, walks with a jerky, unsteady gait and has epilepsy. Staff describe him as laughing often and flapping his hands when excited. Which syndrome is most consistent with this picture?
o: Angelman syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
Down syndrome
4.w: Angelman syndrome (loss of maternal UBE3A) causes severe learning disability, minimal or no speech, ataxia, epilepsy, a happy excitable demeanour with frequent laughter and hand-flapping, and sleep problems (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.1: Fragile X usually causes a mild to moderate learning disability with speech, anxiety and social avoidance.
n.2: Prader-Willi typically causes a mild to moderate learning disability with hyperphagia, not ataxia and absent speech.
n.3: Down syndrome does not typically cause absent speech with ataxia and frequent laughter.

4.q: A ward nurse is completing an adult safeguarding referral in England. Under section 42 of the Care Act 2014, the local authority must make enquiries where it has reasonable cause to suspect that an adult has care and support needs and is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect. What is the third condition?
o: The adult has been assessed as lacking capacity to decide
As a result of those needs, the adult cannot protect themselves
The adult has agreed in writing to the referral being made
The abuse has been witnessed by a health or care professional
4.w: Care Act 2014 s42(1): the duty applies where the adult (a) has needs for care and support, (b) is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and (c) as a result of those needs is unable to protect themselves from it.

n.0: Lack of capacity is not a s42 criterion; adults with capacity can also meet the criteria.
n.2: Written agreement is not a statutory condition for the enquiry duty.
n.3: Reasonable cause to suspect is enough; abuse need not have been witnessed.

4.q: Isla, 30, has a profound learning disability. She often rocks and makes humming sounds. During an intensive interaction session, what should the nurse do?
o: Ask Isla simple questions and wait for a response each time
Gently redirect the rocking towards a more purposeful activity
Join in with Isla's humming and rhythm, then wait for her response
Offer a picture choice of activities every few minutes
4.w: Intensive interaction uses imitation and responsive joining-in with the person's own sounds and movements, then pausing for them to respond, creating turn-taking from the person's own behaviour.

n.0: Questions are staff-led and assume language skills Isla may not have.
n.1: Redirecting her behaviour takes control away from Isla and stops her leading the interaction.
n.3: Picture choices are a different approach and interrupt the shared interaction.

4.q: Julie, 58, has motor neurone disease and full capacity. She tells the specialist nurse she wants to make an advance decision refusing mechanical ventilation in the future, even if her life is at risk. In England, what is needed for this refusal to be valid and applicable to life-sustaining treatment?
o: Signed by her GP and registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Written, signed and witnessed, stating it applies even if her life is at risk
Written down and then confirmed in writing by her next of kin
Recorded verbally in her notes and countersigned by two registered nurses
4.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss24-25: a person aged 18 or over with capacity may make an advance decision to refuse treatment. For life-sustaining treatment it must be in writing, signed by the person (or by another in their presence and by their direction), signed by a witness, and contain a statement that it applies even if life is at risk.

n.0: Registration with the Office of the Public Guardian applies to lasting powers of attorney, not advance decisions; no GP signature is required.
n.2: Next of kin confirmation is not a legal requirement; Julie's signature, a witness and the 'even if life is at risk' statement are.
n.3: A verbal advance decision can refuse other treatment, but a refusal of life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed and witnessed (MCA s25(5)-(6)).

4.q: Agnes, the nurse in charge of a busy surgical ward, wants the whole team to share the same understanding of which patients are at risk at the start of each shift. Which practice best supports this?
o: Each nurse reads the full medical notes of all patients before starting
Staff ask the nurse in charge about any patient they are worried about
A brief safety huddle after handover to share key risks and plans
The nurse in charge keeps a written list of risks in the ward office
4.w: Shared situational awareness, the team's common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is supported by short structured safety huddles where risks (deteriorating patients, falls, staffing) are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; P5.2; P6.6).

n.0: Reading all notes is impractical on a busy ward and does not create a shared team picture or agreed actions.
n.1: Relying on individuals to ask means risks are shared reactively and unevenly.
n.3: A list kept by one person does not share awareness across the team.

4.q: Daisy, 19, is autistic and uses a picture communication book. She is admitted to a children's ward after a fall. The nurse notices the book has been packed away in her bag in the locker. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep the book within Daisy's reach and use it when talking with her
Ask her parents to take the book home until she is discharged
Make a set of the ward's own picture cards to use during her stay
Leave the book in the locker so it does not get lost on the ward
4.w: A personal communication aid is Daisy's voice. It must be kept with her and used by staff so she can understand and express needs, including pain (Annexe A 2.4; Accessible Information Standard 'meet').

n.1: Sending it home removes her means of communication during admission.
n.2: Unfamiliar ward cards are less useful than her own book, which she already knows how to use.
n.3: Locked away, the book cannot be used, leaving Daisy unable to communicate.

4.q: Winston, 69, has a long-term urinary catheter. A healthcare support worker is about to empty his drainage bag into a single-use jug. There is a small risk of splashing. Which PPE is most appropriate for this task?
o: Sterile gloves and a disposable apron to protect the closed system
A disposable apron, with hand hygiene once the bag is emptied
Non-sterile gloves, a long-sleeved gown and an FFP3 respirator
Non-sterile gloves and apron, plus eye protection if splashing is likely
4.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves are worn when exposure to body fluids is anticipated, aprons protect clothing when contamination is likely, and eye or face protection is worn when splashing to the face is anticipated. Sterility is not needed to empty a drainage bag.

n.0: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures; emptying a bag via the outlet needs non-sterile gloves.
n.1: Contact with urine is anticipated, so gloves are needed as well as the apron.
n.2: Gowns are for extensive splashing and FFP3 respirators for airborne risks; neither applies to emptying a catheter bag.

4.q: Ruby works as a receptionist in a GP surgery and needs general awareness of learning disability and autism. Her practice manager books her onto the Tier 1 package of the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training. What does this package consist of?
o: A three-hour classroom session led by a learning disability nurse
A 90-minute e-learning module and a one-hour live online interactive session
A one-day face-to-face session followed by a 90-minute e-learning module
A 90-minute e-learning module with an assessed workbook and no live session
4.w: The Tier 1 package is for staff who need general awareness: a 90-minute e-learning module plus a one-hour live online interactive session with at least one person with a learning disability and one autistic person (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: The package is not a nurse-led classroom session; it must be co-delivered by people with lived experience.
n.2: A one-day face-to-face session is the Tier 2 package for staff who provide care and support.
n.3: The live interactive session is a required part of Tier 1; e-learning alone does not meet it.

4.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
4.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

4.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
4.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

4.q: Mr Owusu, 70, has suspected sepsis from a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and the FY2 doctor has reviewed him. Under NICE NG253 (2025), which set of blood tests should the nurse make sure is taken?
o: Urea and electrolytes and FBC, with lactate if the BP falls
Venous gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, FBC and CRP
Arterial gas and troponin, then cultures after antibiotics are given
FBC, CRP and liver function tests, with cultures if fever persists
4.w: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.2-1.8.3 (high risk, NEWS2 7 or more): take a venous blood test including blood gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, full blood count and CRP (plus U&E, creatinine, liver function tests and a clotting screen), and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

n.0: Lactate is part of the initial high-risk bloods and should not depend on a further fall in BP.
n.2: NG253 specifies a venous gas with lactate and blood culture as part of the initial tests; delaying cultures is not recommended.
n.3: Cultures are part of the initial bloods and should not wait for persisting fever.

4.q: On a home visit, community nurse Faye watches Mrs Dobson give her husband his insulin. She injects into the same small area of his abdomen each time and Faye notices lumpy skin there. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to review the insulin dose at the next appointment
Show her how to rotate sites, observe her practice and document it
Take over all of Mr Dobson's insulin injections from now on
Leave an injection technique leaflet for Mrs Dobson to read
4.w: Nurses monitor and evaluate the quality of care delivered by lay carers (P5.7). Teaching site rotation, observing Mrs Dobson's technique and recording the plan supports safe care and independence; lumpy injection sites can alter insulin absorption.

n.0: Dose review may be needed later, but the technique problem must be addressed directly now.
n.2: Taking over removes the couple's independence when the issue can be corrected by teaching.
n.3: A leaflet without demonstration and observation does not confirm the technique has changed.

4.q: Ben, 30, has a learning disability and attends his annual health check with his support worker. His BMI is 35. The nurse wants to discuss diet and activity with him. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Use easy-read materials, allow extra time and involve Ben in each choice
Discuss the plan with his support worker rather than with Ben himself
Use the standard 10-minute appointment and the usual written leaflet
Postpone the conversation, as he may not understand the information
4.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.4: use opportunities, with reasonable adjustments, to discuss diet and exercise. Equality Act 2010 s20 (duty to make reasonable adjustments); Accessible Information Standard (2025). NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014): tailor interventions to the person's capability and needs, including any disability.

n.1: Ben should be involved in decisions about his own health; talking over him is not person-centred.
n.2: Without reasonable adjustments, Ben may be unable to take part; adjustments are a legal duty (Equality Act 2010 s20).
n.3: Assuming he cannot understand breaches MCA s1 and denies him health promotion.

4.q: Ken, 72, had severe delirium with sepsis and lacked capacity, so a covert plan was agreed for his antibiotics. Five days later his delirium has resolved, and an assessment shows he now has capacity to decide about his medicines. What should happen next?
o: Stop all his antibiotics, as the covert plan no longer applies
Stop covert administration and discuss his medicines with him
Continue covertly until the antibiotic course is complete
Continue covertly, as the plan states it runs for 14 days
4.w: Covert administration is lawful only while the person lacks capacity and refuses (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21). Once Ken regains capacity, the plan ends; his medicines are discussed openly and his informed decision respected (MCA 2005 s1).

n.0: The covert method ends, not the treatment; he can be offered the antibiotics openly.
n.2: Continuing covertly once he has capacity overrides his right to decide.
n.3: A plan's stated duration does not authorise covert use once capacity returns.

4.q: Kerry, 35, smokes 20 cigarettes a day. She says, "I know I should stop, but it's the only thing that calms me." Which response reflects motivational interviewing?
o: "Here is a leaflet listing all the risks of smoking."
"You must stop smoking now for the sake of your long-term health."
"What are the good and less good things about smoking for you?"
"Let's agree a date this week when you will stop."
4.w: Annexe A 3.1: motivational interview techniques. MI explores ambivalence through open questions and reflection rather than persuasion.

n.0: Giving information without exploring her views is not MI.
n.1: Direct persuasion tends to increase resistance; MI explores ambivalence.
n.3: Setting a date before exploring her ambivalence skips the MI process.

4.q: A student nurse asks what a Care and Treatment Review (CTR) is for an adult with a learning disability at risk of admission. Which answer is best?
o: A formal complaint process for families who are unhappy with care
An independent review of whether care is safe and community options are used
A Care Act needs assessment completed by a local authority social worker
A review of whether the person meets the criteria for detention
4.w: C(E)TRs bring an independent panel to look at whether the person's care, (education) and treatment are safe and effective, whether community alternatives to admission have been used and what is needed to avoid admission or speed discharge (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy).

n.0: Complaints have their own process; a CTR reviews care and treatment, not complaints.
n.2: A Care Act assessment determines eligible care and support needs; a CTR is a different, NHS-led review.
n.3: Detention criteria are decided under the Mental Health Act by AMHPs and doctors, not by a CTR.

4.q: The Department of Health and Social Care opens a public consultation on changes to nurse education funding. Mariam, a staff nurse, has concerns about the effect on recruitment to her mental health service. What is the most appropriate way for her to influence the policy?
o: Post her views on social media, naming her employer and the vacancies
Respond to the consultation with evidence, directly or through her union
Ask her manager to raise it with the patients' families at visiting
Write to the NMC and ask it to block the proposed funding changes
4.w: P5.12 and P7.13 ask nurses to understand mechanisms for influencing public policy and to use political awareness. Responding to consultations with evidence, individually or through professional bodies and unions, is a legitimate and effective route, consistent with Code 20 (professionalism).

n.0: Naming her employer and service on social media risks breaching Code 20.10 and confidentiality, and is not a formal route of influence.
n.2: Involving visiting families is inappropriate and does not feed into the consultation.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not control government education funding.

4.q: Evie, 37, has a profound learning disability and pulls out her gastrostomy tube. Staff suggest arm splints at all times. The nurse wants the least restrictive option. Which plan is best?
o: Use arm splints at night and remove them for meals during the day
Ask the GP to prescribe sedation so that she does not pull the tube
Fit splints day and night and review them at the next annual review
Use a tube cover and abdominal binder, agreed in a best interests review
4.w: MCA 2005 s1(6) requires the less restrictive option to be considered. A tube cover or binder protects the gastrostomy with far less restriction of movement than splints, and any restriction must be agreed through a best interests decision and reviewed (NICE NG11 1.9.5).

n.0: Night-time splints still restrict her movement for long periods when a less restrictive device could protect the tube.
n.1: Sedation is chemical restraint and is more restrictive than protecting the tube directly.
n.2: Continuous splints are highly restrictive, and waiting a year to review breaches the duty to minimise restriction.

4.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
4.q: Lewis, 30, has a profound learning disability and very limited movement. He sleeps every night on his side with both knees dropped to the same side. Over time, which body shape change is most likely?
o: Windswept hips with risk of hip dislocation
Improved lung expansion on the upper side
Flat feet from lack of weight bearing
Stronger trunk muscles from side lying
4.w: Lying in the same asymmetric position for long periods causes the knees to fall to one side, producing a 'windswept' hip pattern, pelvic rotation, hip dislocation and scoliosis. Supported symmetrical lying protects body shape.

n.1: Lying fixed on one side does not improve lung expansion; the asymmetry it causes can lead to scoliosis that restricts the chest over time.
n.2: Foot posture may change, but the classic risk from this position is windswept hips.
n.3: Side lying in one position does not strengthen the trunk; it promotes asymmetry.

4.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
4.q: A ward is admitting Mohammed, 44, who has a learning disability. The nurse wants to recognise deterioration early. Which information is most useful to gather on admission?
o: His usual baselines from family and his passport
His preferred newspaper and television programmes
His school records and qualifications
His blood group and previous transfusions
4.w: Knowing the person's usual observations, behaviours, eating, sleeping, mobility and how they show pain allows staff to recognise change; family carers and passports are key sources (LeDeR; Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag).

n.1: Preferences support comfort but do not establish clinical baselines.
n.2: Education history does not help recognise physical deterioration.
n.3: Blood group matters only if a transfusion is planned.

4.q: A community nurse attends to verify the expected death of Lena, 83, who had advanced dementia. Lena is cold and rigor mortis is present. The nurse notices fresh, unexplained bruising on Lena's upper arms, and two relatives give conflicting accounts of the evening. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Decline to verify and request the police and the responsible doctor
Begin CPR because the death can no longer be treated as expected
Verify the death as expected and document the bruising in her record
Verify the death, then wash Lena before the funeral director arrives
4.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): verification by an RN applies to expected deaths not accompanied by suspicious circumstances, and the verifying nurse has the right to refuse to verify and to request the responsible doctor or the police in any unusual situation. Care after death guidance: minimal contact with the body when suspicion arises.

n.1: Rigor mortis is a sign of irreversible death, so CPR is not indicated (RNVoEAD; RCUK).
n.2: Verification by an RN is excluded where there are suspicious circumstances (RNVoEAD guidance).
n.3: Washing could destroy evidence; with suspicion, there should be minimal contact with the body.

4.q: Dan, 24, has Prader-Willi syndrome and lives in supported living. He has taken food from housemates' cupboards and gained 6 kg in two months. Staff want to lock the kitchen. What must happen first?
o: Assess his capacity on food access and, if lacking, decide in his best interests
Lock the kitchen straight away, because hyperphagia justifies any food restriction
Lock the kitchen once his parents have agreed to it on his behalf
Leave the kitchen open and record his food choices as unwise decisions
4.w: Two steps: locking the kitchen restricts Dan and his housemates, so it needs a lawful basis. Assess his capacity for this decision (MCA s2-3); if he lacks it, make a best interests decision (s4) choosing the least restrictive option (s1(6)), and review it regularly.

n.1: Restrictions need a lawful basis and proportionality; a diagnosis does not authorise any restriction.
n.2: Parents cannot consent on behalf of an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.3: Calling his choices unwise assumes he has capacity, which has not been assessed, given the compulsive nature of hyperphagia.

4.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
4.q: Nina, 44, has a moderate learning disability and capacity to decide about CPR. Her consultant believes CPR would be unlikely to succeed. Nina says she wants CPR. What should happen?
o: Ask her mother to decide instead of Nina
Record that Nina lacks capacity because she disagrees
Record DNACPR now and discuss it with her at a later review
Explain sensitively why CPR may not work and involve Nina
4.w: Patients with capacity must be involved in discussions about DNACPR; the clinician explains the reasons in an accessible way. A patient cannot demand treatment that will not work, but should be informed unless it would cause physical or psychological harm (Tracey v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014]; Resuscitation Council UK/BMA/RCN guidance).

n.0: Nina has capacity, so her mother cannot decide for her.
n.1: Disagreement with clinicians is not evidence of lack of capacity (MCA s1(4)).
n.2: Under Tracey, a patient with capacity should be involved when the decision is made unless discussion would cause harm; delaying the discussion is not lawful.

4.q: A charge nurse asks what a basic business case for funding two additional healthcare assistant posts should contain. Which content is most appropriate?
o: Last year's off-duty rotas to show how often extra shifts were filled
A list of the staff who support the request, with their signatures
The problem, the options considered, their costs and the expected benefits
Details of recent incidents including the patients' names and dates of birth
4.w: A business case explains why change is needed, the options (including doing nothing), costs, expected benefits to patients and the organisation, and how success will be measured (P7.12). Evidence should be anonymised to protect confidentiality (Code 5).

n.0: Past rotas may support part of the argument but are not the core content of a business case.
n.1: Support from colleagues does not show need, cost or benefit.
n.3: Identifiable patient information is not needed and would breach confidentiality; anonymised data should be used.

4.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
4.q: Mo, 39, has a learning disability and is subject to a standard DoLS authorisation in a care home. He repeatedly says he wants to live with his sister, who is his relevant person's representative and wants to challenge the authorisation. What should the nurse do?
o: Support an application to the Court of Protection under section 21A
Ask the care home manager to end the authorisation himself
Advise that a DoLS authorisation cannot be challenged once granted
Help them apply to a mental health tribunal to end the authorisation
4.w: Two steps: recognise Mo's objection and his representative's role; then support the statutory route: under MCA s21A the person or their representative can apply to the Court of Protection to challenge a standard authorisation, and non-means-tested legal aid is available.

n.1: The managing authority cannot simply end an authorisation while it says the criteria are met; the challenge route is the court.
n.2: Authorisations can be challenged; s21A exists for this purpose.
n.3: Mental health tribunals deal with Mental Health Act detention, not DoLS.

4.q: Hannah, 24, has type 1 diabetes and is on an orthopaedic ward. You are called because she is sweaty and confused. Airway is clear, RR 18, SpO2 97%, pulse 98, BP 118/72. She responds to voice. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give her 300 mg aspirin to chew while awaiting review
Complete a 4AT delirium screen before any other test
Request an urgent CT head scan to exclude a stroke
Check her capillary blood glucose straight away
4.w: With A, B and C stable, D includes a capillary blood glucose. In someone with diabetes who is sweaty and confused, hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L, RCUK first aid 2025) is the most likely reversible cause and must be excluded quickly.

n.0: Aspirin is for cardiac-sounding chest pain and is not indicated for confusion.
n.1: Delirium screening is relevant later; a reversible metabolic cause should be excluded first.
n.2: Imaging is not a nursing first step and would delay checking for a common reversible cause.

4.q: Nadia is redressing a deep cavity wound on the sacrum of Ruth, 80. She is wearing non-sterile gloves and using ANTT, but realises she will need to touch the wound bed with her fingers to place the packing. What should she do?
o: Change to sterile gloves, as the Key-Site will be touched directly
Moisten the non-sterile gloves with sterile saline before packing
Rub alcohol handrub onto the gloves before touching the wound
Continue with the non-sterile gloves, as she cleaned her hands first
4.w: Under ANTT, if a Key-Site or Key-Part must be touched directly, sterile gloves are needed so that the hands do not contaminate it (a Surgical-ANTT approach). NIPCM ch 1.4 also requires sterile gloves for contact with a sterile site or body cavity.

n.1: Saline does not sterilise gloves; the gloves would still contaminate the wound bed.
n.2: Gloves are not decontaminated with handrub, and this does not make them sterile.
n.3: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable when Key-Sites are not touched; here she must touch the wound bed directly.

4.q: Sophie is about to insert a peripheral intravenous cannula into the forearm of Malik, 45. She has selected the vein and performed hand hygiene. According to NICE CG139, how should she prepare the skin at the insertion site?
o: Clean with a 70% alcohol wipe, then palpate the vein again
Clean with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride and pat the skin dry with gauze
Apply povidone-iodine and wipe it off before inserting
Clean with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and allow it to dry
4.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate the skin at the insertion site with chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol before inserting a peripheral vascular access device or PICC. The solution must dry to work, and the cleaned site is not re-palpated.

n.0: Re-palpating the vein after cleaning contaminates the Key-Site, and alcohol alone is not the CG139 product.
n.1: Saline cleans but does not decontaminate the skin.
n.2: CG139 specifies chlorhexidine in alcohol; wiping antiseptic off before it has acted also defeats it.

4.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
4.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

4.q: Over 24 hours, Mr Ito, 74, receives 1,000 mL IV fluid and drinks 650 mL. His output is 1,500 mL urine and 600 mL vomit. He is drowsy with a dry mouth. What is the fluid balance and the best action?
o: Minus 450 mL; continue current fluids and recheck tomorrow
Minus 1,100 mL; restrict oral fluids as he is vomiting
Minus 450 mL; report the deficit and signs of dehydration
Plus 450 mL; continue current fluids and recheck tomorrow
4.w: Input 1,000 + 650 = 1,650 mL; output 1,500 + 600 = 2,100 mL; balance = 1,650 - 2,100 = -450 mL. P1.15 numeracy for safe practice; Code 13.1 recognise deterioration and 13.2 refer in a timely way.

n.0: The figure is right, but drowsiness and a dry mouth with a negative balance need prompt escalation.
n.1: 1,650 - 2,100 = -450 mL; restricting fluids would worsen dehydration.
n.3: Input 1,650 mL minus output 2,100 mL gives minus 450 mL, not plus.

4.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
4.q: Martin, 46, has a severe learning disability and is admitted with a chest infection. A junior doctor writes on a DNACPR form, 'Reason: learning disability, poor quality of life.' What should the nurse do?
o: Ask Martin's family to sign the form to confirm it
Accept the form, as DNACPR is a medical decision
File the form and review it on discharge
Raise it with the consultant as an invalid reason
4.w: A learning disability, Down syndrome or autism must never be the reason for a DNACPR decision; decisions must be individual, based on clinical factors and made with the person or, if they lack capacity, in consultation with family under the MCA (NHS England C1146 letter on DNACPR and people with a learning disability and autistic people; Equality Act 2010).

n.0: Family signatures do not validate an unlawful reason; families are consulted, not asked to sign.
n.1: Although clinicians make CPR decisions, a decision based on disability is discriminatory and must be challenged.
n.2: Leaving a discriminatory decision in place risks Martin's life during this admission.

4.q: Bryony, 38, has a profound learning disability and does not use pictures or signs. Staff want to help her anticipate that she is going swimming. Using objects of reference, what should they do?
o: Show her a photograph of the swimming pool
Sign 'swimming' in Makaton as they tell her
Give her a piece of her swimming towel to hold
Hand her a symbol card for swimming
4.w: An object of reference is a real object that stands for an activity, person or place, such as a towel for swimming, used with people who do not yet understand pictures or signs. It must be used consistently.

n.0: Photographs are more abstract than objects; Bryony does not use pictures.
n.1: Bryony does not use signs, so a sign alone will not convey the activity.
n.3: Symbols are more abstract than pictures and are not meaningful for her.

4.q: Mr Gray, 70, has capacity and a physical disability. He discloses that his son pushes him when angry, but asks the nurse to do nothing. The nurse discusses the options, and there is no apparent risk to anyone else. Which of the six adult safeguarding principles requires the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk?
o: Empowerment
Protection
Accountability
Proportionality
4.w: The six principles (Care Act statutory guidance ch 14) are empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership and accountability. Proportionality means the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk presented.

n.0: Empowerment concerns person-led decisions and informed consent, not the scale of response.
n.1: Protection concerns support and representation for those in greatest need.
n.2: Accountability concerns accountability and transparency in delivering safeguarding, not the scale of the response.

4.q: Ray, 58, smokes, drinks about 30 units a week and takes little exercise. He tells the nurse he wants to be healthier but feels overwhelmed by everything he 'should' change. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise him to stop smoking and drinking on the same day
Tell him to start with alcohol, as it carries the greatest risk
Give leaflets on all three topics and review him in six months
Ask which change he feels most motivated to tackle first
4.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) rec 8: tailor interventions by assessing the person's behaviour, capability, context and how motivated they are to change; if many behaviours need to change, assess which one or ones the person is most motivated to tackle. NMC Annexe A 2.7: assess motivation and capacity for behaviour change.

n.0: Tackling several behaviours at once when he feels overwhelmed may reduce his chance of success; PH49 asks which he is most motivated to change.
n.1: Choosing for him ignores his motivation; PH49 recommends assessing which behaviour he is most motivated to tackle.
n.2: Leaflets without a plan miss the chance to agree goals; PH49 recommends goals, action plans and planned review.

4.q: Kofi, 72, has a NEWS2 of 6. You have completed an ABCDE assessment, given oxygen and called the doctor using SBAR. The doctor will arrive in 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate next action?
o: Hand over to the next shift that he has been reviewed
Leave him to rest and record observations again in 4 hours
Repeat the ABCDE assessment to check his response to interventions
Start the oral antibiotics left on his drug chart from yesterday
4.w: ABCDE is cyclical: after each intervention reassess from A. A NEWS2 of 5 or more requires at least hourly monitoring, and any deterioration should trigger re-escalation (RCP 2017 chart 4).
