n.0: He has not yet been reviewed, so this handover would be inaccurate and unsafe.
n.1: A NEWS2 of 5-6 requires at least hourly observations, not 4-hourly.
n.3: Oral antibiotics from yesterday are not a response to an acute deterioration and need medical review.

4.q: Philip, 66, is drowsy after surgery and has had no food for 6 days. His BMI is 23 kg/m² and he has no other refeeding risk factors. Nutrition support is planned. Under NICE CG32, what is the maximum initial intake for the first 2 days?
o: His full estimated requirements
No more than 50% of his estimated requirements
No more than 25% of his estimated requirements
No more than 10 kcal/kg/day
4.w: NICE CG32: people who have eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days should have nutrition support started at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days, before increasing if clinical and biochemical monitoring reveals no refeeding problems. The 10 kcal/kg/day limit is for those at high refeeding risk.

n.0: Full requirements after more than 5 days of little intake risk refeeding problems.
n.2: 25% is lower than the CG32 recommendation for this group.
n.3: 10 kcal/kg/day is the starting level for people at high refeeding risk, which he is not.

4.q: Ben, 31, has a severe learning disability and no speech. Over two days he has stopped eating and has been pushing staff away. A support worker writes in the notes, 'Ben is being difficult again, it is his learning disability.' Which concept best describes this note?
o: Diagnostic overshadowing
Learned helplessness
Behavioural extinction
Positive risk-taking
4.w: Explaining a new change in eating and behaviour as part of Ben's learning disability, without considering pain or illness, is diagnostic overshadowing. Behaviour change is a common way people without speech communicate pain or illness.

n.1: Learned helplessness describes passivity after repeated loss of control; it does not fit a note blaming the disability.
n.2: Extinction is a behavioural term for a behaviour fading when it is no longer reinforced; it does not describe this note.
n.3: Positive risk-taking is a planned approach to supporting choice and independence, not a missed illness.

4.q: Vera, 81, is recovering from pneumonia and is keen to return home. She can wash her face and upper body slowly but tires easily. A healthcare support worker suggests giving her a full bed bath to save time. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Postpone her wash until she can manage it without help
Set her up to wash what she can and help with the rest
Give her a full bed bath so that she can rest afterwards
Ask her daughter to wash her during the afternoon visit
4.w: Annexe B 4.3: assist with washing and dressing in a way that promotes independence. Encouraging Vera to do what she can, with help for the rest, maintains her abilities and dignity and supports her goal of going home (Code 1.2, 2.1).

n.0: Postponing hygiene leaves her needs unmet and risks skin problems.
n.2: A full bed bath removes the independence she needs to regain.
n.3: Hygiene is a fundamental of care that the nursing team is responsible for providing.

4.q: Kieran, 26, has a learning disability and takes risperidone prescribed for behaviour that challenges. His learning disability nurse is helping the GP practice prepare his annual health check. According to NICE NG11, which area should the check specifically review?
o: A full functional assessment of his behaviour by a clinical psychologist
His medicines and side effects, and links between behaviour and physical health
A capacity assessment covering each of his major life decisions
A repeat IQ test to confirm the severity of his learning disability
4.w: NICE NG11 (1.2.1) says the annual health check should include reviewing behaviour that challenges and any links with physical health, and reviewing medication including side effects.

n.0: Functional assessment is a specialist process when behaviour is a concern, not a routine element of the GP check.
n.2: Capacity is decision-specific and assessed when a decision arises, not as a blanket review at the health check.
n.3: Re-testing IQ is not part of the annual health check and does not change his care.

4.q: Ellie, 5, is having a cannula inserted tomorrow. Today the play specialist uses a doll with a cannula to show Ellie what will happen and let her practise on it. Which approach is this?
o: Distraction and diversion
Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Therapeutic play
4.w: Annexe A 3.7: play therapy. Therapeutic play prepares children for procedures and helps them express feelings.

n.0: Distraction is used during the procedure; this prepares her beforehand.
n.1: CBT addresses thoughts and behaviour; this uses play to prepare.
n.2: Solution-focused work looks for exceptions and goals.

4.q: Frank, 68, has COPD and pneumonia. Two days ago the team thought he was dying and started an end of life care plan. Today he is more alert, has eaten some breakfast and his breathing is easier. The doctors disagree about whether he is still dying. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue the end of life care plan unchanged, as improvement is often brief
Seek advice from the specialist palliative care team about the uncertainty
Request daily full blood counts and renal function to clarify his prognosis
Stop the end of life care plan and restart all of his previous medicines
4.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.7: seek advice from colleagues with more experience of end of life care when there is a high level of uncertainty, for example conflicting signs, about whether a person is dying, stabilising or may recover. Rec 1.1.3: improvement could indicate stabilising or recovery.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.1.3 warns that improvement may mean the person is stabilising or recovering, so the plan cannot simply continue unchanged.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.1.4 advises avoiding investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last days of life.
n.3: Reversing all care without a shared review is premature; the guidance is to seek experienced advice when the picture is uncertain.

4.q: Ida, 79, is being fed through a nasogastric tube. During the feed she starts coughing, becomes breathless and her SpO2 falls from 96% to 89%. What should the nurse do first?
o: Slow the feed rate and recheck her saturation
Flush the tube with water to clear any blockage
Stop the feed, sit her up and call for urgent help
Check the tube length mark and continue feeding
4.w: Sudden coughing, breathlessness and desaturation during a feed suggest aspiration or tube misplacement. Stop the feed, sit her upright, give oxygen and get urgent help (Annexe B 5.7; misplaced tubes are a Never Event).

n.0: Continuing a slower feed risks further aspiration.
n.1: Flushing adds more fluid to a possibly misplaced tube.
n.3: Continuing feeding is unsafe until the cause is established.

4.q: Steve, 36, has cerebral palsy and a severe learning disability and does not use words. He cries out and grips the hoist sling when moved and when staff dress his legs. A support worker suggests adding this to his behaviour plan. What should the nurse do?
o: Assess for hip or other musculoskeletal pain and review his analgesia
Hoist him less often to reduce the number of distressing transfers
Record it as behaviour that challenges to be managed in his support plan
Ask staff to dress him more quickly to shorten the distress
4.w: Hip displacement, contractures and scoliosis are common in cerebral palsy and cause pain on movement. Crying out during transfers and leg dressing is likely pain communication, so it needs assessment and analgesia review rather than a behavioural label (avoid diagnostic overshadowing).

n.1: Reducing transfers affects his care and position changes without treating the cause.
n.2: Labelling pain as behaviour is diagnostic overshadowing and leaves pain untreated.
n.3: Faster dressing does not address the likely source of pain.

4.q: A trained healthcare worker is giving CPR to an adult with a pocket mask. What ratio of compressions to rescue breaths should be used?
4.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, each breath just enough to make the chest start to rise.

n.1: 15:2 is the ratio used in paediatric life support by healthcare rescuers.
n.2: 5:1 is an obsolete ratio not used in current guidance.
n.3: 30:1 gives too few breaths for adult BLS.

4.q: A nurse is carrying out a whole-body systems assessment of Mr Burns, 80, who has been bedbound for several days. On the skin review she finds a red area over his sacrum that does not blanch with light finger pressure. What should she do?
o: Record it as a category 2 pressure ulcer and apply a dressing
Reassess it at his next weekly skin inspection
Massage the area to restore its circulation and recheck it tomorrow
Start pressure ulcer prevention and recheck the skin at least 2-hourly
4.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy to test blanching; if non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until resolved. A systems assessment includes skin (Annexe B 2.7).

n.0: Intact non-blanching erythema is a category 1 finding, not category 2, which involves partial-thickness skin loss.
n.1: Weekly review is too infrequent; CG179 requires at least 2-hourly reassessment.
n.2: Massaging pressure-damaged skin can cause further harm, and a day's delay is too long.

4.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
4.q: Sasha, 24, has a mild learning disability and has just had her first baby. She is learning to make up formula feeds safely before discharge home. Which teaching approach is most likely to help?
o: Show the steps practically with pictures and repeat them over time
Explain the full process once in detail on the day of discharge
Ask her partner to make all the feeds until she feels confident
Give her the standard written leaflet on formula feeds to take home and keep
4.w: People with a learning disability learn best through practical demonstration, accessible pictorial step-by-step guides, repetition and positive reinforcement (NMC Annexe A 2.6). Ongoing support at home should continue after discharge.

n.1: A single detailed explanation is hard to retain and does not allow practice.
n.2: This removes her opportunity to learn and parent her baby.
n.3: A standard leaflet may not be accessible to Sasha.

4.q: Jasmine, 34, has a profound learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to dental treatment. She needs a tooth extraction under general anaesthetic. Her blood tests and ear examination are also overdue because she cannot tolerate them while awake. What is the best adjustment to propose?
o: Plan, in her best interests, to do the other checks under the same anaesthetic
Ask her GP to try the blood tests again with extra staff support
Book separate appointments for the blood tests and ear examination later
Carry out the extraction and delay the other checks to her annual check
4.w: Coordinating procedures under one general anaesthetic is a recognised reasonable adjustment that avoids repeated distress and anaesthetic risk. Because Jasmine lacks capacity, the plan must be agreed as being in her best interests with those close to her (MCA 2005 s4; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.1: Repeating the tests while she is awake, with more staff to support or hold her, is more restrictive and she has not tolerated them awake.
n.2: Separate appointments she cannot tolerate while awake are likely to fail again.
n.3: Delaying the checks misses a safe opportunity and leaves health needs unmet.

4.q: Nurse Ola realises she gave Leon, 45, 10 mg of oral morphine solution instead of the prescribed 5 mg, 20 minutes ago. Leon is alert with a respiratory rate of 16 and no sedation. What should Ola do?
o: Rewrite the chart entry to 5 mg to avoid confusing the next nurse
Monitor Leon, inform the prescriber, tell Leon and report the incident
Observe Leon and report the error if he shows any signs of harm
Inform the ward manager and leave her to decide whether to tell Leon
4.w: Medication incidents are reported and reflected on (P6.8; NMC Code 19): the priority is the person's safety (monitoring sedation and respiratory rate), then informing the prescriber, being open with Leon (professional duty of candour), and reporting through the local system feeding LFPSE.

n.0: Altering the record to hide an error is dishonest and breaches the Code.
n.2: Incidents, including those without harm, are reported so that learning can occur.
n.3: The professional duty of candour is personal; Ola should be open with Leon herself.

4.q: Frank, 63, is prescribed oral morphine solution 2.5-5 mg as required every 2 hours for pain. He had 2.5 mg 4 hours ago with little effect and now rates his pain 8/10. He is alert with a respiratory rate of 16. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 2.5 mg now and repeat it in 30 minutes if needed
Give 7.5 mg, as the previous 2.5 mg dose was ineffective
Withhold the dose until the doctor increases the prescription
Give 5 mg, the top of the prescribed range, and reassess
4.w: Titration within a prescribed range is a nurse's decision based on assessment (AnnexB.11.5). The previous dose was ineffective, he is not sedated and 2 hours have passed, so the higher dose within the range is appropriate, with reassessment of pain, sedation and respiratory rate.

n.0: Repeating at 30 minutes breaches the 2-hourly minimum interval.
n.1: 7.5 mg exceeds the prescribed range, which the nurse cannot change.
n.2: A suitable dose is available within the range; withholding leaves him in pain.

4.q: Mr Fox, 82, lacks capacity to consent to a hip operation. His nephew produces a registered lasting power of attorney for property and financial affairs and says he will give consent. What should the nurse explain?
o: The nephew can consent because the LPA is registered
The nephew can consent if the surgeon agrees
The LPA covers treatment once two doctors sign it
This LPA does not cover decisions about medical treatment
4.w: MCA 2005 s9(1) distinguishes an LPA for personal welfare (health and welfare, which can cover medical treatment) from one for property and affairs. A property and financial affairs attorney has no authority over health decisions, so the surgeon must decide in Mr Fox's best interests (s4), consulting the nephew.

n.0: Registration does not change the scope of the power; this LPA covers finances, not health.
n.1: A surgeon's agreement cannot widen the authority given by the LPA.
n.2: There is no provision for doctors to extend a financial LPA to cover treatment.

4.q: Nadia, 49, has Down syndrome and lives in supported living. Over six months she has started needing prompts to wash and dress, and has become forgetful and withdrawn. Staff wonder if she has dementia. Which should the nurse ask the GP to check first?
o: Her IQ score compared with childhood
Her serum cholesterol and lipid profile
An urgent CT head scan
Thyroid function, hearing and vision
4.w: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and can mimic dementia or depression; hearing and vision loss also cause apparent cognitive decline. These treatable causes should be excluded before a dementia diagnosis (DSMIG/DSA thyroid guidance; NICE NG54 1.7.4 review physical health).

n.0: IQ tests do not measure change reliably and do not exclude treatable causes; adaptive behaviour compared with a baseline is used instead.
n.1: Lipids are part of general health checks but do not explain new loss of skills.
n.2: Neuroimaging is not the first step; reversible causes such as thyroid and sensory problems are checked first.

4.q: At a major incident, Daniel reaches a young woman lying on the ground with a lower leg wound that is spurting blood. She is conscious. Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool, what should he do?
o: Categorise her as P2 because she is conscious and breathing
Ask her to walk to the casualty clearing area for assessment
Apply pressure or a tourniquet and categorise her as P1
Assess her breathing rate first and then decide her triage category
4.w: Catastrophic bleeding is the first step in MITT (NHS England 2023): control it with pressure, a tourniquet or haemostatic packing and categorise the casualty as P1 (P6.12).

n.0: Being conscious does not lower the priority of catastrophic bleeding, which makes the casualty P1.
n.1: Walking her would worsen the bleeding and delay life-saving control.
n.3: Catastrophic bleeding is assessed and controlled before breathing in MITT; delaying control risks death from haemorrhage.

4.q: Olu and Grace ask why their son Ethan, 4, who has a learning disability, is being offered genetic testing when 'nothing will change his condition'. What is the most accurate explanation?
o: Testing can identify a treatment that reverses the learning disability
A known cause can guide checks for linked conditions and inform family planning
Testing is needed before Ethan can be referred to specialist support services
Testing decides whether Ethan is eligible for an annual health check at 14
4.w: Identifying a cause (for example fragile X or a chromosome deletion) can guide health surveillance for associated conditions, give the family information on recurrence risk, and connect them with condition-specific support.

n.0: Knowing the genetic cause does not reverse a learning disability.
n.2: Support is based on need, not on knowing the cause; many people never have a cause identified.
n.3: Annual health checks are offered to anyone aged 14 or over on the GP learning disability register, whatever the cause.

4.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
4.q: A community learning disability nurse explains when a local authority must make safeguarding enquiries under section 42 of the Care Act 2014. Which set of conditions triggers the duty?
o: Care and support needs; at risk of abuse or neglect; unable to protect themselves as a result
Lacks capacity for the decision; aged over 65; lives alone without daily support from family or friends
Has a learning disability; is known to services; has a family who agree to an enquiry
Is eligible for funded care; has an allocated social worker; consents to an enquiry
4.w: Care Act 2014 s42(1): the duty applies where the local authority has reasonable cause to suspect that an adult in its area (a) has needs for care and support, (b) is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and (c) as a result of those needs is unable to protect themselves.

n.1: Capacity, age and living alone are not the statutory criteria.
n.2: A diagnosis and family agreement are not the statutory criteria.
n.3: Eligibility for funding is not required; care and support needs are enough.

4.q: Gary, 23, is autistic, has a learning disability and his placement is close to breaking down because of increasing distress. His commissioner suggests a specialist hospital 150 miles away. Which response best reflects Building the Right Support?
o: Put intensive support in place in the community close to his home
Move him to a large residential campus with on-site specialist staff
Arrange respite on an acute adult psychiatric ward until he settles
Arrange admission to the hospital as the safest place for him at present
4.w: Building the Right Support (2015) and NICE NG93 aim for people to be supported in the community, close to home, with intensive support to prevent admission; inpatient care should be used when it is genuinely needed for assessment or treatment, not as a response to placement breakdown.

n.1: Large campus settings are a form of institutional care that policy moves away from.
n.2: An acute psychiatric ward is not designed for his needs and is not a respite setting.
n.3: A distant admission removes him from family and community, the pattern policy aims to end.

4.q: Ben, 35, has a moderate learning disability. ABC charts show he hits out on some days when asked to get dressed but not on others. Night staff notes show the incidents follow nights when he slept less than four hours. How should the nurse describe the poor sleep in the formulation?
o: A consequence that keeps the behaviour going
A trigger that immediately precedes the behaviour
A setting event that makes the behaviour more likely
The function the behaviour serves for Ben
4.w: Setting events are background conditions (poor sleep, pain, hunger, illness) that change how likely a trigger is to provoke the behaviour. NICE NG11 1.5.9 asks for setting events to be identified alongside triggers and maintaining consequences.

n.0: Consequences follow the behaviour; poor sleep comes before it.
n.1: The immediate trigger is the request to get dressed; poor sleep is a background condition, not the antecedent.
n.3: The function is what the behaviour achieves (for example escape); sleep loss influences likelihood but is not a function.

4.q: A ward manager asks a learning disability nurse what the national Building the Right Support programme set out to achieve for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Which answer is correct?
o: To increase specialist inpatient beds so that people are treated near home
To reduce reliance on inpatient care by developing community support
To make Care and Treatment Reviews a requirement under the Care Act 2014
To transfer all learning disability services to local authority control
4.w: Building the Right Support (2015) and its 2022 action plan aim to reduce the number of people with a learning disability and autistic people in mental health inpatient settings by developing community services; the action plan target was to halve inpatient numbers from 2015 levels by March 2024, which was missed (BRS; Commons Library SN07058).

n.0: The aim was to reduce, not increase, reliance on inpatient beds.
n.2: C(E)TRs are NHS England policy; the Care Act 2014 did not make them statutory.
n.3: The programme involves NHS and local government jointly; it did not transfer services to councils.

4.q: A ward manager in an English hospital is updating staff training on people who lack capacity and whose care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. A nurse asks which legal scheme is currently in force to authorise such arrangements in hospitals and care homes. What should the manager say?
o: The nurse's holding power under the Mental Health Act 1983
The Liberty Protection Safeguards under the 2019 Amendment Act
The community treatment order scheme under the Mental Health Act
The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards under the MCA 2005
4.w: DoLS (MCA 2005 Schedules A1 and 1A) remain the scheme in force in England and Wales for hospitals and care homes. The Liberty Protection Safeguards in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 have not been implemented.

n.0: The nurse's holding power under MHA s5(4) briefly detains an informal inpatient with mental disorder; it does not authorise care arrangements under the MCA.
n.1: The LPS have not been brought into force; DoLS remain the live scheme.
n.2: Community treatment orders apply to certain detained patients leaving hospital, not to people lacking capacity in hospitals or care homes.

4.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
4.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

4.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
4.q: A nurse is preparing to assess whether Lily, 25, who has a learning disability, has capacity to decide to engage in sexual relations. Following A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52, which information must Lily be able to understand as part of the decision?
o: That her family must be told about any sexual relationship she has
That a written agreement is needed before any sexual activity
That marriage is required before sexual activity becomes lawful
That the other person must be able to consent and consent throughout
4.w: In JB the Supreme Court upheld the Court of Appeal: the information relevant to the decision includes that the other person must have the capacity to consent to the sexual activity and must in fact consent before and throughout it, as well as the mechanics of sex, health risks and the risk of pregnancy.

n.0: An adult does not need to tell her family about a relationship.
n.1: There is no legal requirement for a written agreement.
n.2: Sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful without marriage.

4.q: An audit on Ward 6 found that only 58% of patients had a fully completed fluid balance chart against a standard of 95%. The team then held teaching sessions and introduced a simpler chart. What is the next step that completes the audit cycle?
o: Lower the standard to a level the ward can meet
Re-audit practice against the same 95% standard
Start a new audit on a different topic for the ward
Publish the original results in a nursing journal
4.w: The audit cycle is: agree the standard, measure practice, compare, implement change, then re-audit to check whether the change has improved and sustained practice (HQIP Best Practice in Clinical Audit). Re-measurement against the same standard closes the loop (P6.7).

n.0: Standards are set from evidence and policy, not lowered to match current performance.
n.2: Moving on without re-auditing leaves the cycle incomplete and the change unevaluated.
n.3: Sharing findings can be useful, but publication does not show whether the changes worked.

4.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
4.q: Lena, 24, has a moderate learning disability. Over a week she has stopped eating, seems to respond to voices and is withdrawn, with no aggressive or irresponsible conduct. The team considers admission for assessment under section 2. Does the learning disability conduct qualifier apply?
o: No, the qualifier does not apply to section 2, which may be used if its criteria are met
Yes, section 2 cannot be used for a person who has a learning disability
No, section 2 has its own qualifier based on risk of self-neglect
Yes, section 2 requires abnormally aggressive conduct linked to the learning disability
4.w: The s1(2A) qualifier does not apply to section 2 (assessment for up to 28 days). A person with a learning disability can be detained under section 2 if the usual criteria are met; here there are also signs of possible mental illness.

n.1: Section 2 can be used for people with a learning disability when the criteria are met.
n.2: There is no separate self-neglect qualifier for section 2.
n.3: The qualifier applies to section 3 and related powers, not section 2.

4.q: After Ivan Novak, 79, fell and fractured his hip on a medical ward, the trust begins a learning response under PSIRF. His wife asks whether she can contribute her account of the evening and ask questions. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Advise her to wait for the final report and then decide whether to make a complaint
Explain that incident reviews are internal and that she will receive a summary letter
Welcome her involvement and arrange for her account and questions to inform the review
Ask her to raise her concerns through the Patient Advice and Liaison Service instead
4.w: Compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected is one of PSIRF's four aims; families are invited to share their account and questions so the learning response reflects their perspective (NHS England PSIRF, Engaging and involving patients, families and staff). This applies P6.9, working with people and families on improvement.

n.0: Delaying her involvement until the report is final excludes her perspective from the learning.
n.1: PSIRF expects meaningful involvement of those affected, not a summary sent after the event.
n.3: PALS can support families, but it does not replace involving her directly in the learning response.

4.q: A learning disability nurse is teaching new support workers about Valuing People (2001), the White Paper that shaped modern learning disability services in England. Which four key principles did it set out?
o: Rights, independence, choice and inclusion
Prevention, protection, partnership and accountability
Presence, choice, respect and competence
Safety, care, protection and supervision
4.w: Valuing People (DH 2001) was built on four key principles: rights, independence, choice and inclusion.

n.1: These are among the Care Act safeguarding principles.
n.2: These overlap with O'Brien's five accomplishments, not the Valuing People principles.
n.3: These reflect an institutional care model that Valuing People moved away from.

4.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
4.q: Liam, 24, has a learning disability and epilepsy. He is having a convulsive seizure at home that has lasted 6 minutes. He has no emergency plan with him and his carer has buccal midazolam prescribed for him. What does NICE NG217 recommend as first-line treatment in the community?
o: Buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam immediately
Intravenous lorazepam once paramedics arrive
An extra dose of his usual anti-seizure tablets
Oral diazepam tablets crushed into water
4.w: NICE NG217 7.1.3: if no individualised plan is immediately available, give a benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam) immediately as first-line treatment in the community; IV lorazepam is used where IV access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available.

n.1: IV lorazepam is appropriate when IV access and resuscitation facilities are available, but buccal or rectal treatment should not be delayed waiting for it.
n.2: Usual oral tablets are not emergency treatment and cannot be swallowed safely during a seizure.
n.3: Nothing should be given by mouth during a convulsive seizure because of the choking risk.

4.q: Mr Grant, 72, has COPD and is admitted with breathlessness. His SpO2 is 89% on air. No target saturation range has been prescribed or documented. A colleague says to use NEWS2 SpO2 Scale 2 because he has COPD. What should the nurse do?
o: Use Scale 2, because a diagnosis of COPD is sufficient
Use Scale 1 and ask the medical team to prescribe a target range
Use Scale 2 and give oxygen to reach 94-98% saturations
Leave the SpO2 parameter unscored until a target range is prescribed
4.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): Scale 2 (target 88-92%) is for people with hypercapnic respiratory failure and is used when a clinician has prescribed that target. Until then Scale 1 applies (89% scores 3), and the team should be asked to set a target.

n.0: COPD alone does not authorise Scale 2; it must be prescribed by a clinician.
n.2: Scale 2 corresponds to a target of 88-92%, not 94-98%.
n.3: Leaving the parameter unscored gives a falsely low NEWS2 and delays escalation.

4.q: Lucy, 21, has Down syndrome. Her parents ask the nurse when they should start talking with her about the link between Down syndrome and dementia. Which advice reflects NICE NG96?
o: Wait until Lucy shows the first signs of memory loss
Leave the conversation to her GP when she reaches 40
Explain early and accessibly to Lucy and her family
Talk to her parents and avoid upsetting Lucy
4.w: NICE NG96 1.5.36 advises explaining early to people with learning disabilities, particularly Down syndrome, and their families about the link with dementia, using accessible information so they can plan.

n.0: Waiting until symptoms appear prevents planning while Lucy can take part fully.
n.1: NG96 advises early discussion; delaying to 40 is not supported.
n.3: Excluding Lucy denies her information about her own health.

4.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
4.q: Jasmine is 13 and in year 8. She has a severe learning disability and epilepsy and an education, health and care (EHC) plan. Her mother asks when planning for adult services should start. According to NICE NG43 and the Children and Families Act 2014, what is the answer?
o: From age 17, a year before she turns 18
From year 9, at age 13 or 14
From age 16, when the MCA applies
From age 18, when adult services take over
4.w: NICE NG43 1.2.1: start planning for adulthood from year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest, or immediately if the young person enters services close to transfer. For young people with EHC plans, the SEND Regulations 2014 (made under the Children and Families Act 2014) reg 20(6) require every review from year 9 to consider what provision is needed to prepare for adulthood and independent living.

n.0: Starting at 17 leaves too little time for a gradual, planned transition.
n.2: The MCA applying from 16 is relevant to decisions, but planning should start earlier, from year 9.
n.3: Starting at 18 means no planning before transfer, which NG43 aims to prevent.

4.q: A student nurse on placement asks which of the following conditions is a notifiable disease that a doctor in England must report to UKHSA. Which is correct?
o: MRSA colonisation found on an admission screen
Uncomplicated genital chlamydia infection
Clostridioides difficile infection in a hospital inpatient
Invasive group A streptococcal disease
4.w: The UKHSA list of notifiable diseases includes invasive group A streptococcal disease, classed as urgent. C. difficile and MRSA are monitored through separate healthcare-associated infection surveillance, and chlamydia is not on the notifiable disease list.

n.0: MRSA colonisation is managed through screening and HCAI surveillance, not notification.
n.1: Chlamydia is monitored through sexual health surveillance and is not on the notifiable disease list.
n.2: C. difficile is reported through mandatory HCAI surveillance by trusts, not as a notifiable disease by doctors.

4.q: Imogen, a staff nurse, sees a colleague starting to move Mr Price, 84, from bed to chair using an under-arm drag lift. His care plan states that he must be hoisted. What should Imogen do?
o: Ask her colleague to stop, help hoist Mr Price, then discuss it privately
Help her colleague complete the transfer and mention it to the ward manager later
Speak to her colleague about it privately at the end of the shift
Report the colleague on the incident system without speaking to her about it
4.w: Code 16 requires acting without delay if there is a risk to patient safety. Imogen should stop the unsafe practice first, ensure Mr Price is moved safely according to his care plan, and then challenge constructively in private, agreeing any learning needs (P5.9 challenge and give constructive feedback about care delivered by others). Two steps: make safe, then feedback.

n.1: Joining an unsafe technique exposes Mr Price and both staff to injury.
n.2: Waiting until later allows the unsafe transfer to continue now.
n.3: Reporting may be appropriate, but the immediate risk must be stopped first and a direct conversation supports learning.

4.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
4.q: Peter, 45, has a severe learning disability and is on a medical ward. His sister says, 'He's not himself, he's gone quiet and isn't humming like he usually does.' His NEWS2 score is 1. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck his observations at the next routine time
Reassure her that a NEWS2 of 1 is low risk
Act on her concern, reassess fully and escalate
Ask her to write her concerns down for the doctor
4.w: Family carers know the person's baseline and often notice 'soft signs' of deterioration before observations change. LeDeR and CIPOLD learning show that ignoring carer concern contributes to avoidable deaths; the nurse should reassess (full observations, ABCDE) and escalate, using Martha's Rule routes if needed.

n.0: Waiting for routine observations may miss early deterioration.
n.1: A low score does not override a credible concern from someone who knows his baseline.
n.3: Written concerns delay action; the nurse should act now.

4.q: Before her evening dose, Shirley, 74, says her blood pressure tablets look different from the ones she had last month and asks if they are the wrong tablets. The prescription is for amlodipine 5 mg once daily. What should the nurse do?
o: Give both the old and new tablets so she gets the full effect
Check the drug and strength match and explain generics can look different
Withhold the dose until the original brand can be supplied
Report the change as a dispensing error on the incident reporting system
4.w: Generic medicines contain the same active ingredient and strength as the branded product but may differ in appearance (P4.16). The nurse confirms the label, drug and strength match the prescription before giving it, and explains this to Shirley.

n.0: Giving both would double the dose of amlodipine.
n.2: Withholding an appropriate generic omits a prescribed dose without reason.
n.3: A generic supply matching the prescription is not an error.

4.q: Mrs Lewis, 84, is on day 2 after a hip replacement. Her daughter tells the nurse her mother 'is not making sense today' and keeps asking where she is, which is new. Her other observations are within normal ranges. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recheck her level of consciousness at the next routine set
Record new confusion as scoring 3 and inform the medical team
Record her as Alert, as she is awake and talking with her daughter
Reassure the daughter that this is normal after hip surgery
4.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): new confusion (C on ACVPU) scores 3. A single parameter scoring 3 requires at least hourly monitoring and the RN informing the medical team. NICE CG103 also asks that changes reported by relatives prompt delirium assessment.

n.0: New confusion scores 3 and needs action now, not at the next routine check.
n.2: Being awake and talking does not make a newly confused person 'Alert' on ACVPU.
n.3: New confusion is not an expected finding and may signal delirium, sepsis or other illness.

4.q: Mrs Nolan, 74, has cellulitis of the leg and is otherwise well. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97%, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 84, alert, temperature 39.3°C. Using NEWS2 Chart 1, what is her temperature score and her aggregate score?
o: Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 2
Temperature scores 3, giving a NEWS2 total of 3
Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 4
Temperature scores 1, giving a NEWS2 total of 1
4.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017) Chart 1: temperature 39.1°C or above scores 2; 38.1-39.0 scores 1. All other parameters score 0 (RR 12-20, SpO2 96% or above, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert, on air), so the aggregate is 2.

n.1: No temperature band scores 3 for fever; 3 is for 35.0°C or below.
n.2: The other parameters all score 0, so the total equals the temperature score of 2.
n.3: A score of 1 applies to 38.1-39.0°C; 39.3°C is in the 39.1 or above band.

5.q: Ted, 67, has a PCA pump after bowel surgery. He is very drowsy, difficult to rouse, with RR 8 per minute and pinpoint pupils. His wife says he has been pressing the button for him while he slept. What is the priority?
o: Stop the PCA, support his breathing and call for urgent help
Explain to his wife that Ted must press the PCA button himself
Encourage him to take deep breaths and press the button less
Reduce the PCA bolus dose and recheck his observations in 1 hour
5.w: RR 8 scores 3 on NEWS2 and drowsiness scores 3: this is opioid toxicity. Stop the infusion, open and support the airway, give oxygen and get urgent help so that naloxone can be given as prescribed (P4.15). The PCA safety principle is that the person alone presses the button; this is addressed after the emergency.

n.1: Education is needed, but only after treating life-threatening respiratory depression.
n.2: He cannot respond reliably and needs emergency treatment, not encouragement.
n.3: Altering the dose and waiting an hour leaves respiratory depression untreated.

5.q: Ruth, 63, has cellulitis and suspected sepsis. Her NEWS2 is 6, made up of RR 3 and three single points, and her worsening is thought to be due to the infection. Under NICE NG253 (2025), how should she be managed?
o: As high risk, with IV antibiotics within 1 hour
As very low risk, with standard observation frequency
As medium risk, with antibiotics deferred up to 3 hours
As low risk, with review by a registered practitioner in 1 hour
5.w: NG253: for a NEWS2 of 5-6 that includes a single parameter scoring 3, if this is likely to be due to the infection, manage as high risk. High risk means IV antibiotics within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score.

n.1: Very low risk applies to a NEWS2 of 0.
n.2: Medium-risk deferral does not apply where a single 3 is likely caused by the infection.
n.3: Low-risk management applies to NEWS2 1-4, not 6.

5.q: Alfred, 86, has delirium and MRSA and is nursed in a single room. With the door closed he becomes distressed and has twice tried to climb out of bed. The healthcare support worker suggests propping the door open. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep the door closed and increase checks on Alfred to hourly
Move Alfred back to the open bay where staff can see him
Prop the door open and mention the change at the next handover
Document a risk assessment and agree the door plan with the IPC team
5.w: NIPCM ch 2.1: isolation room doors should remain closed, and if this is not possible a documented risk assessment is needed, with IPC team advice on precautions. Alfred's falls risk and distress must be balanced against transmission risk.

n.0: Hourly checks do not address the falls risk and distress that the closed door is causing.
n.1: Moving him to a bay exposes other patients to MRSA without IPC team assessment.
n.2: Changing isolation conditions needs a documented risk assessment, not an informal handover note.

5.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
5.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

5.q: Lucy brings her 1-year-old son for his MMRV vaccine. Her neighbour's baby is too young to be vaccinated, and Lucy asks how vaccinating her son could help that baby. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Vaccinating children means adults in the area no longer need vaccines
Her son will pass vaccine antibodies to other children he plays with
Vaccinated people are less likely to pass the infection on to others
The vaccine gives lifelong protection, so the disease disappears locally
5.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): vaccinated individuals are less likely to be a source of infection to others, reducing the risk of exposure for unvaccinated individuals, so people who cannot be vaccinated still benefit. This is population (or 'herd') immunity.

n.0: Population immunity does not replace the adult programme; adults are still offered vaccines.
n.1: Antibodies are not passed between children; protection of others comes from reduced transmission.
n.3: No vaccine offers 100% protection, and disease can return if coverage falls.

5.q: Mrs Lowe, 90, lives in a care home in England and lacks capacity to decide where to live. The manager has concluded that her care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. What is needed to make these arrangements lawful?
o: A best interests note in her care plan by the manager
An authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
Her daughter's signed consent to the locked doors
An authorisation under the Liberty Protection Safeguards
5.w: Where a person who lacks capacity is deprived of liberty in a care home or hospital, the arrangements need authorisation under DoLS (MCA 2005 Sch A1). Article 5 of the Human Rights Act 1998 protects liberty, and DoLS supply the required safeguards.

n.0: Recording that the arrangements are in her best interests does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
n.3: The LPS are not in force, so no LPS authorisation can be given.

5.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. Which is the most appropriate way to interpret this information?
o: As a possible sign of acute illness that needs assessment
As part of his learning disability needing no action
As evidence that he lacks capacity for all decisions
As a behavioural issue for the support team to manage
5.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability or dementia; rec 1.4.7 says assessment should include history from family or carers. A change from his baseline is significant.

n.1: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability (diagnostic overshadowing) risks missing illness.
n.2: Behaviour change does not establish incapacity; capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2-3).
n.3: Treating it as behaviour to manage ignores a possible physical cause.

5.q: A caller to a surgical ward says she is the daughter of Mrs Green, 70, who had surgery today, and asks how the operation went. The nurse cannot confirm who the caller is. What should the nurse do?
o: Check Mrs Green's wishes and agreed contacts before sharing anything
Give a brief update, as the caller knows the patient's name
Ask the caller to confirm Mrs Green's date of birth, then answer
Confirm the operation went well but give no further details
5.w: Code 5.1 requires respect for a person's right to privacy, and 5.2 that people know how and why their information is shared. The nurse should establish whether Mrs Green consents to information being given to this caller (for example agreed contacts or a password).

n.1: Knowing a patient's name does not show the caller has a right to her information.
n.2: A date of birth is easily known by others and does not establish Mrs Green's consent.
n.3: Confirming the outcome is still disclosure of confidential information without consent.

5.q: Dorothy, 86, has advanced dementia. For three days she has spat out her anticonvulsant and pushed staff away at medicine rounds. Her son suggests hiding it in her tea. What is the nurse's most appropriate first step?
o: Assess her capacity to make this specific decision about the medicine
Arrange for the medicine to be given by injection instead
Hide the medicine in her tea, as she has a diagnosis of dementia
Stop the anticonvulsant, as she is repeatedly refusing it
5.w: The MCA 2005 (ss1-3) requires a capacity assessment that is decision-specific and time-specific; a diagnosis of dementia alone does not establish incapacity. Only if she lacks capacity can a best interests decision about covert administration follow (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21).

n.1: Changing the route needs a prescriber and does not address capacity or consent.
n.2: A diagnosis does not prove lack of capacity (MCA s2(3)); covert use also needs a best interests process.
n.3: Stopping an anticonvulsant risks seizures; the refusal needs assessment, not unilateral cessation.

5.q: Isla's parents are told that she has Rett syndrome caused by a MECP2 variant. Neither parent has symptoms. They ask about the chance of a future child being affected. What is the most accurate response?
o: Each future daughter has a 50% risk because the condition is X-linked dominant
Future sons have a higher risk than future daughters of being affected
The risk is 25%, as both parents must carry the variant
Most cases are new variants, so the risk is low; genetic counselling is advised
5.w: More than 99% of Rett syndrome cases arise from a new (de novo) MECP2 variant not present in either parent (MedlinePlus Genetics), so recurrence risk is low, but families should be offered genetic counselling to discuss their individual situation.

n.0: A 50% risk would apply if a parent carried the variant; in nearly all families the variant is new.
n.1: Rett syndrome affects almost exclusively girls.
n.2: Rett is not autosomal recessive, so the 25% figure does not apply.

5.q: Jasmine, 34, has a profound learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to dental treatment. She needs a tooth extraction under general anaesthetic. Her blood tests and ear examination are also overdue because she cannot tolerate them while awake. What is the best adjustment to propose?
o: Plan, in her best interests, to do the other checks under the same anaesthetic
Ask her GP to try the blood tests again with extra staff support
Book separate appointments for the blood tests and ear examination later
Carry out the extraction and delay the other checks to her annual check
5.w: Coordinating procedures under one general anaesthetic is a recognised reasonable adjustment that avoids repeated distress and anaesthetic risk. Because Jasmine lacks capacity, the plan must be agreed as being in her best interests with those close to her (MCA 2005 s4; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.1: Repeating the tests while she is awake, with more staff to support or hold her, is more restrictive and she has not tolerated them awake.
n.2: Separate appointments she cannot tolerate while awake are likely to fail again.
n.3: Delaying the checks misses a safe opportunity and leaves health needs unmet.

5.q: For three weeks the call bells in one bay on Kemi's ward have failed intermittently. Each failure has been reported as an incident, but estates staff say a full replacement needs trust funding. What is the most appropriate next step for Kemi as the nurse in charge?
o: Move patients who cannot use a call bell to beds nearer the nurses' station each shift
Keep reporting each failure as an incident until the estates team replaces the system
Write to the local newspaper about the delay to replacing the call bell system
Escalate to the ward manager so the risk can be assessed and added to the risk register
5.w: A persistent risk that cannot be fixed at ward level should be escalated so it is formally assessed, recorded on the organisation's risk register with an owner and controls, and reviewed (P6.3 local and national frameworks for managing and reporting risk; Code 16.1 and 25.1). Interim measures continue alongside escalation.

n.0: Moving patients is a sensible interim control but does not get the underlying risk managed or funded.
n.1: Incident reports record events; they do not on their own place a known, ongoing risk under managed review with an owner.
n.2: Going to the media before using internal escalation routes is not consistent with NMC raising concerns guidance.

5.q: Amira, 46, has Down syndrome. Her support staff report she has lost interest in activities, is tearful and sleeps poorly. She can still dress and cook with her usual prompts. Which possibility should be assessed alongside dementia?
o: Lack of motivation
Normal ageing
Learned helplessness
Depression
5.w: Depression can mimic early dementia (withdrawal, poor sleep, apparent decline) and is treatable. NICE NG54 asks for full assessment of mental and physical health; her preserved skills make depression a strong alternative to exclude.

n.0: Labelling the change as lack of motivation is diagnostic overshadowing.
n.1: Tearfulness and loss of interest are not part of normal ageing.
n.2: This is a behavioural concept, not a diagnosis to exclude; it would not explain tearfulness and poor sleep.

5.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
5.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

5.q: Joan, 56, has a moderate learning disability and lives in supported living. At her annual review the community nurse plans her health monitoring. Which approach is in line with NICE NG96 on growing older with learning disabilities?
o: Focus reviews on behaviour change, because physical decline is an expected part of ageing
Start age-related health checks at 65, the same age as for the general population
Monitor for age-related changes such as hearing and sight loss, dysphagia and osteoporosis
Transfer her care from learning disability services to older people's services at 55
5.w: NICE NG96 (1.5.14) recommends monitoring people with learning disabilities for age-related conditions including hearing loss, sight problems, dysphagia, epilepsy, thyroid problems, osteoporosis, menopausal symptoms and dementia; these can occur earlier than in the general population.

n.0: Assuming decline is expected is diagnostic overshadowing; changes should be assessed.
n.1: Age-related changes may start earlier, so waiting until 65 risks late detection.
n.3: NG96 does not set an age for transfer; it focuses on a single lead practitioner and coordinated support.

5.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
5.q: Lionel, 66, has a profound learning disability and is in the last days of life. He is grimacing and moaning, which his DisDAT shows are his distress cues. He has a syringe pump. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess the cause and seek a review of his symptom control
Increase the pump rate to give more medicine
Record the cues and review at the next drug round
Ask his family to sit with him and offer him comfort for now
5.w: Two-step reasoning: his known distress cues suggest uncontrolled symptoms. The nurse should assess possible causes (pain, position, full bladder, constipation, breathlessness) and seek prompt review of anticipatory or as-needed medicines; pump rates should not be changed without a prescription.

n.1: Changing a pump rate without a prescription is unsafe and outside the nurse's authority.
n.2: Waiting until the next round leaves him in distress.
n.3: Comfort helps, but it does not address possible uncontrolled pain.

5.q: At 21:00 Yusuf arrives to take charge of a 24-bed ward for the night. One registered nurse has phoned in sick and no replacement has been found, leaving Yusuf as the only registered nurse with three healthcare assistants. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the shift and complete an incident report at the end of the night describing it
Start the shift and allocate the medicines round to the most senior healthcare assistant
Escalate immediately to the site manager, as fewer than two registered nurses is a red flag
Ask the day staff to stay until midnight and then manage the remainder of the shift himself
5.w: NICE SG1 Box 2 lists fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift as a nursing red flag, which requires an immediate escalation response. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt action on risks to safety and effective management of staff and resources.

n.0: Reporting after the shift leaves the risk unmanaged throughout the night.
n.1: Healthcare assistants cannot be delegated tasks outside their competence, such as a full registered nurse medicines round (Code 11.1).
n.3: A short extension by tired day staff does not solve the shortfall for most of the night and bypasses escalation.

5.q: Kezia, a second-year adult nursing student, is ending her placement on a surgical ward. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment (SSSA), who conducts the assessment that confirms her achievement of proficiencies for this placement?
o: Her practice assessor, informed by feedback from her supervisors
Her practice supervisor, who has worked most shifts with her
Her academic assessor, who visits the ward at the end of placement
The ward manager, who signs off all students on the ward
5.w: Under the SSSA (NMC 2018), practice supervisors support and supervise and contribute feedback; the practice assessor conducts the assessment and confirms achievement of practice proficiencies, drawing on that feedback; the academic assessor works with the practice assessor on progression decisions (P5.8).

n.1: Practice supervisors contribute to assessment through feedback but do not confirm achievement of proficiencies.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement for progression with the practice assessor, but does not assess practice on the ward.
n.3: SSSA roles are defined by function, not by management position; the ward manager has no automatic assessment role.

5.q: On an acute ward, Mr Stone, 40, is pacing and shouting that he wants to leave. He has not harmed anyone. What is the nurse's most appropriate first approach?
o: Tell him firmly to sit down and stop shouting
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and listen to him
Call security to restrain him before he leaves
Stand in the doorway to block his exit from the ward
5.w: Annexe A 3.5: de-escalation strategies and techniques. Code 13.4 personal safety; calm voice, open posture and listening come before restrictive interventions.

n.0: Commands can escalate agitation; de-escalation uses calm listening.
n.2: Restraint is a last resort; de-escalation should be tried first.
n.3: Blocking his exit increases risk and may escalate the situation.

5.q: Nadia, a ward manager, learns that a staff nurse who raised a concern about a doctor's practice is now being left out of break rotas and ignored by some colleagues. What does the Code require Nadia to do?
o: Act to protect the nurse from detriment or victimisation
Wait for the concern to be investigated before taking any action
Advise the nurse to request a transfer to another ward
Report the nurse's colleagues to the NMC straight away
5.w: Code 16.5-16.6: do not obstruct, intimidate or victimise anyone raising a concern, and protect anyone you have management responsibility for from harm, detriment, victimisation or unwarranted treatment after a concern is raised.

n.1: The victimisation is happening now; Code 16.6 requires her to act to protect the nurse.
n.2: Moving the nurse penalises the person who raised the concern; Code 16.6 requires protection from detriment.
n.3: Local management action comes first; referral may follow if misconduct is serious, but protection is the duty now.

5.q: Mrs Ahmed, 66, has capacity and care needs after a stroke. She discloses that her husband sometimes slaps her but says she does not want any action taken. Nobody else lives in the home. Following the statutory guidance, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a safeguarding referral but do not let her know it has been made
Share her disclosure with relevant professionals via the safeguarding lead
Report her husband directly to the police against her wishes
Respect her wishes, taking no further action and making no record
5.w: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.92: if an adult with capacity does not want action taken, this does not preclude sharing information with relevant professional colleagues to assess risk and check she is not being coerced. It is good practice to tell her this is being done unless that would increase the risk.

n.0: Para 14.92 says she should normally be told, unless telling her would increase the risk; nothing suggests that here.
n.2: Police involvement against her wishes is not the first step without a wider risk or public interest; colleagues should first assess the risk.
n.3: Her wishes carry great weight, but para 14.92 allows information to be shared with professional colleagues, and the disclosure must be recorded.

5.q: A public health team plans to reduce average salt intake across a region by working with manufacturers to lower the salt content of bread and processed foods. Which statement best describes this strategy?
o: Secondary prevention that detects raised blood pressure at an early stage
A high-risk approach targeting people already diagnosed with hypertension
A population approach: a small benefit to each person but a large total benefit
Tertiary prevention to reduce disability in people who have had strokes
5.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the population approach recognises that society influences individual behaviour and reduces risk at population level. The prevention paradox (Rose): most people who lower their risk will not benefit directly, although the total benefit across the population is large.

n.0: No one is being tested or detected; this lowers exposure to a risk factor across the population.
n.1: The change affects everyone who buys the foods, not a selected high-risk group.
n.3: This is aimed at the whole population before disease develops, not at people with established disease.

5.q: Lucy, 33, has a mild learning disability and lives alone with a few hours of support. She has never been invited for a learning disability annual health check, and the community nurse finds she is not on her GP practice's learning disability register. What should the nurse do first?
o: Arrange for the community team to carry out the annual check at home
With Lucy's agreement, ask the practice to add her to the register
Advise Lucy to request a health check at the local walk-in centre
Ask the GP to book her an NHS Health Check, which covers the same review
5.w: Being on the GP learning disability register is the gateway to annual health checks, health action plans and many reasonable adjustments; only about a quarter of people with a learning disability are on registers (NHS.uk; Mencap).

n.0: Annual health checks are provided by GP practices; the gap here is the missing register entry.
n.2: Walk-in centres do not provide learning disability annual health checks or hold the register.
n.3: The NHS Health Check is a different programme for adults aged 40 to 74 and does not replace the learning disability annual check.

5.q: Bea, 29, is autistic and has a learning disability. She attends the emergency department with a wrist injury and is rocking and covering her ears in the busy waiting area. The triage nurse estimates a three-hour wait. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Move her ahead of other patients so she is seen straight away
Give her ear defenders and ask her to stay in the waiting area
Ask her carer to take her home and return when the department is quieter
Move her to a quieter area while she keeps her place in the queue
5.w: A quiet space is a reasonable adjustment that removes the sensory disadvantage while clinical priority is still decided by triage (Equality Act 2010 s20; NICE CG142 1.1.8 on adjusting noise and the environment for autistic adults).

n.0: Priority should follow clinical need; the adjustment is to the environment, not to the triage order.
n.1: Ear defenders may help a little, but keeping her in the busy area leaves the main barrier in place.
n.2: Sending her home delays treatment of an injury.

5.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
5.q: Sean, 34, has a severe learning disability and epilepsy. Over a month his seizures have increased. Staff find tablets in his bedding and he spits out his evening dose. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to increase his anti-seizure medicine dose
Give his tablets covertly in his food from tonight
Find out why he refuses and review the formulation with the prescriber
Record each refusal and keep offering the tablets at the usual times
5.w: Two-step reasoning: the seizure increase is likely due to missed doses, so the cause of refusal must be found (taste, tablet size, swallowing difficulty, side effects, timing) and a solution such as a liquid formulation agreed with the prescriber and pharmacist. Non-adherence is a modifiable SUDEP risk factor (NG217 10.1.2).

n.0: A higher dose will not help if he is not taking the tablets and may cause toxicity when he does.
n.1: Covert administration needs a capacity assessment, best interests decision and pharmacist advice first.
n.3: Simply recording leaves seizures and SUDEP risk unaddressed.

5.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
5.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

5.q: Over 24 hours, Mr Ito, 74, receives 1,000 mL IV fluid and drinks 650 mL. His output is 1,500 mL urine and 600 mL vomit. He is drowsy with a dry mouth. What is the fluid balance and the best action?
o: Minus 450 mL; continue current fluids and recheck tomorrow
Minus 1,100 mL; restrict oral fluids as he is vomiting
Minus 450 mL; report the deficit and signs of dehydration
Plus 450 mL; continue current fluids and recheck tomorrow
5.w: Input 1,000 + 650 = 1,650 mL; output 1,500 + 600 = 2,100 mL; balance = 1,650 - 2,100 = -450 mL. P1.15 numeracy for safe practice; Code 13.1 recognise deterioration and 13.2 refer in a timely way.

n.0: The figure is right, but drowsiness and a dry mouth with a negative balance need prompt escalation.
n.1: 1,650 - 2,100 = -450 mL; restricting fluids would worsen dehydration.
n.3: Input 1,650 mL minus output 2,100 mL gives minus 450 mL, not plus.

5.q: Mrs Nolan, 74, has cellulitis of the leg and is otherwise well. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97%, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 84, alert, temperature 39.3°C. Using NEWS2 Chart 1, what is her temperature score and her aggregate score?
o: Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 2
Temperature scores 3, giving a NEWS2 total of 3
Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 4
Temperature scores 1, giving a NEWS2 total of 1
5.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017) Chart 1: temperature 39.1°C or above scores 2; 38.1-39.0 scores 1. All other parameters score 0 (RR 12-20, SpO2 96% or above, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert, on air), so the aggregate is 2.

n.1: No temperature band scores 3 for fever; 3 is for 35.0°C or below.
n.2: The other parameters all score 0, so the total equals the temperature score of 2.
n.3: A score of 1 applies to 38.1-39.0°C; 39.3°C is in the 39.1 or above band.

5.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
5.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

5.q: Mrs Leila Hassan, 71, is recovering from a hip fracture. She lives in a first-floor flat and is worried about managing her bath and kitchen safely at home. Which professional is best placed to assess her for equipment and adaptations?
o: A district nursing sister
An occupational therapist
A hospital social worker
A community physiotherapist
5.w: Occupational therapists assess a person's ability to carry out activities of daily living and recommend equipment and home adaptations, often through a home visit (P5.4; NICE NG249 recommends home hazard assessment ideally by an occupational therapist).

n.0: District nurses provide nursing care at home but are not the lead for daily living equipment assessment.
n.2: Social workers coordinate care and support arrangements but do not assess for equipment.
n.3: Physiotherapists focus on mobility, strength and exercise rather than assessing the home environment for equipment.

5.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
5.q: Phil, 66, has a learning disability and developed delirium from a urinary tract infection. On day 3 of treatment he cannot discuss whether to move into a care home after discharge, which is planned in about ten days. What should the nurse advise first?
o: Consider whether he will regain capacity and, if so, delay the decision
Instruct an IMCA straight away to make the care home placement decision
Ask his brother to decide, as he is the closest relative
Make the best interests decision now, as he lacks capacity today
5.w: Two steps: recognise that delirium is often temporary; then apply MCA s4(3): the decision-maker must consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. If the decision can wait, it should, so Phil can decide himself.

n.1: An IMCA does not make decisions, and the first step is to consider whether he will regain capacity.
n.2: Relatives are consulted but do not make the decision without legal authority.
n.3: Deciding now ignores the likelihood that he will regain capacity soon.

5.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
5.q: Lee, 34, has a learning disability and cannot read. A hospital clinic's policy is to discharge anyone who misses two appointments. Lee has missed two because he could not read the letters. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discharge him, as the policy applies to all patients equally
Adjust the policy for Lee and use phone or text reminders
Refer him to social services for help with reading his post at home
Ask Lee to bring someone who can read his letters to him in future
5.w: A policy applied to everyone (a provision, criterion or practice) puts Lee at a substantial disadvantage. Equality Act s20(3) requires reasonable steps to avoid it, such as not discharging him and using accessible reminders; his needs should also be flagged under the Accessible Information Standard.

n.0: Applying the same rule to everyone is the provision that causes the disadvantage.
n.2: This does not remove the disadvantage created by the clinic's process.
n.3: This shifts responsibility to Lee rather than changing the practice.

5.q: The father of Chloe, 22, who is being assessed for autism, asks the nurse to arrange a brain scan and blood tests 'to prove it one way or the other'. Which response follows NICE CG142?
o: Arrange an MRI scan if the clinical assessment is inconclusive
Arrange an EEG, because it is the investigation that confirms autism
Arrange blood tests, as a genetic marker confirms most cases of autism
Explain that scans and blood tests are not routine for diagnosing autism
5.w: NICE CG142 1.2.11: do not routinely use biological tests, genetic tests or neuroimaging for the purposes of diagnosing autism in adults. Diagnosis is made by comprehensive clinical assessment.

n.0: An inconclusive assessment is resolved by further clinical assessment, not routine neuroimaging.
n.1: There is no EEG test that confirms autism; EEG is used if seizures are suspected.
n.2: No single genetic marker confirms autism in most people.

5.q: Amira, 29, is admitted to a gynaecology ward. Her notes record a history of sexual assault. When the nurse reaches to hold her hand during an examination, Amira flinches. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop, ask whether touch is acceptable and explain each step first
Ask a colleague to hold her hand in place of the nurse
Continue gently, as touch is a recognised comforting technique
Stop all communication until the examination is finished
5.w: Annexe A 1.3: use appropriate non-verbal communication, including touch, eye contact and personal space. Code 1.1 and 4.2: treat with respect and gain consent before any action.

n.1: Changing who touches her does not address whether she wants touch at all.
n.2: Comforting touch is only therapeutic when welcome; her reaction shows it is not.
n.3: Withdrawing communication leaves her anxious and unsupported.

5.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
5.q: Claire, 39, has a mild learning disability and a progressive illness. She has capacity and wants to plan her future care. Which approach to advance care planning is best?
o: Ask her parents to write the plan for her
Complete the whole plan quickly in a single meeting
Delay planning until she lacks capacity
Record her wishes accessibly over several conversations
5.w: Advance care planning is a voluntary process of discussion over time. For people with a learning disability it should use accessible information (easy read, pictures), take time and involve those Claire chooses, recording her wishes, values and preferences.

n.0: Claire has capacity; the plan should reflect her wishes, not her parents'.
n.1: A single rushed meeting may not give her time to understand and decide.
n.2: Planning while she has capacity lets her own wishes guide future decisions.

5.q: Frank, 63, is prescribed oral morphine solution 2.5-5 mg as required every 2 hours for pain. He had 2.5 mg 4 hours ago with little effect and now rates his pain 8/10. He is alert with a respiratory rate of 16. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 2.5 mg now and repeat it in 30 minutes if needed
Give 7.5 mg, as the previous 2.5 mg dose was ineffective
Withhold the dose until the doctor increases the prescription
Give 5 mg, the top of the prescribed range, and reassess
5.w: Titration within a prescribed range is a nurse's decision based on assessment (AnnexB.11.5). The previous dose was ineffective, he is not sedated and 2 hours have passed, so the higher dose within the range is appropriate, with reassessment of pain, sedation and respiratory rate.

n.0: Repeating at 30 minutes breaches the 2-hourly minimum interval.
n.1: 7.5 mg exceeds the prescribed range, which the nurse cannot change.
n.2: A suitable dose is available within the range; withholding leaves him in pain.

5.q: Bridget, 58, is due to have her first red cell transfusion before surgery. She asks the nurse what she should know about it. According to NICE NG24, which information should the nurse include?
o: That she will be able to give blood herself once she has recovered
That she will no longer be eligible to donate blood after a transfusion
That she cannot refuse once the transfusion has been prescribed
That a transfusion has no risks if the bedside checks are completed
5.w: NICE NG24 rec 1.14.2: give verbal and written information on the reason for transfusion, risks and benefits, the process, alternatives, that the person is no longer eligible to donate blood, and encourage questions; document the discussion (1.14.3).

n.0: NG24 states people who have had a transfusion are no longer eligible to donate blood.
n.2: A person with capacity may refuse a transfusion; consent remains her decision.
n.3: Transfusion carries risks that must be explained even with correct checks.

5.q: Dolores, 88, is frail and drowsy after a stroke. She has a dry, coated tongue and cracked lips, takes nothing by mouth and has an unsafe swallow. Which oral care plan is most appropriate?
o: Daily chlorhexidine mouthwash rinses by mouth
Lemon and glycerine swabs every two hours
Gentle mouth care with a soft brush and lip balm
Mouth care whenever her relatives request it
5.w: People who are nil by mouth and drowsy need frequent oral assessment and gentle care with a soft toothbrush, moistening and lip care. Lemon and glycerine dry the mouth further and mouthwashes risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow (Annexe B 4.5; NICE NG31 advises frequent mouth and lip care).

n.0: Rinses she cannot spit out risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow.
n.1: Lemon and glycerine swabs dry the mucosa further and can damage teeth.
n.3: Oral care is a planned nursing intervention based on assessment, not on request.

5.q: A nurse researcher wants to understand what living with a new stoma is like for young adults, in their own words. Which research approach is most suitable?
o: A qualitative design using in-depth interviews
A randomised controlled trial of stoma care products
A retrospective audit of stoma complication rates
A cross-sectional survey using closed questions
5.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022) recognises qualitative research approaches; interviews explore meaning and experience. Proficiency P1.7: understand research methods to critically analyse findings.

n.1: An RCT compares interventions; it does not explore lived experience.
n.2: An audit measures practice against a standard, not personal experience.
n.3: Closed questions limit responses and do not capture experience in people's own words.

5.q: Ellen, 29, had wheeze, hypotension and urticaria after eating a prawn curry on the ward. She improved after one dose of IM adrenaline and is now stable. The doctor plans her period of observation and later allergy referral. Which blood test should be taken to support the diagnosis?
o: Two sets of blood cultures
Mast cell tryptase level
Serum troponin level
Full blood count and film
5.w: RCUK guidance: take mast cell tryptase samples to help confirm anaphylaxis and support specialist allergy follow-up. Observation is risk-stratified, with a minimum of 6 hours in most people and 12 hours in higher-risk groups, or fast-track after 2 hours in selected cases.

n.0: Blood cultures are taken for suspected infection, not allergy.
n.2: Troponin assesses myocardial injury and does not confirm anaphylaxis.
n.3: FBC does not confirm anaphylaxis.

5.q: Hugh, 70, has had a stroke and cannot bear weight. He needs to be moved from bed to chair. Which approach is safest?
