o: Lift him under the arms with two staff members
Use a drag lift with one person on each side
Use a hoist with an assessed sling
Ask him to stand and pivot using a frame
5.w: Annexe B 7.2-7.3: use moving and handling equipment for people with impaired mobility. A person who cannot bear weight needs a hoist with a correctly sized and assessed sling, operated by trained staff per the handling plan. Underarm drag lifts injure patients and staff.

n.0: Lifting under the arms is a drag lift, which risks shoulder injury to him and back injury to staff.
n.1: A drag lift is an unsafe technique and not part of contemporary practice.
n.3: He cannot bear weight, so a standing pivot transfer is unsafe.

5.q: Mrs Price, 88, has advanced dementia and has been assessed as lacking capacity to decide about a feeding tube. The team is making a best interests decision. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4 checklist, which should the decision maker take into account?
o: Her past wishes, beliefs and values, as reported by those close to her
Her son's own preference, because he is recorded as next of kin
The option that places the least demand on the ward's nursing time
Her age and diagnosis, as the main guide to her likely outcome
5.w: MCA 2005 s4(6) requires consideration of the person's past and present wishes and feelings, beliefs and values; s4(7) requires consulting carers and others interested in her welfare about what she would want. s4(1) prohibits basing the decision on age or condition alone.

n.1: Relatives are consulted about what the person would want; their own preference does not decide the matter.
n.2: Staff convenience is not part of the s4 checklist; the focus is the person's best interests.
n.3: s4(1) states a best interests determination must not be made merely on the basis of age or condition.

5.q: Deborah, 46, received IM adrenaline 500 micrograms for anaphylaxis 5 minutes ago. She remains wheezy with BP 84/52 mmHg. What should happen next?
o: Wait a further 15 minutes before repeating adrenaline
Give chlorphenamine IV and wait for it to take effect
Sit her upright with her legs lowered to ease breathing
Give a second IM adrenaline dose and an IV crystalloid bolus
5.w: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and give an IV crystalloid bolus (adults 500-1,000 mL) for circulatory problems, with high-flow oxygen and monitoring.

n.0: RCUK advises a repeat dose after 5 minutes, not 15.
n.1: Antihistamines are not used to treat ABC problems in anaphylaxis.
n.2: With hypotension she should lie flat with or without legs raised; sitting with legs down worsens circulation.

5.q: Frank Ellis, 74, uses a walking frame and fell once at home last month. He has capacity and wants to walk to the day room for lunch. His daughter asks the nurse to keep him in his chair so he cannot fall again. Which response best reflects positive risk management?
o: Let Mr Ellis walk to the day room after he signs a disclaimer accepting the risk of falling
Arrange for him to use a wheelchair to reach the day room until physiotherapy can review him
Agree with the daughter and keep him seated at lunchtimes until he is discharged home
Agree a plan with Mr Ellis for supervised walking with his frame and record the discussion
5.w: Positive risk management weighs benefits and harms with the person and puts proportionate controls in place so they can do what matters to them, rather than removing all activity (P6.10 risk management versus risk aversion). Mr Ellis has capacity, so his decision is respected (MCA 2005 s1), and the plan and discussion are documented (Code 10).

n.0: A disclaimer does not manage the risk or remove the nurse's duty of care; it replaces planning with paperwork.
n.1: Using a wheelchair when he can walk with his frame reduces independence and mobility without a clinical reason.
n.2: Keeping him seated is risk aversion: it removes activity he values, causes deconditioning and overrides the choice of a person with capacity.

5.q: Mr Gordon Bailey, 79, is recovering from a hip fracture repair. He is not yet safe at home but the team expects he will be able to return home after a few weeks of rehabilitation in a community hospital bed. Which discharge pathway is this?
o: Pathway 3
Pathway 2
Pathway 1
Pathway 0
5.w: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based setting with dedicated recovery support, where short-term care helps the person recover before living independently or receiving longer-term care (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.2: Pathway 1 is discharge home with new support; Mr Bailey is not yet ready to go home.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new needs.

5.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
5.q: Ben, 45, has a learning disability and diabetes treated with insulin. He has a prolonged seizure, which stops after buccal midazolam. He is drowsy and breathing normally. What should the nurse check promptly as a possible cause?
o: Capillary blood glucose
Urinalysis for protein
Peak expiratory flow
Serum cholesterol
5.w: Two-step reasoning: once the seizure has stopped and airway and breathing are secure, consider underlying causes. NICE NG217 7.1.4 lists hypoglycaemia among possible causes of status epilepticus; Ben uses insulin, so a capillary glucose check is a priority.

n.1: Proteinuria is not an acute cause of seizure in this context.
n.2: Peak flow assesses asthma and is not useful in a drowsy post-ictal person.
n.3: Cholesterol does not cause an acute seizure.

5.q: A practice nurse invites people with a BMI over 40 to an intensive weight-management programme rather than offering it to the whole practice population. Which advantage is associated with this high-risk approach?
o: It tackles the social influences on behaviour in the wider community
Those invited are often more motivated, as their personal risk is high
It removes the need to assess each person's individual risk factors
It brings the largest fall in disease across the whole population
5.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the high-risk approach may be more cost-effective than population-wide approaches and targets people who are more motivated to change their behaviour; the population approach achieves risk reduction at population level. NICE PH49 (2014) rec 9: high-intensity interventions for people at high risk, for example a BMI over 40.

n.0: Addressing social influences on the whole community is a feature of the population approach.
n.2: A high-risk approach depends on identifying individuals by assessing their risk.
n.3: A large fall in total disease is the strength of the population approach, not a high-risk approach.

5.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
5.q: George, 55, has a learning disability, lacks capacity for the decision and needs chemotherapy for bowel cancer. He has no family or friends; only paid support staff are involved. What must happen?
o: Treatment is delayed until a deputy is appointed
The oncologist decides without consulting anyone
His support manager can consent on his behalf
An IMCA must be instructed before the decision
5.w: Under MCA 2005 ss37-38, an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate must be instructed for serious medical treatment by the NHS when the person lacks capacity and there is no one, other than paid carers, appropriate to consult. Chemotherapy is serious medical treatment.

n.0: Deputyship is not needed; the IMCA route allows a timely best interests decision.
n.1: Best interests decisions require consultation; with no family an IMCA is required.
n.2: Paid staff cannot consent for an adult and do not count as 'appropriate to consult' for IMCA purposes.

5.q: A nurse hears that the Mental Health Act 2025 changes how people with a learning disability can be detained. A colleague says that from now on a person cannot be detained under section 3 because of a learning disability. What is the correct position in October 2026?
o: Correct, the change came into force with the new Code of Practice in 2026
Incorrect, the change has been enacted but is not yet in force
Incorrect, the 2025 Act did not change the rules for learning disability
Correct, the 2025 Act removed learning disability from section 3 on Royal Assent
5.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 (Royal Assent 18 Dec 2025) will stop learning disability or autism alone justifying s3 detention, but ss3-4 and Sch 1 are prospective and not in force; the 1983 Act as amended applies, including the 'abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct' qualifier for s3 (MHA83 s1(2A)-(2B)).

n.0: No commencement has brought the s3 change into force, and a code of practice cannot do so.
n.2: The 2025 Act does contain this change; it is simply not yet in force.
n.3: Royal Assent did not bring this change into force; legislation.gov.uk shows the provisions as prospective.

5.q: Phyllis, 85, on a medical ward, has had three episodes of loose, watery stool (Bristol type 7) since this morning with no obvious cause. She started antibiotics 5 days ago. What is the priority action?
o: Wait for two more episodes before sending a sample
Give her prescribed loperamide and continue to monitor her
Move her nearer the toilet in the shared bay
Isolate her in a single room and send a stool sample
5.w: Unexplained diarrhoea, especially after antibiotics, may be infective (for example C. difficile). Isolate promptly in a single room with contact precautions, send a stool sample, and use soap and water for hand hygiene (NIPCM; Annexe B 6.4).

n.0: Delay increases the risk of spread and delays diagnosis.
n.1: Antidiarrhoeals can be harmful in suspected C. difficile and do not reduce spread.
n.2: Staying in a shared bay risks transmission to other patients.

5.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
5.q: A hospital's outpatient manager says, 'We make reasonable adjustments for people with a learning disability as soon as someone asks us to.' Which response by the liaison nurse is most accurate?
o: That is correct, because the duty is triggered by a request from the patient
The duty is anticipatory, so adjustments should be planned before people attend
The duty applies to private providers rather than to NHS hospitals
That is correct when a formal diagnosis appears on the referral letter
5.w: For service providers, including the NHS, the reasonable adjustments duty is anticipatory: they must think in advance about what disabled people generally may need, such as easy read letters and longer appointments, rather than waiting for a request.

n.0: Waiting for a request breaches the anticipatory nature of the duty.
n.2: The duty applies to NHS services as service providers.
n.3: The duty does not depend on a formal diagnosis being supplied.

5.q: Bryony, 38, has a profound learning disability and does not use pictures or signs. Staff want to help her anticipate that she is going swimming. Using objects of reference, what should they do?
o: Show her a photograph of the swimming pool
Sign 'swimming' in Makaton as they tell her
Give her a piece of her swimming towel to hold
Hand her a symbol card for swimming
5.w: An object of reference is a real object that stands for an activity, person or place, such as a towel for swimming, used with people who do not yet understand pictures or signs. It must be used consistently.

n.0: Photographs are more abstract than objects; Bryony does not use pictures.
n.1: Bryony does not use signs, so a sign alone will not convey the activity.
n.3: Symbols are more abstract than pictures and are not meaningful for her.

5.q: A ward manager wants to check whether patients' falls risk assessments are completed within 6 hours of admission, as the trust policy requires, by reviewing 50 sets of notes. How should this project be classified?
o: Research, which needs NHS research ethics committee review
Health surveillance, which tracks outbreaks and health threats
Service evaluation, which judges a service without a standard
Clinical audit, which measures practice against a set standard
5.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (October 2022): clinical audit answers 'Does this service reach a predetermined standard?', uses care already in use and does not require REC review.

n.0: It tests no hypothesis and seeks no generalisable knowledge; it compares practice with an existing standard.
n.1: Surveillance monitors threats to population health, not compliance with a ward policy.
n.2: Service evaluation does not measure against a predetermined standard; this project does.

5.q: Two staff nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station about who should admit a new patient. Patients and visitors nearby are watching. Lorna is the nurse in charge. What should Lorna do first?
o: Admit the new patient herself so that the disagreement is no longer relevant
Calmly ask them both to step into the office and talk the issue through there
Tell both nurses firmly that they will each be reported to the ward manager
Leave them to resolve it between themselves, as they are both experienced nurses
5.w: A calm presence and moving the conflict to a private place protects patients' dignity and the team's professionalism and allows the issue to be resolved (AnnexA.4.2.3 calm presence when dealing with conflict; Code 20.1 and 20.3). The admission can then be allocated clearly.

n.0: Taking the task herself avoids the conflict without addressing it and adds to her workload.
n.2: Threatening sanctions in public escalates the conflict and does not resolve the allocation.
n.3: A public argument is affecting patients now; the nurse in charge needs to intervene.

5.q: Ben, 31, has a severe learning disability and no speech. Over two days he has stopped eating and has been pushing staff away. A support worker writes in the notes, 'Ben is being difficult again, it is his learning disability.' Which concept best describes this note?
o: Diagnostic overshadowing
Learned helplessness
Behavioural extinction
Positive risk-taking
5.w: Explaining a new change in eating and behaviour as part of Ben's learning disability, without considering pain or illness, is diagnostic overshadowing. Behaviour change is a common way people without speech communicate pain or illness.

n.1: Learned helplessness describes passivity after repeated loss of control; it does not fit a note blaming the disability.
n.2: Extinction is a behavioural term for a behaviour fading when it is no longer reinforced; it does not describe this note.
n.3: Positive risk-taking is a planned approach to supporting choice and independence, not a missed illness.

5.q: Mrs Webb, 72, takes ibuprofen for arthritis. She vomits a moderate amount of dark brown material that looks like coffee grounds. Her pulse is 108 and her blood pressure is lower than earlier. What should the nurse do?
o: Send a stool sample to the laboratory for testing
Dispose of the vomit and offer her mouth care and a drink
Give an antiemetic and recheck all her observations in 4 hours
Escalate urgently as a possible upper GI bleed and keep a record
5.w: Coffee-ground vomit suggests partly digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal bleed; NSAID use is a risk factor. With a rising pulse and falling blood pressure she needs urgent escalation (P3.12) and accurate recording of the amount and appearance (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: A stool sample does not address an acute bleed with haemodynamic change.
n.1: Disposing of it without escalation ignores a possible bleed; oral fluids may need withholding pending review.
n.2: An antiemetic does not address a possible bleed, and 4-hourly observations are too infrequent.

5.q: A trained healthcare worker is giving CPR to an adult with a pocket mask. What ratio of compressions to rescue breaths should be used?
5.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, each breath just enough to make the chest start to rise.

n.1: 15:2 is the ratio used in paediatric life support by healthcare rescuers.
n.2: 5:1 is an obsolete ratio not used in current guidance.
n.3: 30:1 gives too few breaths for adult BLS.

5.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
5.q: Bill, 54, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about his care. He lives in a care home and has started trying to leave in the afternoons, saying he wants to 'go to work'. Staff suggest locking the front door and giving PRN sedation. What should be considered first?
o: Less restrictive ways to meet his need, such as accompanied walks
PRN sedation in the afternoons to reduce his attempts to leave the home
A locked front door as a blanket rule applied to all residents
His family's consent to the door being locked and the sedation
5.w: MCA s1(6): before acting, regard must be had to whether the purpose can be achieved in a way that is less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom. Understanding the meaning of his behaviour and offering accompanied walks or meaningful activity may meet the need without restriction (STOMP; NICE NG11).

n.1: Sedation to control behaviour is a chemical restraint and contrary to STOMP as a first response.
n.2: Blanket restrictions affect everyone and are not individually justified.
n.3: Family cannot consent to restrictions for an adult without legal authority.

5.q: Bethany, 38, has a tracheostomy and needs suctioning for audible secretions. Her SpO2 is 95% before the procedure. Which practice is correct?
o: Set the suction pressure to about -300 mmHg for better clearance
Limit each suction pass to about 10 seconds and monitor saturation
Instil 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% before each pass
Apply suction while advancing the catheter to clear secretions
5.w: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (Suctioning guidance): suctioning can cause hypoxia, trauma and vagal stimulation. Do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; apply it on withdrawal, keep each period of suction to no more than 10 seconds, use a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg, and observe the patient (saturation, heart rate, colour) throughout, reattaching oxygen promptly.

n.0: The National Tracheostomy Safety Project advises a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg (-20 kPa) for most patients; higher pressure traumatises the mucosa and worsens hypoxia.
n.2: NTSP does not advise routine saline instillation; tenacious secretions are managed with better humidification, and saline is reserved for specific situations.
n.3: NTSP: do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; suction on insertion causes mucosal damage and hypoxia.

5.q: A ward's budget is overspent. The manager explains that money spent on agency staff this year means the planned purchase of new pressure-relieving mattresses cannot go ahead. Which economic concept does this illustrate?
o: Value for money
Opportunity cost
Cost-effectiveness
Economies of scale
5.w: Opportunity cost is the benefit lost from the next best use of a resource when it is spent on something else. In a fixed budget, spending on one item means another cannot be funded (P7.3 principles of health economics and resource allocation).

n.0: Value for money describes how well spending achieves outcomes, not the forgone alternative.
n.2: Cost-effectiveness compares the costs and outcomes of alternatives; it is not the loss of the forgone option.
n.3: Economies of scale are lower unit costs from producing more; they are not shown here.

5.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
5.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

5.q: Alys, 38, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to a medical ward. Her long-standing support worker asks to stay overnight because Alys becomes frightened in unfamiliar places. Ward visiting ends at 8 pm. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse in charge?
o: Agree a trial stay and review whether to extend it in the morning
Ask the support worker to return at 8 am to help with personal care
Explain that ward visiting times apply to all visitors equally
Agree she can stay and plan how she will support Alys's care
5.w: Allowing a familiar carer to stay is a recognised reasonable adjustment (Equality Act 2010 s20). Agreeing roles in advance helps staff work with the carer while remaining responsible for Alys's nursing care.

n.0: Making the stay a trial overnight adds uncertainty for Alys without reason; her need for a familiar person is already known.
n.1: Returning in the morning leaves Alys frightened overnight, which is when she most needs support.
n.2: Applying the same rule to everyone can put a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage; the duty is to adjust.

5.q: Cathy, 66, has a new itchy, raised red rash on her trunk two days after starting a new antibiotic. She is alert, her observations are normal and her lips and tongue are not swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Advise her to stop the antibiotic once she is at home
Wait until the rash has spread before reporting it
Give the next dose and apply an emollient to the rash
Withhold the next dose and inform the prescriber promptly
5.w: A new rash after starting a medicine may be an adverse drug reaction. Without anaphylaxis features, withhold the next dose pending review and inform the prescriber promptly; document it and consider a Yellow Card report (Annexe B 4.4; P4.15).

n.0: Advice to stop treatment needs prescriber review and does not address her current care.
n.1: Delay risks progression of a drug reaction.
n.2: Giving another dose of a possible cause risks a more serious reaction.

5.q: A community learning disability nurse is arranging a C(E)TR for Zara, 15. Which panel members must be present in addition to the chair?
o: Zara's GP and her head teacher
A clinical expert and an expert by experience
A police officer and a safeguarding lead
A consultant psychiatrist and an approved mental health professional
5.w: Under the NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy (2023) every review panel includes a chair (usually the commissioner), an independent clinical expert and an independent expert by experience (a person with lived experience or a family carer).

n.0: The GP and school provide information; the independent panel members are a clinical expert and an expert by experience.
n.2: Police and safeguarding leads are not core C(E)TR panel members.
n.3: These professionals may contribute evidence but are not the required independent panel members.

5.q: Kofi, 20, scored 67 on an IQ test taken during a stressful college assessment. He works part-time, travels alone by bus, cooks for himself and manages his own money. His tutor asks the nurse whether Kofi has a learning disability. What is the best response?
o: Refer him for genetic testing to identify the cause of his learning disability
The definition also needs impaired social functioning, which is not evident
Yes, because a score below 70 confirms a mild learning disability
Repeat the IQ test, because a second score below 70 would confirm it
5.w: Two steps: the definition needs impaired intelligence AND impaired social (adaptive) functioning starting before adulthood. Kofi's daily living skills show no significant impairment of social functioning, so a single IQ score cannot establish a learning disability; adaptive functioning matters as much as IQ.

n.0: Genetic testing does not decide whether the definition is met, and on these facts social functioning is not impaired.
n.2: An IQ score alone does not define a learning disability; adaptive functioning must also be impaired.
n.3: Repeating the test still ignores the adaptive functioning limb, which on these facts is not impaired.

5.q: Sinead, a learning disability nurse, is running healthy eating support for Josh, 29, who has a mild learning disability and type 2 diabetes. Which plan is most likely to help Josh learn and keep the key messages?
o: Short repeated sessions using pictures, practice and praise
A leaflet from the diabetes clinic for Josh to read at home
A weekly text message with a different healthy eating tip
One detailed hour-long session covering all dietary advice
5.w: Repetition, practical learning with pictures and positive reinforcement help people with a learning disability understand and retain health information (Annexe A; P2.10 health promotion using accessible methods).

n.1: A standard leaflet may be inaccessible and gives no repetition or practice.
n.2: A new tip each week lacks repetition of the key messages and practice.
n.3: A single long session overloads processing and memory.

5.q: A communal commode has just been used by Frank, 78, who has suspected C. difficile. It must be decontaminated before use by anyone else, and there is no visible blood. Following NIPCM appendix 7, how should it be cleaned?
o: Clean with detergent, then 1,000 ppm available chlorine, rinse and dry
Clean with detergent, then 10,000 ppm available chlorine, and dry
Wipe all surfaces with 70% isopropyl alcohol wipes and dry
Clean with detergent wipes and leave it to air dry before reuse
5.w: NIPCM appendix 7: equipment contaminated with faeces or used on a patient with known or suspected infection is cleaned with detergent then a 1,000 ppm available chlorine solution (or a combined product), rinsed and dried. 10,000 ppm is reserved for blood and high-risk body fluids. Equipment for an isolated patient should ideally be dedicated to them.

n.1: 10,000 ppm is for contamination with blood or high-risk body fluids, not faeces without blood.
n.2: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores and is not the appendix 7 method.
n.3: Detergent alone is for equipment not exposed to infection; this commode was used by a patient with suspected C. difficile.

5.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
5.q: Dean, 26, has a mild learning disability and his own tenancy. His community nurse finds several new 'friends' staying at his flat, packages being passed at the door, and Dean looking frightened and saying they 'look after him'. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record it as his lifestyle choice, as he has capacity about visitors
Advise Dean to tell his new friends that they must leave the flat
Raise a safeguarding concern and, as crime is likely, involve the police
Wait for clearer evidence at the next planned visit in a fortnight
5.w: This suggests cuckooing (exploitation of a vulnerable person's home, often for drug dealing) and exploitation by people posing as friends. Dean has care and support needs, is at risk and appears unable to protect himself, so a safeguarding concern is raised (Care Act s42) and the police informed because a crime is likely.

n.0: Fear and probable criminal exploitation are not a lifestyle choice; capacity does not remove the need to safeguard.
n.1: Asking Dean to confront the people exploiting him could put him at greater risk.
n.3: Delay leaves Dean at risk of serious harm.

5.q: Ruth, 45, has a moderate learning disability and is moving from her family home to supported living. Her new provider asks the community nurse which assessment will best show the support Ruth needs day to day. What is the best answer?
o: A genetic test to establish the cause of her learning disability
A repeat IQ test to confirm her current severity band
An assessment of adaptive skills such as self-care, safety and money
A review of the diagnosis letter written during her childhood
5.w: Support needs depend on adaptive (social) functioning: self-care, communication, managing money, keeping safe. A severity label or IQ score says little about the specific help a person needs in a new setting.

n.0: Knowing the cause may help with health surveillance but does not show her daily support needs.
n.1: An IQ score does not describe the practical help Ruth needs, and her severity is already known.
n.3: A childhood letter will not reflect Ruth's current skills as an adult.

5.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
5.q: Daisy, 35, has profound and multiple learning disabilities and lacks capacity to decide about a gastrostomy. Her parents strongly oppose it; the team believes it is in her best interests. After further meetings they still disagree. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Follow her parents' wishes, as next of kin decide for adults lacking capacity
Consider mediation or an application to the Court of Protection to resolve it
Proceed with the gastrostomy, as clinicians make best interests decisions
Stop involving the parents, as they are not the decision-maker
5.w: Families must be consulted (MCA s4(7)), but the decision-maker weighs all views. Where a serious dispute about serious medical treatment cannot be resolved locally, mediation and then an application to the Court of Protection are appropriate (MCA Code of Practice ch.5 and 15).

n.0: Next of kin have no legal power to decide for an adult unless they hold an LPA or deputyship.
n.2: Proceeding despite an unresolved serious dispute risks acting unlawfully; disputes should be resolved first.
n.3: Families must continue to be consulted; excluding them breaches s4(7).

5.q: In a supported living service, staff keep the kitchen cupboards locked because Alfie, 33, who has Prader-Willi syndrome, eats food compulsively. A new support worker asks the learning disability nurse what kind of practice this is. Which answer is correct?
o: A mechanical restrictive practice
A seclusion-based restrictive practice
An environmental restrictive practice
A chemical restrictive practice
5.w: Locking doors or cupboards to limit a person's access to their environment or belongings is an environmental restriction. Like all restrictive practices it needs a lawful basis (for example an MCA best interests decision), must be the least restrictive option and should be reviewed (NICE NG11 1.9; MCA 2005 s1(6)).

n.0: Mechanical restraint uses a device (for example arm splints or a belt) to restrict movement; locked cupboards restrict access, not movement.
n.1: Seclusion is confining a person alone in a room they cannot leave, which is not what is happening.
n.3: Chemical restraint is the use of medication to control behaviour, which is not described here.

5.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
5.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

5.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
5.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

5.q: Sophie, 14, has Rett syndrome and is reviewed by the community learning disability nurse. Which complication is most important to monitor for as part of her condition?
o: Large ears and joint hypermobility
Curvature of the spine (scoliosis)
Hyperphagia with rapid weight gain
Early-onset Alzheimer's disease
5.w: Scoliosis is a recognised feature of Rett syndrome, alongside seizures, breathing irregularities, slow growth and loss of hand use (MedlinePlus Genetics), and needs regular monitoring and postural care.

n.0: Large ears and flexible joints are features of fragile X syndrome.
n.2: Hyperphagia is characteristic of Prader-Willi syndrome; slow growth is more typical in Rett.
n.3: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease is linked with Down syndrome.

5.q: Ellie qualified six weeks ago. At the start of a night shift she is told she will be the only registered nurse for 28 patients on an unfamiliar ward, and has never taken charge. What should she do first?
o: Accept the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Raise her concerns at once with the person in charge and record it
Leave the ward and return to her own ward for safety
Accept the shift and phone her own ward manager at home
5.w: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Code 13.3 and NMC Raising concerns guidance support escalation and keeping a record.

n.0: Delaying until the morning leaves patients at risk; Code 16.2 requires her to raise concerns immediately.
n.2: Leaving abandons patients; she must raise the concern so safe cover is arranged.
n.3: Her absent manager cannot change tonight's staffing; the site lead or person in charge must be told now.

5.q: A learning disability nurse is assessing the mental health of Kofi, 29, who has a moderate learning disability and limited verbal communication. According to NICE NG54, who should usually be involved in the assessment?
o: Kofi, with his family or carers who know him well
His GP, using his records from the annual health check
Kofi, seen privately so that his confidentiality is protected
His consultant psychiatrist, without carers present
5.w: NICE NG54 1.7.5 says assess recent changes in behaviour using information from family members, carers and staff as well as records, taking into account their relationship with the person; they can describe change from Kofi's usual presentation and help with communication.

n.1: Records help, but an assessment needs Kofi himself and those who know him, not records alone.
n.2: Confidentiality matters, but excluding everyone who knows Kofi would lose crucial information about change from his baseline.
n.3: Specialist input may be needed, but excluding carers loses the knowledge of his usual behaviour.

5.q: A newly qualified nurse is learning which ward medicines must be entered in the controlled drugs register. Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, which of these medicines is a Schedule 2 controlled drug?
o: Diazepam 5 mg tablets
Oxycodone 5 mg in 5 mL oral solution
Tramadol 50 mg capsules
Midazolam injection 10 mg in 2 mL
5.w: Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 (Home Office controlled drugs list), oxycodone is in Schedule 2, alongside morphine, diamorphine and fentanyl, and needs a CD register entry (NICE NG46). Midazolam and tramadol are Schedule 3; diazepam is Schedule 4 Part 1.

n.0: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 Part 1 benzodiazepine.
n.2: Tramadol is in Schedule 3.
n.3: Midazolam is a Schedule 3 controlled drug, although many hospitals record it in the register by local policy.

5.q: Gwen, 70, is in the last days of life with metastatic cancer and new bone pain. She has not taken opioids before. The team agree to start subcutaneous morphine for symptom control, and the nurse is planning her care. Which approach to dosing is recommended?
o: Wait until her pain is severe before giving the first dose of morphine
Start with the lowest effective dose and titrate to her symptoms
Start at the top of the prescribed range so that she is comfortable quickly
Give a loading dose by intramuscular injection, then change to subcutaneous
5.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.7 and 1.5.8: for people starting treatment who have not previously had medicines for symptom management, start with the lowest effective dose and titrate as clinically indicated, reassessing symptoms at least daily.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.11 asks for pain to be managed promptly and effectively once identified.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.7 recommends starting with the lowest effective dose for people not previously given symptom-control medicines.
n.3: Intramuscular injections should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.5.5).

5.q: Mrs Shah, 58, asks a practice nurse whether a herbal supplement she has bought online will help her blood pressure alongside her prescribed amlodipine. The nurse is unsure. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her that nurses cannot discuss non-prescribed products
Check a reliable source or the pharmacist before advising her
Advise her that herbal products are natural and safe to take
Advise her to stop the amlodipine while she tries the supplement
5.w: Code 6.1: information or advice must be evidence-based, including about health products; Code 18.3: check compatibility with other treatment, including over-the-counter medicines; Code 13.3 seek help when unsure.

n.0: Code 18.3 expects compatibility with other treatments, including over-the-counter products, to be checked.
n.2: This is not evidence-based and ignores possible interactions (Code 6.1, 18.3).
n.3: Stopping a prescribed medicine without review could be harmful and is outside the nurse's evidence base.

5.q: A laboratory scientist phones the ward with a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L for Mr Shaw. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to take this result?
o: Ask the laboratory to email the result to the doctor directly
Remember it and tell the doctor at the next ward round
Write it on the handover sheet for the night team to act on
Write it down, read it back, then tell the doctor at once
5.w: Annexe A 1.9 and 1.11: share verbal information clearly. Writing a telephoned result down and reading it back confirms it was heard correctly, and a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L needs the doctor told at once (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.0: Email may not be seen promptly; the nurse must act on it now.
n.1: Relying on memory risks error, and waiting delays urgent treatment.
n.2: A critical result needs immediate action, not handover.

5.q: Albert, a resident in a care home, died last night. This morning his close friend Ted, another resident, asks the nurse where Albert is, as he did not come to breakfast. Albert's family have been informed. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask the activities coordinator to tell residents at next week's meeting
Avoid telling Ted, to prevent him becoming upset during breakfast
Tell Ted sensitively that Albert has died and offer him time and support
Say that Albert has gone into hospital so that Ted is not distressed
5.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): residents in communal settings such as care homes often build significant relationships with other residents and will need to be informed; the RNVoEAD guidance asks the nurse to recognise the emotional impact on surrounding residents and prompt support. Code 2 and 20.2: act with honesty.

n.0: Delaying news for a week is not compassionate support for a close friend who is asking now.
n.1: Residents in communal settings have often built close relationships and need to be informed and supported.
n.3: Giving false information is dishonest (Code 20.2) and delays Ted's grieving.

5.q: Nadia is redressing a deep cavity wound on the sacrum of Ruth, 80. She is wearing non-sterile gloves and using ANTT, but realises she will need to touch the wound bed with her fingers to place the packing. What should she do?
o: Change to sterile gloves, as the Key-Site will be touched directly
Moisten the non-sterile gloves with sterile saline before packing
Rub alcohol handrub onto the gloves before touching the wound
Continue with the non-sterile gloves, as she cleaned her hands first
5.w: Under ANTT, if a Key-Site or Key-Part must be touched directly, sterile gloves are needed so that the hands do not contaminate it (a Surgical-ANTT approach). NIPCM ch 1.4 also requires sterile gloves for contact with a sterile site or body cavity.

n.1: Saline does not sterilise gloves; the gloves would still contaminate the wound bed.
n.2: Gloves are not decontaminated with handrub, and this does not make them sterile.
n.3: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable when Key-Sites are not touched; here she must touch the wound bed directly.

5.q: Asif, 32, has a moderate learning disability. His sister reports he has been talking to someone who is not there, and he is frightened in his room at night. Staff say he has always talked to himself. What is the best next step for the learning disability nurse?
o: Move him to a different bedroom and see whether his fear settles over a week
Compare with his known baseline and arrange a mental health assessment
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to help him sleep at night
Record that this is his usual self-talk and close the concern
5.w: Two-step reasoning: self-talk can be normal for some people with a learning disability, so the nurse first compares with the person's baseline; a change in content (frightened, responding to voices) suggests possible psychosis and needs a specialist mental health assessment (NICE NG54 1.1.2 differences in presentation; 1.6.5 refer suspected serious mental illness to a psychiatrist with expertise in learning disabilities).

n.0: Changing rooms may help comfort but does not assess a possible mental illness.
n.2: Medication before assessment is not appropriate and conflicts with STOMP.
n.3: Dismissing the change as usual self-talk is diagnostic overshadowing; the sister describes something new.

5.q: Under NICE guidance on violence and aggression (NG10), when may manual restraint be used in a health setting?
o: As the first response whenever a person raises their voice
As a last resort when de-escalation fails and harm is likely
As a routine measure to give medicines a person has refused
As a punishment for breaking ward rules on two occasions
5.w: NICE NG10 and Annexe B 2.17: restrictive interventions are used as a last resort, after de-escalation and other strategies fail, when there is a real risk of harm, and must be proportionate and for the shortest time possible.

n.0: Raised voices call for de-escalation, not restraint.
n.2: Restraint is not a routine method of giving refused medicines; covert or compulsory treatment has its own legal safeguards.
n.3: Restraint is never punitive; this would breach human rights and the Code.

5.q: Mr Owusu, 81, says he 'came over funny' before his fall at home. The nurse needs to understand what happened. Which response best clarifies his account?
o: "So you fainted, then. How long were you unconscious?"
"What did 'came over funny' feel like for you?"
"Lots of older people feel funny. Let's move on."
"Did you trip on something on the floor?"
5.w: Annexe A 1.6: use clarification techniques; P1.11 communicate effectively with people at all stages of life. Code 7.4 keep misunderstanding to a minimum.

n.0: This assumes a faint and leads him to a particular answer.
n.2: This dismisses an important symptom and stops clarification.
n.3: This closed question narrows to one cause before his experience is understood.

5.q: On a dementia ward, Mr Payne, 81, lacks capacity and needed to be briefly held by two trained staff to stop him hitting another patient. He is now calm. Besides checking him for injury, what should the nurse record about the incident?
o: The details in the incident system, rather than his care record
A brief note that restraint was needed, to avoid labelling him
The reasons for the hold, technique used, duration and his response
That he was held in his best interests, with the names of staff
5.w: Code 10.1-10.4 requires accurate, timely records that attribute, date and time entries. Any restraint must be justified as necessary and proportionate (MCA s6), so the record should show why it was used, how, for how long and its effect, supporting review and learning.

n.0: Incident reporting is appropriate, but the care record must also document what happened to him.
n.1: A minimal note fails Code 10 and prevents review of whether the restraint was justified.
n.3: Stating 'best interests' without reasons, technique and duration does not show the hold was necessary and proportionate.

5.q: Graham, 46, has a moderate learning disability. His mother, who lived with him, died suddenly last night. His support team asks the community nurse how to tell him. Which approach is best?
o: Wait until after the funeral so he is not upset during it
Ask his GP to tell him at his next appointment
Tell him plainly that she has died, with someone he trusts present
Tell him his mother has 'gone to sleep' to soften the news for him
5.w: People with a learning disability need honest, concrete words (such as 'died') delivered by someone they trust in a familiar place, with time to repeat information and include them in mourning rituals. Euphemisms confuse and delays exclude (Annexe A 2.9).

n.0: Delaying the news excludes him from the funeral and grieving with family.
n.1: Waiting for a routine appointment delays the news and removes the support of familiar people.
n.3: Euphemisms like 'gone to sleep' are confusing and can cause fear of sleep.

5.q: Archie, 11, is autistic and has a mild learning disability. He is due to have his tonsils removed next month and becomes very anxious about new situations. His community nurse suggests writing a Social Story. What is the purpose of a Social Story?
o: To record Archie's medical history for the anaesthetist to read
To describe what will happen and why, so the situation is predictable
To reward Archie with stickers each time he stays calm at hospital
To teach Archie the medical words used by hospital staff
5.w: Social Stories, created by Carol Gray (1991), describe a situation, event or activity in a clear, reassuring way, so an autistic person knows what to expect. They are widely used to prepare people for hospital visits and procedures.

n.0: Medical history belongs in the clinical record or hospital passport.
n.2: Rewards are a behavioural strategy; a Social Story gives information to make events predictable.
n.3: Social Stories use everyday language to explain events, not to teach medical vocabulary.

5.q: A community nurse attends to verify the expected death of Lena, 83, who had advanced dementia. Lena is cold and rigor mortis is present. The nurse notices fresh, unexplained bruising on Lena's upper arms, and two relatives give conflicting accounts of the evening. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Decline to verify and request the police and the responsible doctor
Begin CPR because the death can no longer be treated as expected
Verify the death as expected and document the bruising in her record
Verify the death, then wash Lena before the funeral director arrives
5.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): verification by an RN applies to expected deaths not accompanied by suspicious circumstances, and the verifying nurse has the right to refuse to verify and to request the responsible doctor or the police in any unusual situation. Care after death guidance: minimal contact with the body when suspicion arises.

n.1: Rigor mortis is a sign of irreversible death, so CPR is not indicated (RNVoEAD; RCUK).
n.2: Verification by an RN is excluded where there are suspicious circumstances (RNVoEAD guidance).
n.3: Washing could destroy evidence; with suspicion, there should be minimal contact with the body.

5.q: Brenda, 58, completed a bowel screening kit six months ago and the result was normal. She now tells the nurse she has had blood in her stools and looser bowel movements for four weeks. What should the nurse advise?
o: Wait for her next routine kit, due in about 18 months' time
See her GP about these symptoms now, despite the normal screen
Her normal screening result means bowel cancer can be ruled out
Request an extra screening kit to repeat the test this month
5.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): screening identifies increased risk in apparently healthy people; even with a normal result you could still develop the condition, and people with symptoms should speak to a GP. Screening tests are not 100% accurate (false negatives occur).

n.0: Symptoms need GP assessment now; screening is for people without symptoms.
n.2: A normal (screen-negative) result means low risk at the time; it does not exclude disease developing later.
n.3: Screening is not a test for symptoms; she needs clinical assessment by her GP.

5.q: Ms Grey, 34, has symptoms of a urinary tract infection and needs a urine sample sent for culture. She is independent and mobile. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Collect urine from the toilet bowl after passing it
Discard the first part of the stream and collect the midstream urine
Collect the last few drops of urine at the end of passing it
Collect the first part of the urine stream into a clean pot
5.w: A clean-catch midstream specimen reduces contamination by skin and urethral organisms. The first part of the stream is discarded and the midstream portion collected into a sterile container, labelled and sent promptly (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: Urine from the toilet bowl is contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
n.2: The end of the stream is not the midstream sample required for culture.
n.3: First-catch urine carries urethral and skin organisms that contaminate a culture; it is the sample used for chlamydia testing, not for MSU culture.

5.q: Ruth, 85, has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible but no bone, tendon or muscle is exposed. Using the international NPIAP-EPUAP classification, which category is this?
o: Category 2
Suspected deep tissue injury
Category 3
Category 4
5.w: NPIAP-EPUAP classification (used per NICE CG179): category 3 is full-thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible but bone, tendon or muscle not exposed. Category 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle; category 2 is partial-thickness loss.

n.0: Category 2 is partial-thickness loss of dermis, such as a shallow open wound or blister.
n.1: Suspected deep tissue injury is an area of purple or maroon intact skin or a blood-filled blister.
n.3: Category 4 involves exposed bone, tendon or muscle.

5.q: Maureen, 87, lacks capacity and has life-threatening pneumonia. Her daughter holds a registered health and welfare lasting power of attorney (LPA). The LPA does not contain express authority over life-sustaining treatment. Her daughter says she refuses intravenous antibiotics. How should the team proceed?
o: Delay treatment until the Court of Protection has confirmed that the LPA is valid
Ask the daughter to agree as nearest relative, which overrides the terms of the LPA
Follow the daughter's refusal, as the LPA is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Decide in her best interests, consulting her daughter, who cannot refuse this treatment
5.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s9 (an LPA must be registered) and s11(7)-(8): a health and welfare attorney can give or refuse consent to treatment when the person lacks capacity, but this does not extend to life-sustaining treatment unless the LPA contains express provision. The team decide in Maureen's best interests (s4), consulting her daughter.

n.0: The registered LPA does not need court confirmation, and delaying antibiotics would put Maureen's life at risk.
n.1: There is no 'nearest relative' power under the MCA; decisions are made in Maureen's best interests.
n.2: Registration is required, but under MCA s11(8) an attorney cannot refuse life-sustaining treatment without express authority in the LPA.

5.q: Agnes, the nurse in charge of a busy surgical ward, wants the whole team to share the same understanding of which patients are at risk at the start of each shift. Which practice best supports this?
o: Each nurse reads the full medical notes of all patients before starting
Staff ask the nurse in charge about any patient they are worried about
A brief safety huddle after handover to share key risks and plans
The nurse in charge keeps a written list of risks in the ward office
5.w: Shared situational awareness, the team's common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is supported by short structured safety huddles where risks (deteriorating patients, falls, staffing) are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; P5.2; P6.6).

n.0: Reading all notes is impractical on a busy ward and does not create a shared team picture or agreed actions.
n.1: Relying on individuals to ask means risks are shared reactively and unevenly.
n.3: A list kept by one person does not share awareness across the team.

5.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
5.q: Ruby, 38, has a profound learning disability and has been sitting in her wheelchair for six hours at a day centre. Her postural care plan says she should change position every two hours. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask her family to reposition her when she gets home
Leave Ruby in her chair as she seems content
Tilt the wheelchair back for the rest of the day
Reposition Ruby out of her chair as her plan sets out
5.w: Prolonged sitting in one position increases pressure damage and body shape distortion. The plan's schedule should be followed, using supported lying or standing as set out (24-hour postural care principles).

n.0: Delaying repositioning until she goes home breaches the plan and risks harm.
n.1: Appearing content does not mean her body is protected from prolonged sitting.
n.2: Tilting changes pressure but she has already exceeded the planned time in her chair.

5.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
5.q: Aaron, a learning disability nurse, is teaching a new supported living team about the health risks faced by the people they support. A support worker asks which serious illness LeDeR reports as one of the most common causes of death, often linked to aspiration. Which illness is it?
o: Asthma
Kidney failure
Pneumonia
Meningitis
5.w: LeDeR reports consistently list pneumonia and other lung infections among the most common causes of death, alongside cancer and heart conditions; in 2021 pneumonia accounted for 35% of respiratory deaths reported to LeDeR, many linked to aspiration (LeDeR 2023 report; LeDeR pneumonia report 2024).

n.0: Asthma is not among the leading causes of death in LeDeR reports.
n.1: Kidney failure is not among the leading causes highlighted.
n.3: Meningitis is not a leading cause of death in LeDeR reports.

5.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
5.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

5.q: George Hall, 80, has a NEWS2 score of 1. His nurse, Precious, feels uneasy: he is quieter than usual and has not eaten, though nothing specific is abnormal. She is unsure whether to act on this feeling. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase his observations and discuss her concern with the medical team
Ask the healthcare assistant to repeat the observations at the next round
Record her impression and continue observations at the planned frequency
Wait until his score reaches 5 so that escalation is clearly justified
5.w: NEWS2 supports, and does not replace, clinical judgement (RCP 2017; NICE NG253). For scores of 1-4 the registered nurse decides on monitoring frequency and escalation. Acting on clinical concern under uncertainty, by increasing monitoring and escalating, is safe practice (P6.11 accept and manage uncertainty; Code 13.3 ask for help).

n.1: Repeating routine observations later does not address her clinical concern now.
n.2: Recording a concern without acting on it leaves a possible deterioration unaddressed.
n.3: Waiting for a threshold ignores the nurse's assessment and may delay recognition of deterioration.

5.q: Dan, 24, has Prader-Willi syndrome and lives in supported living. He has taken food from housemates' cupboards and gained 6 kg in two months. Staff want to lock the kitchen. What must happen first?
o: Assess his capacity on food access and, if lacking, decide in his best interests
Lock the kitchen straight away, because hyperphagia justifies any food restriction
Lock the kitchen once his parents have agreed to it on his behalf
Leave the kitchen open and record his food choices as unwise decisions
5.w: Two steps: locking the kitchen restricts Dan and his housemates, so it needs a lawful basis. Assess his capacity for this decision (MCA s2-3); if he lacks it, make a best interests decision (s4) choosing the least restrictive option (s1(6)), and review it regularly.

n.1: Restrictions need a lawful basis and proportionality; a diagnosis does not authorise any restriction.
n.2: Parents cannot consent on behalf of an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.3: Calling his choices unwise assumes he has capacity, which has not been assessed, given the compulsive nature of hyperphagia.

6.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
6.q: Shona, 35, has a moderate learning disability and her friend at the day centre has died. Staff want to help her understand. Which approach is best?
o: Say her friend has 'gone to sleep' to soften it
Use clear words such as 'died' with pictures
Avoid mentioning the friend so she does not get upset
Tell her the friend has moved to another day centre
6.w: Clear, concrete language ('died', 'dead') with pictures or easy read is easier to understand than euphemisms. 'Gone to sleep' can cause confusion and fear about sleeping; honesty supports grieving.

n.0: Euphemisms are confusing and may cause fear of sleep.
n.2: Avoiding the subject leaves her confused and unsupported.
n.3: Lying undermines trust and prevents her from grieving.

6.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
6.q: Phil, 49, has Down syndrome and dementia. He is now sleeping most of the day, barely drinking and his breathing has changed. Care staff say this is 'just his dementia getting worse'. What should the nurse consider?
o: That he is depressed and needs an antidepressant
That Phil may be dying and needs assessment
That his dementia is progressing and his plan stays the same
That he is tired after a busy week
6.w: Increased sleep, reduced intake and changes in breathing may indicate the last days of life, or a reversible cause such as infection. Recognising possible dying allows assessment, review of reversible causes and planning for comfort (NICE NG31 principles; LeDeR learning on overshadowing).

n.0: Depression does not explain these physical changes.
n.2: Attributing all change to dementia risks missing dying or a treatable illness.
n.3: Tiredness does not explain reduced drinking and changed breathing.

6.q: Steve, 36, has cerebral palsy and a severe learning disability and does not use words. He cries out and grips the hoist sling when moved and when staff dress his legs. A support worker suggests adding this to his behaviour plan. What should the nurse do?
o: Assess for hip or other musculoskeletal pain and review his analgesia
Hoist him less often to reduce the number of distressing transfers
Record it as behaviour that challenges to be managed in his support plan
Ask staff to dress him more quickly to shorten the distress
6.w: Hip displacement, contractures and scoliosis are common in cerebral palsy and cause pain on movement. Crying out during transfers and leg dressing is likely pain communication, so it needs assessment and analgesia review rather than a behavioural label (avoid diagnostic overshadowing).

n.1: Reducing transfers affects his care and position changes without treating the cause.
n.2: Labelling pain as behaviour is diagnostic overshadowing and leaves pain untreated.
n.3: Faster dressing does not address the likely source of pain.

6.q: Alys, 38, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to a medical ward. Her long-standing support worker asks to stay overnight because Alys becomes frightened in unfamiliar places. Ward visiting ends at 8 pm. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse in charge?
o: Agree a trial stay and review whether to extend it in the morning
Ask the support worker to return at 8 am to help with personal care
Explain that ward visiting times apply to all visitors equally
Agree she can stay and plan how she will support Alys's care
6.w: Allowing a familiar carer to stay is a recognised reasonable adjustment (Equality Act 2010 s20). Agreeing roles in advance helps staff work with the carer while remaining responsible for Alys's nursing care.

n.0: Making the stay a trial overnight adds uncertainty for Alys without reason; her need for a familiar person is already known.
n.1: Returning in the morning leaves Alys frightened overnight, which is when she most needs support.
n.2: Applying the same rule to everyone can put a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage; the duty is to adjust.

6.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
6.q: Dean, 26, has a mild learning disability and his own tenancy. His community nurse finds several new 'friends' staying at his flat, packages being passed at the door, and Dean looking frightened and saying they 'look after him'. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record it as his lifestyle choice, as he has capacity about visitors
Advise Dean to tell his new friends that they must leave the flat
Raise a safeguarding concern and, as crime is likely, involve the police
Wait for clearer evidence at the next planned visit in a fortnight
6.w: This suggests cuckooing (exploitation of a vulnerable person's home, often for drug dealing) and exploitation by people posing as friends. Dean has care and support needs, is at risk and appears unable to protect himself, so a safeguarding concern is raised (Care Act s42) and the police informed because a crime is likely.

n.0: Fear and probable criminal exploitation are not a lifestyle choice; capacity does not remove the need to safeguard.
n.1: Asking Dean to confront the people exploiting him could put him at greater risk.
n.3: Delay leaves Dean at risk of serious harm.

6.q: Before giving the first dose of oral amoxicillin to Stanley, 67, the nurse notices he is wearing a red allergy wristband labelled 'penicillin'. The allergy section of his drug chart is blank and the prescriber has gone home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose with an antihistamine to cover any possible reaction
Withhold it, clarify the allergy with Stanley and contact a prescriber
Give the dose, as the drug chart has no allergy recorded
Give half the dose and observe Stanley closely for any reaction
6.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 requires the person administering to check allergies or previous adverse drug reactions, and to raise ambiguities with the prescriber or pharmacy without delay. Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so the dose is withheld, the reaction history clarified, the chart updated and an alternative sought.

n.0: An antihistamine would not prevent anaphylaxis and the nurse cannot add a medicine.
n.2: The wristband is a warning that must be resolved; a blank chart is an omission, not evidence of no allergy.
n.3: Altering the prescribed dose is not within the nurse's role, and any dose risks anaphylaxis.

6.q: Lily, 5, has Down syndrome. Her teacher reports that over the past term she has stopped responding when her name is called and seems 'in her own world'. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Refer to the educational psychologist for an attention assessment
Arrange a hearing assessment, as hearing loss and glue ear are common
Refer to CAMHS because she may be showing new autistic features
Record the change as behaviour linked to her learning disability
6.w: Hearing loss, including glue ear, is common in children with Down syndrome (NHS.uk). A child who stops responding to her name needs her hearing checked first, before other explanations are explored.

n.0: Attention assessment may follow, but hearing is the likely and treatable cause to check first.
n.2: Autism can occur with Down syndrome, but a treatable hearing problem should be excluded first.
n.3: Recording it as part of her learning disability is diagnostic overshadowing.

6.q: Ben, a theatre nurse, has developed persistent back pain that is making patient transfers difficult. He has not told anyone. Which action best reflects his professional responsibility for his own health?
o: Wait until his annual appraisal to mention the problem
Seek occupational health advice and discuss adjustments
Take regular painkillers and keep doing transfers as before
Avoid transfers by swapping tasks with colleagues informally
6.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need to carry out your professional role. Proficiency P1.6: take responsibility for a healthy lifestyle to maintain fitness for practice; Code 19.4 personal precautions.

n.0: Waiting delays support; Code 20.9 requires maintaining the health needed for the role now.
n.2: Masking symptoms risks harm to himself and patients and does not address fitness for his role.
n.3: Informal swaps hide the problem and may leave the team short of safe handlers.

6.q: Dolores, 88, is frail and drowsy after a stroke. She has a dry, coated tongue and cracked lips, takes nothing by mouth and has an unsafe swallow. Which oral care plan is most appropriate?
o: Daily chlorhexidine mouthwash rinses by mouth
Lemon and glycerine swabs every two hours
Gentle mouth care with a soft brush and lip balm
Mouth care whenever her relatives request it
6.w: People who are nil by mouth and drowsy need frequent oral assessment and gentle care with a soft toothbrush, moistening and lip care. Lemon and glycerine dry the mouth further and mouthwashes risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow (Annexe B 4.5; NICE NG31 advises frequent mouth and lip care).

n.0: Rinses she cannot spit out risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow.
n.1: Lemon and glycerine swabs dry the mucosa further and can damage teeth.
n.3: Oral care is a planned nursing intervention based on assessment, not on request.

6.q: Sidney, 76, has fallen twice in the past year at home and could not get up without help after the second fall. His GP practice nurse sees him for a routine review. What does NICE NG249 recommend?
o: Refer him for a bone scan without other assessment
Offer him a comprehensive falls assessment and management
Give him a leaflet on falls and review him in a year
Advise him to stay in his chair to avoid further falls
6.w: NICE NG249: in the community, offer a comprehensive falls assessment and management to people who have fallen in the past year and meet any criterion, such as being unable to get up independently or having 2 or more falls in the year. Sidney meets both.

n.0: Osteoporosis risk is part of the assessment, but not the whole of it.
n.2: A leaflet alone does not meet his assessed needs.
n.3: Reducing activity increases deconditioning and falls risk; exercise programmes are recommended.

6.q: Ms Grey, 34, has symptoms of a urinary tract infection and needs a urine sample sent for culture. She is independent and mobile. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Collect urine from the toilet bowl after passing it
Discard the first part of the stream and collect the midstream urine
Collect the last few drops of urine at the end of passing it
Collect the first part of the urine stream into a clean pot
6.w: A clean-catch midstream specimen reduces contamination by skin and urethral organisms. The first part of the stream is discarded and the midstream portion collected into a sterile container, labelled and sent promptly (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: Urine from the toilet bowl is contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
n.2: The end of the stream is not the midstream sample required for culture.
n.3: First-catch urine carries urethral and skin organisms that contaminate a culture; it is the sample used for chlamydia testing, not for MSU culture.

6.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
6.q: Mia, 30, has a profound learning disability and an SLT eating and drinking plan. She is about to be given her lunch. Which position is safest during the meal?
o: Semi-reclined in her chair with her feet raised
Lying on her side in bed facing the carer
Reclined at 45 degrees with her head tilted back
Sitting upright with her chin slightly tucked
6.w: Sitting as upright as possible, with the head in midline and the chin slightly tucked, protects the airway during swallowing; her SLT plan and 24-hour postural care plan give the specific position (SLT dysphagia guidance).

n.0: A semi-reclined position increases the risk of food entering the airway.
n.1: Side-lying is not a safe eating position unless a specialist plan states it.
n.2: Reclining with the head tilted back opens the airway to food and fluid, increasing aspiration risk.

6.q: Mrs Kowalska, 74, speaks Polish and little English. She needs to consent to a planned procedure. Her 12-year-old grandson offers to interpret. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a bilingual ward housekeeper to interpret during her break
Accept the grandson's offer as he is a trusted relative
Give her the English consent form to take home overnight
Book a professional interpreter before discussing consent
6.w: NHS England Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services in primary care (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; use of anyone under 16 is not acceptable except when immediate and necessary treatment is required. Code 7.2.

n.0: An untrained staff member is not a registered interpreter; reliance on unqualified interpreters is discouraged.
n.1: NHS England guidance says use of anyone under 16 is not acceptable except for immediate necessary treatment.
n.2: An English form does not meet her language needs and is not informed consent.

6.q: Ivy, 84, has dementia and becomes agitated each evening, trying to leave the ward and hitting out during personal care. Her pain has not been assessed. Which action best responds to her behaviour?
o: Ask her family to stay overnight so that staff can step back
Assess for pain and unmet needs and adapt her care around them
Keep her in a chair with a lap belt to stop her leaving
Request a prescription for regular antipsychotic medicine
6.w: Behaviour that challenges often communicates unmet need, such as pain, constipation, infection or fear. Assess pain with a behavioural observation tool where self-report is difficult (the 2018 UK guideline recommends PAINAD or Doloplus-2; Abbey is widely used) (UK guidance on pain assessment in older people, Age and Ageing 2018) and adapt care, using positive behaviour support before any restrictive or pharmacological option (Annexe A 3.5, P4.4).

n.0: Family involvement is helpful, but staff remain responsible for assessing and meeting her needs.
n.2: A lap belt is a restrictive practice and a potential deprivation of liberty, not a first response.
n.3: Antipsychotics carry significant risks in dementia and do not address the cause.

6.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
6.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

6.q: Daniel Morgan, 32, has a learning disability and is very anxious about needles. He missed his last two blood test appointments at a busy GP practice clinic. Which reasonable adjustment is most appropriate for the practice nurse to offer?
o: Offer the first appointment of the day with extra time and easy read information
Ask his support worker to bring him in and stay outside the room during the test
Arrange for the test to be done when he next attends hospital as an inpatient
Book him into the next routine clinic slot and send a standard reminder letter
6.w: Equality Act 2010 s20 places a duty to make reasonable adjustments so that disabled people are not at a substantial disadvantage. A quiet first appointment, extra time and accessible information reduce anxiety and support his access (P3.7 principles of reasonable adjustments; P7.9; Accessible Information Standard).

n.1: A familiar support worker can help, but asking them to wait outside removes the support he may need.
n.2: Waiting for an unplanned admission denies him timely, equitable access to routine care.
n.3: Repeating the arrangement that has failed twice makes no adjustment for his disability.

6.q: A student nurse says that normalisation means 'making people with learning disabilities behave like everyone else'. How should the mentor correct this?
o: It means making ordinary patterns and conditions of everyday life available to people
It means people follow the same rules as staff so that services run smoothly
It means grouping people with similar needs so that they share specialist services
It means treating the impairment so that the person becomes as typical as possible
6.w: Normalisation (Nirje; Wolfensberger) means making the patterns and conditions of everyday life, such as a home, routines, work, leisure and relationships, as close as possible to the norms of mainstream society. It is about conditions of life, not changing the person.

n.1: Normalisation is about ordinary life patterns, not compliance with staff rules.
n.2: Grouping people with similar needs in specialist settings is the opposite of normalisation.
n.3: Normalisation is not about treating the impairment or changing the person.

6.q: Grace, 68, is admitted to a surgical ward. Three months ago she was an inpatient in a hospital abroad after a car accident. She has no symptoms of infection. What is the most appropriate placement while admission screening is arranged?
o: A single room with contact precautions while screening for CPE
A bay with other patients recently treated abroad, pending results
An open bay, after starting prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
An open bay, with screening repeated if she develops a fever
6.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 lists patients who have been inpatients in any hospital in the UK or abroad as a possible cross-infection risk for multidrug-resistant organisms such as carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE). She should be placed in a single room with contact precautions pending screening, and the decision documented.

n.1: Cohorting is for patients with the same confirmed infection; unscreened patients may carry different organisms.
n.2: Prophylactic antibiotics do not clear carriage and drive resistance, contrary to NICE NG15 stewardship.
n.3: CPE carriage is usually symptomless, so waiting for a fever leaves the bay exposed.

6.q: During the morning medication round, Lewis notices the sharps container on the drug trolley has reached the manufacturer's fill line. Several injections are still due. What should Lewis do with the full container?
o: Close and lock it, label it with origin and date, and replace it
Leave it open and start a second container beside it on the trolley
Press the contents down to make room for the remaining needles
Use it until it is completely full, then seal it before lunch
6.w: NIPCM ch 1.9: sharps containers must be disposed of when the manufacturer's fill line is reached, labelled with point of origin and dates of assembly and disposal, and use the temporary closure when not in use.

n.1: A full container left open is a sharps hazard; it should be locked and removed.
n.2: Pushing down sharps risks a needlestick injury and overfills the container.
n.3: Filling past the fill line risks protruding sharps and injury.

6.q: Winifred, 86, lives alone and takes 12 regular medicines from three prescribers. She has fallen twice this month and her daughter reports increasing daytime drowsiness. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the community nurse's most appropriate action?
o: Request a structured medication review with her GP and pharmacist
Spread her doses across the day to reduce side effects
Advise her daughter to buy a pill organiser for the medicines
Stop the medicines most likely to cause drowsiness and falls
