6.w: Polypharmacy with falls and drowsiness is a trigger for a structured medication review (NICE NG5 medicines optimisation; P4.15). Prescribers and pharmacists can review the indication, risks and benefits of each medicine together with Winifred.

n.1: Retiming doses without review may cause errors and does not address inappropriate medicines.
n.2: A pill organiser may help adherence but does not address why she is falling.
n.3: Stopping medicines is a prescribing decision and abrupt withdrawal can cause harm.

6.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
6.q: A learning disability liaison nurse is teaching ward staff about section 20 of the Equality Act 2010. Which three requirements make up the duty to make reasonable adjustments?
o: Instruct an IMCA; arrange an independent advocate; send all letters in an easy read format
Assess capacity; consult the family; record a best interests decision in the notes
Provide a paid carer; offer a single room; give extra funding for each admission
Change a provision, criterion or practice; alter physical features; provide auxiliary aids
6.w: Equality Act 2010 s20(3)-(5): the duty has three requirements: to avoid substantial disadvantage caused by a provision, criterion or practice; by a physical feature; and by a lack of an auxiliary aid.

n.0: IMCAs and advocacy arise under the MCA and Care Act, not as the s20 requirements.
n.1: These describe MCA processes, not the Equality Act duty.
n.2: These may be adjustments in some cases but are not the three statutory requirements.

6.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
6.q: Isla, 26, has a learning disability and dysphagia. Her weight has dropped by 4 kg in two months, and staff say meals now take over an hour and she often refuses food. What is the priority?
o: Offer larger portions at each meal to restore her weight
Record her weight monthly and review in three months
Give her meals faster so that she does not tire
Refer back to SLT and a dietitian for urgent review
6.w: Prolonged meals, food refusal and weight loss suggest her swallowing has worsened or the plan no longer meets her needs; she needs prompt SLT re-assessment and dietetic review (NICE CG32 nutrition support principles; LeDeR learning on dysphagia).

n.0: Larger portions may increase fatigue and aspiration risk without addressing the cause.
n.1: Waiting three months allows further weight loss and aspiration risk.
n.2: Faster feeding increases aspiration risk; pacing should match her swallow.

6.q: Ernest, 81, has Parkinson's disease with a tremor and struggles to get food to his mouth. He is eating less than half his meals. Which intervention should be tried first to help him eat?
o: Provide adapted cutlery, a plate guard and help
Give his meals later, when the ward is quieter
Refer him for insertion of a nasogastric feeding tube
Prescribe oral nutritional supplements three times a day
6.w: Annexe B 5.3: assist with eating and drinking and use feeding and drinking aids. Adapted cutlery, plate guards and non-slip mats, plus assistance (for example via a red tray system or protected mealtimes), address the cause of his poor intake.

n.1: Delaying meals does not address his difficulty and may mean food is cold.
n.2: Enteral feeding is not indicated when oral intake can be improved with help.
n.3: Supplements may follow, but his barrier is a physical one that aids can address first.

6.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
6.q: A learning disability nurse is preparing a teaching session on international policy. Which statement about the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) is accurate?
o: It is a UK Act of Parliament that can be enforced directly in any UK court
It is a NICE guideline setting national quality standards for disability services
It is a European directive that replaced the Equality Act 2010 in the UK
It is an international treaty including the right to live independently in the community
6.w: The UNCRPD is a United Nations human rights treaty ratified by the UK. It sets out the rights of disabled people, including Article 19, living independently and being included in the community, and Article 12, equal recognition before the law.

n.0: It is an international treaty, not a UK statute directly enforceable in the courts.
n.1: It is not a NICE guideline.
n.2: It is a UN convention, and the Equality Act 2010 remains in force.

6.q: Mrs Adeyemi, 72, has capacity and a leg ulcer. When the nurse arrives to change the dressing she says firmly that she does not want it done today because she is tired. The dressing is not urgent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Change the dressing gently because it is in her best interests
Respect her decision, explore her reasons and record the refusal
Ask her daughter to persuade her to accept the dressing change
Assess her capacity because she is refusing recommended care
6.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment. Mrs Adeyemi has capacity, so her refusal is valid. The nurse should explore why, explain any consequences, offer another time and document the refusal.

n.0: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity (MCA s4); treating a capacitous person against her refusal is unlawful.
n.2: Using a relative to pressure her undermines the voluntariness of any later consent.
n.3: Refusing care is not evidence of incapacity; MCA s1(4) says an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity, and capacity is presumed.

6.q: Sana, a nurse who trained in Canada, joins a UK learning disability team and refers to 'people with an intellectual disability'. A colleague asks whether this is the same group. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is the international term for the group UK services describe as having a learning disability
It refers to specific learning difficulties such as dyslexia, dyscalculia and dyspraxia
It describes a milder condition than a learning disability as defined by UK services
It is the statutory term used for this group in section 1 of the Mental Health Act 1983
6.w: 'Intellectual disability' is the term used internationally (and in ICD-11 as disorders of intellectual development) for the same group described as having a learning disability in UK health and social care.

n.1: Dyslexia and dyspraxia are specific learning difficulties; they do not affect general intellectual ability.
n.2: The terms describe the same range of severity, not a milder group.
n.3: The 1983 Act uses 'learning disability' (s1(4)), not 'intellectual disability'.

6.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
6.q: Lewis, 30, has a profound learning disability and very limited movement. He sleeps every night on his side with both knees dropped to the same side. Over time, which body shape change is most likely?
o: Windswept hips with risk of hip dislocation
Improved lung expansion on the upper side
Flat feet from lack of weight bearing
Stronger trunk muscles from side lying
6.w: Lying in the same asymmetric position for long periods causes the knees to fall to one side, producing a 'windswept' hip pattern, pelvic rotation, hip dislocation and scoliosis. Supported symmetrical lying protects body shape.

n.1: Lying fixed on one side does not improve lung expansion; the asymmetry it causes can lead to scoliosis that restricts the chest over time.
n.2: Foot posture may change, but the classic risk from this position is windswept hips.
n.3: Side lying in one position does not strengthen the trunk; it promotes asymmetry.

6.q: Kemi, a newly qualified nurse on an assessment and treatment unit, notices staff mocking a patient, restraint episodes left unrecorded and families discouraged from visiting the ward. Mindful of the lessons of Winterbourne View and Whorlton Hall, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Speak privately to the staff involved and monitor whether it continues
Record her observations in her reflective account for revalidation
Raise the concern at the next team meeting so standards can be agreed together
Escalate promptly to senior managers and the safeguarding lead
6.w: These are warning signs of a closed culture and possible abuse. The Code requires nurses to act without delay where there is a risk to patient safety, raising and escalating concerns (standard 16 and 16.1), and to raise concerns immediately where a person is vulnerable or at risk (standard 17 and 17.1), using whistleblowing routes if needed; safeguarding procedures must be followed (Care Act 2014 s42).

n.0: Informal monitoring allows abuse to continue and leaves no formal record; escalation is required.
n.1: Reflection is no substitute for acting; patients remain at risk while nothing is reported.
n.2: Waiting for a team meeting delays protection and may expose the concern to the people involved.

6.q: Tunde, a student learning disability nurse, is writing an essay on how healthcare for people with a learning disability came under scrutiny. He needs the 2007 Mencap report that described the deaths of six people in NHS care and argued that the NHS institutionally discriminated against them. Which report is this?
o: Death by Indifference
Healthcare for All
The Confidential Inquiry (CIPOLD)
Building the Right Support
6.w: Mencap's Death by Indifference (2007) set out six avoidable deaths of people with a learning disability in NHS care and alleged institutional discrimination. On publication the Health Secretary ordered an independent inquiry led by Sir Jonathan Michael (Mencap).

n.1: Healthcare for All (2008) was the independent inquiry set up in response to Death by Indifference, not the Mencap report itself.
n.2: CIPOLD (2013) reviewed a large population of deaths in south west England; it did not focus on six cases.
n.3: Building the Right Support (2015) is the national plan to reduce inpatient care after Winterbourne View.

6.q: Mr Evans, 69, has expressive aphasia after a stroke. He understands speech but struggles to find words. Which approach best supports communication?
o: Finish his sentences for him to reduce his frustration
Use closed questions, picture boards and extra time
Ask his wife to answer all questions on his behalf
Speak more loudly and repeat each sentence twice
6.w: Annexe A 2.5: identify the need for and manage alternative communication techniques. Code 7.3: use a range of verbal and non-verbal methods.

n.0: Finishing sentences may misrepresent what he means and reduces his control.
n.2: He can understand and should be supported to communicate for himself.
n.3: His difficulty is expressing words, not hearing; volume does not help.

6.q: Malik, 50, has suspected sepsis with a NEWS2 of 5. How often should his NEWS2 be recalculated under NICE NG253 (2025)?
o: Hourly
Every 4-6 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 30 minutes
6.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.6.5: recalculate NEWS2 every 30 minutes for high risk, hourly for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6), every 4-6 hours for low risk.

n.1: 4-6 hourly is for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.2: 12-hourly is the general NEWS2 minimum for a score of 0, not for suspected sepsis at 5.
n.3: Every 30 minutes is for high risk (NEWS2 7 or more).

6.q: Mrs Dawson, 84, has a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and is on a ward in England. She tells the nurse she wants to go home today rather than wait for physiotherapy. A junior doctor says, 'She has dementia, so she can't make that decision.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: She can go home, because a person with dementia keeps all their rights
A best interests meeting should be arranged before any assessment
Her capacity for this decision must be assessed, not assumed from diagnosis
Her daughter should be asked to decide, as she is her next of kin
6.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it. s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's condition. Capacity must be assessed for this decision at this time.

n.0: Whether she can safely go home depends on whether she has capacity for this decision; that has not yet been assessed.
n.1: Best interests decisions (s4) follow a finding that the person lacks capacity; the assessment comes first.
n.3: Next of kin has no legal power to make decisions for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.

6.q: Ruby, 24, has a learning disability and has been on an inpatient unit for 14 months. Her clinical team say she no longer needs hospital care, but no community provider has been found. Her mother asks what can help. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Request a C(E)TR to identify discharge barriers and who will act on them
Suggest a transfer to a nearer hospital until a provider is found
Ask the consultant to apply for Ruby to be detained under section 3
Advise that Ruby must stay until her discharge plan is fully funded
6.w: Two-step reasoning: Ruby is clinically ready for discharge but delayed by a lack of community support. C(E)TRs review barriers to discharge and set actions with named owners; Building the Right Support aims to reduce long inpatient stays and develop community services (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy; BRS).

n.1: A move to another hospital keeps her in inpatient care she no longer needs.
n.2: Detention is not justified when she no longer needs hospital treatment and would not help discharge.
n.3: Waiting passively accepts an inappropriate delay rather than challenging the barriers.

6.q: Max, 33, has a moderate learning disability and is anxious about his planned knee operation. His learning disability liaison nurse is planning reasonable adjustments. Which adjustment is most likely to reduce his anxiety on the day?
o: Arranging a pre-admission visit to see the ward and meet staff
Admitting him the night before so he can settle in overnight
Keeping details from him until the day so he does not worry
Giving him a sedative premedication on arrival at the ward
6.w: A pre-admission visit lets the person see the environment and meet staff in advance, making the day familiar and predictable. This is a common reasonable adjustment (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7).

n.1: An extra night in an unfamiliar ward may increase anxiety rather than reduce it.
n.2: Withholding information makes the day less predictable and may increase distress.
n.3: Sedation is a more restrictive option and does not replace preparation.

6.q: Ronald, 80, is prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch, changed every 72 hours. The new patch is due today. His previous patch is on his upper left chest. What is the correct way to apply the new patch?
o: Apply the new patch to the same area once the old one has been removed
Remove the old patch and apply the new one to a different area of skin
Apply the new patch, then remove the old one at the next 72-hour change
Apply the new patch over the old one to maintain a steady dose
6.w: For transdermal patches the old patch is removed before the new one is applied, sites are rotated to reduce skin irritation, and the patch goes on clean, dry, hairless skin (AnnexB.11.8). Leaving an old fentanyl patch in place causes opioid toxicity.

n.0: Reusing the same site raises the risk of skin irritation and altered absorption.
n.2: Leaving the old patch for another 72 hours doubles the dose for that period.
n.3: Two patches at once would double the fentanyl dose and risk respiratory depression.

6.q: Marcus Bell, 66, is on a surgical ward. His observations are: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on air, BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, alert, temperature 37.2°C. His NEWS2 total is 3. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Increase observations to at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat the observations in 4 hours and escalate if the total rises
Continue 4 to 6 hourly observations as the total score is below 5
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
6.w: A respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3 in a single parameter (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Chart 1). A score of 3 in any one parameter triggers a low-medium clinical risk response: minimum 1-hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team, who decide whether escalation is needed (Chart 4). Two steps: calculate the parameter score, then apply the single-parameter rule.

n.1: Four-hourly review delays recognition of deterioration when a single parameter is already scoring 3.
n.2: The aggregate of 3 is low, but a single red score of 3 overrides this and requires at least hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.3: Emergency critical care assessment is the response to an aggregate of 7 or more; this is an urgent ward-based response.

6.q: On a busy surgical ward, a doctor asks Holly, a staff nurse, to get a healthcare assistant to give a prescribed dose of intravenous antibiotic so that it is not late. The healthcare assistant has not been trained in IV administration. What should Holly do?
o: Delay the dose until the evening medicines round, when more nurses are on duty
Give the IV dose herself or arrange for another competent registrant to give it
Delegate the IV dose and supervise the healthcare assistant closely at the bedside
Ask the doctor to give the dose, as the healthcare assistant is not trained
6.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence. An untrained healthcare assistant cannot safely give IV medicines, so the dose must be given by a competent registrant without undue delay (Code 18.1; P5.4 roles and scope of practice of team members).

n.0: Delaying a prescribed antibiotic risks harm when a competent nurse can give it now.
n.2: Supervision does not make delegation appropriate when the person lacks the training and competence for the task.
n.3: The doctor could give it, but medicine administration is within Holly's own role; passing it back adds delay without a reason.

6.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
6.q: Carl, 29, is autistic and has a learning disability. A gym run by the council bars him after he became distressed and shouted when the music was too loud, which staff know relates to his sensory needs. Which form of discrimination is most likely?
o: Discrimination arising from disability, unless a proportionate means of a legitimate aim
Direct discrimination, because the gym treated him less favourably for being disabled
Harassment, because the gym's decision violated his dignity and created a hostile environment
Victimisation, because he was barred after making a complaint
6.w: Equality Act 2010 s15: unfavourable treatment because of something arising in consequence of a person's disability (here distress linked to sensory needs), which the provider knows about, is discrimination unless it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. A failure to adjust (turning the music down) may also apply.

n.1: Direct discrimination is less favourable treatment because of disability itself; here it is because of behaviour arising from it.
n.2: Harassment is unwanted conduct related to disability that creates a hostile environment; this is a decision to bar him.
n.3: Victimisation is treatment because of a protected act such as a complaint, which did not happen here.

6.q: Code standard 19.2 asks nurses to take account of current evidence and knowledge about human factors. During preceptorship, Jade is asked which definition of human factors the Code refers to. Which is correct?
o: The physical and mental health conditions that may affect a registrant's fitness to practise safely
The personal values and beliefs that staff bring to their work and that can influence patient care
The study of individual mistakes so that staff responsible for errors can be identified and retrained
Environmental, organisational and job factors, and individual characteristics that affect behaviour at work
6.w: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety (P5.2).

n.0: Health and fitness to practise is covered by Code 20.9 and NMC processes, not by the definition of human factors.
n.1: Personal beliefs are addressed by Code 20.7; the human factors definition is wider and centres on work systems.
n.2: Human factors looks at how systems shape performance, not at singling out individuals for blame or retraining.

6.q: Ellen, 29, had wheeze, hypotension and urticaria after eating a prawn curry on the ward. She improved after one dose of IM adrenaline and is now stable. The doctor plans her period of observation and later allergy referral. Which blood test should be taken to support the diagnosis?
o: Two sets of blood cultures
Mast cell tryptase level
Serum troponin level
Full blood count and film
6.w: RCUK guidance: take mast cell tryptase samples to help confirm anaphylaxis and support specialist allergy follow-up. Observation is risk-stratified, with a minimum of 6 hours in most people and 12 hours in higher-risk groups, or fast-track after 2 hours in selected cases.

n.0: Blood cultures are taken for suspected infection, not allergy.
n.2: Troponin assesses myocardial injury and does not confirm anaphylaxis.
n.3: FBC does not confirm anaphylaxis.

6.q: Mr Pearce, 67, has capacity and peripheral vascular disease. After a full explanation of the risks, he declines a recommended below-knee amputation, saying he would rather take his chances. The team thinks this is an unwise choice. Which principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies most directly?
o: Making an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity
Any act done for a person must be in their best interests
The less restrictive option must be considered first
All practicable steps must be taken to help the person decide
6.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Mr Pearce has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (Code 2.5).

n.1: Best interests (s1(5)) applies to acts for people who lack capacity; Mr Pearce has capacity.
n.2: The less restrictive principle (s1(6)) applies when acting for someone who lacks capacity.
n.3: Supporting decision-making (s1(3)) has already been met by the full explanation; the issue now is respecting an unwise choice.

6.q: A learning disability nurse joins a review of an inpatient unit. Learning from long-stay hospitals, Winterbourne View and Whorlton Hall, which combination of features most strongly suggests a risk of abuse?
o: A large staff team with a mix of registered nurses and support workers
A service that holds weekly multidisciplinary reviews with families
A unit that uses positive behaviour support plans for every patient
A closed culture: isolation, people far from home and few outside visitors
6.w: Abuse in learning disability settings has repeatedly occurred in closed cultures: people placed far from home, isolated from families and outside scrutiny, with poor leadership and power imbalances (CQC closed cultures learning after Whorlton Hall).

n.0: A mixed staff team is normal and not in itself a warning sign.
n.1: Regular family involvement increases outside scrutiny and reduces risk.
n.2: PBS plans for each person are good practice, not a warning sign.

6.q: Eve, a practice development nurse, is writing a policy on learning disability and autism training. She needs to cite the legal source and start date of the requirement for CQC-registered providers. Which citation is correct?
o: Care Act 2014 section 42, in force from 1 April 2015
Equality Act 2010 section 20, in force from 1 October 2010
Mental Capacity Act 2005 section 1, in force from 1 October 2007
Health and Care Act 2022 section 181, in force from 1 July 2022
6.w: Section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 introduced the requirement, through the Health and Social Care Act 2008 and regulation 18 of the 2014 Regulations, that from 1 July 2022 CQC-registered providers ensure staff receive learning disability and autism training appropriate to their role (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: Section 42 of the Care Act 2014 is the safeguarding enquiry duty.
n.1: Section 20 of the Equality Act 2010 is the reasonable adjustment duty.
n.2: Section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 sets out its five principles.

6.q: While walking to the nurses' station, Chloe, a staff nurse, notices a large pool of spilled water on the corridor floor outside a bay where several patients walk with frames. Nobody else is nearby. What should Chloe do first?
o: Complete an incident report so the hazard is recorded for the ward manager
Ask the domestic team to mop the floor when they reach the ward this afternoon
Make the area safe straight away with a warning sign and arrange for it to be dried
Tell the patients in the bay at the next ward round to avoid that corridor
6.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 require nurses to act promptly on hazards, and s7 Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires reasonable care for others. Removing an immediate slip hazard comes first; reporting follows (P6.6 respond to potential hazards).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate but should follow making the area safe; the hazard remains while the form is completed.
n.1: Leaving a known slip hazard until the afternoon exposes patients with frames to falls.
n.3: Warning patients later does not remove the hazard now and relies on people remembering.

6.q: A healthcare assistant in a care home in England is found to have left Mr Garner, who lacks capacity, in a soiled bed without food for a whole day on purpose. The manager asks the nurse what legal status this conduct has. What should the nurse say?
o: It is an offence under the Care Act 2014 safeguarding section
It may be a criminal offence of wilful neglect under MCA s44
It is a regulatory matter for the CQC with no criminal liability
It is a disciplinary matter for the employer to deal with
6.w: MCA 2005 s44 makes it an offence for a person who has the care of someone who lacks capacity to ill-treat or wilfully neglect them; on indictment the maximum is 5 years' imprisonment. It should also be raised as a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Care Act s42 places a duty on the local authority to make enquiries; it does not create this offence.
n.2: CQC regulates the provider, but s44 creates individual criminal liability.
n.3: Employer discipline may follow, but deliberate neglect of a person lacking capacity is also a potential criminal offence.

6.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
6.q: In October 2026, a ward manager says that under the Mental Health Act 2025 a person can no longer be detained under section 3 on the basis of a learning disability or autism alone. Is she correct?
o: No, the change is in the 2025 Act but has not yet come into force
Yes, the change took effect on Royal Assent in December 2025
Yes, the change was commenced across England in April 2026
No, the change was removed from the Bill before Royal Assent
6.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 (Royal Assent 18 December 2025) amends the 1983 Act so that section 3 will require a psychiatric disorder, but sections 3-4 and Schedule 1 are shown as prospective (not in force) on legislation.gov.uk in October 2026. The 1983 Act as amended remains the current law.

n.1: Royal Assent did not bring these provisions into force; they await commencement.
n.2: These provisions were not commenced in April 2026.
n.3: The change is in the Act as passed; it simply has not been commenced.

6.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
6.q: Rina, 40, has a learning disability and does not use speech. She communicates with Makaton signs and eye pointing to pictures. Staff are satisfied she understands and weighs the choice of having a flu vaccine. How should her decision be treated?
o: As not valid, because she cannot state her decision in spoken words
As valid once a family member has confirmed what she meant
As not valid until she has confirmed it in writing with a witness
As valid, because she can communicate it by signs or eye pointing
6.w: MCA s3(1)(d): a person is unable to make a decision if they cannot communicate it 'by talking, using sign language or any other means'. Rina can communicate by signs and eye pointing, so she meets this part of the test.

n.0: The Act accepts any means of communication, not only speech.
n.1: Her decision is her own; a relative's confirmation is not required for validity.
n.2: There is no requirement for written confirmation of consent to a vaccine.

6.q: Rose, 70, an inpatient on a medical ward, has new dysuria and frequency. She is alert with a NEWS2 score of 1. The doctor prescribes oral nitrofurantoin. No urine sample has been sent. What should the nurse do before giving the first dose?
o: Send a sample after 48 hours if her symptoms have not improved
Obtain a urine sample first, then give the antibiotic without delay
Give the first dose now and send a sample with her next void
Withhold the antibiotic until the urine culture result is available
6.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.27: for patients in hospital who have suspected infections, take microbiological samples before prescribing an antimicrobial and review the prescription when results are available. Collecting the sample first takes minutes and does not delay treatment.

n.0: Delaying the sample for 48 hours loses the chance to guide treatment, contrary to NG15.
n.2: A sample taken after the antibiotic may give a false negative culture, so the prescription cannot be reviewed against reliable results.
n.3: Treatment is not delayed until culture returns; the sample is taken first and the drug given promptly.

6.q: Mr Price, 69, has COPD, type 2 diabetes and depression. He is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. His SpO2 is 85% on air and he is struggling to finish sentences; his capillary glucose is 11.2 mmol/L. Which need should the nurse prioritise first?
o: His dietary intake and weight
His raised blood glucose
His low mood and anxiety
His breathing and oxygenation
6.w: When prioritising care for a person with comorbidities (P3.13), immediate threats to life come first. Severe hypoxaemia and breathlessness are an airway and breathing priority needing escalation and oxygen to a prescribed target; the other needs are addressed once he is stable.

n.0: Nutrition is important for recovery but is not the immediate priority.
n.1: A glucose of 11.2 mmol/L needs monitoring but is not an immediate threat compared with hypoxaemia.
n.2: His mood matters but is not the most urgent need while he is hypoxic.

6.q: Ayesha, 30, has a learning disability and uses her own signs, which her support worker understands. During a consultation the doctor directs all questions to the support worker. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the support worker to leave so Ayesha can answer for herself
Arrange a separate meeting with the support worker to gather the history
Ask the doctor to speak to Ayesha, with the support worker helping interpret
Let the support worker answer, as she knows Ayesha best
6.w: Communication should be directed to the person, with others helping only to support understanding. This respects Ayesha's dignity and right to be involved (Code 2.1, 7; Annexe A 2.5; MCA s1(3)).

n.0: Removing the person who understands her signs would make communication harder.
n.1: A separate meeting still bypasses Ayesha and misses the chance to hear from her.
n.3: Talking about Ayesha rather than to her excludes her from her own care.

6.q: Mr Blake, 85, has dementia and was admitted two days ago with pneumonia. Staff describe him as 'a lovely quiet man' who sleeps most of the day, eats little and is slow to respond. His family say he is usually chatty. What should the nurse suspect?
o: Hypoactive delirium needing assessment
Expected tiredness from his pneumonia
Progression of his dementia over two days
Low mood related to being in hospital
6.w: NICE CG103 notes hypoactive delirium is easily missed. Recent changes in cognition, physical function (reduced movement, appetite, sleep) and social behaviour (withdrawal), reported by family, are indicators of delirium needing assessment with the 4AT (rec 1.3.1, 1.6.1).

n.1: Attributing a marked change from his baseline to tiredness risks missing delirium.
n.2: Dementia progresses gradually; a change over two days points to delirium.
n.3: Low mood may cause withdrawal, but slowed responses and drowsiness developing over days point to delirium first.

6.q: Frank, 63, is prescribed oral morphine solution 2.5-5 mg as required every 2 hours for pain. He had 2.5 mg 4 hours ago with little effect and now rates his pain 8/10. He is alert with a respiratory rate of 16. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 2.5 mg now and repeat it in 30 minutes if needed
Give 7.5 mg, as the previous 2.5 mg dose was ineffective
Withhold the dose until the doctor increases the prescription
Give 5 mg, the top of the prescribed range, and reassess
6.w: Titration within a prescribed range is a nurse's decision based on assessment (AnnexB.11.5). The previous dose was ineffective, he is not sedated and 2 hours have passed, so the higher dose within the range is appropriate, with reassessment of pain, sedation and respiratory rate.

n.0: Repeating at 30 minutes breaches the 2-hourly minimum interval.
n.1: 7.5 mg exceeds the prescribed range, which the nurse cannot change.
n.2: A suitable dose is available within the range; withholding leaves him in pain.

6.q: Liam, 22, attends an emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high using a scoring tool, and says 'low' scores can be discharged without referral. According to NICE NG225, how should the nurse approach this?
o: Not use the score to predict risk or decide on discharge
Complete the score and refer him to liaison psychiatry if it is high
Repeat the score each hour until he is discharged
Use the score to decide whether to refer him to liaison psychiatry
6.w: NICE NG225 (2022) recs 1.6.1-1.6.3: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged; do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification.

n.1: Restricting referral to high scores is risk stratification, which NG225 advises against.
n.2: Repeating a tool does not make it a valid predictor; NG225 advises against using it for this purpose.
n.3: NG225 says tools must not decide who is offered treatment; liaison psychiatry referral should be offered after self-harm.

6.q: The son of a patient on a medical ward is shouting at the nurses' station because he was not told his father had been moved to another bay. He is red-faced and pacing. What should the nurse, Bryony, do first?
o: Call security straight away so that he can be escorted off the ward
Tell him firmly that shouting is unacceptable and that he must lower his voice
Speak calmly, acknowledge his frustration and offer to talk somewhere quieter
Explain that the move happened because of bed pressures beyond her control
6.w: De-escalation uses a calm tone and non-threatening body language, acknowledges the person's feelings, and moves the conversation away from an audience, while keeping a safe distance and exit route (AnnexA.4.2.5 de-escalation strategies when dealing with conflict).

n.0: Security may be needed if there is a risk of violence, but there is no threat here and calling them first may escalate the situation.
n.1: Leading with a demand can escalate anger before his concern is acknowledged.
n.3: Explaining reasons before acknowledging his feelings can sound defensive and does not de-escalate.

6.q: Nadia, 34, has a screen-positive result from an NHS screening programme. She is anxious and asks the nurse what this result means. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: She may have the condition and will be offered tests to confirm it
She has the condition and will now start treatment straight away
The result is likely to be a false positive, so no action is needed
She should repeat the same screening test again in 5 years' time
6.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): a screen-positive (higher-risk) result means you may have the condition; you will be offered diagnostic tests to confirm whether you have it, then treatment, advice and support.

n.1: A screening test is not diagnostic; diagnostic tests are needed to confirm the condition first.
n.2: Screen-positive results lead to diagnostic tests; they cannot be assumed to be false.
n.3: A screen-positive result leads to diagnostic testing, not routine re-screening.

6.q: A learning disability nurse is teaching staff about restraint under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 for adults who lack capacity. Which statement correctly describes when restraint is lawful under s6?
o: When it is needed to make the person follow the daily routine
When it is in the person's best interests and the family have agreed
When it prevents harm to the person and is proportionate to that harm
When it is written in the care plan and signed by the manager
6.w: MCA 2005 s6: restraint is permitted only if the person taking action reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to the person who lacks capacity, and the act is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. It must also be in the person's best interests (s5).

n.0: Securing compliance with a routine is not prevention of harm and does not meet s6.
n.1: Family agreement is not the legal test; s6 requires necessity to prevent harm and proportionality.
n.3: Documentation is good practice, but a signed plan does not make a disproportionate restraint lawful.

6.q: Mr Dunn, 66, is going home on a new medicine. He says he 'doesn't get on with reading' and has left his leaflet unopened. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explain in plain words with pictures, then use teach-back
Explain it once in full medical terms to be accurate
Ask the pharmacist to post a copy of the leaflet to him
Give him a second copy of the leaflet in larger print
6.w: Proficiency P2.10: provide information in accessible ways; Annexe A 2.2 clear language and appropriate materials; Annexe A 2.6 repetition and positive reinforcement; Code 7.4 check understanding.

n.1: Medical terms reduce understanding; Code 7.1 requires terms people can understand.
n.2: Posting the same written information will not help him understand it.
n.3: Larger print does not address difficulty with reading.

6.q: Mrs Price, 88, has advanced dementia and has been assessed as lacking capacity to decide about a feeding tube. The team is making a best interests decision. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4 checklist, which should the decision maker take into account?
o: Her past wishes, beliefs and values, as reported by those close to her
Her son's own preference, because he is recorded as next of kin
The option that places the least demand on the ward's nursing time
Her age and diagnosis, as the main guide to her likely outcome
6.w: MCA 2005 s4(6) requires consideration of the person's past and present wishes and feelings, beliefs and values; s4(7) requires consulting carers and others interested in her welfare about what she would want. s4(1) prohibits basing the decision on age or condition alone.

n.1: Relatives are consulted about what the person would want; their own preference does not decide the matter.
n.2: Staff convenience is not part of the s4 checklist; the focus is the person's best interests.
n.3: s4(1) states a best interests determination must not be made merely on the basis of age or condition.

6.q: Mavis, 81, has died on a medical ward. Her two sons arrive an hour later and say they are unsure whether they want to see her body, as they have never seen someone who has died. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Tell them viewing is possible once she has reached the funeral director
Offer them the chance to see her and prepare them for what to expect
Advise them not to view her so they remember her as she was in life
Explain that viewing on the ward is allowed after the doctor's review
6.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): all key contacts should be offered the opportunity to view the deceased; there is evidence that, even in traumatic circumstances, key contacts found this helpful. Viewing can occur in acute hospitals, some hospices or later at the funeral directors. Prepare people sensitively for changes to the body.

n.0: Viewing can take place in hospitals and hospices, so there is no need to delay it until later.
n.2: Hospice UK guidance says all key contacts should be offered the chance to view; many find it helpful.
n.3: Viewing does not depend on a doctor's review once death has been verified.

6.q: Dennis, 70, has a deep laceration to his forearm from a fall on the ward. Blood is spurting and soaking through the dressing despite firm direct pressure. You have called for help. What should be done next?
o: Elevate the arm and wait for the bleeding to stop
Apply an ice pack directly to the wound site
Apply a tourniquet 5-7 cm above the wound
Remove the soaked dressing and press on a new one
6.w: RCUK first aid 2025: use direct pressure and a haemostatic dressing; apply a tourniquet as soon as possible for life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure, 5-7 cm above the injury and not over a joint, recording the time applied.

n.0: Elevation is not part of the RCUK 2025 escalating approach (pressure, haemostatic dressing, tourniquet) and waiting delays control.
n.1: Ice does not control arterial bleeding.
n.3: Removing the dressing disturbs clot formation; pressure is maintained and escalated.

6.q: Ama is due to revalidate next month. Her CPD log shows 35 hours: 18 hours at a study day and team workshops, and 17 hours reading journal articles on her own. What is the position on her CPD requirement?
o: She needs five more hours of any type of CPD
She needs two more hours of participatory learning
She needs fifteen more hours of participatory learning
She meets it, as she has 35 hours in total
6.w: NMC revalidation CPD requirement (updated 08/09/2021): 35 hours of CPD in three years, of which at least 20 must include participatory learning. 20 - 18 = 2 participatory hours still needed.

n.0: Her total of 35 is already met; the shortfall is in participatory hours, not overall hours.
n.2: She needs 20 participatory hours in total; with 18 already logged, the gap is two hours.
n.3: The total is met, but at least 20 of the 35 hours must be participatory; she has 18.

6.q: Ryan, 12, is autistic and finds noise, bright light and waiting very distressing. He is due for a dental check at a busy community clinic. Which adjustment reflects NICE CG170?
o: Send a written reminder to his parents the day before the visit
Book a mid-morning appointment when the clinic is fully staffed
Ask a staff member to sit with him in the main waiting area throughout
Offer the first or last appointment of the day and a quiet place
6.w: NICE CG170 1.1.9-1.1.10 advises adjusting the environment for autistic children and young people, including attention to lighting, noise and personal space, and offering appointments at the beginning or end of the day to minimise waiting.

n.0: A reminder is helpful but does not reduce the sensory load or wait.
n.1: A mid-morning slot is likely to involve more waiting and a busier environment.
n.2: Company does not remove the noise, light and waiting that cause his distress.

6.q: Single rooms are full on a respiratory ward. Two patients with the same confirmed respiratory virus are to be cohorted in a bay. Under current NIPCM guidance, what is the minimum separation between their beds?
o: At least 0.5 metres between the bed spaces
At least 3 metres between the bed spaces
At least 2 metres between the bed spaces
At least 1 metre between the bed spaces
6.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 states cohorted infectious patients should be separated by at least 3 feet (1 metre) with the door closed. Droplet precautions use at least 1 metre; the 2 metres introduced during COVID-19 has reverted to 1 metre in all areas.

n.0: Half a metre is below the 1 metre minimum for separation in a cohort.
n.1: 3 metres exceeds the NIPCM standard; the distance given is 3 feet, which is about 1 metre.
n.2: 2 metres was a COVID-19 measure that NIPCM says has returned to 1 metre.

6.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
6.q: Bethany, 46, has a learning disability and has had no proper bowel movement for eight days. Staff now report frequent small amounts of liquid stool leaking into her pad. They plan to give loperamide for diarrhoea. What should the nurse advise?
o: Start a stool chart and review in a week
Withhold it and seek review for impaction with overflow
Give the loperamide as planned and monitor her fluid intake
Give extra fluids and restart her normal diet
6.w: Two-step reasoning: liquid leakage after days without a proper stool suggests overflow around impacted faeces. Antidiarrhoeal treatment would worsen the impaction; she needs urgent medical assessment and treatment of constipation.

n.0: Waiting a week risks obstruction and perforation.
n.2: Loperamide slows the bowel and would worsen faecal impaction.
n.3: Fluids help but do not address the impaction needing medical treatment.

6.q: Iris, 70, dies on a general ward. She was on the NHS Organ Donor Register as wanting to donate. Her husband asks the nurse whether her wish to donate can still be met now that she has died on the ward. Which response is accurate?
o: The ward nurse can remove the corneas before transfer to the mortuary
Donation is not possible because she did not die in intensive care
Organs can be retrieved from the ward if it is within 24 hours of death
Tissue such as corneas may still be donated, up to 24 hours after death
6.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): organ donation is possible only from intensive care units and emergency departments and is organised before death; whole-body and tissue donation is possible after death, and cornea donation can take place up to 24 hours after death in hospitals, hospices and funeral homes.

n.0: Ward nurses do not retrieve tissue; donation is arranged with the specialist donation service.
n.1: This is true for organs, but tissue donation, including corneas, remains possible after death.
n.2: Organ donation is organised before death from intensive care or emergency departments; it cannot be arranged after a ward death.

6.q: A district nursing team wants to find out how patients rate their new evening visiting service, with no benchmark to compare against, by asking current patients to complete a short questionnaire. What type of project is this?
o: Qualitative research study
Clinical audit
Randomised controlled trial
Service evaluation
6.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): service evaluation asks 'What standard does this service achieve?', measures the current service without reference to a standard and does not need REC review.

n.0: It aims to judge the current service, not to generate generalisable knowledge.
n.1: Audit compares practice with a predetermined standard; here there is no standard.
n.2: There is no allocation to interventions or randomisation.

6.q: A functional assessment for Leo, 23, who has a learning disability, has been completed and a support plan started. Six weeks later, the nurse is evaluating the plan. Which measure best shows whether the plan is working?
o: The number of staff who have read and signed the plan
The number of PRN doses given during the six weeks
Staff ratings of whether Leo seems calmer than he was before the plan
Behaviour and quality-of-life data compared with the baseline
6.w: NICE NG11 1.5.10 asks for a baseline of the behaviour (frequency, severity, duration) and of quality of life, so that the effect of interventions can be measured against it; evaluation compares current data with that baseline (P3.15).

n.0: Staff sign-off shows the plan was shared, not whether it changed outcomes for Leo.
n.1: PRN use is one indicator, but on its own it does not measure behaviour or quality of life against the baseline.
n.2: Impressions are less reliable than measured data compared with the baseline.

6.q: Amira, 46, has Down syndrome. Her support staff report she has lost interest in activities, is tearful and sleeps poorly. She can still dress and cook with her usual prompts. Which possibility should be assessed alongside dementia?
o: Lack of motivation
Normal ageing
Learned helplessness
Depression
6.w: Depression can mimic early dementia (withdrawal, poor sleep, apparent decline) and is treatable. NICE NG54 asks for full assessment of mental and physical health; her preserved skills make depression a strong alternative to exclude.

n.0: Labelling the change as lack of motivation is diagnostic overshadowing.
n.1: Tearfulness and loss of interest are not part of normal ageing.
n.2: This is a behavioural concept, not a diagnosis to exclude; it would not explain tearfulness and poor sleep.

6.q: Asif, 55, weighs 70 kg and is nil by mouth after surgery. He needs routine IV maintenance fluids. Using NICE CG174, what is the appropriate total daily water range?
6.w: NICE CG174: 25-30 mL/kg/day. 70 kg x 25 = 1,750 mL; 70 kg x 30 = 2,100 mL. CG174 also notes that intake rarely needs to exceed 3 L/day.

n.0: 700-1,050 mL uses 10-15 mL/kg/day, below CG174 maintenance.
n.2: 3,500-4,200 mL is well above maintenance and risks overload.
n.3: 2,800-3,500 mL uses 40-50 mL/kg/day, above maintenance.

6.q: A public health team plans to reduce average salt intake across a region by working with manufacturers to lower the salt content of bread and processed foods. Which statement best describes this strategy?
o: Secondary prevention that detects raised blood pressure at an early stage
A high-risk approach targeting people already diagnosed with hypertension
A population approach: a small benefit to each person but a large total benefit
Tertiary prevention to reduce disability in people who have had strokes
6.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the population approach recognises that society influences individual behaviour and reduces risk at population level. The prevention paradox (Rose): most people who lower their risk will not benefit directly, although the total benefit across the population is large.

n.0: No one is being tested or detected; this lowers exposure to a risk factor across the population.
n.1: The change affects everyone who buys the foods, not a selected high-risk group.
n.3: This is aimed at the whole population before disease develops, not at people with established disease.

6.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
6.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

6.q: Agnes, the nurse in charge of a busy surgical ward, wants the whole team to share the same understanding of which patients are at risk at the start of each shift. Which practice best supports this?
o: Each nurse reads the full medical notes of all patients before starting
Staff ask the nurse in charge about any patient they are worried about
A brief safety huddle after handover to share key risks and plans
The nurse in charge keeps a written list of risks in the ward office
6.w: Shared situational awareness, the team's common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is supported by short structured safety huddles where risks (deteriorating patients, falls, staffing) are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; P5.2; P6.6).

n.0: Reading all notes is impractical on a busy ward and does not create a shared team picture or agreed actions.
n.1: Relying on individuals to ask means risks are shared reactively and unevenly.
n.3: A list kept by one person does not share awareness across the team.

6.q: Nadia, a ward manager, learns that a staff nurse who raised a concern about a doctor's practice is now being left out of break rotas and ignored by some colleagues. What does the Code require Nadia to do?
o: Act to protect the nurse from detriment or victimisation
Wait for the concern to be investigated before taking any action
Advise the nurse to request a transfer to another ward
Report the nurse's colleagues to the NMC straight away
6.w: Code 16.5-16.6: do not obstruct, intimidate or victimise anyone raising a concern, and protect anyone you have management responsibility for from harm, detriment, victimisation or unwarranted treatment after a concern is raised.

n.1: The victimisation is happening now; Code 16.6 requires her to act to protect the nurse.
n.2: Moving the nurse penalises the person who raised the concern; Code 16.6 requires protection from detriment.
n.3: Local management action comes first; referral may follow if misconduct is serious, but protection is the duty now.

6.q: Jodie, a nurse new to a community learning disability team, is told that a 2011 BBC Panorama programme exposed the abuse of patients at Winterbourne View, a private inpatient hospital. Which national programme was the government's direct response?
o: The Transforming Care programme
The LeDeR mortality review programme
The Valuing People white paper
The STOMP medicines programme
6.w: After Winterbourne View the Department of Health published Transforming Care (2012), which aimed to move people out of inpatient units into community support; this led to Building the Right Support (2015) and the 2022 action plan (Commons Library SN07058).

n.1: LeDeR reviews deaths and grew from CIPOLD's recommendations, not the Winterbourne View response.
n.2: Valuing People was the 2001 learning disability white paper, ten years before Winterbourne View.
n.3: STOMP (2016) tackles overuse of psychotropic medicines; it was not the direct policy response to Winterbourne View.

6.q: A student nurse on a learning disability placement asks why the team spends weeks on a functional assessment before writing a behaviour support plan for Ayesha, 27. What is the best explanation?
o: It shows why the behaviour happens so support can target that need
It gives evidence that the behaviour is severe enough for admission
It identifies which staff members are causing the behaviour to happen
It is needed so that a referral for medication can be accepted
6.w: NICE NG11 1.5.6 recommends a written formulation of what led to the behaviour and the function it serves; this understanding is the basis for a support plan that meets the need, rather than simply suppressing the behaviour.

n.1: NG11 aims to support people in the least restrictive setting close to home, not to build a case for admission.
n.2: Staff interactions are one possible influence, but the assessment is not designed to find fault with individuals.
n.3: Medication is not the purpose of functional assessment; NG11 puts psychological and environmental approaches first.

6.q: Bryony, 38, has a profound learning disability and does not use pictures or signs. Staff want to help her anticipate that she is going swimming. Using objects of reference, what should they do?
o: Show her a photograph of the swimming pool
Sign 'swimming' in Makaton as they tell her
Give her a piece of her swimming towel to hold
Hand her a symbol card for swimming
6.w: An object of reference is a real object that stands for an activity, person or place, such as a towel for swimming, used with people who do not yet understand pictures or signs. It must be used consistently.

n.0: Photographs are more abstract than objects; Bryony does not use pictures.
n.1: Bryony does not use signs, so a sign alone will not convey the activity.
n.3: Symbols are more abstract than pictures and are not meaningful for her.

6.q: Leonard, 77, has heart failure and advanced bowel cancer with bowel obstruction. He is in the last days of life with persistent nausea and vomiting. Subcutaneous hyoscine butylbromide was started 24 hours ago, but his symptoms have not improved. Which action should the nurse discuss with the prescriber?
o: Continuing the same hyoscine dose for 72 hours more
Changing hyoscine to the intramuscular route
Adding cyclizine as the next option
Considering octreotide as the next option
6.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.5.22: for nausea or vomiting with obstructive bowel disorders in the last days of life, consider hyoscine butylbromide first line, then octreotide if symptoms do not improve within 24 hours. Rec 1.5.3: take into account risks such as cyclizine exacerbating heart failure.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.22 says consider octreotide if symptoms have not improved within 24 hours.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.3 notes that cyclizine may exacerbate heart failure, which Leonard has; octreotide is the NG31 next step.

6.q: Eric, 58, has a PEG tube. His paracetamol oral suspension, baclofen liquid and a dispersible aspirin tablet are due at 12:00. His feed is running. How should the nurse give these medicines?
o: Give all three, then flush once with water at the end
Give each separately, flushing with water before, between and after
Add the three medicines into the feed bag to run with the feed
Mix all three in one enteral syringe and give them together
6.w: For enteral tubes, each medicine is given separately in a suitable liquid or dispersed form via an enteral syringe, with the tube flushed with water before, between and after each medicine to prevent interactions and blockage (AnnexB.11.9; RPS/RCN references the NEWT guidelines). The feed is paused while medicines are given.

n.0: Without flushing between medicines they may interact in the tube and block it.
n.2: Adding medicines to feed risks incompatibility and unpredictable dosing if the feed stops.
n.3: Mixing medicines can cause physical or chemical incompatibilities and tube blockage.

6.q: At a team meeting, a district nursing team leader explains the integrated care partnership (ICP) in her area. Which statement about the ICP is correct?
o: It inspects and rates the quality of local health services
It is the NHS body that commissions hospital and GP services
It is a joint committee that develops the integrated care strategy
It employs the community nurses who work in the local area
6.w: The ICP is a joint committee run by the NHS organisations and upper-tier local authorities in each ICS, with wider partners such as the voluntary sector. It must develop a long-term integrated care strategy to improve health, care and wellbeing (NHS England, What is integrated care?; P7.1).

n.0: Inspection and rating are carried out by the Care Quality Commission in England.
n.1: Planning NHS services and managing the budget is the role of the integrated care board.
n.3: Community nurses are employed by provider organisations, not by the ICP.

6.q: Jim, 70, has a well-nourished diet and is at high risk of pressure ulcers. His wife asks whether he should take a nutritional supplement drink to prevent ulcers, and whether a nurse could massage his heels. According to NICE CG179, what is the best response?
o: Both are recommended to protect his skin and should be started
A supplement is recommended, but heel massage is not advised
Neither is recommended; focus on repositioning and heel offloading
Heel massage is recommended, but a supplement is not advised
6.w: NICE CG179: do not offer nutritional supplements specifically to prevent pressure ulcers in people whose intake is adequate, and do not offer skin massage or rubbing. Prevention relies on repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces and heel offloading for those at high risk.

n.0: CG179 advises against both measures in this situation.
n.1: Supplements are not recommended for prevention when intake is adequate.
n.3: Skin massage and rubbing are advised against in CG179.

6.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
6.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

6.q: The LeDeR report on deaths in 2023 (republished January 2026) compared deaths by severity of learning disability. Which finding is accurate?
o: People with a profound learning disability died at an average age of around 70
Age at death did not differ between levels of severity of learning disability
People with a severe or profound learning disability died younger, on average at 58
People with a mild learning disability died youngest because they had less support
6.w: LeDeR 2023 (revised January 2026): average age at death was 63 overall, but people with a severe or profound learning disability died at an average of 58 and were more likely to die of something treatable.

n.0: The average for severe or profound learning disability was 58, not around 70.
n.1: There was a clear difference: 58 for severe or profound against 63 overall.
n.3: The report found the opposite: greater severity was linked to earlier death.

6.q: Harold, 76, has COPD with a prescribed target of 88-92%. He is on 28% oxygen via a Venturi mask with SpO2 95%. He is alert and comfortable. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remove the mask and recheck his saturation in 4 hours
Reduce the oxygen concentration and recheck his saturation
Continue the current oxygen, as 95% is a reassuring level
Increase the oxygen to 35% to prevent a fall in saturation
6.w: BTS guideline: titrate oxygen to keep saturation within the prescribed target. Above 92% in someone at risk of hypercapnia risks CO2 retention, so step down (for example to 24%) and monitor closely. On Scale 2, 95% on oxygen also scores 2 points (RCP 2017).

n.0: Stopping oxygen abruptly without close monitoring risks rebound hypoxaemia.
n.2: 95% is above his prescribed range and risks hypercapnia.
n.3: Increasing oxygen pushes his saturation further above target.

6.q: A ward manager is introducing the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF) to her team. Which of the following is one of PSIRF's four stated aims?
o: Identifying the member of staff responsible for each incident
Reporting every patient safety incident directly to the regulator
A root cause analysis for every incident within a fixed timescale
Compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected
6.w: PSIRF (NHS England 2022, replacing the Serious Incident Framework 2015) has four aims: compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected; system-based approaches to learning; considered and proportionate responses; and supportive oversight focused on strengthening the response system (S-PSIRF).

n.0: PSIRF focuses on how incidents happen and contributory system factors, not on attributing individual blame.
n.1: PSIRF is a framework for provider learning responses; it does not require every incident to go to a regulator.
n.2: Fixed-timescale investigation of set categories was a feature of the Serious Incident Framework; PSIRF calls for proportionate, planned responses.

6.q: Zara, a first-year student nurse, asks to insert a urinary catheter for a patient. She has not yet been taught or practised the procedure. Her practice supervisor, Ama, is busy. What is the most appropriate response from Ama?
o: Carry out the procedure with Zara observing and explain each step
Ask a healthcare assistant to supervise Zara during the catheterisation
Ask Zara to read the procedure policy and then insert the catheter
Let Zara insert the catheter while Ama finishes her other tasks nearby
6.w: Delegation must be within the person's competence (Code 11.1). A student who has not been taught a procedure should first observe and then practise under direct supervision. Ama can use the opportunity to teach (P5.8 support and supervise students; AnnexA.4.1.1 clear explanations when teaching).

n.1: Supervision must come from someone competent in the procedure and in supporting the student; this does not meet the student's learning needs.
n.2: Reading a policy does not provide the skill and assessed competence needed.
n.3: Indirect supervision is unsafe for an aseptic invasive procedure the student has not learned.

6.q: Laura, a staff nurse, has worried for several weeks that the night skill mix on her ward is unsafe, with frequent missed observations. She has not yet raised it with anyone. According to NMC guidance, who should she raise it with first?
o: The NMC, so that it can investigate the ward's safety
The trust chief executive, as the person accountable for staffing
The Care Quality Commission, as the regulator for the ward
Her line manager, verbally or in writing, keeping a record
6.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: stage 1 line manager (verbally or in writing, keep a record); stage 2 designated person; stage 3 higher level; stage 4 regulator or helpline. Code 16.1.

n.0: The NMC regulates individual professionals; this is a system concern for the line manager first.
n.1: A higher level in the organisation is stage 3, after the line manager and designated person.
n.2: Going to a regulator is stage 4 of the NMC guidance, used if internal routes fail or are unsuitable.

6.q: Ruth, 63, has cellulitis and suspected sepsis. Her NEWS2 is 6, made up of RR 3 and three single points, and her worsening is thought to be due to the infection. Under NICE NG253 (2025), how should she be managed?
o: As high risk, with IV antibiotics within 1 hour
As very low risk, with standard observation frequency
As medium risk, with antibiotics deferred up to 3 hours
As low risk, with review by a registered practitioner in 1 hour
6.w: NG253: for a NEWS2 of 5-6 that includes a single parameter scoring 3, if this is likely to be due to the infection, manage as high risk. High risk means IV antibiotics within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score.

n.1: Very low risk applies to a NEWS2 of 0.
n.2: Medium-risk deferral does not apply where a single 3 is likely caused by the infection.
n.3: Low-risk management applies to NEWS2 1-4, not 6.

6.q: A community nurse is learning about the NHS England Core20PLUS5 approach to reducing healthcare inequalities in adults. What does 'Core20' refer to?
o: The 20% of the population who are aged 65 and over in each region
The 20% of adults living with the highest number of long-term health conditions
The most deprived 20% of the population, by the Index of Multiple Deprivation
The 20% of local areas with the highest rates of emergency hospital admission
6.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): Core20 is the most deprived 20% of the national population as identified by the national Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD); PLUS groups are identified locally; the 5 are clinical areas of focus.

n.0: Age is not the basis of Core20; it is the most deprived fifth of the population.
n.1: Core20 is defined by deprivation, not by the number of long-term conditions a person has.
n.3: Admission rates are not the measure; Core20 uses the national Index of Multiple Deprivation.

6.q: Monica, 55, had abdominal surgery five days ago. Her wound edges are now red and swollen, the area is hot and tender, and there is cloudy discharge. Her temperature is 38.4°C. Which conclusion best fits these findings?
o: The wound is in the normal maturation phase
The wound is showing signs of a moisture lesion
The wound shows a normal inflammatory response
The wound shows signs of infection
6.w: Increasing redness, swelling, heat, pain, purulent or cloudy exudate and fever at day 5 indicate wound infection, which needs escalation and review. Mild early inflammation in the first few days is normal, but it should be settling, not worsening (Annexe B 4.6).

n.0: Maturation (remodelling) is a late phase lasting months and does not cause fever and pus.
n.1: Moisture lesions are caused by incontinence or sweat on the skin, not surgical wound infection.
n.2: Normal inflammation is mild and settles early; worsening signs with fever suggest infection.

6.q: Sam, 41, has a moderate learning disability and lives in a group home. Since the death of a housemate he has been tearful and has told staff 'I want to be with Pete in heaven'. Staff think he does not understand what he is saying. What should the nurse do?
o: Wait until the next annual health check to raise it with the GP
Ask Sam directly and gently about thoughts of ending his life
Reassure staff that Sam is grieving and needs no further action
Distract Sam from talking about Pete to avoid upsetting him
6.w: People with a learning disability can experience suicidal thoughts and must not be assumed not to mean what they say. Asking directly and gently about suicidal thoughts is the first step to assessing and managing any risk, and research indicates that asking does not increase suicidal thinking. Mental health problems are common in people with a learning disability and may present differently (NICE NG54 1.2.8).

n.0: Delaying months leaves a possible risk unassessed now.
n.2: Grief is likely, but the statement needs exploring before deciding no action is needed.
n.3: Avoiding the subject denies Sam support and leaves any risk unassessed.

6.q: A doctor needs to tell Mrs Ibrahim, 70, who speaks Somali and limited English, that her husband has died in intensive care. Her adult niece is with her. What is the most appropriate way to communicate?
o: Wait until her son arrives to translate later that day
Use a professional Somali interpreter for the conversation
Give the news in simple English and check she understands
Ask the niece to interpret, as she is family and will support her
6.w: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; reliance on family is strongly discouraged. Code 7.2 meet language needs; Annexe A 2.9.

n.0: Delaying the news without reason causes distress; an interpreter can be arranged now.
n.2: Simple English risks misunderstanding when news is this serious.
n.3: Relying on family is discouraged; the niece is also grieving and may filter the news.

6.q: Ellie qualified six weeks ago. At the start of a night shift she is told she will be the only registered nurse for 28 patients on an unfamiliar ward, and has never taken charge. What should she do first?
o: Accept the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Raise her concerns at once with the person in charge and record it
Leave the ward and return to her own ward for safety
Accept the shift and phone her own ward manager at home
6.w: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Code 13.3 and NMC Raising concerns guidance support escalation and keeping a record.

n.0: Delaying until the morning leaves patients at risk; Code 16.2 requires her to raise concerns immediately.
n.2: Leaving abandons patients; she must raise the concern so safe cover is arranged.
n.3: Her absent manager cannot change tonight's staffing; the site lead or person in charge must be told now.

6.q: A practice nurse invites people with a BMI over 40 to an intensive weight-management programme rather than offering it to the whole practice population. Which advantage is associated with this high-risk approach?
o: It tackles the social influences on behaviour in the wider community
Those invited are often more motivated, as their personal risk is high
It removes the need to assess each person's individual risk factors
It brings the largest fall in disease across the whole population
6.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the high-risk approach may be more cost-effective than population-wide approaches and targets people who are more motivated to change their behaviour; the population approach achieves risk reduction at population level. NICE PH49 (2014) rec 9: high-intensity interventions for people at high risk, for example a BMI over 40.

n.0: Addressing social influences on the whole community is a feature of the population approach.
n.2: A high-risk approach depends on identifying individuals by assessing their risk.
n.3: A large fall in total disease is the strength of the population approach, not a high-risk approach.

6.q: Joanne is registered with the NMC as both a nurse and a midwife and is preparing to revalidate both registrations. How many practice hours must she show over the three-year period?
o: 900 hours, including 450 for each registration
675 hours, as half of the second registration counts
1,350 hours, including 450 for each registration
450 hours across both registrations combined
6.w: NMC revalidation, practice hours (page updated 26/05/2021): 450 hours for one registration, 900 hours for nurse and midwife (450 each), 1,350 for triple registration.

n.1: There is no pro rata reduction; each registration needs its own 450 hours.
n.2: 1,350 hours applies to triple registration as nurse, midwife and nursing associate.
n.3: 450 hours is the figure for a single registration; dual nurse and midwife registration requires 900.

6.q: A nurse on an intensive care unit in England is caring for four patients for whom organ donation after death may be possible. None has recorded a decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. Which patient is excluded from deemed consent?
o: Leah, 30, who had not discussed donation with her family
Amy, 17, a student who has lived in England all her life
Victor, 75, who completed treatment for bowel cancer last year
Paul, 60, who moved to England from Wales three years ago
6.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England: the opt-out law does not apply to people under 18, people who lack capacity to understand the arrangements for a significant period before death, visitors and people not living in England voluntarily, or people who lived in England for less than 12 months before their death.

n.0: Not having discussed donation does not exclude an adult; her family are approached about any known views.
n.2: Medical history affects suitability, not whether deemed consent applies; age 75 is not an exclusion.
n.3: He has lived in England for more than 12 months and is an adult, so he is not in an excluded group.

6.q: During the breakfast round, Norma, 85, says she would like to take her tablets after she has eaten and asks the nurse to leave them on her table. Norma has capacity but no self-administration assessment has been done. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the tablets as refused and offer them at lunchtime
Return after breakfast to give them and record once taken
Leave the tablets and sign the chart as given
Leave the tablets and ask a support worker to check later
6.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-4 and 15-17: unless a self-administration risk assessment allows it, the nurse administering remains accountable and must see the dose taken; the record is completed at the time of administration (NICE SC1: record only after the dose is taken).

n.0: Norma has not refused; she asked to take them later, which can be accommodated.
n.2: Signing before the dose is taken creates an inaccurate record and the tablets may be lost or taken by others.
n.3: Delegating a check does not confirm administration and leaves medicines unattended.

6.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
6.q: Katie, 42, has a learning disability and has had three chest infections in six months, each treated with antibiotics by her GP. No one has reviewed why they keep happening. What should the learning disability nurse recommend?
o: Request a review of swallowing, posture and oral care to find the cause
Request a flu vaccine as the main preventive step
Ask for a rescue pack of antibiotics to keep at home
Advise that recurrent infections are expected in learning disability
6.w: Recurrent chest infections can be a sign of aspiration. LeDeR learning shows treating each infection without investigating cause misses dysphagia, postural problems and poor oral care; a multidisciplinary review (SLT, physiotherapy, postural care) targets prevention.

n.1: Vaccination is important but does not address likely aspiration.
n.2: Rescue antibiotics treat episodes but do not address the cause.
n.3: Accepting recurrent infection as expected is diagnostic overshadowing.

6.q: Kian, 5, is autistic and does not speak. His team starts the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS). In the first phase, what is Kian taught to do?
o: Hand a picture to a partner to receive the item he wants
Choose between two pictures to get the item he prefers
Answer the question 'What do you want?' with a picture
Build an 'I want' sentence strip with a picture of the item
6.w: PECS Phase 1 is the physically assisted exchange: the person learns to pick up a single picture and hand it to a communication partner in exchange for a desired item (Bondy and Frost, PECS).

n.1: Choosing between pictures is Phase 3, picture discrimination.
n.2: Responding to 'What do you want?' is Phase 5.
n.3: Sentence strips are Phase 4, sentence structure.

6.q: Mrs Doyle, 63, is receiving 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannulae. Her observations are: respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96%, systolic BP 130, pulse 80, alert, temperature 36.8°C. Her SpO2 is scored on Scale 1. What is her NEWS2 score?
o: 1, because supplemental oxygen scores 1
3, because oxygen scores 3 on Scale 1
0, because each vital sign is in range
2, because supplemental oxygen scores 2
6.w: NEWS2 Chart 1: SpO2 96% or above on Scale 1 scores 0, but the 'air or oxygen' parameter scores 2 for any supplemental oxygen. All other values score 0, so the total is 2.

n.0: Supplemental oxygen scores 2, not 1.
n.1: Oxygen use scores 2; 3 is not a value in the air or oxygen parameter.
n.2: The use of supplemental oxygen is scored separately and adds 2 points.

7.q: Maureen, 87, lacks capacity and has life-threatening pneumonia. Her daughter holds a registered health and welfare lasting power of attorney (LPA). The LPA does not contain express authority over life-sustaining treatment. Her daughter says she refuses intravenous antibiotics. How should the team proceed?
o: Delay treatment until the Court of Protection has confirmed that the LPA is valid
Ask the daughter to agree as nearest relative, which overrides the terms of the LPA
