Follow the daughter's refusal, as the LPA is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Decide in her best interests, consulting her daughter, who cannot refuse this treatment
7.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s9 (an LPA must be registered) and s11(7)-(8): a health and welfare attorney can give or refuse consent to treatment when the person lacks capacity, but this does not extend to life-sustaining treatment unless the LPA contains express provision. The team decide in Maureen's best interests (s4), consulting her daughter.

n.0: The registered LPA does not need court confirmation, and delaying antibiotics would put Maureen's life at risk.
n.1: There is no 'nearest relative' power under the MCA; decisions are made in Maureen's best interests.
n.2: Registration is required, but under MCA s11(8) an attorney cannot refuse life-sustaining treatment without express authority in the LPA.

7.q: Mr Mensah, 59, has Black African heritage and is recovering from pneumonia. His pulse oximeter reads 94% on air. He is a little more breathless than earlier. Which consideration is most important when interpreting this reading?
o: Oximeters underestimate saturations in people with dark skin
Oximeters can overestimate saturations in people with dark skin
His reading is within target, so his breathlessness is not significant
An SpO2 of 94% on air means oxygen therapy should be started
7.w: NICE NG253 (practical information on pulse oximeters): some oximeters underestimate or overestimate saturations, especially when borderline, and overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin. His true saturation may be lower, so the reading should be interpreted with his clinical picture and escalated if concerned.

n.0: The reported error in people with dark skin is overestimation, not underestimation.
n.2: Increasing breathlessness is significant even when the oximeter reading is within target.
n.3: 94% on air is within the 94-98% target for most adults; starting oxygen is not indicated by the number alone.

7.q: A nurse is recording a 12-lead ECG for Mr Ford, 76, who is cold and shivering. The trace has a wandering, fuzzy baseline in several leads. What is the best way to improve the recording?
o: Accept the trace, as shivering does not affect how it is interpreted
Warm him, help him relax and lie still, then check electrode contact
Increase the paper speed and record the trace again at once
Record the trace with him standing to reduce the shivering
7.w: Muscle tremor, movement and poor electrode contact cause artefact. Making the person warm, comfortable and still, usually lying or semi-recumbent, with clean dry skin and good electrode contact, gives an interpretable trace (Annexe B 2.3).

n.0: Artefact can mimic or hide abnormalities, so the trace may not be interpretable.
n.2: Changing paper speed alters the appearance of the trace and does not remove tremor artefact.
n.3: Standing increases muscle activity and movement; ECGs are recorded with the person at rest.

7.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
7.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

7.q: After the unexpected death of a young patient, several members of the ward team seem shaken. The ward manager wants to support the team's resilience. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Offer the team extra shifts to keep them occupied
Ask each nurse to write a statement about what went wrong
Encourage the team to move on and focus on the next shift
Hold a supportive debrief and signpost wellbeing services
7.w: Proficiency P6.11: accept and manage uncertainty and develop resilience in self and others. Code 8.7 support colleagues; Code 25.2 support staff you are responsible for.

n.0: More shifts may increase fatigue and do not address distress.
n.1: Statements may be needed for review, but they do not address the team's wellbeing.
n.2: This dismisses the emotional impact and misses the chance to support resilience.

7.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
7.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

7.q: Dominic, 47, has a severe learning disability. He is usually very active, walking around the house and humming. For two days he has stayed in his chair, quiet and still. Staff say he is 'having a calm few days'. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Encourage him to join activities to lift his mood
Note the change and review him again at the end of the week
Treat this as a possible sign of pain or illness and assess him
Agree that this is positive and continue to monitor him
7.w: Distress and pain may show as withdrawal and reduced activity, not only as agitation. A marked change from Dominic's baseline needs assessment for pain or illness (DisDAT; deteriorating patient learning from LeDeR).

n.0: Encouraging activity ignores a possible physical cause.
n.1: Waiting a week risks delayed diagnosis.
n.3: Interpreting withdrawal as calm may miss pain or illness.

7.q: At a team meeting, a district nursing team leader explains the integrated care partnership (ICP) in her area. Which statement about the ICP is correct?
o: It inspects and rates the quality of local health services
It is the NHS body that commissions hospital and GP services
It is a joint committee that develops the integrated care strategy
It employs the community nurses who work in the local area
7.w: The ICP is a joint committee run by the NHS organisations and upper-tier local authorities in each ICS, with wider partners such as the voluntary sector. It must develop a long-term integrated care strategy to improve health, care and wellbeing (NHS England, What is integrated care?; P7.1).

n.0: Inspection and rating are carried out by the Care Quality Commission in England.
n.1: Planning NHS services and managing the budget is the role of the integrated care board.
n.3: Community nurses are employed by provider organisations, not by the ICP.

7.q: A ward manager is reviewing staffing on an acute adult medical ward. Which statement about nurse-to-patient ratios reflects NICE SG1 (2014)?
o: A ratio of one registered nurse to six patients applies on all wards, day and night
A ratio of one registered nurse to eight patients is a legal minimum in England
There is no single ratio, but over 8 patients per nurse by day is linked to harm
Staffing ratios for adult wards are set by the NMC for each type of hospital ward
7.w: NICE SG1 rec 1.5.3: there is no single nursing staff-to-patient ratio for all acute adult wards, but there is evidence of increased risk of harm when a registered nurse cares for more than 8 patients on day shifts, which should prompt close monitoring of red flags and safe nursing indicators.

n.0: SG1 does not set a 1:6 ratio; it uses patients' nursing needs and professional judgement.
n.1: The 1:8 figure is an evidence threshold for monitoring, not a legal minimum in England.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not set ward staffing ratios.

7.q: In 2019, Dennis made a valid written advance decision refusing artificial nutrition. In 2023, with capacity, he made a health and welfare LPA giving his son express authority to decide on that treatment, including if life-sustaining. Dennis now lacks capacity. Whose decision about artificial nutrition applies?
o: The consultant's, because the two documents conflict
His son's, as the later LPA covers the same treatment
The Court of Protection's, as both documents exist
The advance decision, because it was made first
7.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s25(2)(b): an advance decision is not valid if the person has, under an LPA created after the advance decision was made, conferred authority on the attorney to give or refuse consent to the treatment to which the advance decision relates.

n.0: There is no conflict for the consultant to resolve; the later LPA displaces the earlier advance decision.
n.2: Court involvement is not needed when the law gives a clear answer on these facts.
n.3: MCA s25(2)(b): an advance decision is not valid if a later LPA gives the attorney authority over the same treatment.

7.q: A community mental health nurse asks Leon, 27, "Think of a day recently when things were a little better. What was different about that day?" Which approach is the nurse using?
o: Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Motivational interviewing
Reminiscence therapy
7.w: Annexe A 3.2: solution-focused therapies. Asking about exceptions, when the problem was less present, builds on existing strengths.

n.0: CBT works on links between thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
n.2: MI explores ambivalence about change.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories to support wellbeing, mainly in older adults.

7.q: During the morning medication round, Lewis notices the sharps container on the drug trolley has reached the manufacturer's fill line. Several injections are still due. What should Lewis do with the full container?
o: Close and lock it, label it with origin and date, and replace it
Leave it open and start a second container beside it on the trolley
Press the contents down to make room for the remaining needles
Use it until it is completely full, then seal it before lunch
7.w: NIPCM ch 1.9: sharps containers must be disposed of when the manufacturer's fill line is reached, labelled with point of origin and dates of assembly and disposal, and use the temporary closure when not in use.

n.1: A full container left open is a sharps hazard; it should be locked and removed.
n.2: Pushing down sharps risks a needlestick injury and overfills the container.
n.3: Filling past the fill line risks protruding sharps and injury.

7.q: A student nurse says that normalisation means 'making people with learning disabilities behave like everyone else'. How should the mentor correct this?
o: It means making ordinary patterns and conditions of everyday life available to people
It means people follow the same rules as staff so that services run smoothly
It means grouping people with similar needs so that they share specialist services
It means treating the impairment so that the person becomes as typical as possible
7.w: Normalisation (Nirje; Wolfensberger) means making the patterns and conditions of everyday life, such as a home, routines, work, leisure and relationships, as close as possible to the norms of mainstream society. It is about conditions of life, not changing the person.

n.1: Normalisation is about ordinary life patterns, not compliance with staff rules.
n.2: Grouping people with similar needs in specialist settings is the opposite of normalisation.
n.3: Normalisation is not about treating the impairment or changing the person.

7.q: A district nursing team wants to find out how patients rate their new evening visiting service, with no benchmark to compare against, by asking current patients to complete a short questionnaire. What type of project is this?
o: Qualitative research study
Clinical audit
Randomised controlled trial
Service evaluation
7.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): service evaluation asks 'What standard does this service achieve?', measures the current service without reference to a standard and does not need REC review.

n.0: It aims to judge the current service, not to generate generalisable knowledge.
n.1: Audit compares practice with a predetermined standard; here there is no standard.
n.2: There is no allocation to interventions or randomisation.

7.q: Raymond, 74, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He usually wet shaves with a blade razor and asks for help to shave while in hospital. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply pressure to any cuts for 30 seconds afterwards
Use an electric razor to reduce the risk of bleeding
Postpone shaving until his anticoagulant is stopped
Use a new disposable blade razor and press gently
7.w: Annexe B 4.3: when assisting with shaving, consider risks such as anticoagulation. An electric razor reduces the risk of cuts and bleeding in people taking anticoagulants such as apixaban.

n.0: This responds to cuts rather than preventing them.
n.2: His anticoagulant is needed for stroke prevention and shaving is part of his personal care.
n.3: A blade razor still risks cuts that bleed more with anticoagulation.

7.q: Using his DisDAT, staff recognise that Abdul, 39, who has a severe learning disability, is showing his distress cues: grimacing, rubbing his hands and refusing food. What should the nurse do next?
o: Give his PRN medicine for agitation as written in his care plan
Start his behaviour support plan's de-escalation strategies
Assess for possible causes such as pain, infection or constipation
Record the cues and review them again tomorrow
7.w: DisDAT identifies that the person is distressed, not why. The next step is a clinical assessment for causes such as pain, infection, constipation, dental problems or emotional causes, then treating the cause and reassessing.

n.0: Sedative PRN treats the behaviour without finding the cause and may mask pain.
n.1: De-escalation addresses behaviour but leaves a possible physical cause untreated.
n.3: Waiting a day delays treatment of a possibly painful condition.

7.q: Carol, 41, tells the nurse at a health check that she drinks most weekends: about 7 units on Friday night and 7 units on Saturday night, and nothing during the week. Which advice is most accurate?
o: Her drinking is above the weekly guideline, which is 10 units for women
Her drinking is low risk because her weekly total is within 14 units
Spread drinking over 3 or more days, as heavy sessions raise her risk
She should drink a small amount daily, as this protects her heart
7.w: UK Chief Medical Officers' low risk drinking guidelines (2016): it is safest not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, for men and women; if drinking as much as 14 units a week, spread it evenly over 3 or more days, as one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase the risk of death from long-term illness and from accidents and injuries.

n.0: The CMO guideline is 14 units a week for both men and women.
n.1: The CMOs advise that one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase risks of long-term illness, accidents and injuries.
n.3: The CMOs do not advise drinking for health; risk rises with regular drinking.

7.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
7.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

7.q: Nia, 40, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her hospital passport lists her medicines, but the nurse notices it names an antiepileptic that her GP record shows was stopped a year ago. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her family to update the passport after discharge and continue as listed
Stop using the passport and rely on the trust's own records for her stay
Give the medicines listed on the passport, as it is written by those who know her
Reconcile her medicines with current records and update the passport with Nia
7.w: Medicines reconciliation on admission must use current, verified sources. Passports go out of date, so the nurse should confirm the current medicines and support Nia and those close to her to update the passport so it stays accurate (Code 10.2, 18).

n.0: Continuing an inaccurate list risks a medication error now; the update should not wait until discharge.
n.1: The passport still contains valuable information on communication, pain and preferences; it needs correcting, not discarding.
n.2: Giving a discontinued antiepileptic could cause harm; passport medicine lists must be checked against current records.

7.q: An audit on Ward 6 found that only 58% of patients had a fully completed fluid balance chart against a standard of 95%. The team then held teaching sessions and introduced a simpler chart. What is the next step that completes the audit cycle?
o: Lower the standard to a level the ward can meet
Re-audit practice against the same 95% standard
Start a new audit on a different topic for the ward
Publish the original results in a nursing journal
7.w: The audit cycle is: agree the standard, measure practice, compare, implement change, then re-audit to check whether the change has improved and sustained practice (HQIP Best Practice in Clinical Audit). Re-measurement against the same standard closes the loop (P6.7).

n.0: Standards are set from evidence and policy, not lowered to match current performance.
n.2: Moving on without re-auditing leaves the cycle incomplete and the change unevaluated.
n.3: Sharing findings can be useful, but publication does not show whether the changes worked.

7.q: A ward manager, Leon, has noticed over three weeks that a staff nurse, Abi, regularly completes her patients' records several hours after care. Patient care has otherwise been good. What is Leon's most appropriate first step?
o: Start a formal capability process with a written warning
Meet Abi privately, give examples, explore reasons and agree a plan
Refer Abi to the NMC for failing to keep records as required
Move Abi to a different ward with a lighter workload
7.w: Performance management starts with an informal, supportive conversation using specific examples, exploring causes (for example workload or skills) and agreeing objectives, support and a review date, escalating to formal processes only if problems continue (P5.3 principles and processes of performance management; Code 10.1 records completed at the time or as soon as possible after).

n.0: Formal processes are disproportionate before an informal discussion and support have been tried.
n.2: This is a local performance issue, not a fitness to practise concern at this stage.
n.3: Moving her does not address the reasons for the delay or support her improvement.

7.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
7.q: Jordan, 37, has a severe learning disability and cerebral palsy and lives in a residential home. His bowel chart shows Bristol type 1 stools every four or five days. He takes an anticholinergic medicine for drooling. A new support worker asks why this matters. What should the nurse explain?
o: Infrequent stools need action once he reports abdominal pain
Constipation can lead to obstruction and has contributed to deaths
Bristol type 1 stools show that his diet has enough fibre
Hard stools are expected in people with cerebral palsy
7.w: Bristol type 1 (separate hard lumps) indicates constipation. In people with a learning disability constipation is common, is worsened by immobility and anticholinergic medicines, and can cause bowel obstruction, perforation and aspiration from vomiting; LeDeR reports constipation still contributing to deaths (LeDeR 2023).

n.0: Jordan may not be able to report pain; waiting for a complaint is unsafe.
n.2: Type 1 stools suggest constipation, not adequate fibre.
n.3: Treating constipation as expected is diagnostic overshadowing; it needs active management.

7.q: After inserting a peripheral cannula into the hand of Agnes, 88, the nurse needs to secure and cover the site. Which type of dressing is recommended so that the site can be inspected?
o: A sterile hydrocolloid dressing over the hub
A sterile gauze dressing and crepe bandage
Non-sterile adhesive tape over a gauze square
A sterile transparent semipermeable dressing
7.w: Vascular access device care (NICE CG139 and the IPC facts sheet) uses a sterile, transparent, semipermeable membrane dressing so the insertion site can be observed for signs of infection or phlebitis without removing it.

n.0: Hydrocolloid dressings are for wounds; they are opaque and not designed for cannula sites.
n.1: A bandage over gauze prevents regular inspection of the insertion site.
n.2: Non-sterile tape and gauze hide the site and are not a sterile covering for a Key-Site.

7.q: Before a transfer, Rosa checks the mobile hoist on her ward. The examination label shows that its last thorough examination under LOLER was eight months ago, and no examination scheme with different intervals is displayed. What should Rosa do?
o: Use the hoist, because lifting equipment is examined every 12 months
Take the hoist out of use, report it and use another hoist that is in date
Carry out a visual pre-use check and continue if the hoist looks sound
Use the hoist for this transfer and report the overdue date at handover
7.w: Under LOLER 1998, lifting equipment and accessories used for lifting people must be thoroughly examined at least every 6 months (other lifting equipment every 12 months) unless an examination scheme sets other intervals. A hoist overdue for examination should not be used to lift a person and should be reported (HSE, Thorough examinations and inspections of lifting equipment).

n.0: The 12-month interval applies to lifting equipment that is not used to lift people; patient hoists fall under the 6-month interval.
n.2: A pre-use check is good practice but does not replace the thorough examination by a competent person that LOLER requires.
n.3: Knowingly using equipment that is overdue for its statutory examination puts the patient at risk; the problem must be dealt with before the transfer.

7.q: Simone, 37, has Down syndrome and attends her annual health check with her support worker. She has no new symptoms. Alongside the standard check, which additional test should be offered every year?
o: An X-ray of the cervical spine
A resting electrocardiogram
A cervical screening test
A thyroid function blood test
7.w: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and the risk rises with age, so thyroid function should be tested every year throughout life (DSMIG thyroid guideline; Down's Syndrome Association).

n.0: Routine X-ray screening of the neck is not recommended in adults without symptoms.
n.1: Heart problems are common from birth, but an annual ECG is not part of routine surveillance in an adult without symptoms.
n.2: Cervical screening follows the national recall schedule of several years between tests, not an annual test.

7.q: Eileen, 76, is prescribed morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously. The ward stocks morphine sulfate 10 mg in 1 mL ampoules. A second nurse witnesses throughout. Which controlled drugs register entry correctly records the dose and the remainder?
o: 2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.4 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.6 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) returned to the CD cupboard
2.5 mg (2.5 mL) given; ampoule recorded as used with no remainder
7.w: Volume = 2.5 / 10 x 1 = 0.25 mL, leaving 7.5 mg (0.75 mL). NICE NG46: for CDs left over after administration, record the amount disposed of and the signatures of the person disposing and any witness. Opened ampoules are not returned to stock.

n.1: 0.4 mL contains 4 mg, so the volume is wrong for a 2.5 mg dose.
n.2: Opened ampoules cannot be returned to stock; the remainder is disposed of and recorded.
n.3: 2.5 mL exceeds the 1 mL ampoule and would be a tenfold miscalculation.

7.q: Leon, 39, stopped smoking three months ago with support. He tells the nurse he is worried he will start again at a family wedding next month, where many guests smoke. What is the most appropriate support?
o: Help him make an 'if-then' plan for moments when he is tempted
Advise him to avoid weddings and other social events for a year
Close his episode of care, as his quit attempt is now complete
Reassure him that relapse is rare once three months have passed
7.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) recs 6 and 10: interventions should address relapse and recognise that it is common; help people maintain change by giving them well-rehearsed action plans such as 'if-then' plans, social support and feedback and monitoring for at least 1 year.

n.1: Avoiding all social contact is unrealistic and removes social support that helps people maintain change.
n.2: PH49 rec 10 recommends feedback and monitoring for at least a year to help maintain change.
n.3: PH49 recognises that relapse is common and asks for interventions to address it.

7.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
7.q: Noah, 27, has a learning disability and constipation. A support worker says he refuses prune juice and fibre-rich foods. What is the best approach for the nurse?
o: Tell Noah he must drink the juice so he avoids going to hospital
Hide fibre supplements in his food
Agree acceptable food and drink with him and review laxatives
Stop offering choices and give the same meal each day
7.w: Person-centred care involves Noah in finding foods and drinks he accepts, using accessible information, and reviewing medical treatment if diet alone is not enough. Covert administration would need a capacity assessment and best interests process.

n.0: Threats are coercive and do not respect his choices.
n.1: Hiding supplements is covert administration without lawful process.
n.3: Removing choice is restrictive and unlikely to help.

7.q: Zoe, 28, has a learning disability and started risperidone for severe self-injury four weeks ago, alongside a psychological intervention. Under NICE NG11, if there is no meaningful response, by when should the antipsychotic be stopped?
o: After 6 weeks
After 12 weeks
After 6 months
After 2 weeks
7.w: NICE NG11 1.8.4: review effectiveness and side effects after 3-4 weeks and stop the antipsychotic if there is no indication of a response at 6 weeks.

n.1: Twelve weeks exceeds the 6-week limit set by NG11.
n.2: Six months would expose Zoe to side effects without benefit for far too long.
n.3: Two weeks is too early; NG11 sets the first review at 3-4 weeks.

7.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
7.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

7.q: Femi, the nurse in charge of a 28-bed surgical ward, is allocating patients. Sara, a newly registered nurse, is in her first week of preceptorship. One bay includes Mr Clarke, 58, who has a new tracheostomy. Sara has not yet been trained in tracheostomy care. Which allocation is most appropriate?
o: Give Sara no patients and ask her to shadow Femi while Femi coordinates the ward
Give Sara the bay and ask a healthcare assistant to look after Mr Clarke's tracheostomy
Give Sara the bay with Mr Clarke so that she can learn tracheostomy care quickly
Give Sara a bay of stable patients with a named nurse to support her during the shift
7.w: Assigning care means matching patients' needs to staff competence and providing support (P5.5 prioritisation, delegation and assignment of care; Code 11.1 and standard 13 (work within the limits of competence)). A preceptee should care for patients within her competence with a named support, while a nurse trained in tracheostomy care looks after Mr Clarke.

n.0: A registered preceptee can safely take a supported caseload; withholding all patients wastes capacity and slows her development.
n.1: Tracheostomy care is outside a healthcare assistant's role unless specifically trained, and Sara could not supervise it.
n.2: Learning tracheostomy care needs training and supervision; allocating an untrained nurse puts Mr Clarke at risk.

7.q: Joanne is registered with the NMC as both a nurse and a midwife and is preparing to revalidate both registrations. How many practice hours must she show over the three-year period?
o: 900 hours, including 450 for each registration
675 hours, as half of the second registration counts
1,350 hours, including 450 for each registration
450 hours across both registrations combined
7.w: NMC revalidation, practice hours (page updated 26/05/2021): 450 hours for one registration, 900 hours for nurse and midwife (450 each), 1,350 for triple registration.

n.1: There is no pro rata reduction; each registration needs its own 450 hours.
n.2: 1,350 hours applies to triple registration as nurse, midwife and nursing associate.
n.3: 450 hours is the figure for a single registration; dual nurse and midwife registration requires 900.

7.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
7.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

7.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
7.q: A ward is admitting Mohammed, 44, who has a learning disability. The nurse wants to recognise deterioration early. Which information is most useful to gather on admission?
o: His usual baselines from family and his passport
His preferred newspaper and television programmes
His school records and qualifications
His blood group and previous transfusions
7.w: Knowing the person's usual observations, behaviours, eating, sleeping, mobility and how they show pain allows staff to recognise change; family carers and passports are key sources (LeDeR; Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag).

n.1: Preferences support comfort but do not establish clinical baselines.
n.2: Education history does not help recognise physical deterioration.
n.3: Blood group matters only if a transfusion is planned.

7.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
7.q: A nurse learns that Dan, a support worker, has begun a sexual relationship with Jess, 28, a woman with a learning disability whom he supports at her home. Jess says she consents and is happy. What is the correct position?
o: It is lawful if Jess is assessed as having capacity to consent to sex
It is lawful, because both are adults and Jess has said she consents
It is a likely criminal offence by a care worker and must be raised as safeguarding
It is a disciplinary matter for his employer rather than a safeguarding issue
7.w: The Sexual Offences Act 2003 (ss38-41) makes sexual activity by a care worker with a person with a mental disorder, including a learning disability, an offence whether or not the person appears to consent, because of the imbalance of power in the care relationship. A safeguarding concern and police referral are required.

n.0: The care worker offences apply even if the person has capacity.
n.1: Apparent consent is not a defence to the care worker offences.
n.3: Employer discipline does not replace safeguarding and police involvement.

7.q: Daniel, 45, is on an intensive care unit in England after a catastrophic brain haemorrhage. Treatment is to be withdrawn. He has lived in England all his life and has not recorded a donation decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. What happens about organ donation?
o: His organs are retrieved without discussion because his consent is deemed
His family are approached to find out whether he held any views about donation
The consultant decides on donation at a best interests meeting
Donation cannot proceed because he did not register as an organ donor
7.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England (opt out from 20 May 2020): adults are considered to agree to donate unless they recorded a decision not to donate or are in an excluded group, and families are still consulted when donation is a possibility, to share any knowledge of the person's decision.

n.0: Under the opt-out law the family are still consulted when donation is possible; retrieval does not proceed without that discussion.
n.2: Donation decisions follow the deemed consent law and the person's known views, not a clinical best interests meeting.
n.3: In England, adults not in an excluded group are considered to agree unless they opted out; registration is not required.

7.q: A nurse hears that the Mental Health Act 2025 changes how people with a learning disability can be detained. A colleague says that from now on a person cannot be detained under section 3 because of a learning disability. What is the correct position in October 2026?
o: Correct, the change came into force with the new Code of Practice in 2026
Incorrect, the change has been enacted but is not yet in force
Incorrect, the 2025 Act did not change the rules for learning disability
Correct, the 2025 Act removed learning disability from section 3 on Royal Assent
7.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 (Royal Assent 18 Dec 2025) will stop learning disability or autism alone justifying s3 detention, but ss3-4 and Sch 1 are prospective and not in force; the 1983 Act as amended applies, including the 'abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct' qualifier for s3 (MHA83 s1(2A)-(2B)).

n.0: No commencement has brought the s3 change into force, and a code of practice cannot do so.
n.2: The 2025 Act does contain this change; it is simply not yet in force.
n.3: Royal Assent did not bring this change into force; legislation.gov.uk shows the provisions as prospective.

7.q: A student nurse asks what a Care and Treatment Review (CTR) is for an adult with a learning disability at risk of admission. Which answer is best?
o: A formal complaint process for families who are unhappy with care
An independent review of whether care is safe and community options are used
A Care Act needs assessment completed by a local authority social worker
A review of whether the person meets the criteria for detention
7.w: C(E)TRs bring an independent panel to look at whether the person's care, (education) and treatment are safe and effective, whether community alternatives to admission have been used and what is needed to avoid admission or speed discharge (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy).

n.0: Complaints have their own process; a CTR reviews care and treatment, not complaints.
n.2: A Care Act assessment determines eligible care and support needs; a CTR is a different, NHS-led review.
n.3: Detention criteria are decided under the Mental Health Act by AMHPs and doctors, not by a CTR.

7.q: Ana, a nurse, is about to start intensive interaction with Leon, 23, who has a profound learning disability and uses a wheelchair. Which non-verbal approach should she use?
o: Sit at his eye level with a relaxed, responsive face and body
Stand in front of him and keep constant eye contact
Sit behind him and talk so he can hear her voice clearly
Stand beside his wheelchair so she does not crowd him
7.w: Being at the person's level with a relaxed, open and responsive manner invites interaction. Non-verbal communication (position, facial expression, body language) is central to Annexe A 1.3 and intensive interaction.

n.1: Standing over him with constant eye contact can feel intimidating.
n.2: Sitting behind him prevents shared attention and facial communication.
n.3: Standing over a seated person is less inviting and makes eye contact hard.

7.q: Maya, 17, is autistic. Her outpatient appointment has been moved to a different clinic room at short notice and she has become very anxious in the waiting area. Which reasonable adjustment would best prevent this next time?
o: Ask Maya's mother to attend instead of Maya to save her stress
Give advance notice of any change with a photo of the new room
Offer Maya a sedative to take an hour before each appointment
Book the longest available slot in the middle of the clinic day
7.w: Unexpected change commonly drives anxiety in autistic people. Advance warning and visual information make change predictable; CG170 1.1.10 also suggests appointments at the start or end of the day to minimise waiting.

n.0: Excluding Maya removes her right to take part in her own care.
n.2: Routine sedation is not a reasonable adjustment and is contrary to STOMP and STAMP.
n.3: Long waits in the middle of a busy clinic day are likely to increase anxiety; start or end of day is preferred.

7.q: A practice nurse is preparing a short presentation for a safeguarding update and reads the 2015 Welsh study of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) among adults. Roughly what proportion of the adults surveyed reported four or more ACEs?
o: About 47%
About 30%
About 5%
About 14%
7.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): 47% of Welsh adults reported at least one ACE and 14% reported four or more.

n.0: Forty-seven per cent reported at least one ACE, not four or more.
n.1: Thirty per cent is not a figure from the study for 4+ ACEs.
n.2: Five per cent was the prevalence of individual ACEs such as parental drug use or incarceration.

7.q: You are alone on a quiet community visit when Sandra, 55, collapses. She is unresponsive and you have a mobile phone. According to RCUK 2025, what should you do next?
o: Give 2 minutes of CPR before calling 999
Call 999 on speaker, then assess breathing
Leave her to find a defibrillator first
Assess her breathing for one minute before calling
7.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: if alone with a phone, call 999 on speakerphone as soon as unresponsiveness is identified, before assessing breathing, so the call handler can guide CPR and locate an AED.

n.0: Delaying the call delays emergency help and AED location.
n.2: Leaving her delays both the call and CPR; the call handler can direct others to an AED.
n.3: Breathing is assessed for no more than 10 seconds, and the 2025 guideline calls 999 first if alone.

7.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
7.q: Priya, 18, has a learning disability and has just moved from children's to adult services. Her mother is used to making all health decisions for her. At her first adult appointment, how should the nurse approach decision-making?
o: Wait until Priya's mother arrives before any decision
Assume Priya lacks capacity because of her disability
Ask her mother to sign consent as she did before
Presume Priya has capacity and support her to decide
7.w: Adults (and young people aged 16+ under the MCA) are presumed to have capacity (MCA 2005 s1(2)) and must be given all practicable support to decide (s1(3)). Parental responsibility ends at 18, so a parent cannot consent on behalf of an adult; if Priya lacks capacity for a decision, a best interests process applies.

n.0: Her mother's views matter, but Priya should be supported to decide for herself.
n.1: A learning disability does not by itself mean lack of capacity.
n.2: A parent has no legal power to consent for an adult unless appointed as a deputy or attorney.

7.q: Molly, 45, has a learning disability and needs a double-length dental appointment so she can become familiar with the room and equipment. The practice manager says Molly will have to pay an extra fee for the longer slot. What is the correct position under the Equality Act 2010?
o: Molly can be charged if the adjustment costs more than a set amount
Molly can be charged a reduced fee for the additional time
Molly's family can be charged in place of Molly herself
Molly must not be charged for the cost of a reasonable adjustment
7.w: Section 20(7) of the Equality Act 2010 states that a disabled person must not be required to pay for the costs of complying with the duty to make reasonable adjustments.

n.0: There is no cost threshold above which the disabled person can be charged; cost is considered when deciding what is reasonable.
n.1: A reduced fee is still a charge for the adjustment, which s20(7) prohibits.
n.2: Passing the cost to family is still charging for the adjustment and is not permitted.

7.q: Lionel, 79, has had a stroke and cannot reposition himself. He is incontinent and his assessment shows he is at high risk of developing a pressure ulcer. His skin is currently intact. Under NICE CG179, what is the minimum frequency at which he should be helped to change position?
o: At least every 8 hours
At least every 6 hours
At least every 12 hours
At least every 4 hours
7.w: NICE CG179: reposition adults at risk at least every 6 hours, and adults at high risk at least every 4 hours.

n.0: Every 8 hours is longer than any CG179 interval.
n.1: Every 6 hours is the minimum for adults at risk, not high risk.
n.2: Every 12 hours is far longer than CG179 recommends.

7.q: Which factor is most likely to give a falsely reassuring pulse oximetry reading?
o: A fever of 38.2°C on admission
Mild iron-deficiency anaemia
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Mild dehydration after vomiting
7.w: Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so carbon monoxide poisoning can show normal or high SpO2 despite severe hypoxia. Other pitfalls include poor perfusion, nail varnish, movement and reduced accuracy in people with darker skin tones.

n.0: Fever does not directly cause oximeters to over-read.
n.1: Mild anaemia does not by itself produce a falsely high SpO2.
n.3: Mild dehydration is not a recognised cause of falsely high oximeter readings.

7.q: Nurse Ali phones a doctor about Mr Cole using SBAR. He says, "I think he may be developing sepsis." Which part of SBAR is this?
o: Assessment
Situation
Background
Recommendation
7.w: NHS England SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation): Assessment is the nurse's evaluation of the problem.

n.1: Situation states the immediate problem, for example 'his NEWS2 is 6'.
n.2: Background gives history and context.
n.3: Recommendation states what the nurse wants done.

7.q: Derek, 70, has COPD and has been admitted twice this winter with exacerbations. He tells the nurse that his flat is damp and that he cannot afford to heat it. Which action by the nurse best addresses the factors affecting his health?
o: Ask the prescriber to increase his inhaler dose for the winter months
Refer or signpost him to local housing and energy support services
Advise him to spend more time in bed to conserve his energy
Record the housing issue and note it is outside the nursing role
7.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.2 and P2.7: understand the wider determinants of health and explain the contribution of social influences and circumstances to health outcomes. NICE PH49 (2014): assess the context in which people live, including their physical, economic and social environment.

n.0: Medicines do not address the damp, cold housing that is affecting his health.
n.2: This does not address the housing problem and reduces his activity.
n.3: NMC P2.7 expects nurses to recognise social circumstances as influences on health and act on them.

7.q: A caller to a surgical ward says she is the daughter of Mrs Green, 70, who had surgery today, and asks how the operation went. The nurse cannot confirm who the caller is. What should the nurse do?
o: Check Mrs Green's wishes and agreed contacts before sharing anything
Give a brief update, as the caller knows the patient's name
Ask the caller to confirm Mrs Green's date of birth, then answer
Confirm the operation went well but give no further details
7.w: Code 5.1 requires respect for a person's right to privacy, and 5.2 that people know how and why their information is shared. The nurse should establish whether Mrs Green consents to information being given to this caller (for example agreed contacts or a password).

n.1: Knowing a patient's name does not show the caller has a right to her information.
n.2: A date of birth is easily known by others and does not establish Mrs Green's consent.
n.3: Confirming the outcome is still disclosure of confidential information without consent.

7.q: Miss Patel, 45, has a learning disability and has substantial difficulty understanding the safeguarding process. Her only relative is the person suspected of abusing her. The local authority is starting a section 42 enquiry. What should happen?
o: The local authority arranges an independent advocate for her
Her relative supports her, as her closest family member
The enquiry continues without her views, to avoid distress
The nurse acts as her advocate throughout the enquiry
7.w: Care Act 2014 s68 and statutory guidance para 7.3: the local authority must arrange an independent advocate for a safeguarding enquiry where the adult has substantial difficulty being involved and there is no appropriate person to support them. The suspected abuser cannot be that person.

n.1: A relative suspected of abuse is not an appropriate person to support her.
n.2: Excluding her views contradicts Making Safeguarding Personal and the advocacy duty.
n.3: The nurse is not an independent advocate under the Care Act and has a different role.

7.q: You find Brenda, 72, unresponsive in a day room. She is not breathing normally and is making occasional gasping sounds. What does this indicate?
o: Sleep apnoea, so open her airway and observe
Cardiac arrest, so start CPR
A seizure, so protect her head
A faint, so raise her legs
7.w: RCUK 2025: if a person is unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing, assume cardiac arrest and start CPR. Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest, and brief seizure-like activity may occur at onset.

n.0: Observing an unresponsive person with abnormal breathing delays CPR.
n.2: Treating gasping as a seizure delays CPR in someone in cardiac arrest.
n.3: A faint does not cause unresponsiveness with agonal breathing.

7.q: A nurse preparing a presentation on Building the Right Support checks progress on reducing inpatient numbers for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Which statement is accurate?
o: Inpatient numbers had not changed since the 2015 baseline
The halving target was met on time in March 2024
Numbers fell by about 29% by February 2025, missing the target
Inpatient numbers had fallen by about 75% by February 2025, beating it
7.w: In February 2025 there were 2,055 inpatients, down 29% from 2,905 in March 2015, so the target to halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 was missed (House of Commons Library SN07058).

n.0: Numbers did fall, from 2,905 to 2,055.
n.1: The target was not met; numbers fell by under a third.
n.3: The fall was about 29%, not 75%.

7.q: Noah, 23, is seen after self-harm. A colleague suggests using a risk scale to decide whether he can be discharged. Under NICE NG225, what should happen instead?
o: A person-centred psychosocial assessment and an agreed safety plan
A higher-risk score threshold before he is allowed to go home
Discharge if his risk is rated as low on the global scale
A repeat of the same scale after 24 hours of observation
7.w: NICE NG225 (2022): do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict suicide or repetition of self-harm or to decide who is discharged, and do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification. Develop a safety plan with, and agreed by, the person.

n.1: Adjusting a scale threshold still relies on a risk tool to make the decision.
n.2: Global low, medium or high stratification is specifically advised against.
n.3: Repeating the scale does not make it a valid basis for decisions.

7.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
7.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

7.q: Incident reporting on a surgical ward has fallen sharply since a new manager publicly criticised a nurse who reported an error. Staff say they now worry about being blamed. Which action by the matron would best improve the ward's safety culture?
o: Remind staff in writing that failing to report is a breach of the Code
Model openness, thank staff for reporting and share the learning
Make incident reporting a target in each nurse's annual appraisal
Ask the manager to review each report before it is submitted
7.w: Organisational culture is shaped by leaders' behaviour. A just, open culture where reporting is thanked and learning shared encourages reporting (P5.1 group and organisational dynamics and culture; Code 16.5 and 25.1; PSIRF).

n.0: Threats increase fear and do not rebuild trust.
n.2: Targets can encourage low-value reports without addressing the fear that is suppressing reporting.
n.3: Managerial filtering of reports adds to the fear and may suppress reporting further.

7.q: Agnes, the nurse in charge of a busy surgical ward, wants the whole team to share the same understanding of which patients are at risk at the start of each shift. Which practice best supports this?
o: Each nurse reads the full medical notes of all patients before starting
Staff ask the nurse in charge about any patient they are worried about
A brief safety huddle after handover to share key risks and plans
The nurse in charge keeps a written list of risks in the ward office
7.w: Shared situational awareness, the team's common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is supported by short structured safety huddles where risks (deteriorating patients, falls, staffing) are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; P5.2; P6.6).

n.0: Reading all notes is impractical on a busy ward and does not create a shared team picture or agreed actions.
n.1: Relying on individuals to ask means risks are shared reactively and unevenly.
n.3: A list kept by one person does not share awareness across the team.

7.q: After hearing his cancer has spread, Mr Ward, 70, falls silent and starts to cry. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Step out of the room and return once he is calmer
Reassure him that many people live for years with this
Stay with him, allow silence and acknowledge his feelings
Explain the treatment options to him while he takes it in
7.w: Annexe A 2.9 convey compassion during difficult conversations; Code 2.6 respond compassionately to distress; P1.12 support people who are emotionally vulnerable.

n.0: Leaving may feel like abandonment at a vulnerable moment.
n.1: This may be inaccurate and closes down his emotions.
n.3: Giving more information while he is distressed is unlikely to be absorbed.

7.q: Daniel, 41, is prescribed a 3 mL deep intramuscular injection. He is of average build and has no contraindications at any site. The nurse is choosing between the available sites. Which site is preferred for this volume?
o: The abdomen, at least 5 cm from the umbilicus
The ventrogluteal site over the gluteus medius
The dorsogluteal site in the upper outer buttock
The deltoid muscle of the upper arm
7.w: The ventrogluteal site is the preferred IM site for larger volumes in adults: the muscle is thick, the subcutaneous layer is relatively thin and it is away from major nerves and vessels (AnnexB.11.7). The deltoid takes small volumes, and the dorsogluteal site risks sciatic nerve injury.

n.0: The abdomen is a subcutaneous site, not an intramuscular one.
n.2: The dorsogluteal site carries a risk of sciatic nerve and gluteal artery injury.
n.3: The deltoid is a small muscle used for small volumes such as vaccines, not 3 mL.

7.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
7.q: Sasha, 24, has a mild learning disability and is 20 weeks pregnant. A professional suggests a referral to children's social care 'because of her learning disability'. There are no other concerns. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Assess her support needs as a parent and offer adapted support
Wait until the baby is born before considering any support
Plan for the baby to be placed with her grandparents at birth
Make a child protection referral because of her learning disability
7.w: A learning disability alone is not evidence that a child is at risk. Parents with a learning disability should have their needs assessed early and receive adapted, ongoing support; referral to children's social care follows if there are actual concerns about the child (balanced safeguarding; Equality Act 2010).

n.1: Delaying support until after birth misses the chance to prepare and support her.
n.2: Planning removal without evidence of risk breaches Article 8 and is discriminatory.
n.3: A diagnosis alone is not a child protection concern and assuming risk is discriminatory.

7.q: At 16:30 the laboratory phones the ward with a potassium result of 6.9 mmol/L for Mr Hayes, 74, who has chronic kidney disease. He feels 'a bit weak' but is otherwise as before. The doctor who requested the test has gone home. What should the nurse do?
o: Escalate to the on-call doctor now and document the result
Recheck his observations in 4 hours and escalate if they change
Record the result for the day team to review in the morning
Ask the laboratory to send the result to his GP for review
7.w: NMC proficiency P3.12 requires nurses to interpret results and act promptly, escalating when required. A potassium of 6.9 mmol/L is markedly raised and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, so the on-call doctor must be told now and the communication documented (Code 10).

n.1: Normal-looking observations do not exclude the risk of arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia.
n.2: Waiting until morning leaves a dangerous result untreated for hours.
n.3: The GP is not responsible for an inpatient's urgent results.

7.q: Hamid, 74, takes warfarin for a mechanical heart valve. His INR today is 8.5 (target 2.5 to 3.5). He has no bleeding, bruising or other symptoms, and his 18:00 dose is due. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the usual dose, as he has no signs of bleeding
Give oral vitamin K from ward stock to lower the INR
Withhold the warfarin and inform the prescriber urgently
Give half the usual dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
7.w: An INR well above target raises the risk of serious bleeding. Anticoagulants are high-risk medicines (P4.15): the dose is withheld and the prescriber informed promptly, who decides on dose changes or reversal such as vitamin K.

n.0: No bleeding now does not remove the high bleeding risk at INR 8.5.
n.1: Vitamin K must be prescribed; giving it from stock without a prescription is unlawful.
n.3: Altering the warfarin dose is a prescriber decision.

7.q: Tunde, a student learning disability nurse, is writing an essay on how healthcare for people with a learning disability came under scrutiny. He needs the 2007 Mencap report that described the deaths of six people in NHS care and argued that the NHS institutionally discriminated against them. Which report is this?
o: Death by Indifference
Healthcare for All
The Confidential Inquiry (CIPOLD)
Building the Right Support
7.w: Mencap's Death by Indifference (2007) set out six avoidable deaths of people with a learning disability in NHS care and alleged institutional discrimination. On publication the Health Secretary ordered an independent inquiry led by Sir Jonathan Michael (Mencap).

n.1: Healthcare for All (2008) was the independent inquiry set up in response to Death by Indifference, not the Mencap report itself.
n.2: CIPOLD (2013) reviewed a large population of deaths in south west England; it did not focus on six cases.
n.3: Building the Right Support (2015) is the national plan to reduce inpatient care after Winterbourne View.

7.q: Ms Okoro, 24, has type 1 diabetes and has been vomiting since last night. Her urinalysis shows glucose 3+ and ketones 3+. She is breathing quickly and her capillary glucose is 22.6 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Encourage oral fluids and recheck her urine in 4 hours
Check her blood ketones and inform the doctor urgently
Record the results and send the urine for culture
Give her usual insulin dose and recheck in the morning
7.w: High glucose with heavy ketonuria, vomiting and rapid breathing in type 1 diabetes suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, a medical emergency. The nurse should check capillary blood ketones per local protocol and escalate urgently (P3.11, P3.12; Annexe B 2.10).

n.0: Oral fluids and a 4-hour recheck delay treatment of possible ketoacidosis.
n.2: Culture does not address the immediate danger shown by the results.
n.3: Her usual dose does not treat ketoacidosis, and waiting until morning is unsafe.

7.q: A learning disability nurse uses O'Brien's five service accomplishments to review a supported living service. Which of these is one of the five accomplishments?
o: Community presence
Social integration
Protection from harm
Independent living
7.w: O'Brien's five accomplishments are community presence, relationships (community participation), choice, respect and competence. They describe what good services should help people to achieve.

n.1: Social integration is linked to normalisation but is not one of the five accomplishments.
n.2: Protection is a safeguarding aim, not one of the five accomplishments.
n.3: Independent living is valued, but the accomplishment is competence (developing skills).

7.q: A support worker new to a residential home asks the learning disability nurse what cerebral palsy is. Which description is most accurate?
o: Permanent movement and posture disorders from non-progressive injury to the developing brain
A form of learning disability that is defined by difficulty with movement
An inherited muscle disease that causes gradually increasing weakness from early childhood
A progressive degeneration of the motor neurones in the spinal cord that begins in early childhood
7.w: Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain. It is often accompanied by epilepsy, dysphagia, reflux, constipation and orthopaedic problems.

n.1: Cerebral palsy is a movement disorder; a learning disability may or may not occur with it.
n.2: Muscular dystrophies are inherited muscle diseases; cerebral palsy arises from the developing brain.
n.3: Motor neurone degeneration is progressive; the brain disturbance in cerebral palsy is not.

7.q: Asif, 32, has a moderate learning disability. His sister reports he has been talking to someone who is not there, and he is frightened in his room at night. Staff say he has always talked to himself. What is the best next step for the learning disability nurse?
o: Move him to a different bedroom and see whether his fear settles over a week
Compare with his known baseline and arrange a mental health assessment
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to help him sleep at night
Record that this is his usual self-talk and close the concern
7.w: Two-step reasoning: self-talk can be normal for some people with a learning disability, so the nurse first compares with the person's baseline; a change in content (frightened, responding to voices) suggests possible psychosis and needs a specialist mental health assessment (NICE NG54 1.1.2 differences in presentation; 1.6.5 refer suspected serious mental illness to a psychiatrist with expertise in learning disabilities).

n.0: Changing rooms may help comfort but does not assess a possible mental illness.
n.2: Medication before assessment is not appropriate and conflicts with STOMP.
n.3: Dismissing the change as usual self-talk is diagnostic overshadowing; the sister describes something new.

7.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
7.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

7.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
7.q: Helen, 61, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about breast screening. A support worker says, 'People with her level of disability don't really benefit from screening.' What is the best response?
o: Refer the decision to her GP, who can decide without consulting her carers or family
Agree, as screening is less useful for people with severe disabilities
Explain that best interests cannot rest on her condition but on her circumstances
Leave screening off her plan and review at her next health check
7.w: MCA s4(1): a best interests decision must not be made merely on the basis of a person's age, appearance, condition or behaviour. The decision-maker must consider Helen's individual circumstances, wishes and the benefits and burdens, with reasonable adjustments to make screening possible.

n.0: The decision-maker must consult those caring for her and interested in her welfare (s4(7)).
n.1: Assuming less benefit because of disability is discriminatory and breaches s4(1).
n.3: Removing screening on the basis of disability repeats the same unlawful reasoning.

7.q: Bill, 85, has advanced dementia and cannot describe his pain. After a fall he grimaces, groans and guards his left hip when moved. Which assessment is most appropriate?
o: A visual analogue scale explained slowly to him
A behavioural pain tool such as the Abbey pain scale
A 0-10 numerical rating scale completed by Bill himself
His daughter's estimate of his pain on a 0-10 scale
7.w: Where a person cannot reliably self-report, for example because of dementia or a learning disability, use a validated behavioural or observational pain assessment tool such as the Abbey pain scale or PAINAD (NICE NG31 principle; Annexe B 3.1).

n.0: A visual analogue scale still needs him to self-report, which he cannot reliably do.
n.2: Numerical self-report relies on abilities Bill no longer has.
n.3: Family insight is valuable, but a proxy number is not a validated assessment.

7.q: Alys, 38, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to a medical ward. Her long-standing support worker asks to stay overnight because Alys becomes frightened in unfamiliar places. Ward visiting ends at 8 pm. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse in charge?
o: Agree a trial stay and review whether to extend it in the morning
Ask the support worker to return at 8 am to help with personal care
Explain that ward visiting times apply to all visitors equally
Agree she can stay and plan how she will support Alys's care
7.w: Allowing a familiar carer to stay is a recognised reasonable adjustment (Equality Act 2010 s20). Agreeing roles in advance helps staff work with the carer while remaining responsible for Alys's nursing care.

n.0: Making the stay a trial overnight adds uncertainty for Alys without reason; her need for a familiar person is already known.
n.1: Returning in the morning leaves Alys frightened overnight, which is when she most needs support.
n.2: Applying the same rule to everyone can put a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage; the duty is to adjust.

7.q: Ruth, 64, has chronic kidney disease and symptomatic anaemia with a haemoglobin of 68 g/L. She is not bleeding and does not have acute coronary syndrome. The doctor plans a red cell transfusion. In line with NICE NG24, what is the recommended approach?
o: Transfuse 1 unit, then reassess and check haemoglobin
Transfuse until haemoglobin reaches at least 110 g/L
Transfuse 2 units, then check haemoglobin the next day
Transfuse 3 units to avoid repeated cannulation
7.w: NICE NG24 (updated 2026): use a restrictive threshold of 70 g/L with a target of 70-90 g/L after transfusion, and consider single-unit transfusions for adults without active bleeding, clinically reassessing and checking haemoglobin after each unit before giving more.

n.1: 110 g/L is well above the NG24 post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L.
n.2: Two units without reassessment risks overtransfusion and circulatory overload.
n.3: Multiple units without reassessment conflicts with single-unit transfusion and raises overload risk.

7.q: Noah, 5, has developmental delay, anxiety and hand-flapping. His paediatrician requests a genetic test. Which result would confirm fragile X syndrome?
o: More than 200 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene
An extra copy of chromosome 21 in the cells
A pathogenic variant in the MECP2 gene
Loss of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15
7.w: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a full mutation in FMR1 on the X chromosome: more than 200 CGG repeats (typical range about 5 to 40), which silences the gene (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.1: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.
n.2: MECP2 variants cause Rett syndrome.
n.3: Loss of maternal UBE3A causes Angelman syndrome.

7.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
7.q: Tara, 17, has a profound learning disability. Her family are worried that her care package will stop at 18. Which duty under the Care Act 2014 helps plan for this?
o: A transition assessment before she turns 18
A continuing healthcare checklist at age 21
A carer's assessment once she turns 18
A safeguarding enquiry under section 42
7.w: The Care Act 2014 requires local authorities to carry out transition assessments for children likely to have needs for care and support after turning 18 where it would be of significant benefit (ss58-66), so that support continues without a gap.

n.1: Continuing healthcare is a different NHS process and is not triggered at 21.
n.2: A carer's assessment is for her family's needs and does not replace planning for Tara's own care.
n.3: Section 42 enquiries concern abuse or neglect, not transition planning.

7.q: Grace, 34, develops a widespread rash, lip swelling and wheeze minutes after starting an IV antibiotic infusion. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the first action after calling for help?
o: Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first drug
Give oral cetirizine and recheck her in 15 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and continue to observe her
7.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, current): remove the trigger (stop the infusion) and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Adults and children over 12: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh.

n.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
n.2: Antihistamines are third-line and do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
n.3: Continuing the infusion, even slowed, keeps exposing her to the trigger.

7.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
7.q: Carl, 29, is autistic and has a learning disability. A gym run by the council bars him after he became distressed and shouted when the music was too loud, which staff know relates to his sensory needs. Which form of discrimination is most likely?
o: Discrimination arising from disability, unless a proportionate means of a legitimate aim
Direct discrimination, because the gym treated him less favourably for being disabled
Harassment, because the gym's decision violated his dignity and created a hostile environment
Victimisation, because he was barred after making a complaint
7.w: Equality Act 2010 s15: unfavourable treatment because of something arising in consequence of a person's disability (here distress linked to sensory needs), which the provider knows about, is discrimination unless it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. A failure to adjust (turning the music down) may also apply.

n.1: Direct discrimination is less favourable treatment because of disability itself; here it is because of behaviour arising from it.
n.2: Harassment is unwanted conduct related to disability that creates a hostile environment; this is a decision to bar him.
n.3: Victimisation is treatment because of a protected act such as a complaint, which did not happen here.

7.q: Mrs Adeyemi, 72, has capacity and a leg ulcer. When the nurse arrives to change the dressing she says firmly that she does not want it done today because she is tired. The dressing is not urgent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Change the dressing gently because it is in her best interests
Respect her decision, explore her reasons and record the refusal
Ask her daughter to persuade her to accept the dressing change
Assess her capacity because she is refusing recommended care
7.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment. Mrs Adeyemi has capacity, so her refusal is valid. The nurse should explore why, explain any consequences, offer another time and document the refusal.

n.0: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity (MCA s4); treating a capacitous person against her refusal is unlawful.
n.2: Using a relative to pressure her undermines the voluntariness of any later consent.
n.3: Refusing care is not evidence of incapacity; MCA s1(4) says an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity, and capacity is presumed.

7.q: Jas, a learning disability nurse, is writing a Social Story for Riley, 15, who is autistic and is having a blood test. Which sentence fits the Social Story approach best?
o: The nurse will put a band on my arm. It will feel tight for a short time.
If I do not keep still, the nurse will have to try again.
Most young people are brave and do not cry when they have blood taken.
The needle is tiny, so it will not hurt me when it goes in.
7.w: Social Stories use descriptive, accurate and reassuring sentences, often in the first person, that explain what will happen and how it may feel. They avoid threats, comparisons and false promises (Carol Gray).

n.1: This frames the story as a warning, which can increase anxiety.
n.2: Comparisons and pressure to be 'brave' are not descriptive and can cause shame.
n.3: Promising it will not hurt is inaccurate and can damage trust.

7.q: A practice nurse needs to send a patient's wound photographs and care plan to the community nursing team. Which method is most appropriate?
o: Send them by WhatsApp to the community nurse's phone
Print them and post them by second class mail
Email them from her personal account as it is faster
Send them through an approved, secure NHS system
7.w: Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely. Code 10.5 keep records secure; Caldicott principles; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality.

n.0: Personal messaging apps are not approved secure systems for clinical data.
n.1: Post is slower and less secure than approved electronic routes.
n.2: Personal email breaches data security (Code 10.5).

7.q: Frank, 70, has a nasogastric tube. Before his morning feed you aspirate and the pH is 6.5. He takes a proton pump inhibitor. He is comfortable with normal observations. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the feed, as the pH is close to the safe range
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Use the whoosh test to confirm the tube position
Flush with 50 mL of water and start feeding
7.w: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not feed; follow local protocol, which may involve waiting and retesting, or an X-ray. CG32 rec 1.7.17 notes that pH may be invalid with acid suppression, which local protocols must address. Air auscultation (the whoosh test) is not a safe method.

n.0: Feeding with an unconfirmed tube position risks feed entering the lungs.
n.2: The whoosh test is unreliable and was removed from practice by the NPSA in 2005.
n.3: Flushing an unconfirmed tube risks fluid entering the lungs.

7.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
7.q: A student nurse asks when a learning disability, on its own, can count as a mental disorder for detention for treatment under section 3 of the Mental Health Act 1983. What does section 1(2A) require?
o: Association with a serious and continuing risk of self-neglect or exploitation
Association with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct
Assessment of the learning disability as severe or profound
A coexisting diagnosis of autism or of a personality disorder of any kind
7.w: MHA 1983 s1(2A)-(2B): for section 3, guardianship, CTOs and most Part 3 provisions, a person with a learning disability is not considered to have a mental disorder by reason of that disability unless it is associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.

n.0: Self-neglect or exploitation is not the statutory qualifier.
n.2: The qualifier concerns conduct, not the severity of the learning disability.
n.3: A second diagnosis is not what the qualifier requires.

7.q: On a dementia ward, Mr Payne, 81, lacks capacity and needed to be briefly held by two trained staff to stop him hitting another patient. He is now calm. Besides checking him for injury, what should the nurse record about the incident?
o: The details in the incident system, rather than his care record
A brief note that restraint was needed, to avoid labelling him
The reasons for the hold, technique used, duration and his response
That he was held in his best interests, with the names of staff
7.w: Code 10.1-10.4 requires accurate, timely records that attribute, date and time entries. Any restraint must be justified as necessary and proportionate (MCA s6), so the record should show why it was used, how, for how long and its effect, supporting review and learning.

n.0: Incident reporting is appropriate, but the care record must also document what happened to him.
n.1: A minimal note fails Code 10 and prevents review of whether the restraint was justified.
n.3: Stating 'best interests' without reasons, technique and duration does not show the hold was necessary and proportionate.

7.q: After staff use a two-person hold to stop Kieran, 20, from hitting another resident, the learning disability nurse leads the response. Kieran has a moderate learning disability. Which action should follow once everyone is safe?
o: Ask the GP for regular sedation to prevent further incidents
Add the hold to Kieran's plan as the first response for the future
Move Kieran to another service so that the other resident is protected
Record the hold and hold a debrief with Kieran and with staff
7.w: NICE NG11 1.9.6: every restrictive intervention is recorded and followed by a debrief with the person (in an accessible way) and with staff, to support recovery and learn how to prevent recurrence; data feed into the reduction programme.

n.0: Regular sedation is chemical restraint and is not supported by NG11 or STOMP after one incident.
n.1: Restrictive interventions are a last resort; making the hold the first response increases restriction.
n.2: A placement move is a major decision that is not justified by a single incident and does not address the cause.

7.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
