An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
7.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

7.q: Ida, 79, is being fed through a nasogastric tube. During the feed she starts coughing, becomes breathless and her SpO2 falls from 96% to 89%. What should the nurse do first?
o: Slow the feed rate and recheck her saturation
Flush the tube with water to clear any blockage
Stop the feed, sit her up and call for urgent help
Check the tube length mark and continue feeding
7.w: Sudden coughing, breathlessness and desaturation during a feed suggest aspiration or tube misplacement. Stop the feed, sit her upright, give oxygen and get urgent help (Annexe B 5.7; misplaced tubes are a Never Event).

n.0: Continuing a slower feed risks further aspiration.
n.1: Flushing adds more fluid to a possibly misplaced tube.
n.3: Continuing feeding is unsafe until the cause is established.

7.q: Mr Hussain, 69, has died on a medical ward after an expected death. The death is not being referred to the coroner. His family tell the nurse that their faith requires family members to wash his body and that they would like to do this themselves. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that hospital policy requires staff to wash all deceased patients
Leave the washing to the family and support them with the rest of his care
Ask the mortuary staff to wash him before he is released to the family
Wash him before the family arrive so that they are spared any distress
7.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): wash the deceased unless requested not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons, or the death is being referred to the coroner; key contacts may wish to assist and should be supported. NMC Code 1.3 and 1.5: recognise diversity and individual choice, and respect and uphold people's human rights.

n.0: Care after death guidance says wash the deceased unless asked not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons.
n.2: Washing by mortuary staff would also override the family's wish to carry out the washing themselves.
n.3: This disregards the family's stated religious wishes, which the guidance says must be respected.

7.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, is treated for alcohol intoxication. She mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone. She refuses to let staff contact anyone. Under the Children Act 2004 s16LA duty in force since 30 September 2026, what should the nurse do?
o: Seek Kerry's consent again and share the information if she agrees
Share once a safeguarding threshold has been reached
Record the concern and share if it happens again
Share the relevant information with children's social care now
7.w: Children Act 2004 s16LA (inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, in force 30 September 2026) requires bodies under the s11 duty, including NHS bodies, to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, without a threshold and without needing consent, unless sharing would be more harmful to the child. A young child alone at home needs immediate action.

n.0: Consent is not required under s16LA, and waiting for it delays protection of a child at immediate risk.
n.1: s16LA sets no threshold; the information is relevant to his safety and must be shared.
n.2: A 3-year-old alone at home is at immediate risk; waiting for a repeat leaves him unprotected.

7.q: Which is the correct order of the phases of wound healing?
o: Inflammation, haemostasis, maturation, proliferation
Proliferation, haemostasis, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, proliferation, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation
7.w: Wounds heal through overlapping phases: haemostasis (clotting), inflammation (clearing debris and bacteria), proliferation (granulation tissue and epithelialisation) and maturation or remodelling (collagen reorganisation, which can last months).

n.0: Haemostasis comes first, and proliferation precedes maturation.
n.1: Proliferation follows inflammation; it does not begin the process.
n.2: Inflammation precedes proliferation, not the other way round.

7.q: A student nurse asks Priti why she called the outreach team for a patient whose NEWS2 is 4, when the escalation chart only requires a ward review. Priti had noticed new subtle confusion. Which response best shows sound professional judgement?
o: Explain that her clinical concern justified the escalation
Explain that students should not question escalation decisions
Explain that the score required outreach review at that level
Explain that she prefers to escalate every patient to be safe
7.w: Proficiency P1.10: demonstrate resilience and emotional intelligence and explain the rationale for judgements and decisions. NEWS2 (RCP 2017): clinical concern can prompt escalation beyond the aggregate score; new confusion scores 3.

n.1: This shuts down learning; Code 9.4 requires her to support students' learning.
n.2: Under NEWS2 (RCP 2017) an aggregate of 4 calls for a ward-based response, urgent review by the ward medical team if one parameter scores 3, not outreach; her call rested on clinical concern.
n.3: Blanket escalation is not a reasoned judgement; P1.10 requires the rationale to be explained.

7.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
7.q: Amira, 50, has a profound learning disability. Her NEWS2 score has risen from 2 to 5 over four hours, and her mother reports she is 'very different'. What is the correct escalation?
o: Change her observations to every 12 hours overnight
Repeat her observations again in four hours
Urgent review by a clinician skilled in acute illness
Inform the nurse in charge at the next handover
7.w: A NEWS2 aggregate of 5 or more triggers an urgent response: urgent review by a clinician with competence in assessing acute illness and at least hourly observations (RCP NEWS2). Her mother's concern adds weight to escalation.

n.0: Twelve-hourly observations are for scores of 0.
n.1: Four-hourly observations are too infrequent for a score of 5.
n.3: Waiting for handover delays an urgent response.

7.q: A ward team wants to reduce the number of missed doses of time-critical medicines. Using the Model for Improvement, which question should they answer first?
o: Who was responsible for the missed doses last month?
What change can we make that will result in improvement?
What are we trying to accomplish?
How will we know that a change is an improvement?
7.w: The Model for Improvement (used in NHS England improvement resources) asks three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? (the aim); How will we know that a change is an improvement? (measures); What change can we make that will result in improvement? (change ideas). Changes are then tested with PDSA cycles. Setting the aim comes first (P6.4).

n.0: Improvement methods look at system causes rather than individual blame, and this is not one of the model's questions.
n.1: Change ideas are the third question, chosen once the aim and measures are agreed.
n.3: Measures are the second question; they depend on a clear aim.

7.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
7.q: Ken, 56, has a learning disability and lives in a privately owned care home. His place is arranged and paid for by the local authority. His sister asks whether the home must respect his rights under the Human Rights Act 1998. What is the most accurate answer?
o: Yes, as care arranged or paid for by a council is treated as a public function
No, the Act binds NHS and council-run services rather than private homes
Yes, because every private company is bound by the Human Rights Act
No, unless Ken has been detained under the Mental Health Act
7.w: Two steps: the Human Rights Act binds public authorities (s6); the Care Act 2014 s73 provides that registered care providers delivering care and support arranged or paid for by a local authority are treated as exercising a public function, so they must act compatibly with Convention rights.

n.1: The Care Act extends HRA duties to private providers of council-arranged care.
n.2: The Act does not bind every private company; it depends on public functions.
n.3: MHA detention is not the trigger; council-arranged care is.

7.q: Maria, 29, is from a Gypsy, Roma and Traveller community and lives on an unauthorised site. A GP receptionist has told her she cannot register without proof of address. The practice nurse is asked for advice. What is correct?
o: She must register as a temporary resident, having no fixed address
She can register without proof of address or identification
She can attend the emergency department for routine care instead
She must provide a utility bill before she can register
7.w: NHS England guidance states that anyone in England can register with a GP practice and that proof of address, identification or immigration status is not needed to register. Facilitating equitable access for groups who face barriers is part of P7.9 (Core20PLUS5 recognises such inclusion health groups; Equality Act 2010, race is a protected characteristic).

n.0: Temporary registration is for people staying in an area for a short time; having no fixed address does not restrict her to it, and she is entitled to full registration.
n.2: Directing routine care to the emergency department is inappropriate and deepens inequality of access.
n.3: Lack of proof of address is not a reason to refuse registration.

7.q: On a ward, an AED is attached to Kevin, 63, during CPR. The AED announces it is analysing the rhythm. What should the team do?
o: Stop compressions and ensure nobody touches him
Continue compressions during the rhythm analysis
Check his carotid pulse while it analyses
Give two rescue breaths while it analyses
7.w: RCUK 2025: follow AED prompts; nobody should touch the person during rhythm analysis, as movement interferes with analysis. Resume compressions immediately after the shock or no-shock prompt.

n.1: Compressions during analysis cause artefact and can delay or prevent a shock.
n.2: Pulse checks involve touching him and delay the AED's decision.
n.3: Breaths involve touching him and interfere with analysis.

7.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion with a fever of 38.4°C. The doctor requests a catheter specimen of urine (CSU) before antibiotics are started. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
o: Decontaminate hands and aspirate from the sampling port aseptically
Disconnect the bag and collect urine from the end of the catheter
Collect urine from the drainage bag outlet into a sterile pot
Replace the catheter and send a sample from the new catheter
7.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and obtain urine samples from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the drainage system closed.

n.1: Breaking the closed drainage system raises the risk of introducing infection.
n.2: Urine in the bag has stood and may be colonised, so it does not reflect bladder urine.
n.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary; changing it just to obtain a sample is not the CG139 method.

7.q: Mrs Wood, 82, lives alone in England and receives daily care visits for help with washing and meals. She tells the community nurse that her grandson takes her bank card and she now cannot afford food. She says she is frightened of him. Which type of abuse is most clearly described?
o: Financial or material abuse
Self-neglect by Mrs Wood
Organisational abuse by the care agency
Discriminatory abuse by a relative
7.w: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.17 lists financial or material abuse, including theft and misuse of a person's money or possessions. Taking her bank card so she cannot buy food fits this type.

n.1: Self-neglect is a person neglecting their own care; here the harm is caused by her grandson.
n.2: Organisational abuse arises within a care setting or service, not from a family member at home.
n.3: Discriminatory abuse is harm motivated by a protected characteristic; nothing suggests this.

7.q: Lily, 5, has Down syndrome. Her teacher reports that over the past term she has stopped responding when her name is called and seems 'in her own world'. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Refer to the educational psychologist for an attention assessment
Arrange a hearing assessment, as hearing loss and glue ear are common
Refer to CAMHS because she may be showing new autistic features
Record the change as behaviour linked to her learning disability
7.w: Hearing loss, including glue ear, is common in children with Down syndrome (NHS.uk). A child who stops responding to her name needs her hearing checked first, before other explanations are explored.

n.0: Attention assessment may follow, but hearing is the likely and treatable cause to check first.
n.2: Autism can occur with Down syndrome, but a treatable hearing problem should be excluded first.
n.3: Recording it as part of her learning disability is diagnostic overshadowing.

7.q: An NHS trust plans to move all outpatient bookings to an online-only app. A senior nurse on the project group is asked what the public sector equality duty requires. Which answer is correct?
o: Obtain written consent from disabled patients before making the change
Have due regard to the effect on people with protected characteristics
Seek approval for the change from the CQC before launch
Ensure that every patient has a smartphone before the change
7.w: Equality Act 2010 s149: public authorities must have due regard to the need to eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations between people with and without protected characteristics.

n.0: Section 149 does not require individual consent; it requires due regard when making decisions.
n.2: The CQC does not approve booking systems; s149 places the due regard duty on the trust itself.
n.3: The duty is to have due regard to equality aims, not to supply equipment to every patient.

7.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
7.q: A support worker who has completed buccal midazolam training is preparing to give it to Owen, 29, during a prolonged seizure. Where should the midazolam be given?
o: Onto the back of the throat
Into the nostril
Between the gum and the cheek
Under the tongue (sublingual)
7.w: Buccal midazolam is given into the buccal cavity, between the gum and the cheek, where it is absorbed through the lining of the mouth. Half may be given on each side if the person's plan states so.

n.0: Giving liquid onto the back of the throat risks aspiration.
n.1: Intranasal midazolam exists but is a different preparation and route from buccal midazolam.
n.3: Sublingual administration is not the buccal route, and the tongue may obstruct during a seizure.

7.q: Asha, 19, has a learning disability and is leaving residential school. Which approach best reflects person-centred planning?
o: Her parents agree her plan on her behalf, as they know her best
A plan is built around what matters to Asha, with her and the people she chooses
Professionals write a plan from her assessed needs and the services available
The plan focuses on reducing the risks that her school has identified
7.w: Person-centred planning puts the person at the centre: it starts with what is important to and for them, involves people they choose, and shapes services around them (Valuing People; NMC Code 2). It supports the P3.4 proficiency of working in partnership with people.

n.0: Families are important partners, but the plan must be built with Asha, not for her.
n.2: Starting from available services is service-led rather than person-centred.
n.3: Risk matters, but a plan focused on risk is not built around her aspirations.

8.q: Nina, 33, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name and her pain score is 9 while she is using her phone. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
o: Accept her report of pain and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Delay analgesia until her behaviour matches her pain score
Offer paracetamol until the doctor has assessed her pain
Ask her to stop using her phone before reassessing her pain
8.w: Pain is what the person says it is; self-report is the most reliable measure. People with long-term painful conditions often know which analgesia works and may cope with distraction. Prompt analgesia is essential, and judgement based on stereotypes breaches Code 20.2 and 1.1.

n.1: Behaviour is a poor guide to pain in people with recurrent pain, and delay causes harm.
n.2: Withholding effective prescribed analgesia leaves severe pain undertreated.
n.3: Distraction is a coping strategy and does not invalidate her pain score.

8.q: Ravi, 30, is autistic with a learning disability and is in hospital after a fall. He becomes distressed every morning when a different nurse arrives. Staff are short and have to rotate allocation. Which is the best adjustment?
o: Ask the ward to allocate him whichever nurse is least busy
Let him stay in bed until he has calmed down each morning
Explain to Ravi that staff changes are unavoidable on a busy ward
Use a photo board each morning showing who is caring for him that day
8.w: Two-step reasoning: the trigger is unpredictability, and constant staff cannot be guaranteed, so the next best adjustment is to make the change predictable with visual information (NICE CG142 1.1.8 visual supports for autistic adults). Where possible, consistent staffing should also be considered.

n.0: Allocation by workload increases unpredictability rather than reducing it.
n.1: Staying in bed delays recovery after a fall and does not address the trigger.
n.2: An explanation alone does not reduce the unpredictability causing his distress.

8.q: Nurse Ola realises she gave Leon, 45, 10 mg of oral morphine solution instead of the prescribed 5 mg, 20 minutes ago. Leon is alert with a respiratory rate of 16 and no sedation. What should Ola do?
o: Rewrite the chart entry to 5 mg to avoid confusing the next nurse
Monitor Leon, inform the prescriber, tell Leon and report the incident
Observe Leon and report the error if he shows any signs of harm
Inform the ward manager and leave her to decide whether to tell Leon
8.w: Medication incidents are reported and reflected on (P6.8; NMC Code 19): the priority is the person's safety (monitoring sedation and respiratory rate), then informing the prescriber, being open with Leon (professional duty of candour), and reporting through the local system feeding LFPSE.

n.0: Altering the record to hide an error is dishonest and breaches the Code.
n.2: Incidents, including those without harm, are reported so that learning can occur.
n.3: The professional duty of candour is personal; Ola should be open with Leon herself.

8.q: Mrs Ross, 77, is ventilated in the intensive care unit after major emergency surgery. Over the last few hours she has become agitated at times and keeps picking at her lines. The nurse is concerned she may be developing delirium. Which assessment tool is recommended in this setting by NICE CG103?
o: CAM-ICU or ICDSC
The Glasgow Coma Scale
The 4AT
The Abbey pain scale
8.w: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.1: in critical care or the recovery room after surgery, use CAM-ICU or the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist instead of the 4AT.

n.1: GCS measures level of consciousness and does not assess delirium.
n.2: The 4AT is recommended for most settings, but CG103 specifies CAM-ICU or ICDSC in critical care.
n.3: The Abbey scale assesses pain in people who cannot communicate, not delirium.

8.q: A nurse joining a care home finds that Ada, 90, has been given her medicines covertly for 10 months. The best interests decision and management plan are filed, but there is no record of any review since. What should the nurse do?
o: Continue, as a plan is in place and signed
Ask Ada's daughter to confirm she still agrees with the plan
Stop all covert medicines until the GP's next visit
Arrange a review of the plan with the multidisciplinary team
8.w: Covert administration requires a documented management plan that is reviewed regularly (NICE SC1 1.15; RPS/RCN 2019 paras 21-23). Ada's capacity, the need for each medicine and the method should be reconsidered by the team, including the prescriber and pharmacist.

n.0: A plan without review may be out of date; review is a required safeguard.
n.1: Family views are part of the review, but the daughter cannot authorise continuation alone.
n.2: Abruptly stopping all medicines could cause harm; a prompt review is needed instead.

8.q: Mr Okonjo, 74, now lacks capacity after a cardiac arrest. He has a valid and applicable advance decision refusing CPR, written and signed, witnessed and stating it applies even if his life is at risk. His daughter is distressed and demands that CPR be given if he arrests again. What should the nurse do?
o: Seek a best interests decision from the medical team
Follow the advance decision and support his daughter
Give CPR because the daughter is the next of kin
Ask the daughter to sign a form overriding the refusal
8.w: A valid and applicable advance decision has the same effect as a contemporaneous refusal (MCA 2005 s26(1)), and the s25 formalities for life-sustaining treatment are met. Relatives cannot override it. The nurse should explain this sensitively and support the daughter.

n.0: A best interests decision is not made where a valid and applicable advance decision already refuses the treatment.
n.2: Next of kin has no power to override a valid advance decision.
n.3: A relative cannot sign away a valid advance decision made by the person.

8.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
8.q: Sarah, 40, has a learning disability. Her father is dying in a hospice. Staff in her supported living home think she should not visit or go to the funeral because she 'won't understand'. What should the nurse advise?
o: Decide for her once her father has died
Support Sarah to choose whether to visit and attend
Agree that she should stay at home to avoid distress
Let her attend the funeral but not visit the hospice
8.w: Including people with a learning disability in saying goodbye and in rituals such as funerals supports healthy grieving. Assumptions that a person 'won't understand' are discriminatory; Sarah should be prepared accessibly and supported to make her own choice.

n.0: Delaying the decision removes her chance to see her father.
n.2: Excluding her denies her the chance to say goodbye and can complicate grief.
n.3: Restricting her to the funeral is a choice made for her, not by her.

8.q: A learning disability nurse is supporting Ben, 25, who has Down syndrome, at his annual health check. NICE NG54 recommends a particular assessment for all adults with Down syndrome to help detect later decline. Which is it?
o: Genetic testing for the APP gene
A yearly brain MRI from the age of 25
A baseline memory clinic referral at age 25
A baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour
8.w: NICE NG54 1.7.13: complete a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour with all adults with Down's syndrome, so that later changes in skills can be measured against it.

n.0: Genetic testing does not establish a functional baseline and is not recommended for this purpose.
n.1: Routine imaging is not recommended for screening.
n.2: Memory clinic referral is for suspected dementia, not a routine baseline.

8.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
8.q: Sam, 16, has a learning disability. A nurse is planning his transition meeting. Which approach to his involvement best reflects NICE NG43?
o: Let professionals agree the plan and then share it
Hold the meeting with his parents and inform Sam later
Postpone involving Sam until he is 18
Involve Sam in planning and agree goals with him
8.w: NICE NG43 1.1.4 and 1.2.4: transition planning should fully involve the young person, agree goals with them and build their confidence to direct their own care, with the family involved as appropriate; it should be reviewed at least annually.

n.0: A plan agreed without him is not person-centred.
n.1: Excluding Sam from his own planning breaches NG43's person-centred approach.
n.2: Waiting until 18 misses years of planning and skill-building.

8.q: Ella, 14, is in school Year 9. The school nurse assesses her as Gillick competent, and Ella consents to her MenACWY vaccine. Her mother has returned a form refusing the vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the vaccine, as a parent cannot override a Gillick competent child's consent
Delay the vaccine until Ella is 16 and can legally consent for herself
Ask the head teacher to decide whether the vaccine should be given
Withhold the vaccine, because a parent's refusal takes priority under age 16
8.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): children under 16 who understand fully what is involved (Gillick competent) can give consent, ideally with parental involvement; where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent. UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: MenACWY at 14 years (school Year 9).

n.1: Gillick competent children under 16 can consent, so waiting is unnecessary.
n.2: The head teacher has no role in consent to Ella's treatment.
n.3: The Green Book states that where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent.

8.q: Frank Ellis, 74, uses a walking frame and fell once at home last month. He has capacity and wants to walk to the day room for lunch. His daughter asks the nurse to keep him in his chair so he cannot fall again. Which response best reflects positive risk management?
o: Let Mr Ellis walk to the day room after he signs a disclaimer accepting the risk of falling
Arrange for him to use a wheelchair to reach the day room until physiotherapy can review him
Agree with the daughter and keep him seated at lunchtimes until he is discharged home
Agree a plan with Mr Ellis for supervised walking with his frame and record the discussion
8.w: Positive risk management weighs benefits and harms with the person and puts proportionate controls in place so they can do what matters to them, rather than removing all activity (P6.10 risk management versus risk aversion). Mr Ellis has capacity, so his decision is respected (MCA 2005 s1), and the plan and discussion are documented (Code 10).

n.0: A disclaimer does not manage the risk or remove the nurse's duty of care; it replaces planning with paperwork.
n.1: Using a wheelchair when he can walk with his frame reduces independence and mobility without a clinical reason.
n.2: Keeping him seated is risk aversion: it removes activity he values, causes deconditioning and overrides the choice of a person with capacity.

8.q: Hilda, 74, has had a nasogastric tube inserted for feeding after a stroke. You aspirate gastric contents and test them on CE-marked pH paper. Which reading confirms gastric placement so that feeding can start?
o: pH 8.5 or above
pH 6.0 or below
pH 7.0 or above
pH 5.5 or below
8.w: NICE CG32: gastric tube position is confirmed by pH 5.5 or below on pH paper. Position must be confirmed after placement and before each use by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary (rec 1.7.17).

n.0: pH 8.5 is alkaline and suggests a non-gastric position.
n.1: pH 6.0 is above the 5.5 threshold and does not confirm gastric placement.
n.2: pH 7 or above may indicate the tube is in the lung or intestine.

8.q: Frank, 70, has a nasogastric tube. Before his morning feed you aspirate and the pH is 6.5. He takes a proton pump inhibitor. He is comfortable with normal observations. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the feed, as the pH is close to the safe range
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Use the whoosh test to confirm the tube position
Flush with 50 mL of water and start feeding
8.w: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not feed; follow local protocol, which may involve waiting and retesting, or an X-ray. CG32 rec 1.7.17 notes that pH may be invalid with acid suppression, which local protocols must address. Air auscultation (the whoosh test) is not a safe method.

n.0: Feeding with an unconfirmed tube position risks feed entering the lungs.
n.2: The whoosh test is unreliable and was removed from practice by the NPSA in 2005.
n.3: Flushing an unconfirmed tube risks fluid entering the lungs.

8.q: A ward manager, Leon, has noticed over three weeks that a staff nurse, Abi, regularly completes her patients' records several hours after care. Patient care has otherwise been good. What is Leon's most appropriate first step?
o: Start a formal capability process with a written warning
Meet Abi privately, give examples, explore reasons and agree a plan
Refer Abi to the NMC for failing to keep records as required
Move Abi to a different ward with a lighter workload
8.w: Performance management starts with an informal, supportive conversation using specific examples, exploring causes (for example workload or skills) and agreeing objectives, support and a review date, escalating to formal processes only if problems continue (P5.3 principles and processes of performance management; Code 10.1 records completed at the time or as soon as possible after).

n.0: Formal processes are disproportionate before an informal discussion and support have been tried.
n.2: This is a local performance issue, not a fitness to practise concern at this stage.
n.3: Moving her does not address the reasons for the delay or support her improvement.

8.q: Kai, 34, is on an intensive care unit, and the team have decided to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. The bedside nurse thinks organ donation may be possible and Kai's parents are at the bedside. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Raise donation with Kai's parents yourself at the bedside straight away
Contact the specialist nurse for organ donation to lead the approach
Wait to see whether Kai's parents ask about organ donation
Ask Kai's GP to discuss donation with his parents by phone
8.w: NHS Blood and Transplant / British Transplantation Society best practice: the specialist nurse for organ donation is the main professional who makes the family approach, in collaboration with the hospital team, after checking the NHS Organ Donor Register for a recorded decision or nominated representative. Families are always approached if donation is possible.

n.0: The family approach is planned jointly and led by the specialist nurse, who checks the Organ Donor Register first.
n.2: Families are approached whenever donation is possible; waiting may lose the chance to honour Kai's decision.
n.3: The GP is not part of the donation pathway; the specialist nurse for organ donation leads it.

8.q: Ayesha, 30, has a learning disability and uses her own signs, which her support worker understands. During a consultation the doctor directs all questions to the support worker. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the support worker to leave so Ayesha can answer for herself
Arrange a separate meeting with the support worker to gather the history
Ask the doctor to speak to Ayesha, with the support worker helping interpret
Let the support worker answer, as she knows Ayesha best
8.w: Communication should be directed to the person, with others helping only to support understanding. This respects Ayesha's dignity and right to be involved (Code 2.1, 7; Annexe A 2.5; MCA s1(3)).

n.0: Removing the person who understands her signs would make communication harder.
n.1: A separate meeting still bypasses Ayesha and misses the chance to hear from her.
n.3: Talking about Ayesha rather than to her excludes her from her own care.

8.q: A nurse is helping to design a local prevention strategy and wants to apply a life course approach. Which statement best reflects that approach?
o: Accept that adult health is fixed by genes, so early action changes little
Begin prevention once a long-term condition has been diagnosed in the person
Act early and at key transitions, as health is shaped across the whole of life
Focus prevention on older adults, as most long-term disease occurs in later life
8.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): a life course approach considers the critical stages, transitions and settings where large differences can be made, taking action early and appropriately across the life course and reducing health inequalities throughout life.

n.0: The approach rests on evidence that early and timely action changes lifelong outcomes.
n.1: Waiting for diagnosis misses the critical earlier stages the approach targets.
n.3: A life course approach acts at every stage, including early years, not just in later life.

8.q: Toby, 8, has Angelman syndrome and uses no spoken words. His new teaching assistant asks how best to communicate with him. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Offer signs, symbols or a communication aid alongside speech
Avoid signs and pictures, so that he is encouraged to develop speech
Speak more loudly, as hearing loss explains the lack of speech
Rely on written instructions, as reading is usually a relative strength
8.w: Severe speech impairment is a core feature of Angelman syndrome. A total communication approach using signs, symbols, objects or a communication aid alongside speech gives him ways to understand and express himself.

n.1: Alternative communication supports rather than blocks speech, and withholding it removes his means of communicating.
n.2: The lack of speech is part of the syndrome, not caused by hearing loss.
n.3: Most people with Angelman syndrome have a severe learning disability and do not read.

8.q: At the start of an early shift, Nina, a staff nurse, is allocated four patients on a medical ward. Which patient should she see first?
o: Mr Ali, 66, whose insulin is due with breakfast in 45 minutes
Mrs Dunn, 74, whose respiratory rate is 28/min, SpO2 89% and who is newly confused
Ms Reid, 52, who reports post-operative pain of 5/10, last analgesia 3 hours ago
Mr Shaw, 59, who is to be discharged today and needs his discharge letter
8.w: Prioritisation uses an ABCDE approach and early warning scores: Mrs Dunn has a respiratory rate of 28 (scores 3), SpO2 89% (scores 3) and new confusion (scores 3) on NEWS2 (RCP 2017), indicating possible life-threatening deterioration needing immediate assessment and escalation (P5.5 lead and manage care of a group of people with prioritisation).

n.0: Time-critical insulin matters, but there are 45 minutes before it is due and he is not unwell.
n.2: Her pain needs prompt attention, possibly by another team member, but is not life-threatening.
n.3: Discharge paperwork can safely wait while a deteriorating patient is assessed.

8.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
8.q: A hospital's outpatient manager says, 'We make reasonable adjustments for people with a learning disability as soon as someone asks us to.' Which response by the liaison nurse is most accurate?
o: That is correct, because the duty is triggered by a request from the patient
The duty is anticipatory, so adjustments should be planned before people attend
The duty applies to private providers rather than to NHS hospitals
That is correct when a formal diagnosis appears on the referral letter
8.w: For service providers, including the NHS, the reasonable adjustments duty is anticipatory: they must think in advance about what disabled people generally may need, such as easy read letters and longer appointments, rather than waiting for a request.

n.0: Waiting for a request breaches the anticipatory nature of the duty.
n.2: The duty applies to NHS services as service providers.
n.3: The duty does not depend on a formal diagnosis being supplied.

8.q: Ivy, 84, now has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to decide where she lives or how she is cared for. Some years ago, with capacity, she wrote a signed letter saying she would like to be cared for at home and prefers baths to showers. How should staff treat this letter?
o: As having no weight now that she lacks capacity to confirm her wishes
As a legally binding instruction that must be followed in the same way as an ADRT
As a statement of her wishes that must be considered in best interests decisions
As binding once her GP has countersigned it and placed it in her record
8.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6)(a): in deciding best interests, consider so far as reasonably ascertainable the person's past and present wishes and feelings, in particular any relevant written statement made when they had capacity. An advance statement of this kind is considered but is not legally binding, unlike a valid and applicable ADRT (ss24-26).

n.0: MCA s4(6)(a) requires decision makers to consider past wishes, in particular relevant written statements made with capacity.
n.1: A statement of wishes and preferences is not legally binding; only a valid, applicable ADRT binds staff to a refusal of treatment.
n.3: A GP signature does not convert a statement of wishes into a binding document.

8.q: Ms Ford, 50, is due to have surgery this afternoon. She is restless, keeps asking the same questions and says she cannot stop thinking she will not wake up. Her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate initial nursing intervention?
o: Give her a leaflet about the operation and leave her to rest
Ask the anaesthetist to prescribe a sedative premedication
Tell her that modern anaesthetics are very safe and move on
Sit with her, explore her fears and explain what will happen
8.w: NMC proficiency P4.8 requires nurses to initiate interventions for common symptoms including anxiety. Listening, exploring specific fears and giving clear information are first-line, person-centred interventions for pre-operative anxiety.

n.0: A leaflet without discussion leaves her specific fears unexplored.
n.1: Medication may be considered later, but non-drug measures come first for anxiety with normal observations.
n.2: Brief reassurance without exploring her fears does not address her anxiety.

8.q: A GP practice nurse sees Mia, 4, who has a high fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a spreading maculopapular rash. She is unvaccinated. The GP suspects measles. Which statement about notification in England is accurate?
o: It is notified on suspicion, urgently by phone to the health protection team
It is reported online within 7 days as a routine notifiable disease
It is notified by the school nurse once two linked cases are confirmed
It is notified once laboratory confirmation of measles has been received
8.w: Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, registered medical practitioners must notify UKHSA on suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Measles is listed as urgent, so it is phoned to the local health protection team within 24 hours, and all cases are reported within 3 days (UKHSA guidance).

n.1: Measles is an urgent notifiable disease, and the reporting deadline for all cases is 3 days, not 7.
n.2: The duty sits with the registered medical practitioner and applies to a single suspected case.
n.3: UKHSA states do not wait for laboratory confirmation; notification is on clinical suspicion.

8.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
8.q: A LeDeR review finds that Ahmed, 52, who had a learning disability, died after signs of pneumonia were attributed to his 'usual behaviour' and treatment was delayed for days. Which Human Rights Act article places a positive duty on the NHS in this context?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial
Article 3, the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 2, the right to life
8.w: Article 2 protects the right to life and places positive obligations on public authorities such as the NHS to protect life, including through proper systems of care; avoidable deaths linked to diagnostic overshadowing engage it.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings, not clinical care.
n.1: Article 3 concerns ill-treatment; the central issue in an avoidable death is the right to life.
n.2: Article 9 concerns belief and religion, not the delay in treatment.

8.q: Mr Nowak, 70, has expressive aphasia after a stroke and cannot speak clearly. A decision is needed about moving him to a rehabilitation unit. Before anyone concludes he lacks capacity, what should the nurse do?
o: Wait for his speech to recover fully before discussing the move
Record that he lacks capacity because he cannot speak clearly
Ask his wife to make the decision as she knows his wishes best
Arrange communication aids or speech and language therapy input
8.w: MCA 2005 s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. s3(1)(d) allows communication by any means, so aids and specialist input should be tried.

n.0: Delaying indefinitely is not required; the duty is to take practicable steps to support his decision now.
n.1: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; s3(1)(d) covers any means.
n.2: His wife cannot decide for him unless she holds a relevant LPA; the first step is to support him to decide.

8.q: Mr Ali, 41, is given IV co-amoxiclav. Within minutes he says his throat feels tight, and the nurse hears a harsh, high-pitched noise each time he breathes in. What does this sound indicate, and what is the priority?
o: Normal breath sounds; reassure him and continue the infusion
Crackles from fluid; sit him up and recheck later
Wheeze from asthma; give his inhaler and observe him
Stridor from upper airway obstruction; call for emergency help
8.w: A harsh, high-pitched inspiratory sound is stridor, indicating upper airway narrowing. After an IV antibiotic this suggests anaphylaxis, an airway emergency: stop the infusion, call for help and treat following the RCUK ABCDE approach and anaphylaxis algorithm.

n.0: Stridor with throat tightness is never a normal finding and continuing the drug is dangerous.
n.1: Crackles are added sounds in the lungs and are not the harsh inspiratory sound described.
n.2: Wheeze is usually expiratory from narrowed lower airways; an inhaler does not treat airway swelling in anaphylaxis.

8.q: Ivy, 82, has fallen on the ward and is lying on the floor. She is alert, says her hip hurts and her right leg looks shortened and externally rotated. What should the nurse do?
o: Help her to stand with two staff and walk her back to bed
Leave her on the floor until her family arrive
Use a standing hoist to lift her straight back into the chair
Keep her still, get her reviewed and use flat-lift equipment
8.w: After a fall, check for injury before moving. A shortened, externally rotated leg suggests a hip fracture: keep her still, call for medical review, give analgesia as prescribed and use flat-lifting equipment such as a scoop stretcher, in line with local post-fall protocols and Annexe B 7.3.

n.0: Standing a person with a suspected fracture risks further injury and pain.
n.1: Waiting for family delays medical review and pain relief.
n.2: A standing hoist needs weight bearing, which is unsafe with a suspected fracture.

8.q: Mr Owusu, 81, says he 'came over funny' before his fall at home. The nurse needs to understand what happened. Which response best clarifies his account?
o: "So you fainted, then. How long were you unconscious?"
"What did 'came over funny' feel like for you?"
"Lots of older people feel funny. Let's move on."
"Did you trip on something on the floor?"
8.w: Annexe A 1.6: use clarification techniques; P1.11 communicate effectively with people at all stages of life. Code 7.4 keep misunderstanding to a minimum.

n.0: This assumes a faint and leads him to a particular answer.
n.2: This dismisses an important symptom and stops clarification.
n.3: This closed question narrows to one cause before his experience is understood.

8.q: Ellie has worked 60 hours a week for a month to cover vacancies. She has twice nearly given the wrong dose and feels exhausted. Her manager asks her to do another extra shift. What should Ellie do?
o: Accept the shift and ask colleagues to double-check her work
Decline the shift and tell her manager about the near misses
Accept the shift and rest fully on her next day off
Decline the shift and keep the near misses to herself
8.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need for your role. Code 16.3: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity about problems that may prevent you working within the Code. Proficiency P1.5.

n.0: Working while exhausted keeps patients at risk; she must address her fitness for practice (Code 20.9).
n.2: Planning rest later does not address the current risk she has recognised.
n.3: Declining helps, but Code 16.3 requires her to tell someone in authority about problems affecting safe practice.

8.q: Clive, 76, has moved from hospital to a nursing home. The nurse is asked to transcribe his discharge medicines onto the home's MAR chart. The insulin entry on the discharge letter reads '10U' with a smudged figure in front of it. What should the nurse do?
o: Transcribe it as 100 units, reading the smudge as a zero
Transcribe it as 10 units, as that is the most legible figure
Contact the prescriber to clarify the dose before transcribing it
Leave the insulin off the MAR until his next GP review
8.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 31: medicines are not transcribed where details are illegible, unclear, ambiguous or incomplete, with particular care for high-risk medicines such as insulin. The abbreviation 'U' is itself a recognised cause of insulin overdose. Clarification is sought without delay.

n.0: Reading 'U' or a smudge as a zero is the classic tenfold insulin error.
n.1: Guessing at an illegible insulin dose risks a serious error.
n.3: Omitting insulin until a routine review risks hyperglycaemia; prompt clarification is needed.

8.q: Wearing non-sterile gloves and an apron, Sam has just emptied the stoma bag of Kofi, 47. Sam now needs to give Kofi mouth care before leaving the bed space. What should Sam do before starting the mouth care?
o: Pull a second pair of gloves over the first pair and continue
Keep the same gloves, as both tasks are for the same patient
Remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene and put on new gloves
Apply alcohol handrub over the gloves, then continue with mouth care
8.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves must be changed after completing a procedure or task even on the same patient, and hand hygiene must be performed between glove changes. Gloves must not be decontaminated with handrub.

n.0: Double gloving is not recommended for routine care and still leaves the contaminated outer layer touching the mouth.
n.1: Gloves are changed between tasks on the same patient, so contamination from the stoma is not carried to the mouth.
n.3: NIPCM states gloves are not decontaminated with handrub or soap and water between uses.

8.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation attempt on a medical ward, Sofia, the nurse in charge, arranges a short team debrief once the immediate tasks are complete. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: Identify which member of staff made an error so that it can be dealt with formally
Reflect together on what went well and what could improve, and support staff
Complete the incident report and the statutory notification to the regulator
Decide as a team what information the family should and should not be given
8.w: Team reflection and debriefing support staff wellbeing and turn experience into learning for future practice (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; Code 8 work cooperatively; human factors and just culture principles).

n.0: A debrief is a supportive learning discussion, not a disciplinary process; a blame focus discourages openness.
n.2: Reporting is a separate governance step and is not the purpose of a team debrief.
n.3: Communication with the family is guided by candour and the person's wishes, not by a team agreement to withhold information.

8.q: Josh, 19, has a learning disability and autism. His family say he has been hitting the side of his head much more than usual for three days and is sleeping poorly. Staff at his college want to restart his behaviour support plan. What should the learning disability nurse do first?
o: Reduce demands at college until the behaviour returns to his usual level
Ask the GP to review the dose of his regular medication for behaviour
Restart the behaviour support plan and record each incident on an ABC chart
Arrange a physical assessment for causes of pain such as ear or dental problems
8.w: A new or increased behaviour may communicate pain or illness. Hitting the side of the head with poor sleep can indicate ear infection or dental pain, so a physical assessment comes before behavioural interventions (NICE NG11 assessment; LeDeR learning on overshadowing).

n.0: Reducing demands may ease distress but leaves a possible painful condition untreated.
n.1: Changing psychotropic medication without assessing for pain repeats the overshadowing error.
n.2: Behavioural recording may be useful later, but treating this as behaviour first risks missing a physical cause.

8.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
8.q: Lionel, 66, has a profound learning disability and is in the last days of life. He is grimacing and moaning, which his DisDAT shows are his distress cues. He has a syringe pump. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess the cause and seek a review of his symptom control
Increase the pump rate to give more medicine
Record the cues and review at the next drug round
Ask his family to sit with him and offer him comfort for now
8.w: Two-step reasoning: his known distress cues suggest uncontrolled symptoms. The nurse should assess possible causes (pain, position, full bladder, constipation, breathlessness) and seek prompt review of anticipatory or as-needed medicines; pump rates should not be changed without a prescription.

n.1: Changing a pump rate without a prescription is unsafe and outside the nurse's authority.
n.2: Waiting until the next round leaves him in distress.
n.3: Comfort helps, but it does not address possible uncontrolled pain.

8.q: Isaac, 47, has been in hospital for a week. His wife says his breathing has worsened and she raised this with the ward team twice today without response. She asks how she can get a different team to review him. Under Martha's Rule, what should you tell her?
o: She should ask his consultant to arrange a formal second opinion
She can request a transfer to another hospital through the GP
She can request an urgent review by a different clinical team herself
She needs to submit a written complaint to the Patient Advice and Liaison Service
8.w: Martha's Rule (NHS England) lets patients, families and carers request an urgent review from a different team, usually critical care outreach, if they are worried about deterioration and feel they are not being heard. It is a rapid review, not a second opinion.

n.0: Martha's Rule escalation is distinct from a formal second opinion by another consultant.
n.1: Transfer through the GP is not the route for an urgent inpatient review.
n.3: PALS and complaints are not designed for urgent clinical deterioration and would delay review.

8.q: Simon, 38, has anaphylaxis after an iodinated contrast injection in the radiology department. The nurse opens the emergency drug box, which contains several adrenaline preparations. Which preparation should be drawn up for his intramuscular injection?
o: 5 mg/mL (1 in 200)
10 micrograms/mL (1 in 100,000)
100 micrograms/mL (1 in 10,000)
8.w: RCUK: IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis uses the 1 mg/mL (1 in 1,000) preparation, for example 0.5 mL = 500 micrograms in an adult.

n.0: 5 mg/mL is not a standard adrenaline preparation for anaphylaxis.
n.1: 1 in 100,000 is a dilution used by specialists for IV infusion, not IM.
n.2: 1 in 10,000 is the IV preparation used in cardiac arrest, not for IM anaphylaxis treatment.

8.q: Mr Ortiz, 66, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. He is being admitted for elective surgery at an English NHS hospital. Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should the nurse do as part of the admission assessment?
o: Use written notes with him, as these work for all deaf people
Identify, record and flag his communication needs and arrange support
Ask his daughter to interpret during his stay to save time
Note his deafness in the record so staff know to speak more loudly
8.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet information and communication needs related to disability or sensory loss. For a BSL user this means arranging a qualified interpreter and flagging the need.

n.0: BSL is a distinct language; written English may not meet his needs.
n.2: Relying on a relative does not meet his needs and compromises confidentiality and accuracy.
n.3: Speaking louder does not help a profoundly deaf BSL user and does not meet the Standard.

8.q: Stanley, 83, has a nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. The tube was confirmed in the stomach by X-ray yesterday and is secured at 60 cm at the nostril. He needs medicines, flushes and feeds today. Under NICE CG32, when must the tube position be confirmed?
o: Before the first feed of each day
When the person reports discomfort
After placement and before each use
After placement and then once a day
8.w: NICE CG32 rec 1.7.17: confirm the position of all nasogastric tubes after placement and before each use (each feed, flush or medicine) by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary.

n.0: A single check at the start misses later displacement from coughing, vomiting or movement.
n.1: Displacement may cause no symptoms, so checks cannot wait for discomfort.
n.3: Daily checks miss displacement between uses.

8.q: Harold, 79, has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids. Overnight he becomes breathless with RR 26, SpO2 92% on air, crackles at both lung bases and new ankle swelling. His fluid balance is positive 2,300 mL over 24 hours. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase the infusion rate to correct the dehydration
Give a prescribed diuretic before informing anyone
Stop the infusion, sit him up and escalate urgently
Continue the infusion and recheck in 4 hours
8.w: Breathlessness, crackles, oedema and a large positive balance suggest fluid overload. Stop the infusion, sit him upright, give oxygen to target and escalate urgently: NEWS2 RR 26 = 3 and SpO2 92% = 2 gives at least 5 (RCP 2017). CG174 asks for fluid mismanagement to be reported as an incident.

n.0: More fluid worsens overload.
n.1: Treatment decisions need urgent medical review; giving a diuretic first delays escalation.
n.3: Continuing the infusion worsens overload and 4 hours is too long.

8.q: Joan, 56, has a moderate learning disability and lives in supported living. At her annual review the community nurse plans her health monitoring. Which approach is in line with NICE NG96 on growing older with learning disabilities?
o: Focus reviews on behaviour change, because physical decline is an expected part of ageing
Start age-related health checks at 65, the same age as for the general population
Monitor for age-related changes such as hearing and sight loss, dysphagia and osteoporosis
Transfer her care from learning disability services to older people's services at 55
8.w: NICE NG96 (1.5.14) recommends monitoring people with learning disabilities for age-related conditions including hearing loss, sight problems, dysphagia, epilepsy, thyroid problems, osteoporosis, menopausal symptoms and dementia; these can occur earlier than in the general population.

n.0: Assuming decline is expected is diagnostic overshadowing; changes should be assessed.
n.1: Age-related changes may start earlier, so waiting until 65 risks late detection.
n.3: NG96 does not set an age for transfer; it focuses on a single lead practitioner and coordinated support.

8.q: Lily, 5, has Down syndrome. Her teacher reports that over the past term she has stopped responding when her name is called and seems 'in her own world'. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Refer to the educational psychologist for an attention assessment
Arrange a hearing assessment, as hearing loss and glue ear are common
Refer to CAMHS because she may be showing new autistic features
Record the change as behaviour linked to her learning disability
8.w: Hearing loss, including glue ear, is common in children with Down syndrome (NHS.uk). A child who stops responding to her name needs her hearing checked first, before other explanations are explored.

n.0: Attention assessment may follow, but hearing is the likely and treatable cause to check first.
n.2: Autism can occur with Down syndrome, but a treatable hearing problem should be excluded first.
n.3: Recording it as part of her learning disability is diagnostic overshadowing.

8.q: A nurse researcher wants to understand what living with a new stoma is like for young adults, in their own words. Which research approach is most suitable?
o: A qualitative design using in-depth interviews
A randomised controlled trial of stoma care products
A retrospective audit of stoma complication rates
A cross-sectional survey using closed questions
8.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022) recognises qualitative research approaches; interviews explore meaning and experience. Proficiency P1.7: understand research methods to critically analyse findings.

n.1: An RCT compares interventions; it does not explore lived experience.
n.2: An audit measures practice against a standard, not personal experience.
n.3: Closed questions limit responses and do not capture experience in people's own words.

8.q: During a major incident, Amir is triaging with the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool. A man is unable to walk, has no catastrophic bleeding, is breathing and responds to voice. His respiratory rate is 32/min. Which category is correct?
o: P2, because he is breathing and responds to voice
P1, because his respiratory rate is outside 12 to 23
P3, because he has no catastrophic bleeding
Dead, because he cannot walk and is breathing fast
8.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) steps: catastrophic bleeding (no); walking (no); breathing (yes); responds to voice (yes); respiratory rate 12-23? A rate of 32 is outside this range, so the casualty is P1. Two steps: work through the algorithm in order, then apply the respiratory rate criterion (P6.12).

n.0: Breathing and responding to voice move him on to the respiratory rate check; an abnormal rate makes him P1, not P2.
n.2: P3 is for casualties who can walk; this man cannot.
n.3: 'Dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened; this man is breathing.

8.q: Ellie, 23, has a mild learning disability and has been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. She would like a talking therapy. Which approach is most consistent with NICE NG54?
o: Offer a psychological intervention adapted to her communication and needs
Offer an antidepressant first and review the need for therapy in six months
Advise that talking therapies are unsuitable for people with a learning disability
Refer her to a general group therapy course with no adjustments
8.w: NICE NG54 1.8.2-1.8.3 says tailor psychological interventions to the person's understanding, communication and sensory needs and agree goals with them (and carers if appropriate); for anxiety, 1.8.6-1.8.7 suggest relaxation therapy or graded exposure, adapted for people with learning disabilities.

n.1: Medication is not the first offer when she wants therapy, and delaying therapy is not supported.
n.2: Psychological therapies are recommended when adapted; excluding Ellie would be discriminatory.
n.3: Without adjustments a standard group is unlikely to meet her needs and fails the reasonable adjustment duty.

8.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
8.q: Kelly, 39, has a moderate learning disability and lacks capacity to manage her finances. A neighbour has started collecting her benefits and keeps most of the money, giving Kelly a small allowance. Kelly says she likes the neighbour and is happy. What should the community nurse do?
o: Raise a safeguarding concern, as Kelly meets the section 42 criteria
Respect Kelly's wishes, as she is happy with the arrangement
Ask the neighbour to keep receipts for everything that is spent
Apply to become Kelly's benefits appointee to control the money
8.w: Two steps: Kelly has care and support needs, is at risk of financial abuse and, lacking capacity about money, cannot protect herself (Care Act s42); so raise a safeguarding concern. Her wishes are important but do not remove the duty to protect.

n.1: Her wishes matter but she lacks capacity about finances and is at risk.
n.2: Receipts do not stop the neighbour keeping her money and do not address the abuse.
n.3: A nurse becoming her appointee creates a conflict of interest and bypasses safeguarding.

8.q: Nurse Ali phones a doctor about Mr Cole using SBAR. He says, "I think he may be developing sepsis." Which part of SBAR is this?
o: Assessment
Situation
Background
Recommendation
8.w: NHS England SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation): Assessment is the nurse's evaluation of the problem.

n.1: Situation states the immediate problem, for example 'his NEWS2 is 6'.
n.2: Background gives history and context.
n.3: Recommendation states what the nurse wants done.

8.q: An integrated care board's LeDeR reviews found that several people waited weeks for blood tests and scans because hospital staff had not planned adjustments such as longer slots or sedation. Hana, a learning disability liaison nurse, is asked to propose one change. Which proposal best addresses this learning?
o: Admit adults with a learning disability to a side room on every admission
Check the reasonable adjustment flag before tests and plan adjustments in advance
Refer every adult with a learning disability to the liaison team after admission
Ask families to attend each appointment so they can explain needs to staff
8.w: LeDeR repeatedly identifies missing reasonable adjustments and delays to tests and treatment. The Equality Act 2010 duty is anticipatory, and the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag exists so that recorded adjustments are seen and acted on before care is delivered (LeDeR 2023; DAPB4019).

n.0: A blanket side room is not person-centred and does not address the planning failure behind the delayed tests.
n.2: Referral after admission comes too late for outpatient tests and scans; adjustments need planning before the appointment.
n.3: Families are valuable partners, but the duty to adjust rests with the service; relying on relatives shifts the burden and fails people without family.

8.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
8.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

8.q: A nurse on placement with the local public health team reads a report stating that 120 people in a town of 100,000 were newly diagnosed with tuberculosis between January and December 2025. Which epidemiological measure does this figure describe?
o: Prevalence
Mortality rate
Case fatality rate
Incidence
8.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: incidence is the number of new cases of a disease arising in a population over a given period; prevalence is the total number of existing cases at a point or over a period. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2 (epidemiology).

n.0: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or period, not only the new cases arising in the year.
n.1: A mortality rate counts deaths in a population, not new diagnoses.
n.2: Case fatality is the proportion of people with a disease who die from it.

8.q: Ethan, 23, is autistic with a mild learning disability. He becomes very distressed in busy waiting rooms and left his last outpatient appointment before being seen. The clinic nurse is rebooking his diabetes review. Which adjustment is most likely to help?
o: Book the first or last appointment of the day with a quiet place to wait
Book a mid-morning appointment and ask him to arrive 30 minutes early
Offer a telephone review so he does not need to attend in person
Ask his GP to take over his diabetes review from the clinic
8.w: Appointments at the start or end of the day minimise waiting (an adjustment NICE gives in CG170 1.1.10), and a quiet waiting space reduces sensory overload (NICE CG142 1.1.8 on adjusting the environment for autistic adults; Equality Act 2010 s20). This keeps the face-to-face review he needs.

n.1: Arriving early lengthens the wait in the environment that caused distress.
n.2: A telephone call cannot replace the examination and tests a diabetes review needs, so it removes care rather than adjusting it.
n.3: Moving his care elsewhere avoids the duty to adjust and may not suit his needs.

8.q: Kian, 5, is autistic and does not speak. His team starts the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS). In the first phase, what is Kian taught to do?
o: Hand a picture to a partner to receive the item he wants
Choose between two pictures to get the item he prefers
Answer the question 'What do you want?' with a picture
Build an 'I want' sentence strip with a picture of the item
8.w: PECS Phase 1 is the physically assisted exchange: the person learns to pick up a single picture and hand it to a communication partner in exchange for a desired item (Bondy and Frost, PECS).

n.1: Choosing between pictures is Phase 3, picture discrimination.
n.2: Responding to 'What do you want?' is Phase 5.
n.3: Sentence strips are Phase 4, sentence structure.

8.q: Mrs Shah, 58, asks a practice nurse whether a herbal supplement she has bought online will help her blood pressure alongside her prescribed amlodipine. The nurse is unsure. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her that nurses cannot discuss non-prescribed products
Check a reliable source or the pharmacist before advising her
Advise her that herbal products are natural and safe to take
Advise her to stop the amlodipine while she tries the supplement
8.w: Code 6.1: information or advice must be evidence-based, including about health products; Code 18.3: check compatibility with other treatment, including over-the-counter medicines; Code 13.3 seek help when unsure.

n.0: Code 18.3 expects compatibility with other treatments, including over-the-counter products, to be checked.
n.2: This is not evidence-based and ignores possible interactions (Code 6.1, 18.3).
n.3: Stopping a prescribed medicine without review could be harmful and is outside the nurse's evidence base.

8.q: Grace, 34, develops a widespread rash, lip swelling and wheeze minutes after starting an IV antibiotic infusion. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the first action after calling for help?
o: Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first drug
Give oral cetirizine and recheck her in 15 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and continue to observe her
8.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, current): remove the trigger (stop the infusion) and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Adults and children over 12: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh.

n.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
n.2: Antihistamines are third-line and do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
n.3: Continuing the infusion, even slowed, keeps exposing her to the trigger.

8.q: Mr Clarke, 52, is alert, warm and chatting. An automated machine records his blood pressure as 82/50 mmHg; an hour ago it was 128/76. His pulse is 78 and regular. What should the nurse do first?
o: Record it as a machine error because he looks well
Repeat the automated reading at the next routine set
Recheck the blood pressure manually and assess him now
Score it as 3 and put out a cardiac arrest call
8.w: Annexe B 2.1 requires nurses to take and interpret vital signs manually and by device. An unexpected device reading should be checked promptly by a manual measurement alongside clinical assessment, rather than accepted or dismissed.

n.0: Assuming error without checking risks missing true deterioration.
n.1: Waiting for the next routine set may delay recognition of genuine hypotension.
n.3: He is alert and talking, so he is not in cardiac arrest; the reading needs verifying first.

8.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
8.q: Dora, 54, has a learning disability and terminal cancer. She has said in pictures that she wants to die in her own bed in her supported living home. Staff worry they cannot manage. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange a hospice place because staff feel unsure
Ask her family to decide where she should die
Admit her to hospital when she becomes more unwell at home
Plan with the palliative care team to support her at home
8.w: Preferred place of death should be respected where possible; reasonable adjustments include training staff, district nursing and specialist palliative care in-reach, anticipatory medicines and equipment (NICE NG142; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: A hospice may be right for some, but staff uncertainty is not a reason to override her wishes without trying support.
n.1: Dora has expressed her own wish; her family should be involved but not replace her choice.
n.2: Planned hospital admission ignores her stated preference.

8.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation, Lucy, a staff nurse, is tearful in the clean utility room. She is due to start the next medicines round in ten minutes. What is the most appropriate response from her colleague?
o: Tell her to go home and let the nurse in charge know later
Reassure her that she will get used to deaths over time
Advise her to take a few minutes and then start the round on time
Offer support, ask how she feels and help arrange cover if needed
8.w: Code 8.7: be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems without compromising safety. Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risk.

n.0: Sending her home without discussion or escalation leaves the ward uncovered and her unsupported.
n.1: This dismisses her distress and offers no practical support.
n.2: This overlooks whether she is safe to give medicines right now.

8.q: Tasha is a registered nursing associate working in Manchester. She is moving to Edinburgh and asks whether she can practise there in her registered nursing associate role. What is the most accurate answer?
o: No, until she completes a Scottish conversion course for the role
No, because nursing associates are regulated for practice in England
Yes, once she transfers to the Scottish part of the NMC register
Yes, because NMC registration applies in all four UK nations
8.w: Nurses and midwives are regulated by the NMC across the UK, but nursing associates are regulated in England only (FACTS S-CODE). This is an example of devolved differences in health workforce policy (P7.2).

n.0: No Scottish conversion course creates a regulated nursing associate role in Scotland.
n.2: There is no Scottish part of the register for nursing associates.
n.3: This is true for nurses and midwives, but the nursing associate role is regulated in England only.

8.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
8.q: Joy, 52, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about a hysterectomy. Her only regular contact is Sue, a paid support worker who has known her for 15 years. The surgeon asks whether Sue can be consulted instead of an IMCA. What is the correct answer?
o: No, so the decision has to be referred to the Court of Protection
Yes, because Sue knows Joy's wishes better than anyone else
Yes, because Sue has known Joy for more than five years
No, paid carers are not appropriate to consult; instruct an IMCA
8.w: MCA s37-38: an IMCA is required where there is no one other than a person engaged in providing care or treatment for payment whom it would be appropriate to consult. Sue's views should still be sought in the best interests process, but she cannot replace the IMCA.

n.0: An IMCA, not a court application, is the statutory safeguard here.
n.1: Sue's knowledge is valuable and should inform the decision, but it does not remove the need for an IMCA.
n.2: Length of paid relationship does not change the statutory exclusion of paid carers.

8.q: Max, 33, has a moderate learning disability and is anxious about his planned knee operation. His learning disability liaison nurse is planning reasonable adjustments. Which adjustment is most likely to reduce his anxiety on the day?
o: Arranging a pre-admission visit to see the ward and meet staff
Admitting him the night before so he can settle in overnight
Keeping details from him until the day so he does not worry
Giving him a sedative premedication on arrival at the ward
8.w: A pre-admission visit lets the person see the environment and meet staff in advance, making the day familiar and predictable. This is a common reasonable adjustment (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7).

n.1: An extra night in an unfamiliar ward may increase anxiety rather than reduce it.
n.2: Withholding information makes the day less predictable and may increase distress.
n.3: Sedation is a more restrictive option and does not replace preparation.

8.q: Ravi, 64, is prescribed his routine subcutaneous enoxaparin injection. He has intact skin at the injection site and no known infection. The nurse has prepared the syringe and checked the prescription. Which personal protective equipment approach is appropriate for giving this injection?
o: Wear non-sterile gloves and decontaminate them between patients
Wear non-sterile gloves and an apron for the injection
Perform hand hygiene; gloves are not routinely needed
Wear sterile gloves because the skin will be punctured
8.w: NIPCM ch 1.4 lists administering routine intradermal, subcutaneous and intramuscular injections among tasks where gloves should not routinely be worn because no exposure to blood or body fluids is anticipated. Hand hygiene is still required, and glove use stays a clinical risk assessment.

n.0: NIPCM states gloves must not be decontaminated with handrub or soap between uses; they are changed instead.
n.1: Gloves and apron are for anticipated exposure to blood or body fluids, which a routine SC injection does not involve.
n.3: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures such as catheter insertion, not routine SC injections.

8.q: You find Brenda, 72, unresponsive in a day room. She is not breathing normally and is making occasional gasping sounds. What does this indicate?
o: Sleep apnoea, so open her airway and observe
Cardiac arrest, so start CPR
A seizure, so protect her head
A faint, so raise her legs
8.w: RCUK 2025: if a person is unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing, assume cardiac arrest and start CPR. Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest, and brief seizure-like activity may occur at onset.

n.0: Observing an unresponsive person with abnormal breathing delays CPR.
n.2: Treating gasping as a seizure delays CPR in someone in cardiac arrest.
n.3: A faint does not cause unresponsiveness with agonal breathing.

8.q: Code standard 19.2 asks nurses to take account of current evidence and knowledge about human factors. During preceptorship, Jade is asked which definition of human factors the Code refers to. Which is correct?
o: The physical and mental health conditions that may affect a registrant's fitness to practise safely
The personal values and beliefs that staff bring to their work and that can influence patient care
The study of individual mistakes so that staff responsible for errors can be identified and retrained
Environmental, organisational and job factors, and individual characteristics that affect behaviour at work
8.w: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety (P5.2).

n.0: Health and fitness to practise is covered by Code 20.9 and NMC processes, not by the definition of human factors.
n.1: Personal beliefs are addressed by Code 20.7; the human factors definition is wider and centres on work systems.
n.2: Human factors looks at how systems shape performance, not at singling out individuals for blame or retraining.

8.q: Ben, 34, is admitted to a medical ward after self-harm while intoxicated. He is now talking coherently. A doctor suggests waiting until his breath alcohol is zero before making any referral to liaison psychiatry. What does NICE NG225 recommend?
o: Refer if he repeats his self-harm while on the ward
Refer now, as alcohol levels should not delay the assessment
Wait until his breath alcohol reading has returned to zero
Refer once his physical treatment on the ward is complete
8.w: NICE NG225 recs 1.5.2 and 1.5.4: do not delay the psychosocial assessment until after medical treatment is completed, and do not use breath or blood alcohol levels to delay it. Rec 1.7.21: after admission for self-harm, offer referral to liaison psychiatry as soon as possible, alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting for a repeat episode ignores the need for prompt assessment after this one.
n.2: NG225 states alcohol levels should not be used to delay the assessment.
n.3: NG225 advises not to wait until medical treatment is finished.

8.q: According to NICE CG32, which finding indicates that an adult is malnourished?
o: BMI under 18.5 kg/m²
BMI between 20 and 25 kg/m²
Unintentional weight loss of 3% in 6 months
Eating normally for the past 5 days
8.w: NICE CG32 defines malnutrition as BMI under 18.5 kg/m²; or unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3-6 months; or BMI under 20 kg/m² with unintentional weight loss over 5% in 3-6 months.

n.1: BMI 20-25 is within the healthy range.
n.2: 3% weight loss is below the CG32 thresholds.
n.3: Normal intake is not a malnutrition criterion.
