8.q: Albert, 85, dies at home with his wife present at 02:10. The community nurse arrives at 03:30 and completes verification of his expected death at 03:45. His wife asks what time will be recorded as the time of death. What should the nurse tell her?
o: 03:30, when the nurse arrived at the house
02:10, when she noticed that he had stopped breathing
The time the doctor completes the death certificate
03:45, when verification of death was completed
8.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the time of verification is recognised as the official time of death and is recorded when verification is completed, not when the death is first reported. Families should be advised there may be a difference between the time of the last breath and the official time of death.

n.0: Arrival time is not the time of death; it is recorded when verification is completed.
n.1: The guidance says families should be told that the time of the last breath may differ from the official time of death.
n.2: The MCCD is completed later by a medical practitioner; the official time of death is the time of verification.

8.q: Ruby, 7, is autistic and uses PECS. She now walks across the room to her communication book and hands a single picture to adults to request items. Her teacher asks what the next PECS phase will teach. Which answer is correct?
o: Answering 'What do you want?' using a sentence strip
Commenting on things she sees, such as 'I see a dog'
Building a sentence strip with 'I want' and an item picture
Choosing the correct picture from two or more pictures
8.w: Ruby has achieved Phase 2 (distance and persistence). Phase 3 is picture discrimination: choosing the right picture from several. Phase 4 then adds sentence structure (PECS).

n.0: Responding to 'What do you want?' is Phase 5.
n.1: Commenting is Phase 6, the final phase.
n.2: Sentence structure is Phase 4, after discrimination in Phase 3.

8.q: Valerie, 58, is choking in a hospital café. She cannot cough, speak or breathe but remains conscious. Help has been called. What should you do first?
o: Perform a blind finger sweep
Give up to 5 back blows
Start chest compressions
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts
8.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): for severe obstruction in a conscious person, give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat until relieved.

n.0: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in and are not part of the algorithm.
n.2: Chest compressions start once she becomes unconscious.
n.3: Abdominal thrusts come after 5 back blows.

8.q: June, 72, has a NEWS2 score of 8 and suspected sepsis from a chest infection. Blood cultures and a lactate have been taken, and IV antibiotics are prescribed. Twenty minutes have passed since NEWS2 was calculated. The laboratory says culture results will take 48 hours. What should the nurse do?
o: Give a 250 mL fluid bolus, then wait for culture results
Give the antibiotics now, within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score
Repeat NEWS2 in 30 minutes before giving antibiotics
Wait for the Gram stain before choosing the antibiotic
8.w: NICE NG253 (2025): for people at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more), give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating NEWS2. Cultures are taken first, as NG15 advises, and the prescription is reviewed when results arrive.

n.0: A fluid bolus may be indicated, but antibiotics must not wait for culture results.
n.2: NEWS2 is recalculated every 30 minutes at high risk, but treatment is not delayed to do so.
n.3: Waiting for microbiology would breach the 1-hour target for high-risk sepsis.

8.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
8.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

8.q: Isla, 2, developed as expected until about 12 months. Since then she has lost the few words she had, stopped using her hands to pick up toys, and now repeatedly wrings her hands. Her parents report episodes of breath-holding. Which condition is most likely?
o: Prader-Willi syndrome
Rett syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
Angelman syndrome
8.w: Rett syndrome (MECP2, almost exclusively girls) typically shows 6 to 18 months of apparently normal development followed by regression: loss of purposeful hand use with repetitive hand wringing, loss of speech and breathing irregularities (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.0: Prader-Willi presents with infant hypotonia and later hyperphagia, not regression.
n.2: Fragile X causes developmental delay and anxiety but not regression with loss of hand use.
n.3: Angelman syndrome causes severe speech impairment, ataxia and frequent laughter, but not a period of normal development followed by loss of hand use.

8.q: Eileen, 76, is prescribed morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously. The ward stocks morphine sulfate 10 mg in 1 mL ampoules. A second nurse witnesses throughout. Which controlled drugs register entry correctly records the dose and the remainder?
o: 2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.4 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.6 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) returned to the CD cupboard
2.5 mg (2.5 mL) given; ampoule recorded as used with no remainder
8.w: Volume = 2.5 / 10 x 1 = 0.25 mL, leaving 7.5 mg (0.75 mL). NICE NG46: for CDs left over after administration, record the amount disposed of and the signatures of the person disposing and any witness. Opened ampoules are not returned to stock.

n.1: 0.4 mL contains 4 mg, so the volume is wrong for a 2.5 mg dose.
n.2: Opened ampoules cannot be returned to stock; the remainder is disposed of and recorded.
n.3: 2.5 mL exceeds the 1 mL ampoule and would be a tenfold miscalculation.

8.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
8.q: Ruby, 31, has a learning disability and epilepsy. At her day centre she has a tonic-clonic seizure. Her individual emergency plan says to give buccal midazolam if a seizure lasts 5 minutes. The seizure has now lasted 5 minutes. What should the trained nurse do?
o: Call 999 and wait for paramedics to give any medication
Place a soft object between her teeth and then give the midazolam
Wait until the seizure has lasted 10 minutes, then give the midazolam
Give buccal midazolam as set out in Ruby's emergency plan
8.w: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus. NICE NG217 7.1.1-7.1.2: provide emergency treatment and, if the person has an individualised emergency management plan immediately available, give medication as detailed in it.

n.0: The plan authorises trained staff to give rescue medication now; waiting for paramedics delays treatment.
n.1: Nothing should be placed between the teeth during a seizure; it can cause injury and airway obstruction.
n.2: Waiting longer than the plan states delays treatment of status epilepticus and raises the risk of harm.

8.q: A ward team wants the strongest evidence on whether a new dressing reduces infection in surgical wounds. Which type of study gives the highest level of evidence for this question?
o: An expert consensus opinion paper from specialists
A single large randomised controlled trial
A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
A large prospective cohort study of patients
8.w: Oxford CEBM levels of evidence (therapy): level 1a is a systematic review of randomised controlled trials; expert opinion is level 5. Code 6.1 requires evidence-based information.

n.0: Expert opinion is the lowest level in evidence hierarchies such as the Oxford CEBM levels.
n.1: A well-designed RCT is strong evidence but ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs.
n.3: Cohort studies are observational and rank below RCTs for treatment effects.

8.q: Hollie, 27, has a moderate learning disability and depression and finds it hard to describe how she feels. Her psychiatrist starts an antidepressant. Which approach to dosing best reflects NICE NG54?
o: Stop the tablets if her mood has not improved after one week
Start at the maximum licensed dose so that her mood improves quickly
Aim for the lowest effective dose, watching for side effects she may not report
Keep the dose low and below the therapeutic range to avoid any side effects
8.w: NICE NG54 1.9.5: when deciding the initial dose and increases, aim for the lowest effective dose, taking account of side effects and the person's difficulty in reporting them, and avoid sub-therapeutic doses. 1.9.4: monitor benefits and harms using agreed outcome measures that reflect communication needs.

n.0: Antidepressants usually take weeks to work; one week is too soon to judge and stopping abruptly is not advised.
n.1: Starting at the maximum dose ignores her higher risk of side effects she may be unable to report.
n.3: NG54 1.9.5 warns against sub-therapeutic doses that may not treat the depression effectively.

8.q: Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool (MITT), Lucy is triaging casualties after an explosion at a shopping centre. A man with cuts to his face and arms is walking around asking for help, with no catastrophic bleeding. Which category should she assign?
o: P2
P3
P1
Dead
8.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) first checks for catastrophic bleeding (P1); if absent, anyone who is walking is categorised P3 (minor) before further physiological assessment (P6.12).

n.0: P2 is reached after the walking, breathing, voice and respiratory rate steps in a casualty who cannot walk.
n.2: P1 is for catastrophic bleeding or abnormal findings later in the algorithm; a walking casualty without catastrophic bleeding is not P1.
n.3: The man is walking and talking; 'dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened.

8.q: Using SBAR, Nurse Mai tells the doctor, "She is 74, had a bowel resection two days ago and has COPD." Which SBAR element is this?
o: Recommendation
Assessment
Background
Situation
8.w: NHS England SBAR tool: Background gives the relevant history and context, such as age, admission reason and past medical history.

n.0: Recommendation is what she wants the doctor to do and by when.
n.1: Assessment is her judgement of what the problem is, for example 'I think she is dehydrated'.
n.3: Situation is the opening statement of the current problem, for example her NEWS2.

8.q: Kofi raised a patient safety concern with his manager and then with the trust's director of nursing. Three months later nothing has changed and patients remain at risk. Under NMC guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record his concerns in his reflective accounts for revalidation
Raise the concern again with his manager in writing
Contact a national newspaper to make the risk public
Raise the concern with a regulator such as the CQC
8.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance stage 4: if internal routes have not worked, raise the concern with a regulator or helpline, for example the CQC in England. Code 16.1.

n.0: Reflection does not escalate the risk to anyone able to act.
n.1: He has already used the internal stages without result; repeating stage 1 delays action.
n.2: Media disclosure is not a stage in NMC guidance and may lose legal protection.

8.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
8.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

8.q: Dan, 24, has Prader-Willi syndrome and lives in supported living. He has taken food from housemates' cupboards and gained 6 kg in two months. Staff want to lock the kitchen. What must happen first?
o: Assess his capacity on food access and, if lacking, decide in his best interests
Lock the kitchen straight away, because hyperphagia justifies any food restriction
Lock the kitchen once his parents have agreed to it on his behalf
Leave the kitchen open and record his food choices as unwise decisions
8.w: Two steps: locking the kitchen restricts Dan and his housemates, so it needs a lawful basis. Assess his capacity for this decision (MCA s2-3); if he lacks it, make a best interests decision (s4) choosing the least restrictive option (s1(6)), and review it regularly.

n.1: Restrictions need a lawful basis and proportionality; a diagnosis does not authorise any restriction.
n.2: Parents cannot consent on behalf of an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.3: Calling his choices unwise assumes he has capacity, which has not been assessed, given the compulsive nature of hyperphagia.

8.q: Late at night, the out-of-hours doctor phones the hospice to increase the dose of subcutaneous diamorphine for Albert, 70, who is in pain. The doctor is 40 minutes away. The nurse knows diamorphine is a Schedule 2 controlled drug. What should the nurse do?
o: Explain it cannot be a verbal order and seek a written prescription
Accept it and ask the doctor to sign the chart within 24 hours
Accept it and record the doctor's name and GMC number in the notes
Accept it with a second nurse listening on speakerphone as witness
8.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20 allows verbal orders in exceptional circumstances for medicines other than Schedule 2 controlled drugs. Diamorphine is Schedule 2, so a written prescription is needed; the nurse should escalate so Albert's pain is managed promptly, for example by the doctor attending or using any existing anticipatory prescription.

n.1: Later written confirmation applies to permitted verbal orders, which exclude Schedule 2 CDs.
n.2: Recording the caller's details does not overcome the exclusion of Schedule 2 CDs from verbal orders.
n.3: A witness does not make a verbal order for a Schedule 2 CD acceptable.

8.q: On admission, Gemma, 35, lists citalopram as her only regular medicine. When asked about other products, she says she has been taking St John's wort from a health food shop for low mood. What should the nurse do?
o: Record it as a herbal product that needs no further review or action
Remove it from her locker and dispose of it in the sharps bin
Record it and inform the prescriber, as it interacts with citalopram
Advise her to double her citalopram dose instead of using it
8.w: Medicines reconciliation includes over-the-counter and herbal products (NICE NG5; P4.15). St John's wort taken with an SSRI such as citalopram increases the risk of serotonin syndrome and interacts with many other drugs, so it is documented and the prescriber or pharmacist informed.

n.0: Herbal products can cause significant interactions and must be reviewed.
n.1: Patients' own products are not removed without consent, and sharps bins are not for medicines.
n.3: Changing a prescribed dose is not the nurse's decision and could cause toxicity.

8.q: Jamal, a first-year student nurse, is visibly upset after caring for a patient who died unexpectedly on his shift. Later that day his practice supervisor, Helen, has time to talk. What is the most helpful approach?
o: Invite him to talk through the event and reflect on his feelings and learning
Ask him to write a reflective account for his portfolio before his next shift
Reassure him that he will get used to deaths with more experience
Suggest he takes the rest of the week off and speaks to occupational health
8.w: Supervisors encourage colleagues and students to reflect on practice (AnnexA.4.1.4) and support their wellbeing. A supportive conversation that explores feelings and learning helps the student process the event, with further support offered if needed (P5.8 promote reflection).

n.1: Written reflection may help later, but setting a task first misses the need for supportive discussion now.
n.2: This dismisses his distress and does not support reflection.
n.3: Some students need time off or occupational health input, but the first step is to listen and explore with him.

8.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
8.q: Lou, 45, has a learning disability. She has been assessed as lacking capacity to manage her tenancy but chooses her own clothes and activities every day. She is now offered a flu vaccine. How should her capacity be approached?
o: Ask her benefits appointee to decide on her behalf
Treat her as having capacity, because she makes everyday choices
Treat her as lacking capacity, given the tenancy assessment
Assess her capacity for the vaccine decision itself if it is in doubt
8.w: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific (MCA s2(1)): 'in relation to a matter' 'at the material time'. Lou is presumed to have capacity for the vaccine; if there is doubt, it is assessed for that decision alone.

n.0: A benefits appointee manages benefits only and has no authority over health decisions.
n.1: Capacity for everyday choices does not show capacity for a health decision; if in doubt it must be assessed.
n.2: A lack of capacity for one decision does not carry over to another.

8.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
8.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

8.q: Liam, 22, attends an emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high using a scoring tool, and says 'low' scores can be discharged without referral. According to NICE NG225, how should the nurse approach this?
o: Not use the score to predict risk or decide on discharge
Complete the score and refer him to liaison psychiatry if it is high
Repeat the score each hour until he is discharged
Use the score to decide whether to refer him to liaison psychiatry
8.w: NICE NG225 (2022) recs 1.6.1-1.6.3: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged; do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification.

n.1: Restricting referral to high scores is risk stratification, which NG225 advises against.
n.2: Repeating a tool does not make it a valid predictor; NG225 advises against using it for this purpose.
n.3: NG225 says tools must not decide who is offered treatment; liaison psychiatry referral should be offered after self-harm.

8.q: Monthly data on a learning disability inpatient unit show 40 physical restraints, mostly on three patients and mostly between 4pm and 6pm when staff change shifts. The nurse in charge is asked to lead a reduction plan. Which first step is best?
o: Train all staff in additional holding techniques for late afternoon
Analyse the incidents with patients and staff to find and change the triggers
Increase PRN medication at 3pm for the three patients involved
Ask the three patients' families to visit outside the 4pm to 6pm period
8.w: Two-step reasoning: the data show a pattern (time, people), so the next step is to understand why. NICE NG11 1.9.4 requires a restrictive intervention reduction programme that uses incident data and involves people and staff to change practice, such as how handovers are staffed and how the patients are supported at that time.

n.0: More holding training prepares staff to restrain, rather than reducing the need for restraint.
n.2: Scheduled PRN is chemical restraint and swaps one restriction for another.
n.3: Nothing suggests visits cause the incidents; the pattern points to the shift change.

8.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
8.q: Robert, 62, has a moderate learning disability and has been told he has terminal heart failure. His brother asks staff not to tell Robert he is dying 'because it will upset him'. What should the nurse do?
o: Support Robert to understand his illness in an accessible way
Agree with the brother and avoid any discussion of dying
Tell Robert everything at once so that he knows the facts
Ask the GP to decide whether Robert should be told
8.w: People with a learning disability have the same right as others to information about their health and to be involved in decisions about their care. Information should be given in an accessible, paced way (easy read, pictures, repetition), checking understanding, while supporting the family (NMC Code 2, 4; MCA principles).

n.1: Withholding information denies Robert the chance to make choices and say goodbye.
n.2: Giving everything at once without adapting it may overwhelm him and limit understanding.
n.3: The decision is not the GP's alone; Robert's right to information comes first.

8.q: Sana, a nurse who trained in Canada, joins a UK learning disability team and refers to 'people with an intellectual disability'. A colleague asks whether this is the same group. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is the international term for the group UK services describe as having a learning disability
It refers to specific learning difficulties such as dyslexia, dyscalculia and dyspraxia
It describes a milder condition than a learning disability as defined by UK services
It is the statutory term used for this group in section 1 of the Mental Health Act 1983
8.w: 'Intellectual disability' is the term used internationally (and in ICD-11 as disorders of intellectual development) for the same group described as having a learning disability in UK health and social care.

n.1: Dyslexia and dyspraxia are specific learning difficulties; they do not affect general intellectual ability.
n.2: The terms describe the same range of severity, not a milder group.
n.3: The 1983 Act uses 'learning disability' (s1(4)), not 'intellectual disability'.

8.q: Kwame, 30, is autistic and has a mild learning disability. His aggression at home has had a limited response to a psychosocial intervention, and his psychiatrist is considering an antipsychotic. Which plan is consistent with NICE CG142?
o: Replace the psychosocial intervention with the antipsychotic to avoid duplication
Prescribe two antipsychotics at low doses to reduce the risk of side effects
Continue the antipsychotic for six months before reviewing whether it has helped
Give it alongside the psychosocial intervention and review benefit at 3 to 4 weeks
8.w: NICE CG142 1.5.7: consider antipsychotic medication in conjunction with a psychosocial intervention for behaviour that challenges when there has been no or limited response to psychosocial or other interventions. It should be prescribed by a specialist, with quality of life outcomes monitored; review the effects after 3 to 4 weeks and stop it if there is no clinically important response at 6 weeks. This also reflects STOMP.

n.0: Medication should be combined with, not replace, psychosocial intervention.
n.1: Two antipsychotics increase side-effect risk; a single drug at the lowest effective dose is used.
n.2: Review is due at 3 to 4 weeks, not after six months.

8.q: Ms Novak, 45, is a professional violinist due to have a hand operation. She asks whether there is any risk to the feeling in her fingers. The surgeon says the risk is low, so it is not usually mentioned. Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015], which risks must be disclosed?
o: Risks the patient specifically asks about during the consent discussion
Risks a responsible body of hand surgeons would usually choose to mention to patients
Risks that occur in more than one in a hundred operations of this type
Risks she, or a reasonable person in her position, would see as significant
8.w: Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 requires reasonable care to make the patient aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should know this patient would. A violinist would attach significance to altered sensation.

n.0: Disclosure of material risks is the clinician's duty; it does not depend on the patient knowing what to ask.
n.1: This is the older professional-practice (Bolam) approach that Montgomery replaced for risk disclosure.
n.2: Montgomery rejected a fixed percentage threshold; materiality depends on the person, not a statistic.

8.q: Lee, 45, who has a moderate learning disability, dies on a surgical ward after a bowel obstruction was recognised late. The ward sister tells Chloe, his named nurse, that the trust's own incident review will cover everything so no other notification is needed. What is the most appropriate action for Chloe?
o: Notify LeDeR and report the delayed diagnosis through the incident system
Ask Lee's GP to notify LeDeR, because notifications must come from primary care
Wait for the trust review to finish and then decide whether LeDeR is needed
Notify the coroner and leave the review of Lee's care to the inquest
8.w: Anyone can notify LeDeR, including hospital staff (leder.nhs.uk), and a delay in recognising illness should also be reported as a patient safety incident so the organisation can learn (PSIRF; Code 19). The two processes run alongside each other.

n.1: LeDeR accepts notifications from anyone, including ward nurses and families; there is no primary care rule.
n.2: Waiting delays the national review and risks the death never being notified; both processes can start now.
n.3: An inquest decides how the person died; it does not replace LeDeR's review of the person's care or the trust's incident learning.

8.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
8.q: Ava, 29, has a profound learning disability and no speech. Over two days she has become restless, is pushing food away and is pressing on her abdomen. Her bowel chart shows no stool for six days. What is the most likely explanation to assess first?
o: Boredom because her day centre is closed
Constipation causing abdominal pain
Dental pain from a new tooth
Behaviour that challenges needing a PBS review
8.w: Behaviour change (restlessness, food refusal, pressing the abdomen) may be how Ava communicates pain. With no stool for six days, constipation is the most likely cause and should be assessed promptly, avoiding diagnostic overshadowing (LeDeR; NHS England constipation resources).

n.0: Boredom does not explain six days without a bowel movement and abdominal pressing.
n.2: Pressing on the abdomen and absent stools point to the bowel rather than the teeth.
n.3: Labelling the change as behaviour misses a likely physical cause.

8.q: A community nurse uses a PAS-ADD checklist with support staff caring for Olivia, 45, who has a learning disability. What is the purpose of this tool?
o: To measure Olivia's IQ and adaptive functioning
To diagnose a specific mental illness without a clinical assessment
To screen for possible mental health problems needing full assessment
To assess Olivia's capacity to consent to treatment
8.w: The PAS-ADD family of tools (Psychiatric Assessment Schedules for Adults with Developmental Disabilities) includes checklists completed by carers to screen for possible mental health problems, prompting referral for full assessment. They support, but do not replace, clinical diagnosis.

n.0: IQ and adaptive functioning are measured with different psychometric tools.
n.1: A screening checklist identifies possible problems; diagnosis requires clinical assessment.
n.3: Capacity is assessed under the MCA for a specific decision, not with a PAS-ADD checklist.

8.q: Mia, 6, is due her annual flu vaccine at school. Her parents tell the school nurse they decline the nasal spray vaccine because it contains porcine gelatine, which conflicts with their beliefs, but they want her protected. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that children under 9 must have the nasal vaccine to be protected
Give the nasal vaccine, explaining that gelatine is an inactive ingredient
Discuss the injected inactivated flu vaccine as an alternative for Mia
Advise them that Mia can have a flu vaccine once she reaches adulthood
8.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: the live attenuated influenza vaccine (Fluenz, nasal) contains porcine gelatine; if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used (Green Book chapter 19). UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): consent must be given freely by an appropriately informed person.

n.0: The schedule states that if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used.
n.1: Giving it against the parents' refusal would be without valid consent (Green Book chapter 2).
n.3: An inactivated alternative is available now, so she need not go unprotected.

8.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
8.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

8.q: Peter, 74, has pancreatic cancer and is in the last days of life at home. He can no longer swallow tablets. Over the past 24 hours the community nurse has given three 'as required' subcutaneous doses of morphine for pain, each giving relief for a few hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue 'as required' doses and review the plan in 72 hours
Ask his wife to give oral morphine solution between visits
Discuss with the prescriber starting a continuous syringe pump
Give the next 'as required' doses by intramuscular injection
8.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.5.6: consider a syringe pump to deliver medicines for continuous symptom control if more than 2 or 3 doses of any 'as required' medicine have been given within 24 hours. Rec 1.5.5: avoid intramuscular injections.

n.0: Needing more than 2 or 3 doses in 24 hours is the NG31 trigger to consider a syringe pump; waiting 72 hours leaves pain poorly controlled.
n.1: Peter can no longer swallow safely, so the oral route is unsuitable (NG31 rec 1.5.4).
n.3: NICE NG31 rec 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life; subcutaneous or intravenous routes are used.

8.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
8.q: Rina, 40, has a learning disability and does not use speech. She communicates with Makaton signs and eye pointing to pictures. Staff are satisfied she understands and weighs the choice of having a flu vaccine. How should her decision be treated?
o: As not valid, because she cannot state her decision in spoken words
As valid once a family member has confirmed what she meant
As not valid until she has confirmed it in writing with a witness
As valid, because she can communicate it by signs or eye pointing
8.w: MCA s3(1)(d): a person is unable to make a decision if they cannot communicate it 'by talking, using sign language or any other means'. Rina can communicate by signs and eye pointing, so she meets this part of the test.

n.0: The Act accepts any means of communication, not only speech.
n.1: Her decision is her own; a relative's confirmation is not required for validity.
n.2: There is no requirement for written confirmation of consent to a vaccine.

8.q: Mrs Taylor cares for her husband, 79, who has capacity and is being discharged after a stroke. She says nobody has involved her in his care planning. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her to the GP to discuss her husband's care plan
Ask if he wants her involved, then involve her and offer a carer's assessment
Involve her fully, as she will be the one providing his care at home
Explain that his care plan is confidential and cannot be shared with her
8.w: Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows; Code 2.1 partnership. Care Act 2014 s10: carers have a right to a carer's assessment. Proficiency P1.13 relationships with carers.

n.0: Passing her elsewhere does not involve her in his discharge planning.
n.2: His consent is needed before sharing his information and involving her.
n.3: If he agrees, she can be involved; refusing outright ignores her role.

8.q: Kemi, a newly qualified nurse on an assessment and treatment unit, notices staff mocking a patient, restraint episodes left unrecorded and families discouraged from visiting the ward. Mindful of the lessons of Winterbourne View and Whorlton Hall, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Speak privately to the staff involved and monitor whether it continues
Record her observations in her reflective account for revalidation
Raise the concern at the next team meeting so standards can be agreed together
Escalate promptly to senior managers and the safeguarding lead
8.w: These are warning signs of a closed culture and possible abuse. The Code requires nurses to act without delay where there is a risk to patient safety, raising and escalating concerns (standard 16 and 16.1), and to raise concerns immediately where a person is vulnerable or at risk (standard 17 and 17.1), using whistleblowing routes if needed; safeguarding procedures must be followed (Care Act 2014 s42).

n.0: Informal monitoring allows abuse to continue and leaves no formal record; escalation is required.
n.1: Reflection is no substitute for acting; patients remain at risk while nothing is reported.
n.2: Waiting for a team meeting delays protection and may expose the concern to the people involved.

9.q: A ward's controlled drugs register has been completed and a new book started. The ward clerk asks how long the old register must be kept. Under NICE NG46, what is the minimum retention period?
o: 1 year from the date of the last entry
2 years from the date of the last entry
6 months from the date the book was closed
7 years from the date of the first entry
9.w: NICE NG46: controlled drugs registers must be kept for 2 years from the date of the last entry, in line with the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. (Records of destruction of patients' own CDs are kept for a minimum of 7 years.)

n.0: 1 year is shorter than the legal minimum.
n.2: 6 months is well below the 2-year requirement.
n.3: 7 years applies to records of destruction of patients' own CDs, and the period runs from the last entry.

9.q: At the bedside check, the nurse notices that the compatibility label on a unit of red cells for Catherine, 60, reads 'Catherine Smyth', while her wristband reads 'Catherine Smith'. Her date of birth and hospital number match. What should the nurse do?
o: Proceed, as the date of birth and hospital number both match
Do not start, and contact the transfusion laboratory to resolve it
Ask a second nurse to countersign the discrepancy and proceed
Correct the spelling on the wristband and then proceed
9.w: BSH (2017): all identifiers on the wristband and the component label must match exactly at the bedside; any discrepancy means the component is not given until resolved with the transfusion laboratory. Wrong component transfused is a leading SHOT-reported error.

n.0: Partial matches are not acceptable; every identifier must match.
n.2: A second signature does not resolve a mismatch in identifiers.
n.3: Changing the wristband to fit the unit conceals the discrepancy and is unsafe.

9.q: Kyle, a staff nurse, notices that Bev, a healthcare assistant, has become quiet and withdrawn since a relative criticised her in front of colleagues. Bev's care remains of a good standard. What is the most appropriate way for Kyle to support and motivate her?
o: Give Bev lighter tasks for the next few shifts so that she can recover
Speak with Bev privately, acknowledge her good care and ask how she is
Report Bev's change in mood to the ward manager for a formal welfare review
Tell Bev that complaints are part of the job and she should not take it personally
9.w: Leaders guide, support and motivate others (P5.6) and the Code asks registrants to work cooperatively and support the staff they are responsible for (Code 8, 25.2). Specific recognition and a private, supportive conversation help restore confidence and show that her work is valued.

n.0: Changing her work without discussion may suggest a lack of confidence in her.
n.2: Escalating to a formal process before talking with her is disproportionate.
n.3: Dismissing her feelings is unsupportive and unlikely to restore motivation.

9.q: Daisy, 19, is autistic and uses a picture communication book. She is admitted to a children's ward after a fall. The nurse notices the book has been packed away in her bag in the locker. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep the book within Daisy's reach and use it when talking with her
Ask her parents to take the book home until she is discharged
Make a set of the ward's own picture cards to use during her stay
Leave the book in the locker so it does not get lost on the ward
9.w: A personal communication aid is Daisy's voice. It must be kept with her and used by staff so she can understand and express needs, including pain (Annexe A 2.4; Accessible Information Standard 'meet').

n.1: Sending it home removes her means of communication during admission.
n.2: Unfamiliar ward cards are less useful than her own book, which she already knows how to use.
n.3: Locked away, the book cannot be used, leaving Daisy unable to communicate.

9.q: During an in-hospital arrest, Joyce, 70, is in a non-shockable rhythm. The ALS team has IV access. When should adrenaline 1 mg IV be given according to RCUK 2025?
o: As soon as possible, then every 3-5 minutes
After 30 minutes, if no output has returned
After 10 minutes of CPR, then every 5 minutes
After the third shock, then every 3-5 minutes
9.w: RCUK 2025 ALS: in non-shockable rhythms give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as possible; for shockable rhythms give it after the third shock. Repeat every 3-5 minutes.

n.1: Adrenaline is not reserved until 30 minutes into the arrest.
n.2: Waiting 10 minutes delays adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm.
n.3: After the third shock is the timing for shockable rhythms.

9.q: Sana, a nurse who trained in Canada, joins a UK learning disability team and refers to 'people with an intellectual disability'. A colleague asks whether this is the same group. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is the international term for the group UK services describe as having a learning disability
It refers to specific learning difficulties such as dyslexia, dyscalculia and dyspraxia
It describes a milder condition than a learning disability as defined by UK services
It is the statutory term used for this group in section 1 of the Mental Health Act 1983
9.w: 'Intellectual disability' is the term used internationally (and in ICD-11 as disorders of intellectual development) for the same group described as having a learning disability in UK health and social care.

n.1: Dyslexia and dyspraxia are specific learning difficulties; they do not affect general intellectual ability.
n.2: The terms describe the same range of severity, not a milder group.
n.3: The 1983 Act uses 'learning disability' (s1(4)), not 'intellectual disability'.

9.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
9.q: Ali, 33, has a profound learning disability and is fed by gastrostomy. His mother asks whether he can still get aspiration pneumonia, as he no longer eats by mouth. What should the nurse explain?
o: No, aspiration happens during eating by mouth
Yes, saliva and refluxed feed can still be aspirated
Yes, when the feeding tube becomes blocked
No, a gastrostomy removes the risk of aspiration
9.w: People who are tube fed can still aspirate oral secretions and refluxed stomach contents. Positioning (head raised during and after feeds), oral care and reflux management remain important (NHS England RightCare aspiration pneumonia scenario).

n.0: Aspiration can occur from secretions and reflux as well as eating.
n.2: Tube blockage is not what causes aspiration; reflux and secretions are.
n.3: A gastrostomy reduces oral intake risks but not aspiration of saliva or refluxed feed.

9.q: Mrs Hughes asks the nurse whether the speech therapy and support her son Leo, 6, receives will cure his moderate learning disability by the time he is an adult. Which reply is most accurate?
o: It will improve markedly once any underlying medication is fully optimised
It is lifelong, but the right support helps him keep learning new skills
It is lifelong, and skills cannot develop much further once childhood ends
It usually resolves by adulthood when intervention starts before school age
9.w: A learning disability is a lifelong condition with a lasting effect on development (Valuing People 2001), but people continue to learn throughout life and good support increases independence and quality of life.

n.0: Medication does not treat a learning disability itself.
n.2: People with a learning disability keep developing skills across the lifespan; adulthood does not end learning.
n.3: Early intervention improves outcomes, but a learning disability does not resolve.

9.q: A nurse has completed a detailed physical assessment of Mr Rees, 75, who is admitted after a fall at home. She has recorded his observations, skin, mobility and continence. Which further area is most needed to make the assessment holistic before discharge planning?
o: A second set of skin checks by another registered nurse
His social circumstances, support at home and his own priorities
A full list of every past hospital admission he has had
A full repeat of his observations before the end of the day shift
9.w: Holistic assessment (P3.1, P3.4) combines physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs and the person's own goals. After a fall at home, his living situation, support and priorities are central to safe planning, and NICE NG249 includes a home hazard assessment.

n.0: A second skin check adds to the physical assessment already completed.
n.2: An exhaustive admission history adds little compared with his current social and support needs.
n.3: Repeat observations are part of physical monitoring, not the missing holistic domain.

9.q: Ethan, 23, is autistic with a mild learning disability. He becomes very distressed in busy waiting rooms and left his last outpatient appointment before being seen. The clinic nurse is rebooking his diabetes review. Which adjustment is most likely to help?
o: Book the first or last appointment of the day with a quiet place to wait
Book a mid-morning appointment and ask him to arrive 30 minutes early
Offer a telephone review so he does not need to attend in person
Ask his GP to take over his diabetes review from the clinic
9.w: Appointments at the start or end of the day minimise waiting (an adjustment NICE gives in CG170 1.1.10), and a quiet waiting space reduces sensory overload (NICE CG142 1.1.8 on adjusting the environment for autistic adults; Equality Act 2010 s20). This keeps the face-to-face review he needs.

n.1: Arriving early lengthens the wait in the environment that caused distress.
n.2: A telephone call cannot replace the examination and tests a diabetes review needs, so it removes care rather than adjusting it.
n.3: Moving his care elsewhere avoids the duty to adjust and may not suit his needs.

9.q: A learning disability nurse is assessing the mental health of Kofi, 29, who has a moderate learning disability and limited verbal communication. According to NICE NG54, who should usually be involved in the assessment?
o: Kofi, with his family or carers who know him well
His GP, using his records from the annual health check
Kofi, seen privately so that his confidentiality is protected
His consultant psychiatrist, without carers present
9.w: NICE NG54 1.7.5 says assess recent changes in behaviour using information from family members, carers and staff as well as records, taking into account their relationship with the person; they can describe change from Kofi's usual presentation and help with communication.

n.1: Records help, but an assessment needs Kofi himself and those who know him, not records alone.
n.2: Confidentiality matters, but excluding everyone who knows Kofi would lose crucial information about change from his baseline.
n.3: Specialist input may be needed, but excluding carers loses the knowledge of his usual behaviour.

9.q: At the end of a shift, which item is most important for Nurse Ben to include when handing over Mrs Webb, 77?
o: Her IV antibiotic is due at 18:00; her NEWS2 rose to 4
She was admitted four days ago from her own home
She enjoyed her lunch and watched television all afternoon
Her daughter visited during the afternoon
9.w: Annexe A 1.11: provide clear information when handing over care. Code 10.2 identify risks and problems; Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed.

n.1: Admission date is less urgent than outstanding care and deterioration.
n.2: Social details matter less than risks and time-critical care.
n.3: Visitor details are not the priority for safe handover.

9.q: A ward nurse is referring Mr Kaur, 70, to the community dietitian after finding he has lost 8% of his body weight in 3 months. Which action best supports a safe referral?
o: Ask his GP to make the referral so that it is from a doctor
Send the referral and let the dietitian explain it when they contact him
Send his entire hospital record so that the dietitian has all details
Explain the referral to him and include the reason, urgency and key findings
9.w: P3.16: know when and how to refer safely. The person should understand and agree to the referral (Code 4.2), and the referral should give the reason, urgency and relevant findings, sharing the minimum necessary information (Caldicott principle 3).

n.0: Nurses can refer directly to a dietitian; routing via the GP adds delay.
n.1: He should know about and agree to the referral before it is sent.
n.2: Sending the whole record exceeds the minimum necessary information for the purpose.

9.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
9.q: Ahmed, 36, has a learning disability and is in supported living. His carer gave buccal midazolam 3 minutes ago for a seizure that had lasted 5 minutes, but he is still convulsing. His plan does not say otherwise. What should happen now?
o: Wait 20 minutes for the midazolam to take full effect
Put him in a cool bath to bring the seizure to an end
Give a second dose of midazolam straight away
Call 999 for emergency help
9.w: NICE NG217 7.1.7: if convulsive status epilepticus does not respond to the first dose of benzodiazepine, call emergency services in the community. A second dose is considered if the seizure has not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first (7.1.8).

n.0: Waiting 20 minutes without calling for help delays emergency treatment.
n.1: A bath is dangerous during a seizure because of drowning risk.
n.2: A second dose is considered only after 5 to 10 minutes; giving it at 3 minutes is too early.

9.q: Jade believes her ward manager is altering staffing records to hide unfilled shifts. She does not feel able to raise this with the manager herself. What is the most appropriate step?
o: Raise it with the manager's own staff at the next team meeting
Raise it with the designated person named in the trust's policy
Post her concerns on a professional social media group
Wait until she has more evidence before telling anyone
9.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: if you cannot raise the concern with your line manager, stage 2 is the designated person in your organisation (for example a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian). Code 16.1.

n.0: Discussing it with peers does not escalate it to someone able to act.
n.2: Public posting bypasses proper channels and risks confidentiality; NMC guidance uses internal and regulatory routes.
n.3: Code standard 16 requires her to act without delay; she does not need proof to raise a concern.

9.q: Sophie, a student nurse on an acute medical ward, hears that Callum, 27, who has a learning disability, has brought his hospital passport. She asks her mentor what a hospital passport is. Which description is correct?
o: A legal record of his best interests decisions, signed by his consultant
A trust form completed by the admitting nurse that replaces the nursing assessment
A person-held document telling staff what they must know about him and how to support him
A GP summary of diagnoses and medicines sent with the referral letter
9.w: A hospital (health) passport is held by the person and travels with them. It records things staff must know (allergies, medicines, communication, how the person shows pain, capacity and consent information), things that are important to them, and likes and dislikes.

n.0: Best interests decisions are recorded in the clinical record under the Mental Capacity Act; the passport is not a legal decision record.
n.1: The passport is the person's own document and supports, not replaces, the nursing assessment.
n.3: A GP summary is a clinical referral document; the passport is person-held and describes how to support the person.

9.q: Grace, 68, is admitted to a surgical ward. Three months ago she was an inpatient in a hospital abroad after a car accident. She has no symptoms of infection. What is the most appropriate placement while admission screening is arranged?
o: A single room with contact precautions while screening for CPE
A bay with other patients recently treated abroad, pending results
An open bay, after starting prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
An open bay, with screening repeated if she develops a fever
9.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 lists patients who have been inpatients in any hospital in the UK or abroad as a possible cross-infection risk for multidrug-resistant organisms such as carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE). She should be placed in a single room with contact precautions pending screening, and the decision documented.

n.1: Cohorting is for patients with the same confirmed infection; unscreened patients may carry different organisms.
n.2: Prophylactic antibiotics do not clear carriage and drive resistance, contrary to NICE NG15 stewardship.
n.3: CPE carriage is usually symptomless, so waiting for a fever leaves the bay exposed.

9.q: Rita, 80, has a urinary catheter. A healthcare support worker asks whether a routine bladder washout would prevent infection. According to NICE CG139, what is the best response?
o: Yes, a weekly saline washout prevents infection
Yes, a daily washout is needed to keep it patent
No, but antibiotics should be given to prevent it
No, washouts must not be used to prevent infection
9.w: NICE CG139: bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infection. Daily meatal hygiene with soap and water and a closed drainage system are the key measures.

n.0: Routine washouts break the closed system and do not prevent infection.
n.1: Daily washouts are not recommended for infection prevention.
n.2: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely used and contributes to resistance (NICE NG15).

9.q: In 2019, Dennis made a valid written advance decision refusing artificial nutrition. In 2023, with capacity, he made a health and welfare LPA giving his son express authority to decide on that treatment, including if life-sustaining. Dennis now lacks capacity. Whose decision about artificial nutrition applies?
o: The consultant's, because the two documents conflict
His son's, as the later LPA covers the same treatment
The Court of Protection's, as both documents exist
The advance decision, because it was made first
9.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s25(2)(b): an advance decision is not valid if the person has, under an LPA created after the advance decision was made, conferred authority on the attorney to give or refuse consent to the treatment to which the advance decision relates.

n.0: There is no conflict for the consultant to resolve; the later LPA displaces the earlier advance decision.
n.2: Court involvement is not needed when the law gives a clear answer on these facts.
n.3: MCA s25(2)(b): an advance decision is not valid if a later LPA gives the attorney authority over the same treatment.

9.q: A train derails near a town and the local acute trust is told to expect over 40 casualties, more than the emergency department can manage with normal arrangements. Under NHS emergency preparedness guidance, how is this event best classified?
o: A business continuity incident
A serious incident
A major incident
A critical incident
9.w: NHS England EPRR guidance classes incidents as business continuity, critical or major. A major incident is an event with serious consequences that requires special arrangements by one or more emergency responder agencies; in the NHS this includes casualties in numbers or types that require special arrangements (JESIP/Cabinet Office definition used by NHS England; P6.12).

n.0: A business continuity incident disrupts an organisation's normal service delivery, for example an IT failure; it is not defined by a surge of casualties needing a multi-agency response.
n.1: 'Serious incident' was a patient safety category under the former Serious Incident Framework, not an emergency preparedness classification.
n.3: A critical incident is a localised, principally internal escalation where an organisation loses the ability to deliver critical services; an external mass casualty event needing multi-agency arrangements is a major incident.

9.q: Fatima, 57, is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has no history of lung disease and her SpO2 is 90% on air. What target oxygen saturation range should be prescribed?
9.w: BTS oxygen guideline and NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.10.1: the target for most acutely ill adults is 94-98%.

n.0: 88-92% is for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some people with COPD.
n.2: 92-96% is not the standard BTS adult target range.
n.3: Aiming for 98-100% risks hyperoxaemia; BTS notes higher saturations are associated with harm.

9.q: Mr Daly, 80, has capacity. When the nurse begins to explain his scan results, he says, "I don't want the details. Just tell my daughter." What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain the results fully, as he has a legal right to know them all
Respect his wish, check what he wants to know and his consent to share
Tell his daughter everything and give him no information himself
Delay the conversation until he is ready for all the details
9.w: Code 2.4: respect the level to which people want to be involved in decisions about their care. Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows, with consent.

n.0: Code 2.4 requires respect for the level of involvement he wants.
n.2: He should be asked what he does want to know, and his consent confirmed first.
n.3: He has stated his wish now; delaying ignores it.

9.q: Ellen, 77, who had C. difficile infection, has been discharged home from a single room. The domestic team asks the nurse what terminal cleaning is required. Which instruction is most appropriate?
o: Use detergent wipes on surfaces and send the curtains as used linen
Clean with a 10,000 ppm available chlorine solution and leave the curtains in place
Clean with neutral detergent and change the curtains at the next routine change
Remove the curtains as infectious linen and clean with 1,000 ppm available chlorine
9.w: NIPCM ch 2.3 terminal decontamination: bag and remove waste, manage curtains and bedding as infectious linen, decontaminate equipment, then clean with a combined detergent and 1,000 ppm available chlorine solution (or detergent followed by 1,000 ppm), working from high to low and least to most contaminated.

n.0: Curtains from an infectious patient's room are infectious linen, and wipes alone are not a terminal clean.
n.1: 10,000 ppm is the strength for blood spills; terminal cleaning uses 1,000 ppm, and curtains are removed.
n.2: Detergent alone does not meet the terminal clean standard, and curtains from an isolation room are removed as infectious linen.

9.q: Zara, a first-year student nurse, asks to insert a urinary catheter for a patient. She has not yet been taught or practised the procedure. Her practice supervisor, Ama, is busy. What is the most appropriate response from Ama?
o: Carry out the procedure with Zara observing and explain each step
Ask a healthcare assistant to supervise Zara during the catheterisation
Ask Zara to read the procedure policy and then insert the catheter
Let Zara insert the catheter while Ama finishes her other tasks nearby
9.w: Delegation must be within the person's competence (Code 11.1). A student who has not been taught a procedure should first observe and then practise under direct supervision. Ama can use the opportunity to teach (P5.8 support and supervise students; AnnexA.4.1.1 clear explanations when teaching).

n.1: Supervision must come from someone competent in the procedure and in supporting the student; this does not meet the student's learning needs.
n.2: Reading a policy does not provide the skill and assessed competence needed.
n.3: Indirect supervision is unsafe for an aseptic invasive procedure the student has not learned.

9.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
9.q: Ola, 26, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to admission for urgent treatment. The ward team concludes that his care will amount to a deprivation of liberty that must start today. How can this be authorised under DoLS?
o: Wait for a standard authorisation before applying any restrictions
Ask the Court of Protection for an emergency order before admission
The hospital gives an urgent authorisation and requests a standard one
Hold him under section 5(2) of the Mental Health Act until a decision
9.w: Under MCA Schedule A1, the managing authority (the hospital or care home) can give itself an urgent authorisation, lasting up to 7 days (extendable by 7 days by the supervisory body), when it requests a standard authorisation from the local authority.

n.0: Waiting would mean either delaying urgent treatment or depriving him of liberty without authority.
n.1: DoLS provide the urgent authorisation route in hospitals; a court order is not the first step.
n.3: Section 5(2) is a holding power for informal inpatients with mental disorder needing MHA assessment, not for authorising physical treatment.

9.q: Ahmed, 28, is distressed and tearful after hearing bad news. Which skill is the cornerstone of mental health first aid in this situation?
o: Offering a sedative medicine
Distracting him with other topics
Listening non-judgementally
Giving clear advice on solutions
9.w: Mental health first aid centres on approaching the person, listening non-judgementally, giving support and information, and encouraging appropriate professional help (Annexe B 2.14).

n.0: Medication is not a first aid response to normal distress.
n.1: Distraction can invalidate his feelings and block disclosure.
n.3: Jumping to advice can feel dismissive before the person feels heard.

9.q: An integrated care board is using Core20PLUS5 to plan work on healthcare inequalities. Which group best illustrates the 'PLUS' element of the approach?
o: Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities identified as a local priority
People in one of the five clinical areas, such as maternity
Adults with hypertension who need case-finding and lipid checks
Adults living in the most deprived 20% of neighbourhoods
9.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): PLUS populations are identified locally and include ethnic minority communities, people with a learning disability and autistic people, people with multiple long-term conditions, and inclusion health groups such as people experiencing homelessness and Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities.

n.1: Maternity is one of the '5' clinical areas, not a PLUS population group.
n.2: Hypertension is one of the five clinical areas rather than a PLUS population.
n.3: This describes the Core20 group, which is defined by the national Index of Multiple Deprivation.

9.q: Vincent, 48, attends the practice nurse for a wound dressing. While checking his record, the nurse sees he smokes 20 cigarettes a day. They have about a minute before the next patient. Which approach reflects very brief advice on smoking?
o: Ask about smoking and advise him to cut down gradually by himself
Ask, advise that medicines plus specialist support work best, and offer referral
Explain the diseases caused by smoking in detail over the next 20 minutes
Wait until he says he is ready to quit before raising the topic of smoking
9.w: NCSCT Very Brief Advice on smoking; NICE NG209 (2021, updated 2025): very brief advice is Ask (record smoking status), Advise (the best way to stop is with a combination of medication and specialist support) and Act (offer referral to local stop smoking support); it takes about 30 seconds.

n.0: VBA advises that the most effective way to stop is medication combined with specialist behavioural support, not quitting unaided.
n.2: Very brief advice takes about 30 seconds; a long lecture is not the VBA model and is not feasible here.
n.3: VBA is offered to everyone who smokes at every opportunity, whatever their stated readiness.

9.q: Leah, 34, attends the emergency department after self-harm. A colleague completes a self-harm risk scale, which places her at low risk, and suggests she can be discharged on that basis. According to NICE NG225, what should happen?
o: Assess Leah's needs and agree a safety plan with her, not using the scale
Repeat the scale in four hours and discharge Leah if it is unchanged
Discharge Leah, as the scale places her in the low-risk group
Admit Leah for observation until a medium-risk score can be ruled out
9.w: NICE NG225 (2022) advises not to use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged. Care is based on a psychosocial assessment of needs and a safety plan developed with the person.

n.1: Repeating an invalid tool does not make it a valid basis for discharge.
n.2: NG225 says scales must not be used to decide discharge; a low score gives false reassurance.
n.3: NG225 advises against global low, medium or high risk stratification; admission is decided by assessed needs, not a score band.

9.q: Mrs Kowalski, 79, lacks capacity to decide about a proposed move to long-term residential care. She has no family, friends or unpaid carers who could be consulted about her wishes. Who should be involved to represent her in the decision?
o: Her GP, as the person who knows her best
The ward manager, acting as her advocate
An independent mental capacity advocate
A Court of Protection deputy appointed by the trust
9.w: MCA 2005 s35 establishes independent mental capacity advocates to represent people who lack capacity and have nobody appropriate to consult. An IMCA supports and represents Mrs Kowalski in the best interests decision.

n.0: The GP is a professional involved in her care, not an independent representative of her wishes.
n.1: Ward staff involved in her care cannot act as her independent advocate.
n.3: Deputies are appointed by the Court of Protection, not by a trust, and none is needed here.

9.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
9.q: Joy, 52, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about a hysterectomy. Her only regular contact is Sue, a paid support worker who has known her for 15 years. The surgeon asks whether Sue can be consulted instead of an IMCA. What is the correct answer?
o: No, so the decision has to be referred to the Court of Protection
Yes, because Sue knows Joy's wishes better than anyone else
Yes, because Sue has known Joy for more than five years
No, paid carers are not appropriate to consult; instruct an IMCA
9.w: MCA s37-38: an IMCA is required where there is no one other than a person engaged in providing care or treatment for payment whom it would be appropriate to consult. Sue's views should still be sought in the best interests process, but she cannot replace the IMCA.

n.0: An IMCA, not a court application, is the statutory safeguard here.
n.1: Sue's knowledge is valuable and should inform the decision, but it does not remove the need for an IMCA.
n.2: Length of paid relationship does not change the statutory exclusion of paid carers.

9.q: Ben, 34, is admitted to a medical ward after self-harm while intoxicated. He is now talking coherently. A doctor suggests waiting until his breath alcohol is zero before making any referral to liaison psychiatry. What does NICE NG225 recommend?
o: Refer if he repeats his self-harm while on the ward
Refer now, as alcohol levels should not delay the assessment
Wait until his breath alcohol reading has returned to zero
Refer once his physical treatment on the ward is complete
9.w: NICE NG225 recs 1.5.2 and 1.5.4: do not delay the psychosocial assessment until after medical treatment is completed, and do not use breath or blood alcohol levels to delay it. Rec 1.7.21: after admission for self-harm, offer referral to liaison psychiatry as soon as possible, alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting for a repeat episode ignores the need for prompt assessment after this one.
n.2: NG225 states alcohol levels should not be used to delay the assessment.
n.3: NG225 advises not to wait until medical treatment is finished.

9.q: Raymond, 74, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He usually wet shaves with a blade razor and asks for help to shave while in hospital. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply pressure to any cuts for 30 seconds afterwards
Use an electric razor to reduce the risk of bleeding
Postpone shaving until his anticoagulant is stopped
Use a new disposable blade razor and press gently
9.w: Annexe B 4.3: when assisting with shaving, consider risks such as anticoagulation. An electric razor reduces the risk of cuts and bleeding in people taking anticoagulants such as apixaban.

n.0: This responds to cuts rather than preventing them.
n.2: His anticoagulant is needed for stroke prevention and shaving is part of his personal care.
n.3: A blade razor still risks cuts that bleed more with anticoagulation.

9.q: Stanley, 80, has end-stage heart and kidney disease and full capacity. The consultant judges that CPR would not succeed and records a DNACPR decision. Stanley tells the nurse he does not accept this and wants 'everything done'. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record that CPR will be attempted because Stanley has requested it
Ask his family to confirm the decision on his behalf at the next visit
Leave the decision unexplained to avoid causing Stanley more distress
Explain the decision sensitively and offer him a second opinion
9.w: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BMA, RCUK, RCN): where CPR would not be successful, clinicians have no obligation to offer it, but the patient should be informed sensitively, and if they do not accept the decision a second opinion should be offered. Tracey [2014]: presumption of involving the patient.

n.0: Clinicians are not obliged to offer CPR that would not succeed; a patient request does not require it (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
n.1: Stanley has capacity, so his family cannot confirm or make the decision for him.
n.2: Stanley must be informed and his concerns heard (Tracey [2014]); avoiding the topic denies him the chance to seek another view.

9.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
9.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

9.q: Owen, a nursing student on a stroke unit, is spending a day working with Leanne, a registered physiotherapist, to learn about mobilisation. Under the SSSA, can Leanne act as Owen's practice supervisor for that day?
o: Yes, as a registered health or social care professional
Yes, but the ward manager must countersign her feedback
No, unless she has completed a practice assessor course
No, as practice supervisors must be registered nurses
9.w: The SSSA allows students to be supervised by any registered health and social care professional, not only NMC registrants, so long-standing interprofessional learning is supported. The physiotherapist can supervise and give feedback within her expertise (P5.8; FACTS S-SSSA).

n.1: The SSSA sets no requirement for a manager to countersign a supervisor's feedback.
n.2: Practice supervisors need to be prepared for the role, but practice assessor preparation is a different requirement.
n.3: NMC registrants are well placed to supervise, but supervision is not restricted to nurses under the SSSA.

9.q: Mavis, 81, has died on a medical ward. Her two sons arrive an hour later and say they are unsure whether they want to see her body, as they have never seen someone who has died. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Tell them viewing is possible once she has reached the funeral director
Offer them the chance to see her and prepare them for what to expect
Advise them not to view her so they remember her as she was in life
Explain that viewing on the ward is allowed after the doctor's review
9.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): all key contacts should be offered the opportunity to view the deceased; there is evidence that, even in traumatic circumstances, key contacts found this helpful. Viewing can occur in acute hospitals, some hospices or later at the funeral directors. Prepare people sensitively for changes to the body.

n.0: Viewing can take place in hospitals and hospices, so there is no need to delay it until later.
n.2: Hospice UK guidance says all key contacts should be offered the chance to view; many find it helpful.
n.3: Viewing does not depend on a doctor's review once death has been verified.

9.q: Pat, 75, has a venous leg ulcer with no red flags. Mild compression was started at her first visit, and strong compression bandaging is now being considered. Before strong compression is applied, what assessment must be completed?
o: A wound swab for culture and sensitivity
A Doppler ankle brachial pressure index
A full blood count to check for anaemia
A capillary blood glucose measurement
9.w: NWCSP Leg Ulcer Recommendations (2023): with no red flags, mild compression (up to 20 mmHg) can start straight away, but a full assessment including a Doppler ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI), within 14 days, is needed before strong compression (40 mmHg or more), because strong compression on a limb with arterial insufficiency can cause ischaemia (Annexe B 4.6 pressure bandaging).

n.0: A wound swab is not needed to decide on compression and is taken only with signs of infection.
n.2: FBC does not assess arterial supply to the limb.
n.3: Glucose is relevant to healing but does not determine whether compression is safe.

9.q: Ms Hunt, 55, has had the same leg ulcer care plan for three weeks. Measurements show the wound has not reduced in size, and she says the dressing leaks and stops her going out. What should the nurse do?
o: Reassess the wound with her and revise the plan, referring if needed
Ask her to stay at home more until the leaking settles down
Continue the plan, as wounds can take several months to heal
Change to a more absorbent dressing without discussing it with her
9.w: P3.15: work in partnership to monitor, evaluate and reassess care plans, readjusting goals and documenting progress. Lack of progress and a poor experience for the person mean the plan should be reviewed with her, with referral (for example to tissue viability) if needed (P3.16).

n.1: Restricting her life to suit the dressing is not person-centred and does not address the problem.
n.2: Continuing an unchanged plan ignores evidence that it is not working.
n.3: Changing the plan without her involvement is not partnership working.

9.q: Bethany, 38, has a tracheostomy and needs suctioning for audible secretions. Her SpO2 is 95% before the procedure. Which practice is correct?
o: Set the suction pressure to about -300 mmHg for better clearance
Limit each suction pass to about 10 seconds and monitor saturation
Instil 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% before each pass
Apply suction while advancing the catheter to clear secretions
9.w: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (Suctioning guidance): suctioning can cause hypoxia, trauma and vagal stimulation. Do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; apply it on withdrawal, keep each period of suction to no more than 10 seconds, use a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg, and observe the patient (saturation, heart rate, colour) throughout, reattaching oxygen promptly.

n.0: The National Tracheostomy Safety Project advises a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg (-20 kPa) for most patients; higher pressure traumatises the mucosa and worsens hypoxia.
n.2: NTSP does not advise routine saline instillation; tenacious secretions are managed with better humidification, and saline is reserved for specific situations.
n.3: NTSP: do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; suction on insertion causes mucosal damage and hypoxia.

9.q: Agnes, 55, has received her cervical screening invitation. She tells the nurse she has heard mixed things about screening and is unsure whether to go. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that cervical screening is compulsory for women of her age group
Advise her that screening prevents every case of cervical cancer
Give balanced information on benefits and limits, and support her choice
Book her test now and explain the details at her appointment
9.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): deciding whether to have screening is a personal choice; benefits (early detection, preventing some deaths) are weighed against risks and limitations (false positives and negatives, anxiety, difficult decisions). Code 4.2: make sure informed consent is obtained.

n.0: Screening is a personal choice; NHS screening is offered, not mandated.
n.1: Screening tests are not 100% accurate; this overstates the benefit and is misleading.
n.3: Booking before she has decided bypasses informed choice.

9.q: A ward manager is reviewing staffing on an acute adult medical ward. Which statement about nurse-to-patient ratios reflects NICE SG1 (2014)?
o: A ratio of one registered nurse to six patients applies on all wards, day and night
A ratio of one registered nurse to eight patients is a legal minimum in England
There is no single ratio, but over 8 patients per nurse by day is linked to harm
Staffing ratios for adult wards are set by the NMC for each type of hospital ward
9.w: NICE SG1 rec 1.5.3: there is no single nursing staff-to-patient ratio for all acute adult wards, but there is evidence of increased risk of harm when a registered nurse cares for more than 8 patients on day shifts, which should prompt close monitoring of red flags and safe nursing indicators.

n.0: SG1 does not set a 1:6 ratio; it uses patients' nursing needs and professional judgement.
n.1: The 1:8 figure is an evidence threshold for monitoring, not a legal minimum in England.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not set ward staffing ratios.

9.q: Nia, 40, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her hospital passport lists her medicines, but the nurse notices it names an antiepileptic that her GP record shows was stopped a year ago. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her family to update the passport after discharge and continue as listed
Stop using the passport and rely on the trust's own records for her stay
Give the medicines listed on the passport, as it is written by those who know her
Reconcile her medicines with current records and update the passport with Nia
9.w: Medicines reconciliation on admission must use current, verified sources. Passports go out of date, so the nurse should confirm the current medicines and support Nia and those close to her to update the passport so it stays accurate (Code 10.2, 18).

n.0: Continuing an inaccurate list risks a medication error now; the update should not wait until discharge.
n.1: The passport still contains valuable information on communication, pain and preferences; it needs correcting, not discarding.
n.2: Giving a discontinued antiepileptic could cause harm; passport medicine lists must be checked against current records.

9.q: Ruth, 45, has a moderate learning disability and is moving from her family home to supported living. Her new provider asks the community nurse which assessment will best show the support Ruth needs day to day. What is the best answer?
