o: A genetic test to establish the cause of her learning disability
A repeat IQ test to confirm her current severity band
An assessment of adaptive skills such as self-care, safety and money
A review of the diagnosis letter written during her childhood
9.w: Support needs depend on adaptive (social) functioning: self-care, communication, managing money, keeping safe. A severity label or IQ score says little about the specific help a person needs in a new setting.

n.0: Knowing the cause may help with health surveillance but does not show her daily support needs.
n.1: An IQ score does not describe the practical help Ruth needs, and her severity is already known.
n.3: A childhood letter will not reflect Ruth's current skills as an adult.

9.q: Mr Ortiz, 66, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. He is being admitted for elective surgery at an English NHS hospital. Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should the nurse do as part of the admission assessment?
o: Use written notes with him, as these work for all deaf people
Identify, record and flag his communication needs and arrange support
Ask his daughter to interpret during his stay to save time
Note his deafness in the record so staff know to speak more loudly
9.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet information and communication needs related to disability or sensory loss. For a BSL user this means arranging a qualified interpreter and flagging the need.

n.0: BSL is a distinct language; written English may not meet his needs.
n.2: Relying on a relative does not meet his needs and compromises confidentiality and accuracy.
n.3: Speaking louder does not help a profoundly deaf BSL user and does not meet the Standard.

9.q: Priti, a registered nurse, delegates a simple wound dressing to Dean, a registered nursing associate who is competent in this task. Dean applies the wrong dressing type. Who is accountable for what?
o: Priti for the decision to delegate; Dean for how he carried out the dressing
Priti is accountable for the dressing, as Dean was working under her direction
The ward manager is accountable, as the allocation of staff was set by her each shift
Dean is accountable for all aspects, as he is a registered professional in his own right
9.w: The Code (standard 11) makes the registrant accountable for decisions to delegate and for confirming outcomes. Nursing associates are NMC registrants bound by the Code, so Dean is accountable for his own practice in carrying out the task (P5.4; FACTS S-CODE).

n.1: Dean is a registrant accountable for his own actions in carrying out the dressing; Priti's accountability is for the decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome.
n.2: The manager is accountable for her own decisions, but this does not remove Priti's or Dean's accountability.
n.3: Priti remains accountable for her decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome (Code 11.3).

9.q: Marcus Bell, 66, is on a surgical ward. His observations are: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on air, BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, alert, temperature 37.2°C. His NEWS2 total is 3. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Increase observations to at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat the observations in 4 hours and escalate if the total rises
Continue 4 to 6 hourly observations as the total score is below 5
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
9.w: A respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3 in a single parameter (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Chart 1). A score of 3 in any one parameter triggers a low-medium clinical risk response: minimum 1-hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team, who decide whether escalation is needed (Chart 4). Two steps: calculate the parameter score, then apply the single-parameter rule.

n.1: Four-hourly review delays recognition of deterioration when a single parameter is already scoring 3.
n.2: The aggregate of 3 is low, but a single red score of 3 overrides this and requires at least hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.3: Emergency critical care assessment is the response to an aggregate of 7 or more; this is an urgent ward-based response.

9.q: A unit of red cells for Hannah, 55, was removed from the blood fridge at 10:00. The transfusion was delayed while her cannula was resited and started at 10:40. By what time must the unit be completed?
o: By 14:00, 4 hours after leaving storage
By 13:00, 3 hours after leaving storage
By 14:40, 4 hours after the start
By 12:00, 2 hours after leaving storage
9.w: BSH (2017): red cells should be transfused within 4 hours of leaving temperature-controlled storage, to limit bacterial growth. The clock starts when the unit leaves the fridge, not when the infusion starts.

n.1: 3 hours is not the BSH limit; the standard is 4 hours from leaving storage.
n.2: Timing runs from removal from storage, so 14:40 is 40 minutes too late.
n.3: 2 hours is shorter than the BSH limit for red cells.

9.q: Krishna, 64, is a Hindu man on an acute ward. During his assessment he asks for a female nurse not to wash him and to wash with running water rather than a bowl. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Record his preferences in the care plan and arrange care to meet them
Ask his family to come in and do all his washing during visiting time
Tell him staffing makes it difficult and he will be washed by whoever is free
Explain that a bowl wash is the standard ward practice for every patient
9.w: Code 1.1, 4.1 and Annexe B 3.4: treat people as individuals and respect their cultural and religious preferences in personal care, documenting them so that care can be arranged to meet them where possible.

n.1: Families may help if they wish, but care remains the nurse's responsibility.
n.2: Dismissing his preference fails to respect his dignity and beliefs.
n.3: Standard practice should adapt to individual needs where reasonably possible.

9.q: On an acute ward, Mr Stone, 40, is pacing and shouting that he wants to leave. He has not harmed anyone. What is the nurse's most appropriate first approach?
o: Tell him firmly to sit down and stop shouting
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and listen to him
Call security to restrain him before he leaves
Stand in the doorway to block his exit from the ward
9.w: Annexe A 3.5: de-escalation strategies and techniques. Code 13.4 personal safety; calm voice, open posture and listening come before restrictive interventions.

n.0: Commands can escalate agitation; de-escalation uses calm listening.
n.2: Restraint is a last resort; de-escalation should be tried first.
n.3: Blocking his exit increases risk and may escalate the situation.

9.q: Ade has finished helping Margaret, who has influenza, to wash. He is wearing gloves, an apron, goggles and a fluid-resistant surgical mask. In which order should he remove this PPE?
o: Mask, eye protection, apron, then gloves
Eye protection, gloves, mask, then apron
Apron, gloves, mask, then eye protection
Gloves, apron, eye protection, then mask
9.w: NIPCM appendix 6: remove gloves, then apron or gown, then eye protection, then the FRSM or respirator, followed immediately by hand hygiene. The most contaminated items (gloves and the front of the apron) come off first.

n.0: Removing the mask first means touching the face with contaminated gloves still on.
n.1: Handling goggles before glove removal transfers contamination from the gloves to the face area.
n.2: Gloves are the most contaminated item and come off before the apron, not after it.

9.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
9.q: Tom, 30, has a severe learning disability and lives in a group home. Staff report that he has started masturbating in the shared lounge. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe medication to reduce his sex drive
Lock his bedroom during the day so he spends time in shared areas
Support him to learn that his bedroom is a private place for this
Raise a safeguarding concern that Tom is sexually abusing others
9.w: Sexual expression is a normal part of life. The aim is to teach and support privacy, using consistent, accessible prompts and guiding him to his room, as part of a person-centred plan. Medication to suppress sexuality is not a first-line response (STOMP).

n.0: Using medication to suppress libido is a restrictive response that does not teach privacy.
n.1: Locking his room removes the private place he needs and is a blanket restriction.
n.3: Masturbation in a shared space needs support and teaching; it is not in itself sexual abuse of others.

9.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
9.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

9.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
9.q: Bill, 54, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about his care. He lives in a care home and has started trying to leave in the afternoons, saying he wants to 'go to work'. Staff suggest locking the front door and giving PRN sedation. What should be considered first?
o: Less restrictive ways to meet his need, such as accompanied walks
PRN sedation in the afternoons to reduce his attempts to leave the home
A locked front door as a blanket rule applied to all residents
His family's consent to the door being locked and the sedation
9.w: MCA s1(6): before acting, regard must be had to whether the purpose can be achieved in a way that is less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom. Understanding the meaning of his behaviour and offering accompanied walks or meaningful activity may meet the need without restriction (STOMP; NICE NG11).

n.1: Sedation to control behaviour is a chemical restraint and contrary to STOMP as a first response.
n.2: Blanket restrictions affect everyone and are not individually justified.
n.3: Family cannot consent to restrictions for an adult without legal authority.

9.q: A healthcare assistant in a care home in England is found to have left Mr Garner, who lacks capacity, in a soiled bed without food for a whole day on purpose. The manager asks the nurse what legal status this conduct has. What should the nurse say?
o: It is an offence under the Care Act 2014 safeguarding section
It may be a criminal offence of wilful neglect under MCA s44
It is a regulatory matter for the CQC with no criminal liability
It is a disciplinary matter for the employer to deal with
9.w: MCA 2005 s44 makes it an offence for a person who has the care of someone who lacks capacity to ill-treat or wilfully neglect them; on indictment the maximum is 5 years' imprisonment. It should also be raised as a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Care Act s42 places a duty on the local authority to make enquiries; it does not create this offence.
n.2: CQC regulates the provider, but s44 creates individual criminal liability.
n.3: Employer discipline may follow, but deliberate neglect of a person lacking capacity is also a potential criminal offence.

9.q: Hamid, 20, is autistic and uses a picture schedule prepared for his day-case procedure. On arrival he learns that theatre is running two hours late. He starts pacing and flapping his hands. What should the nurse do first?
o: Update his schedule with him, adding a waiting activity
Ask his carer to take him for a long walk until theatre calls
Give him the prescribed PRN medicine to help him wait calmly
Reassure him verbally that everything is fine and he will go soon
9.w: Unexpected change is distressing for many autistic people. Promptly updating the visual schedule and adding a planned waiting activity restores predictability (NICE CG142 1.1.8 visual supports for autistic adults; Annexe A 2.8).

n.1: Leaving without a clear plan adds uncertainty and may cause him to miss his slot.
n.2: PRN sedation is a more restrictive response when an adjustment can address the cause.
n.3: Vague reassurance does not restore predictability and 'soon' may be inaccurate.

9.q: Grace, 34, develops a widespread rash, lip swelling and wheeze minutes after starting an IV antibiotic infusion. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the first action after calling for help?
o: Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first drug
Give oral cetirizine and recheck her in 15 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and continue to observe her
9.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, current): remove the trigger (stop the infusion) and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Adults and children over 12: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh.

n.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
n.2: Antihistamines are third-line and do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
n.3: Continuing the infusion, even slowed, keeps exposing her to the trigger.

9.q: During a weekly stock check, two nurses find that the oxycodone 5 mg capsule count is one lower than the balance in the controlled drugs register. They have rechecked the cupboard and the most recent entries. What should they do next?
o: Report the discrepancy to the nurse in charge and pharmacy
Wait for the next weekly check to see if the count resolves
Borrow a capsule from another ward to restore the balance
Correct the register balance to match the stock and initial it
9.w: NICE NG46: stock check SOPs include reporting and managing discrepancies between stock and records. Once rechecked, unresolved discrepancies are reported promptly to the person in charge and pharmacy (and the CD accountable officer as required) and an incident is recorded.

n.1: Delaying a week loses the trail needed to investigate a possible diversion or error.
n.2: Borrowing stock conceals the loss and creates a second unrecorded transfer.
n.3: Altering a balance to hide a discrepancy falsifies a legal record.

9.q: A student nurse asks Eleni to explain the difference between the two duties of candour that apply in English hospitals. Which statement is correct?
o: The statutory duty applies to doctors; the professional duty applies to nurses
The statutory duty applies to individual nurses; the professional duty applies to NHS trusts
Both duties apply to individual nurses and are enforced by the CQC
Statutory duty binds registered providers; professional duty binds individual registrants
9.w: Regulation 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 places the statutory duty on registered providers (regulated by CQC). The professional duty (Code 14, NMC/GMC guidance refreshed December 2024) applies to individual registrants.

n.0: The professional duty applies to all regulated professionals including doctors; the statutory duty binds organisations.
n.1: This reverses the two duties; reg 20 binds registered providers and the Code binds individual registrants.
n.2: The CQC regulates the statutory duty on providers; the NMC oversees the professional duty on nurses.

9.q: Which contemporary tool is most widely used in UK adult care settings to screen for malnutrition?
o: The Braden scale for predicting risk
The 4AT rapid assessment test
The Waterlow risk assessment score
The 'MUST' screening tool
9.w: 'MUST' (BAPEN) combines BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect to give a low, medium or high risk of malnutrition, with a management plan for each (Annexe B 5.2).

n.0: Braden assesses pressure ulcer risk.
n.1: The 4AT screens for delirium.
n.2: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

9.q: Mrs Ivy Turner, 86, is admitted with a chest infection and has urinary incontinence at night. A colleague suggests inserting a urinary catheter so her bed stays dry. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Insert the catheter and review it after one week
Use continence pads overnight until she is discharged
Insert the catheter overnight and remove it each morning
Carry out a continence assessment and plan alternatives
9.w: Catheters carry risks of infection and loss of continence function and should not be used for staff convenience. A continence assessment identifies causes and less invasive options such as prompted toileting (P7.8 avoid unnecessary interventions; NICE CG139 urinary catheter use only after considering alternatives).

n.0: Catheterising for convenience exposes her to infection risk without a clinical indication.
n.1: Pads without a continence assessment leave the cause unidentified and may reduce continence and dignity.
n.2: Repeated insertion increases infection and trauma risk and is not a continence plan.

9.q: Liam, 22, attends an emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high using a scoring tool, and says 'low' scores can be discharged without referral. According to NICE NG225, how should the nurse approach this?
o: Not use the score to predict risk or decide on discharge
Complete the score and refer him to liaison psychiatry if it is high
Repeat the score each hour until he is discharged
Use the score to decide whether to refer him to liaison psychiatry
9.w: NICE NG225 (2022) recs 1.6.1-1.6.3: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged; do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification.

n.1: Restricting referral to high scores is risk stratification, which NG225 advises against.
n.2: Repeating a tool does not make it a valid predictor; NG225 advises against using it for this purpose.
n.3: NG225 says tools must not decide who is offered treatment; liaison psychiatry referral should be offered after self-harm.

9.q: Mr Osei, 80, has mild cognitive impairment. The nurse explains the options for his discharge. He understands, weighs the options and chooses home with carers, but 20 minutes later he cannot recall the details of the conversation. What should the nurse conclude?
o: He lacks capacity, because his cognitive impairment is lifelong
His capacity must be reassessed by a psychiatrist before discharge
He lacks capacity, because he could not recall the information
He can still make the decision, as retaining it briefly is enough
9.w: MCA 2005 s3(3): the fact that a person can retain information for a short period only does not prevent him from being regarded as able to make the decision. Mr Osei retained it long enough to make his choice.

n.0: A condition cannot establish incapacity (s2(3)); the test is functional and decision-specific.
n.1: Any suitably skilled decision maker can assess capacity; a psychiatrist is not required when the s3 test is already met.
n.2: s3(3) states that short-term retention is sufficient; later forgetting does not mean he lacked capacity.

9.q: Caroline, an off-duty theatre nurse, hears on the news that a major incident has been declared at her hospital after a building collapse. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make herself available and respond if the trust contacts her
Drive to the scene of the collapse to help the ambulance crews
Go straight to the emergency department to offer her help
Phone the theatre suite to ask whether she should come in
9.w: In a major incident, staff are called in through the trust's coordinated call-in process so that the right skills arrive at the right time and staff remain for later phases. Self-deployment to the scene or hospital can hamper command and control, and phone lines are needed for the response (P6.12).

n.1: Health staff at the scene are deployed by the ambulance service; self-deploying can add to the risk and confusion.
n.2: Self-presenting bypasses the hospital's command structure, and the trust may need her rested for later shifts.
n.3: Calling the department ties up phone lines needed for the incident response.

9.q: In a GP surgery waiting room, the practice nurse notices Colin, 56, coughing repeatedly into his hands. He has a fever and says he has no tissues. Other patients are seated close by. Which action best applies respiratory and cough hygiene?
o: Give tissues, a bin and a facemask, and seat him at least 1 metre from others
Ask him to cough into his hands and seat him at least 2 metres from others
Give him an FFP3 respirator to wear until he is called in for his appointment
Ask him to wait outside the building in his car until the nurse is ready to see him
9.w: NIPCM ch 1.3 and ch 2: cover the nose and mouth with a disposable tissue, dispose of it promptly and clean hands; outpatients with respiratory symptoms should be asked to wear a facemask if tolerated and be separated from others by at least 1 metre. Prioritising his appointment also helps.

n.1: Coughing into hands contaminates them; the crook of the arm is the fallback, and the NIPCM distance is 1 metre, not the pandemic-era 2 metres.
n.2: NIPCM states an FFP3 respirator must not be worn by an infectious patient, as it filters incoming rather than expelled air.
n.3: Sending a febrile patient to wait outside delays assessment and is not a standard respiratory hygiene measure.

9.q: A patient's family was told in person, with an apology, about a notifiable safety incident on the day it was identified. Under regulation 20, what must the provider do next?
o: Follow it with a written notification and keep a copy
Arrange a further meeting within 28 days to repeat the apology
Report the incident to the NMC for each nurse involved
Wait for the investigation to finish before any further contact
9.w: Reg 20(3)-(4): notification must be given in person, include an apology and be followed by a written notification; the provider must keep a copy and written records.

n.1: Reg 20 requires a written notification after the in-person one; a repeat meeting is not the specified step.
n.2: Reg 20 is about notifying the relevant person; NMC referral relates to fitness to practise concerns, not candour steps.
n.3: The written notification follows the in-person notification and gives what is known so far; it does not wait for the investigation to finish.

9.q: Winston, 73, has a red area over his sacrum. You want to check whether it is blanching. Which method is recommended by NICE CG179?
o: Applying a barrier cream and checking in a week
Measuring the area's temperature with a probe
Rubbing the area firmly to restore circulation
Finger palpation or diascopy with a clear disc
9.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy (pressing a transparent disc onto the skin) to test whether erythema blanches. Non-blanching erythema can present as colour change or discolouration in darker skin tones.

n.0: Barrier cream does not assess blanching and a week's delay misses early damage.
n.1: Temperature probes are not the CG179 method for testing blanching.
n.2: Skin massage or rubbing is advised against in CG179 and can cause damage.

9.q: Molly, 33, has a learning disability and a PRN antipsychotic for agitation. Her records show it was given 14 times last month, often in the early evening. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse?
o: Remove the PRN from her chart without discussion with the prescriber
Review the PRN use, look for triggers and request a medicines review
Ask the GP to make the PRN a regular evening dose
Continue as now, because each dose was within the prescribed limit
9.w: NICE NG11 1.8.4 says PRN antipsychotics should be used for as short a time as possible and their use recorded and reviewed. Frequent use at a regular time suggests an unmet need or trigger that should be explored, with a prescriber review (STOMP).

n.0: Nurses cannot unilaterally stop a prescribed medicine; changes need the prescriber.
n.2: Converting to a regular dose increases medication exposure without understanding the cause.
n.3: Staying within limits does not answer whether the medicine is needed so often.

9.q: Mr Adeyemi, 52, has type 2 diabetes and feels he 'always gets it wrong'. Which statement by the nurse best reflects a strengths-based approach?
o: "Your HbA1c is still too high, so we need to fix your diet."
"Most people find diabetes hard. Keep trying your best."
"Let's list all the things that went wrong this month."
"You've walked every day this month. How could we build on that?"
9.w: Proficiency P2.9: use communication skills and strength-based approaches to support people to make informed choices. Code 2.2 recognise the contribution people make to their own health.

n.0: This focuses on deficits rather than his strengths.
n.1: This is generic and does not identify or use his strengths.
n.2: Focusing on failures reinforces his belief that he gets it wrong.

9.q: Gordon, 66, dies unexpectedly on a surgical ward on the day after a planned procedure. There are no suspicious circumstances, but his death will be referred to the coroner to investigate the cause. He has a peripheral cannula and a urinary catheter. How should the nurse manage these devices during care after death?
o: Leave the cannula in place and spigot the urinary catheter
Remove both and send them with him in a labelled bag
Remove the cannula and catheter before washing him
Remove the cannula but leave the catheter bag attached
9.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause and there are no suspicious circumstances, leave IV cannulae and lines in situ and catheters spigotted; personal care can then be given. Deaths that may be related to a medical procedure or treatment require coroner referral.

n.1: Removing devices could affect the coroner's investigation of a death that may relate to a procedure.
n.2: Devices are left in situ when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause.
n.3: The cannula must stay in situ; the catheter is spigotted, and the bag contents may be discarded per policy.

9.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
9.q: In a supported living service, staff are asked what 'soft signs' of deterioration might look like in Lena, 33, who has a profound learning disability and no speech. Which example best fits?
o: A new oxygen saturation of 88% on air
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
A systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg
Eating less and sleeping more than usual
9.w: Soft signs are subtle changes from the person's baseline (eating, drinking, sleeping, mobility, mood, behaviour) that may precede changes in vital signs. Recognising them depends on knowing the person's usual presentation.

n.0: Saturation of 88% on air is a measured abnormality, not a soft sign.
n.1: A respiratory rate of 30 is a hard, measured sign that scores highly on NEWS2.
n.2: Systolic BP of 85 is a measured red-flag sign, not a soft sign.

9.q: Maya, 17, is autistic. Her outpatient appointment has been moved to a different clinic room at short notice and she has become very anxious in the waiting area. Which reasonable adjustment would best prevent this next time?
o: Ask Maya's mother to attend instead of Maya to save her stress
Give advance notice of any change with a photo of the new room
Offer Maya a sedative to take an hour before each appointment
Book the longest available slot in the middle of the clinic day
9.w: Unexpected change commonly drives anxiety in autistic people. Advance warning and visual information make change predictable; CG170 1.1.10 also suggests appointments at the start or end of the day to minimise waiting.

n.0: Excluding Maya removes her right to take part in her own care.
n.2: Routine sedation is not a reasonable adjustment and is contrary to STOMP and STAMP.
n.3: Long waits in the middle of a busy clinic day are likely to increase anxiety; start or end of day is preferred.

9.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is planning CPD for revalidation. Which activity would count as participatory learning under the NMC requirements?
o: Completing a self-directed e-learning module on sepsis
A live online workshop discussing cases with other nurses
Watching a recorded conference lecture on wound care
Reading a systematic review and writing summary notes
9.w: NMC CPD guidance: participatory learning means activity involving interaction with one or more other professionals, in a physical or virtual environment; you do not have to be in the same room.

n.0: E-learning completed alone involves no interaction with other professionals, so it is non-participatory.
n.2: A recording watched alone has no interaction; participatory learning needs engagement with others.
n.3: Independent reading is valuable CPD but does not involve interaction with another professional.

9.q: Sofia, 28, has a severe learning disability. Her PBS plan includes a planned restrictive intervention: briefly holding her wrists if she scratches her face hard enough to bleed. A new nurse asks what must also be in place for this to be lawful and ethical. Which answer is best?
o: A Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards authorisation covering the use of physical holds
A signed instruction from the consultant psychiatrist authorising the hold for Sofia
A record that Sofia's family agreed to the hold when the plan was written
A best interests decision that it is necessary and proportionate, with review
9.w: NICE NG11 1.9.5-1.9.6: planned restrictive interventions must be lawful (MCA, HRA), in the person's best interests where they lack capacity, a reasonable, necessary and proportionate response to the risk, the least restrictive option, documented, debriefed and reviewed within a reduction programme.

n.0: DoLS authorises a deprivation of liberty in a care home or hospital; it is not the authority for a brief planned hold, which rests on MCA ss5-6.
n.1: A doctor's instruction does not replace the MCA best interests process and proportionality test.
n.2: Families must be consulted, but family agreement does not on its own make an intervention lawful for an adult who lacks capacity.

9.q: Nurse Ola realises she gave Leon, 45, 10 mg of oral morphine solution instead of the prescribed 5 mg, 20 minutes ago. Leon is alert with a respiratory rate of 16 and no sedation. What should Ola do?
o: Rewrite the chart entry to 5 mg to avoid confusing the next nurse
Monitor Leon, inform the prescriber, tell Leon and report the incident
Observe Leon and report the error if he shows any signs of harm
Inform the ward manager and leave her to decide whether to tell Leon
9.w: Medication incidents are reported and reflected on (P6.8; NMC Code 19): the priority is the person's safety (monitoring sedation and respiratory rate), then informing the prescriber, being open with Leon (professional duty of candour), and reporting through the local system feeding LFPSE.

n.0: Altering the record to hide an error is dishonest and breaches the Code.
n.2: Incidents, including those without harm, are reported so that learning can occur.
n.3: The professional duty of candour is personal; Ola should be open with Leon herself.

9.q: At 22:00 two registered nurses phone in sick on a 30-bed ward with three acutely unwell patients. The nurse in charge has one registered nurse and two healthcare assistants. What is the priority action?
o: Escalate to the site manager now and request extra staff
Ask the healthcare assistants to give the evening medicines
Complete an incident report at the end of the shift
Reallocate patients and report the shortfall at the morning huddle
9.w: Proficiency P6.2: understand the relationship between safe staffing, skill mix, safety and quality and escalate concerns. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt escalation of risks; an incident report follows.

n.1: Delegating medicines beyond competence adds risk (Code 11.1) and does not solve the staffing gap.
n.2: Reporting is needed but does not resolve the immediate risk; escalation comes first.
n.3: Waiting until morning leaves an unsafe skill mix all night; it needs escalating now.

9.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
9.q: A LeDeR review of the death of Paul, 51, who had a learning disability, found his death certificate gave 'cerebral palsy' as the cause of death; he died of aspiration pneumonia. Why does LeDeR treat this as an issue?
o: Cerebral palsy should be listed after the learning disability
The actual illness that caused his death was hidden
LeDeR reviews do not look at the recorded cause of death
Pneumonia deaths are certified by the coroner, not a doctor
9.w: LeDeR highlights that people do not die 'of' cerebral palsy or a learning disability but of illnesses such as pneumonia; recording the disability as the cause hides potentially preventable causes and prevents learning (LeDeR 2023 report).

n.0: The order of the conditions is not the problem; the disability should not be given as the cause of death.
n.2: LeDeR reviews do consider cause of death information, including certificates.
n.3: Doctors routinely certify deaths from pneumonia; it does not need certifying by the coroner.

9.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
9.q: Kai, 16, has a learning disability and complex health needs. Several professionals are involved in his transition. His father says no one knows who is coordinating things. What does NICE NG43 recommend?
o: Wait until adult services allocate a social worker
Identify a named worker to coordinate his transition
Ask the GP to take over all of his care at 18
Ask Kai's father to coordinate all of the services
9.w: NICE NG43 1.2.5-1.2.7: help the young person identify a single practitioner as 'named worker' to coordinate transition care and support, link with practitioners and the GP, and support the family; ideally someone with whom the young person has a meaningful relationship.

n.0: Waiting for adult services leaves a gap in coordination before transfer.
n.2: The GP is important but is not expected to take over all specialist care.
n.3: Families should be supported, not left to coordinate complex services alone.

9.q: Ellis, 30, is autistic, has a university degree and no impairment of general intelligence. He is admitted to a surgical ward and the ward manager asks whether he should be referred to the learning disability liaison team as 'a patient with a learning disability'. Which statement is accurate?
o: Ellis has a mild learning disability because autism affects social functioning
Ellis is autistic but does not have a learning disability
Ellis must be added to the GP learning disability register before any referral
Ellis falls under the learning disability qualifier in section 1 of the Mental Health Act
9.w: Autism and learning disability are distinct conditions that can, but need not, occur together. Ellis has no impairment of intelligence, so he does not meet the definition, although he may still need autism-related reasonable adjustments (many liaison teams support autistic people too).

n.0: Differences in social communication from autism are not the same as the impaired intelligence required for a learning disability.
n.2: The register is for people with a learning disability; Ellis does not meet that definition.
n.3: The s1(2A) qualifier applies to learning disability; autism is treated as a mental disorder without that qualifier under the 1983 Act.

9.q: Jas, a learning disability nurse, is writing a Social Story for Riley, 15, who is autistic and is having a blood test. Which sentence fits the Social Story approach best?
o: The nurse will put a band on my arm. It will feel tight for a short time.
If I do not keep still, the nurse will have to try again.
Most young people are brave and do not cry when they have blood taken.
The needle is tiny, so it will not hurt me when it goes in.
9.w: Social Stories use descriptive, accurate and reassuring sentences, often in the first person, that explain what will happen and how it may feel. They avoid threats, comparisons and false promises (Carol Gray).

n.1: This frames the story as a warning, which can increase anxiety.
n.2: Comparisons and pressure to be 'brave' are not descriptive and can cause shame.
n.3: Promising it will not hurt is inaccurate and can damage trust.

9.q: A community learning disability nurse is teaching carers about causes of learning disability. Which example is a perinatal cause?
o: Rubella infection in the mother during the first trimester
Bacterial meningitis at 18 months of age
Hypoxic brain injury during a prolonged and complicated birth
An extra copy of chromosome 21 present from conception
9.w: Perinatal causes act around the time of birth: hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury in labour, extreme prematurity and its complications, and severe neonatal jaundice are examples.

n.0: Maternal rubella in early pregnancy is a prenatal (congenital infection) cause.
n.1: Meningitis in later infancy is a postnatal cause.
n.3: Trisomy 21 is a genetic (chromosomal) prenatal cause.

9.q: Nurse Adebayo nearly gives insulin to the wrong patient but notices at the bedside check, so no dose is given. A colleague says there is no need to report it because nothing happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discuss it at the next team meeting without making a report
Make a note in her own reflective log for revalidation
Tell the patient about the near miss and make no further record
Report the near miss through the local incident reporting system
9.w: The NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (refreshed December 2024) covers openness within organisations, including reporting adverse incidents and near misses. Code 19.1 requires action to reduce the likelihood of mistakes and near misses.

n.0: Discussion helps learning, but candour guidance expects near misses to be reported formally so the system can learn.
n.1: Personal reflection is useful but does not replace organisational reporting of the near miss.
n.2: Telling the patient is not enough; the near miss must still be documented and reported (Code 14.3, 19.1).

9.q: Jacob, 26, is autistic with a moderate learning disability. During a fire alarm test at his day service he stops responding, sits very still and does not answer questions for 20 minutes. Which response by staff is best?
o: Record it as non-compliance in his daily notes
Guide him to a quiet space, stay calm and give him time
Keep asking him questions to keep him engaged
Call an ambulance because he is not responding to speech
9.w: Withdrawal and reduced responsiveness after overwhelming sensory input can be a shutdown response. Reducing demands and stimulation, staying nearby calmly and allowing recovery time is the supportive approach (NICE CG142 1.1.8 adjusting noise and the environment for autistic adults).

n.0: This is a response to overload, not a choice to refuse, so recording it as non-compliance is inaccurate.
n.2: Repeated questions add demands and sensory input and may prolong the shutdown.
n.3: He is breathing, sitting and recovering after a known trigger; there is no sign of a medical emergency.

9.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
9.q: Peter, 45, has a severe learning disability and is on a medical ward. His sister says, 'He's not himself, he's gone quiet and isn't humming like he usually does.' His NEWS2 score is 1. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck his observations at the next routine time
Reassure her that a NEWS2 of 1 is low risk
Act on her concern, reassess fully and escalate
Ask her to write her concerns down for the doctor
9.w: Family carers know the person's baseline and often notice 'soft signs' of deterioration before observations change. LeDeR and CIPOLD learning show that ignoring carer concern contributes to avoidable deaths; the nurse should reassess (full observations, ABCDE) and escalate, using Martha's Rule routes if needed.

n.0: Waiting for routine observations may miss early deterioration.
n.1: A low score does not override a credible concern from someone who knows his baseline.
n.3: Written concerns delay action; the nurse should act now.

9.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
9.q: Phil, 48, has a learning disability and lives in supported living, where staff help him manage his money. Which finding is most suggestive of financial abuse?
o: Phil asking staff to help him check his bank statement at the end of each month
Phil choosing to spend a large amount on a football season ticket
Unexplained cash withdrawals and no money for food despite benefits
A planned increase in Phil's rent agreed at his tenancy review
9.w: Unexplained withdrawals and a lack of money for basics when income is adequate are recognised indicators of financial abuse and need a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Seeking help to check statements is a protective habit, not a sign of abuse.
n.1: A person's own spending choice, even if large, is not abuse.
n.3: An agreed rent increase is an expected, transparent cost.

9.q: A learning disability nurse joins a review of an inpatient unit. Learning from long-stay hospitals, Winterbourne View and Whorlton Hall, which combination of features most strongly suggests a risk of abuse?
o: A large staff team with a mix of registered nurses and support workers
A service that holds weekly multidisciplinary reviews with families
A unit that uses positive behaviour support plans for every patient
A closed culture: isolation, people far from home and few outside visitors
9.w: Abuse in learning disability settings has repeatedly occurred in closed cultures: people placed far from home, isolated from families and outside scrutiny, with poor leadership and power imbalances (CQC closed cultures learning after Whorlton Hall).

n.0: A mixed staff team is normal and not in itself a warning sign.
n.1: Regular family involvement increases outside scrutiny and reduces risk.
n.2: PBS plans for each person are good practice, not a warning sign.

9.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
9.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

9.q: Jordan, 28, has a mild learning disability and is about to sign a consent form for a hernia repair. He speaks fluently and says 'yes, that's fine' to everything the surgeon explains. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
o: Check what he has understood, as fluent speech can mask poor comprehension
Accept his signature, as a mild learning disability rarely affects consent
Ask his mother, who attends with him, to sign the form on his behalf
Request a formal capacity assessment by a psychiatrist before surgery
9.w: People with a mild learning disability may have expressive language that exceeds their understanding and may agree to please. Asking Jordan to explain the procedure in his own words, with accessible information, checks understanding before consent is relied on (MCA s1(3): all practicable steps).

n.1: Capacity is presumed, but agreement alone does not show that Jordan has understood the information.
n.2: Another adult cannot consent for Jordan; a parent has no legal authority to sign for an adult.
n.3: There is no reason yet to doubt capacity formally; the first step is to check and support understanding, which any clinician can do.

9.q: Mr Nowak, 70, has expressive aphasia after a stroke and cannot speak clearly. A decision is needed about moving him to a rehabilitation unit. Before anyone concludes he lacks capacity, what should the nurse do?
o: Wait for his speech to recover fully before discussing the move
Record that he lacks capacity because he cannot speak clearly
Ask his wife to make the decision as she knows his wishes best
Arrange communication aids or speech and language therapy input
9.w: MCA 2005 s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. s3(1)(d) allows communication by any means, so aids and specialist input should be tried.

n.0: Delaying indefinitely is not required; the duty is to take practicable steps to support his decision now.
n.1: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; s3(1)(d) covers any means.
n.2: His wife cannot decide for him unless she holds a relevant LPA; the first step is to support him to decide.

9.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
9.q: Sian, 33, has a learning disability and lives in a group home with a house rule that all residents must be in their rooms by 9pm. Sian has capacity and wants to watch late football matches in the lounge. What is the most appropriate action by the community nurse?
o: Challenge the blanket rule and support Sian to access advocacy
Raise the issue at Sian's annual review in eight months' time
Suggest Sian complains to the NMC about the staff who set the rule
Explain that she must follow house rules that apply to everyone
9.w: Rights-based practice means challenging blanket restrictions that interfere with Article 8 and the person's choices (NMC Code 3.4, 16; O'Brien's choice). The nurse should raise the rule with the provider and help Sian access advocacy.

n.1: Delaying eight months leaves an unjustified restriction in place.
n.2: The NMC regulates nurses; the issue is a service rule, not a registrant's fitness to practise.
n.3: A blanket rule for a capacitous adult is not justified simply because it applies to all.

9.q: Your close colleague, going through a divorce, asks you not to mention that she has given several time-critical medicines over an hour late this week. She promises it will stop. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Agree to keep it confidential if she promises to improve
Offer support but explain you must tell the nurse in charge
Give her time-critical medicines for her so the delays stop
Report her to the NMC without speaking to anyone locally
9.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but this must never compromise patient safety. Code 16.1: raise and escalate safety concerns; 19.1 reduce harm.

n.0: Code 8.7 says support must not compromise patient safety; late time-critical medicines need escalating.
n.2: Covering for her hides the problem and leaves the risk unmanaged.
n.3: Local escalation and support should come first; referral is not the immediate proportionate step.

9.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
9.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

9.q: A community nurse uses a PAS-ADD checklist with support staff caring for Olivia, 45, who has a learning disability. What is the purpose of this tool?
o: To measure Olivia's IQ and adaptive functioning
To diagnose a specific mental illness without a clinical assessment
To screen for possible mental health problems needing full assessment
To assess Olivia's capacity to consent to treatment
9.w: The PAS-ADD family of tools (Psychiatric Assessment Schedules for Adults with Developmental Disabilities) includes checklists completed by carers to screen for possible mental health problems, prompting referral for full assessment. They support, but do not replace, clinical diagnosis.

n.0: IQ and adaptive functioning are measured with different psychometric tools.
n.1: A screening checklist identifies possible problems; diagnosis requires clinical assessment.
n.3: Capacity is assessed under the MCA for a specific decision, not with a PAS-ADD checklist.

9.q: A ward manager is reviewing last month's incident reports with the team. She explains that some incidents are classed as Never Events because strong national safety barriers exist to prevent them. Which of the following incidents is classed as a Never Event in NHS England?
o: A fall resulting in a hip fracture on a ward
A missed dose of a prescribed antibiotic
Misplaced nasogastric tube not detected before use
A category 3 pressure ulcer acquired in hospital
9.w: The NHS England Never Events list (2018, updated 2021, still active) includes misplaced naso- or oro-gastric tubes not detected before use, as strong national barriers (pH testing and X-ray protocols) exist.

n.0: Inpatient falls are serious incidents but are not on the Never Events list.
n.1: Missed doses are medication incidents but are not Never Events.
n.3: Pressure ulcers are reported as incidents but are not Never Events.

9.q: Ella, 14, is in school Year 9. The school nurse assesses her as Gillick competent, and Ella consents to her MenACWY vaccine. Her mother has returned a form refusing the vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the vaccine, as a parent cannot override a Gillick competent child's consent
Delay the vaccine until Ella is 16 and can legally consent for herself
Ask the head teacher to decide whether the vaccine should be given
Withhold the vaccine, because a parent's refusal takes priority under age 16
9.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): children under 16 who understand fully what is involved (Gillick competent) can give consent, ideally with parental involvement; where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent. UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: MenACWY at 14 years (school Year 9).

n.1: Gillick competent children under 16 can consent, so waiting is unnecessary.
n.2: The head teacher has no role in consent to Ella's treatment.
n.3: The Green Book states that where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent.

9.q: Adam, 30, has a learning disability and uses Makaton. A healthcare assistant who has learned some signs explains Adam's meal choices by signing silently so as not to 'confuse him with words'. What advice should the nurse give?
o: Use speech and save signing for when Adam seems confused
Write the choices down for Adam and point to each one
Sign every word of each sentence while staying silent
Sign key words while speaking, in normal word order
9.w: Makaton signs are used with speech, signing the key words in spoken word order. Speech plus sign gives two channels and supports understanding.

n.0: Waiting until confusion appears loses the benefit of signs supporting understanding from the start.
n.1: Written words may not be accessible to Adam; he uses Makaton.
n.2: Makaton signs key words, not every word, and is not used silently.

9.q: Tariq, 26, has a mild learning disability and capacity to decide about blood tests. He has a strong fear of needles and pulled away at his last two attempts. He needs regular blood tests to monitor his lithium. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Record that he has refused blood tests and inform the prescriber
Arrange a graded desensitisation programme with numbing cream
Ask the GP to prescribe a sedative before the next attempt
Ask two staff to hold his arm still for a quick test
9.w: Tariq has capacity, so holding him would be unlawful restraint. A reasonable adjustment such as gradual desensitisation over several visits, with a familiar person and topical anaesthetic, supports him to have the test he needs (MCA 2005 s1; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: His fear is a barrier that adjustments can address; recording refusal without trying them risks unsafe lithium monitoring.
n.2: Sedation is a restrictive option to consider only after less restrictive adjustments have been tried, and needs his consent.
n.3: Holding a person with capacity against his will is assault and not a reasonable adjustment.

9.q: Priya, a community learning disability nurse, is preparing a briefing for her ICB on the January 2026 republished LeDeR report for 2023. She wants one accurate headline about how many adult deaths were rated avoidable. Which statement should she use?
o: About 2 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable, matching the general population
About 1 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
About 4 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
About 7 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
9.w: The revised 2023 report rated 40.2% of adult deaths as avoidable (about 4 in 10), slightly higher than first published before the report was withdrawn for data errors and republished on 27 January 2026 (LeDeR 2023 revised).

n.0: About 22% is the comparable general population figure cited for 2022; people with a learning disability were roughly twice as likely to die avoidably.
n.1: 1 in 10 greatly understates the reported figure of about 40%.
n.3: 7 in 10 overstates the reported figure of about 40%.

9.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
9.q: Tony, 60, has a learning disability and lacks capacity. His sister holds a registered health and welfare Lasting Power of Attorney that expressly covers life-sustaining treatment. Doctors are considering stopping antibiotics. Who makes the decision?
o: His sister, as attorney, in his best interests
The consultant, after informing his sister
An IMCA appointed by the hospital
The Court of Protection, on application
9.w: Under MCA 2005 s9-11, a health and welfare attorney can make decisions about life-sustaining treatment if the LPA expressly authorises it, acting in the person's best interests. Doctors advise on clinical options but the attorney makes the decision.

n.1: Where a valid LPA covers the decision, the attorney decides, not the clinician alone.
n.2: An IMCA is not needed when there is an attorney to make the decision.
n.3: Court involvement is needed for disputes, not for every decision when an attorney exists.

10.q: Ellie has worked 60 hours a week for a month to cover vacancies. She has twice nearly given the wrong dose and feels exhausted. Her manager asks her to do another extra shift. What should Ellie do?
o: Accept the shift and ask colleagues to double-check her work
Decline the shift and tell her manager about the near misses
Accept the shift and rest fully on her next day off
Decline the shift and keep the near misses to herself
10.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need for your role. Code 16.3: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity about problems that may prevent you working within the Code. Proficiency P1.5.

n.0: Working while exhausted keeps patients at risk; she must address her fitness for practice (Code 20.9).
n.2: Planning rest later does not address the current risk she has recognised.
n.3: Declining helps, but Code 16.3 requires her to tell someone in authority about problems affecting safe practice.

10.q: Gordon, 74, is in a single room with a suspected respiratory infection and needs a chest X-ray. The radiology department cannot bring a portable machine today. He is stable and can tolerate a mask. How should the nurse arrange his transfer?
o: Postpone the X-ray until his infection status has been confirmed
Transfer him without a mask and clean the wheelchair once the journey is complete
Ask him to wear an FFP3 respirator during the transfer and X-ray
Ask him to wear a surgical mask if tolerated and inform radiology of his status
10.w: NIPCM ch 2.1: infectious patients are transferred only when clinically necessary, and should wear a surgical mask in communal areas during transfer if tolerated; the receiving department and transport staff must be made aware of the precautions needed.

n.0: The X-ray is clinically needed, and transfer with precautions is appropriate rather than delaying diagnosis.
n.1: Without a mask he exposes others in corridors and waiting areas; cleaning afterwards does not prevent that exposure.
n.2: FFP3 respirators filter incoming air and must not be worn by infectious patients.

10.q: Margaret, 64, is breathless and anxious. Her SpO2 is 82% on air and she is drowsy with RR 30. She has no history of lung disease. Help has been called. What oxygen should be given first?
o: 28% oxygen via a Venturi mask with humidification
4 L/min via a simple face mask and reassess
15 L/min via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask
2 L/min via nasal cannulae and titrate up
10.w: BTS guideline: in critical illness or severe hypoxaemia start high-concentration oxygen via a reservoir mask at 15 L/min, then titrate down to a target of 94-98% once stable (NG253 rec 1.10.1).

n.0: 28% Venturi is a controlled low-concentration device for people at risk of hypercapnia.
n.1: A simple face mask at 4 L/min risks CO2 rebreathing and is inadequate here.
n.3: 2 L/min nasal cannulae delivers far too little oxygen for severe hypoxaemia.

10.q: On a children's ward in England, the nurse is caring for Lily, 15, who needs a decision about a minor procedure. A student nurse asks whether the Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs this decision. Which statement is correct?
o: It applies to children of any age if parents agree
Its powers generally apply to people aged 16 and over
Its powers apply to people aged 18 and over
It applies to anyone over 12 who is in hospital
10.w: MCA 2005 s2(5): the powers under the Act do not generally apply to a person under 16 (subject to s18(3), which concerns property). Decisions for Lily follow the law on children's consent and parental responsibility.

n.0: Parental agreement does not bring a child under 16 within the MCA.
n.2: The MCA starts at 16, not 18; it covers 16 and 17 year olds.
n.3: There is no age-12 threshold in the MCA; s2(5) sets 16.

10.q: Marta, a registered nurse, asks Lewis, a healthcare assistant who is trained and assessed in clinical observations, to record observations on three stable patients in her bay. What must Marta do to delegate this task appropriately?
o: Tell Lewis which patients to observe and leave the escalation decisions to him
Explain what to report and when, check he understands and review the results
Ask Lewis to record the observations and to calculate the NEWS2 for each patient
Ask Lewis to observe the patients if he feels confident and has time this morning
10.w: Code 11.1-11.3: delegate only within the other person's competence, make sure they understand the instructions and are supervised and supported, and confirm the outcome meets the required standard. AnnexA.4.1.2 requires clear instructions and checking understanding when delegating. Marta remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for reviewing findings.

n.0: Escalation decisions require registered nurse assessment; leaving them to Lewis passes on responsibility Marta cannot delegate in this way.
n.2: Recording a score without clear thresholds for reporting and review does not meet Code 11.2-11.3.
n.3: Delegation must be clear and planned; leaving it to his confidence and time does not ensure the care is done.

10.q: Reviewing the night's charts, Nurse Hana sees that a healthcare assistant recorded hourly observations for a patient who was off the ward in theatre for three of those hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Mention it informally to the healthcare assistant next week
Amend the entries herself so the chart is accurate
Leave it, as the patient has now returned safely
Escalate it to the nurse in charge straight away
10.w: Code 10.3: complete records without falsification, taking immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to these requirements. Code 16.1 escalate concerns.

n.0: Falsified observations are a safety concern; Code 10.3 requires immediate action.
n.1: Altering another person's entries is itself inappropriate; the concern must be escalated.
n.2: The patient's safety now does not remove the falsification; it must be acted upon.

10.q: Daniel, a staff nurse with a full beard, is asked to care for Tariq, 30, who has suspected measles and is in a negative-pressure room. Daniel passed an FFP3 fit test two years ago when he was clean-shaven. What is the most appropriate course of action?
o: Wear a powered respirator hood in place of the tight-fitting FFP3
Wear two fluid-resistant surgical masks layered over each other
Wear the same FFP3 model and perform a fit check on entry
Wear a Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with a visor
10.w: Measles spreads by the airborne route, so respiratory protective equipment is needed. NIPCM ch 2.4 states facial hair must not cross the respirator sealing surface and staff must pass a fit test for any tight-fitting RPE; powered respirator hoods are an alternative when fit testing cannot be achieved.

n.1: Layering surgical masks does not create a sealed respirator and gives no airborne protection.
n.2: A beard crossing the seal means a tight-fitting respirator cannot seal, and a fit check does not replace a valid fit test.
n.3: An FRSM with a visor protects against droplets and splashes, not airborne particles.

10.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
10.q: Freya, 29, has a learning disability and epilepsy. She wants to start swimming at her local leisure centre. Her support worker thinks she should not be allowed. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Suggest she swims after her seizures have stopped for five years
Support a risk assessment and plan so that she can swim safely
Agree she should not swim because drowning is a risk
Advise her to swim in the shallow end without any supervision
10.w: People with epilepsy should be supported to live full lives; risks are managed through individual risk assessment and planning (for example a trained companion who knows her seizures, lifeguard awareness), rather than blanket restriction (NG217 principles; positive risk-taking; MCA unwise decisions).

n.0: There is no five-year seizure-free rule for swimming; individual risk assessment applies.
n.2: A blanket ban is overly restrictive; the risk can be reduced with planning.
n.3: Swimming unsupervised is unsafe for a person with active seizures, even in shallow water.

10.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, is treated for alcohol intoxication. She mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone. She refuses to let staff contact anyone. Under the Children Act 2004 s16LA duty in force since 30 September 2026, what should the nurse do?
o: Seek Kerry's consent again and share the information if she agrees
Share once a safeguarding threshold has been reached
Record the concern and share if it happens again
Share the relevant information with children's social care now
10.w: Children Act 2004 s16LA (inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, in force 30 September 2026) requires bodies under the s11 duty, including NHS bodies, to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, without a threshold and without needing consent, unless sharing would be more harmful to the child. A young child alone at home needs immediate action.

n.0: Consent is not required under s16LA, and waiting for it delays protection of a child at immediate risk.
n.1: s16LA sets no threshold; the information is relevant to his safety and must be shared.
n.2: A 3-year-old alone at home is at immediate risk; waiting for a repeat leaves him unprotected.

10.q: Nurse Ola realises she gave Leon, 45, 10 mg of oral morphine solution instead of the prescribed 5 mg, 20 minutes ago. Leon is alert with a respiratory rate of 16 and no sedation. What should Ola do?
o: Rewrite the chart entry to 5 mg to avoid confusing the next nurse
Monitor Leon, inform the prescriber, tell Leon and report the incident
Observe Leon and report the error if he shows any signs of harm
Inform the ward manager and leave her to decide whether to tell Leon
10.w: Medication incidents are reported and reflected on (P6.8; NMC Code 19): the priority is the person's safety (monitoring sedation and respiratory rate), then informing the prescriber, being open with Leon (professional duty of candour), and reporting through the local system feeding LFPSE.

n.0: Altering the record to hide an error is dishonest and breaches the Code.
n.2: Incidents, including those without harm, are reported so that learning can occur.
n.3: The professional duty of candour is personal; Ola should be open with Leon herself.

10.q: Tom, 34, attends an acute medical unit with a urinary tract infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and sepsis is suspected. Under NICE NG253 (2025), within what time should broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics be given?
o: Within 3 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 6 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 4 hours of arrival in the department
10.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.3: for people at high risk (NEWS2 7 or more), give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score.

n.0: Up to 3 hours is the deferral window a clinician may use for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6).
n.2: Up to 6 hours is the deferral window for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.3: A 4-hour arrival target is not a sepsis treatment standard.

10.q: In theatre, Callum, a newly registered scrub nurse, sees the surgeon pick up the scalpel before the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist time out has been done. The team seems not to have noticed. What should Callum do?
o: Complete an incident report after the operation so the omission is recorded
Note the omission and raise it at the team debrief at the end of the list
Quietly tell the anaesthetist so that the surgeon is not challenged openly
Say clearly that the time out has not been done and ask the team to pause
10.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 (preserve safety) require nurses to intervene. Checklists work only if anyone can stop the process; speaking up clearly and directly at the moment of risk is the safest action, whatever the speaker's seniority (P6.6; P5.2).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate later, but the immediate risk must be addressed before the incision.
n.1: Raising it afterwards allows the operation to proceed without the safety check that prevents wrong site and wrong patient surgery.
n.2: An indirect approach delays action and may not stop the procedure in time.

10.q: Hilda, 74, has had a nasogastric tube inserted for feeding after a stroke. You aspirate gastric contents and test them on CE-marked pH paper. Which reading confirms gastric placement so that feeding can start?
o: pH 8.5 or above
pH 6.0 or below
pH 7.0 or above
pH 5.5 or below
10.w: NICE CG32: gastric tube position is confirmed by pH 5.5 or below on pH paper. Position must be confirmed after placement and before each use by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary (rec 1.7.17).

n.0: pH 8.5 is alkaline and suggests a non-gastric position.
n.1: pH 6.0 is above the 5.5 threshold and does not confirm gastric placement.
n.2: pH 7 or above may indicate the tube is in the lung or intestine.

10.q: A healthcare assistant tells Nurse Ade that she has seen poor care but wants to raise it anonymously because she fears losing her job. What advice reflects NMC raising concerns guidance?
o: Giving her name aids investigation and gives her better legal protection
Anonymous concerns cannot be investigated, so she must give her name
She should wait until she has written evidence before raising anything formally
She should tell the patient's family so they can raise it instead
10.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance recommends giving your name because the concern is easier to investigate and you get the best legal protection; concerns can be raised confidentially within limits.

n.1: NMC guidance allows confidential raising, though naming oneself is recommended; anonymous concerns can still be looked at.
n.2: No proof is needed to raise a concern; waiting delays action on a possible risk.
n.3: Passing the duty to relatives is not an NMC route and does not protect patients promptly.

10.q: A community nurse is monitoring Joseph, 55, who has Down syndrome and suspected dementia. Which tool would NICE NG54 suggest to supplement the assessment?
o: The standard Mini-Mental State Examination, unadapted
Dementia Questionnaire for People with Learning Disabilities
The Abbey Pain Scale designed for people living with dementia
The Waterlow score
10.w: NICE NG54 1.7.12: consider supplementing a dementia assessment with measures designed for people with learning disabilities, such as the DLD, the Down Syndrome Dementia Scale or the DSQIID, plus cognitive and adaptive measures over time.

n.0: Standard cognitive tests are not designed for people with learning disabilities and are hard to interpret (NG54 1.7.9).
n.2: The Abbey scale assesses pain in people with dementia, not dementia itself.
n.3: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

10.q: Marcus Bell, 66, is on a surgical ward. His observations are: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on air, BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, alert, temperature 37.2°C. His NEWS2 total is 3. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Increase observations to at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat the observations in 4 hours and escalate if the total rises
Continue 4 to 6 hourly observations as the total score is below 5
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
10.w: A respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3 in a single parameter (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Chart 1). A score of 3 in any one parameter triggers a low-medium clinical risk response: minimum 1-hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team, who decide whether escalation is needed (Chart 4). Two steps: calculate the parameter score, then apply the single-parameter rule.

n.1: Four-hourly review delays recognition of deterioration when a single parameter is already scoring 3.
n.2: The aggregate of 3 is low, but a single red score of 3 overrides this and requires at least hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.3: Emergency critical care assessment is the response to an aggregate of 7 or more; this is an urgent ward-based response.

10.q: A registered nurse is reviewing four recent deaths on a care of older people ward. All were verified, and none involved suspicious circumstances. Which death should be referred to the coroner?
o: Bill, 74, who died an expected death in a hospice from motor neurone disease
Harold, 79, who died an expected death from confirmed COVID-19
Edith, 88, who died five days after a hip fracture from a fall at home
Joan, 91, who died an expected death from heart failure under her GP
10.w: RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024), Appendix 1 (Ministry of Justice): refer to the coroner where the death may have been caused by violence, trauma or physical injury, whether intentional or otherwise, among other criteria. A notifiable disease such as COVID-19 is not a reason to refer.

n.0: An expected death from a diagnosed progressive illness is not, on these facts, reportable to the coroner.
n.1: A notifiable infectious disease such as COVID-19 is not, by itself, a reason to refer a death to the coroner.
n.3: An expected death from a known natural cause with an attending practitioner does not need coroner referral.

10.q: Noah, 5, has developmental delay, anxiety and hand-flapping. His paediatrician requests a genetic test. Which result would confirm fragile X syndrome?
o: More than 200 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene
An extra copy of chromosome 21 in the cells
A pathogenic variant in the MECP2 gene
Loss of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15
10.w: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a full mutation in FMR1 on the X chromosome: more than 200 CGG repeats (typical range about 5 to 40), which silences the gene (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.1: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.
n.2: MECP2 variants cause Rett syndrome.
n.3: Loss of maternal UBE3A causes Angelman syndrome.

10.q: An occupational health nurse is giving an intradermal tuberculin skin test into the inner forearm of Leila, 24. Which finding confirms that the injection has been placed correctly?
o: The fluid flows freely and leaves no mark on the skin
Blood flashback is seen in the hub of the syringe
A small pale bleb forms raising the skin at the site
A bruise appears at the site within a few minutes
10.w: Intradermal injections are given at a shallow angle of about 10-15 degrees with the bevel up, just under the epidermis; correct placement raises a small pale bleb (AnnexB.11.7). No bleb suggests a deeper, subcutaneous injection.

n.0: Free flow with no bleb suggests the fluid has gone into subcutaneous tissue.
n.1: Flashback indicates the needle is in a blood vessel, not the dermis.
n.3: Bruising suggests trauma to vessels, not correct dermal placement.

10.q: Vincent, 48, attends the practice nurse for a wound dressing. While checking his record, the nurse sees he smokes 20 cigarettes a day. They have about a minute before the next patient. Which approach reflects very brief advice on smoking?
o: Ask about smoking and advise him to cut down gradually by himself
Ask, advise that medicines plus specialist support work best, and offer referral
Explain the diseases caused by smoking in detail over the next 20 minutes
Wait until he says he is ready to quit before raising the topic of smoking
10.w: NCSCT Very Brief Advice on smoking; NICE NG209 (2021, updated 2025): very brief advice is Ask (record smoking status), Advise (the best way to stop is with a combination of medication and specialist support) and Act (offer referral to local stop smoking support); it takes about 30 seconds.

n.0: VBA advises that the most effective way to stop is medication combined with specialist behavioural support, not quitting unaided.
n.2: Very brief advice takes about 30 seconds; a long lecture is not the VBA model and is not feasible here.
n.3: VBA is offered to everyone who smokes at every opportunity, whatever their stated readiness.

10.q: A nurse researcher wants to understand what living with a new stoma is like for young adults, in their own words. Which research approach is most suitable?
o: A qualitative design using in-depth interviews
A randomised controlled trial of stoma care products
A retrospective audit of stoma complication rates
A cross-sectional survey using closed questions
10.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022) recognises qualitative research approaches; interviews explore meaning and experience. Proficiency P1.7: understand research methods to critically analyse findings.

n.1: An RCT compares interventions; it does not explore lived experience.
n.2: An audit measures practice against a standard, not personal experience.
n.3: Closed questions limit responses and do not capture experience in people's own words.

10.q: Isla's parents are told that she has Rett syndrome caused by a MECP2 variant. Neither parent has symptoms. They ask about the chance of a future child being affected. What is the most accurate response?
o: Each future daughter has a 50% risk because the condition is X-linked dominant
Future sons have a higher risk than future daughters of being affected
The risk is 25%, as both parents must carry the variant
Most cases are new variants, so the risk is low; genetic counselling is advised
10.w: More than 99% of Rett syndrome cases arise from a new (de novo) MECP2 variant not present in either parent (MedlinePlus Genetics), so recurrence risk is low, but families should be offered genetic counselling to discuss their individual situation.

n.0: A 50% risk would apply if a parent carried the variant; in nearly all families the variant is new.
n.1: Rett syndrome affects almost exclusively girls.
n.2: Rett is not autosomal recessive, so the 25% figure does not apply.

10.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
10.q: A learning disability nurse is preparing a teaching session on international policy. Which statement about the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) is accurate?
o: It is a UK Act of Parliament that can be enforced directly in any UK court
It is a NICE guideline setting national quality standards for disability services
It is a European directive that replaced the Equality Act 2010 in the UK
It is an international treaty including the right to live independently in the community
10.w: The UNCRPD is a United Nations human rights treaty ratified by the UK. It sets out the rights of disabled people, including Article 19, living independently and being included in the community, and Article 12, equal recognition before the law.

n.0: It is an international treaty, not a UK statute directly enforceable in the courts.
n.1: It is not a NICE guideline.
n.2: It is a UN convention, and the Equality Act 2010 remains in force.

10.q: Mr Rowe, 74, is recovering from a hip fracture. The nurse and Mr Rowe are agreeing a mobility goal. Which goal is most appropriate?
o: Improve his mobility as much as possible before discharge
Walk to the day room with his frame by Friday, as he chose
Follow the physiotherapy plan written for all hip patients
Walk 200 metres unaided by tomorrow, as set by the team
10.w: Proficiency P3.4: apply a person-centred approach to shared assessment, planning, decision making and goal setting. Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This is vague and not measurable or time-bound.
n.2: A standard plan is not a personal, shared goal.
n.3: This is set for him, not with him, and may be unrealistic.

10.q: A ward's controlled drugs register has been completed and a new book started. The ward clerk asks how long the old register must be kept. Under NICE NG46, what is the minimum retention period?
o: 1 year from the date of the last entry
2 years from the date of the last entry
6 months from the date the book was closed
7 years from the date of the first entry
