10.w: NICE NG46: controlled drugs registers must be kept for 2 years from the date of the last entry, in line with the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. (Records of destruction of patients' own CDs are kept for a minimum of 7 years.)

n.0: 1 year is shorter than the legal minimum.
n.2: 6 months is well below the 2-year requirement.
n.3: 7 years applies to records of destruction of patients' own CDs, and the period runs from the last entry.

10.q: A community learning disability team is deciding who would benefit most from intensive interaction. For which person is the approach most suitable?
o: Maya, 34, with a mild learning disability who reads easy read well
Callum, 28, with a profound learning disability and very limited communication
Sean, 45, who has dementia after many years of fluent speech
Lena, 19, with a moderate learning disability who uses Makaton fluently
10.w: Intensive interaction is used with people at early stages of communication development, such as people with profound and multiple learning disabilities and some autistic people with limited communication.

n.0: Maya already communicates through reading and speech; she does not need early communication fundamentals.
n.2: Sean's needs relate to dementia; he already has established communication.
n.3: Lena is a fluent Makaton user and already has a working communication system.

10.q: Beatrice, 67, has rheumatoid arthritis. She tells the nurse she would like to be more active but finds long walks painful. She enjoys swimming and used to garden. Which response best supports Beatrice to make an informed choice within the limits of her condition?
o: Explain that exercise is unsuitable for people with rheumatoid arthritis
Advise her to walk 10,000 steps a day, as recommended for everyone
Explore activities she enjoys and can manage, and agree a goal together
Give her a leaflet on exercise and ask her to decide at home
10.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.9: use appropriate communication skills and strength-based approaches to support people to make informed choices about their care within the limits of illness or disability. NICE PH49 (2014): agree goals and develop action plans with the person.

n.0: This is inaccurate and removes her choice; activity within her limits can be supported.
n.1: A fixed target ignores her pain and preferences; P2.9 asks for strength-based, person-centred support.
n.3: A leaflet alone misses the chance to build on her strengths and agree a plan with her.

10.q: Laura, a staff nurse, has worried for several weeks that the night skill mix on her ward is unsafe, with frequent missed observations. She has not yet raised it with anyone. According to NMC guidance, who should she raise it with first?
o: The NMC, so that it can investigate the ward's safety
The trust chief executive, as the person accountable for staffing
The Care Quality Commission, as the regulator for the ward
Her line manager, verbally or in writing, keeping a record
10.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: stage 1 line manager (verbally or in writing, keep a record); stage 2 designated person; stage 3 higher level; stage 4 regulator or helpline. Code 16.1.

n.0: The NMC regulates individual professionals; this is a system concern for the line manager first.
n.1: A higher level in the organisation is stage 3, after the line manager and designated person.
n.2: Going to a regulator is stage 4 of the NMC guidance, used if internal routes fail or are unsuitable.

10.q: Carol, a healthcare assistant, tells Ifeoma, the nurse in charge, that she is anxious about the new 12-hour shift pattern because of her childcare. The ward is busy. Which response best shows active listening?
o: 'Everyone has had to adjust to the new shifts, so I am sure you will manage.'
'Lots of people find it easier once they settle in, so try it for a month first.'
'It sounds as if the longer shifts are making childcare hard. Can you tell me more?'
'You should talk to the ward manager, as I cannot change the shift pattern.'
10.w: Active listening involves giving attention, reflecting back the person's concern and inviting them to say more, which shows the concern has been heard before solutions are discussed (AnnexA.4.2.2 active listening to team members' concerns and anxieties).

n.0: This dismisses her individual concern and closes the conversation.
n.1: Offering reassurance and advice before understanding the problem is not active listening.
n.3: Signposting may be needed later, but responding first with a referral shows she has not been heard.

10.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
10.q: Helen, 61, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about breast screening. A support worker says, 'People with her level of disability don't really benefit from screening.' What is the best response?
o: Refer the decision to her GP, who can decide without consulting her carers or family
Agree, as screening is less useful for people with severe disabilities
Explain that best interests cannot rest on her condition but on her circumstances
Leave screening off her plan and review at her next health check
10.w: MCA s4(1): a best interests decision must not be made merely on the basis of a person's age, appearance, condition or behaviour. The decision-maker must consider Helen's individual circumstances, wishes and the benefits and burdens, with reasonable adjustments to make screening possible.

n.0: The decision-maker must consult those caring for her and interested in her welfare (s4(7)).
n.1: Assuming less benefit because of disability is discriminatory and breaches s4(1).
n.3: Removing screening on the basis of disability repeats the same unlawful reasoning.

10.q: A ward manager wants to check whether patients' falls risk assessments are completed within 6 hours of admission, as the trust policy requires, by reviewing 50 sets of notes. How should this project be classified?
o: Research, which needs NHS research ethics committee review
Health surveillance, which tracks outbreaks and health threats
Service evaluation, which judges a service without a standard
Clinical audit, which measures practice against a set standard
10.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (October 2022): clinical audit answers 'Does this service reach a predetermined standard?', uses care already in use and does not require REC review.

n.0: It tests no hypothesis and seeks no generalisable knowledge; it compares practice with an existing standard.
n.1: Surveillance monitors threats to population health, not compliance with a ward policy.
n.2: Service evaluation does not measure against a predetermined standard; this project does.

10.q: Nia, 40, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her hospital passport lists her medicines, but the nurse notices it names an antiepileptic that her GP record shows was stopped a year ago. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her family to update the passport after discharge and continue as listed
Stop using the passport and rely on the trust's own records for her stay
Give the medicines listed on the passport, as it is written by those who know her
Reconcile her medicines with current records and update the passport with Nia
10.w: Medicines reconciliation on admission must use current, verified sources. Passports go out of date, so the nurse should confirm the current medicines and support Nia and those close to her to update the passport so it stays accurate (Code 10.2, 18).

n.0: Continuing an inaccurate list risks a medication error now; the update should not wait until discharge.
n.1: The passport still contains valuable information on communication, pain and preferences; it needs correcting, not discarding.
n.2: Giving a discontinued antiepileptic could cause harm; passport medicine lists must be checked against current records.

10.q: Nadia, a learning disability nurse, is preparing a briefing on inpatient care. She needs to state the Building the Right Support target for people with a learning disability and autistic people in mental health inpatient settings in England, and whether it was met. Which statement is accurate?
o: Close every specialist inpatient unit by March 2020; the target was missed
Halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with 2015; the target was missed
Reduce inpatient numbers by a quarter by March 2030; progress is on track
Halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with 2015; the target was met
10.w: The Building the Right Support action plan (July 2022) aimed to halve the number of inpatients by March 2024 against March 2015. In February 2025 there were 2,055 inpatients, down about 29% from 2,905, so the target was missed (Commons Library SN07058).

n.0: The policy aimed to reduce reliance on inpatient care, not to close all specialist units by 2020.
n.2: The target was a halving by March 2024, not a quarter by 2030.
n.3: The target was not met; the fall was about 29%, short of 50%.

10.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
10.q: Tony, 60, has a learning disability and lacks capacity. His sister holds a registered health and welfare Lasting Power of Attorney that expressly covers life-sustaining treatment. Doctors are considering stopping antibiotics. Who makes the decision?
o: His sister, as attorney, in his best interests
The consultant, after informing his sister
An IMCA appointed by the hospital
The Court of Protection, on application
10.w: Under MCA 2005 s9-11, a health and welfare attorney can make decisions about life-sustaining treatment if the LPA expressly authorises it, acting in the person's best interests. Doctors advise on clinical options but the attorney makes the decision.

n.1: Where a valid LPA covers the decision, the attorney decides, not the clinician alone.
n.2: An IMCA is not needed when there is an attorney to make the decision.
n.3: Court involvement is needed for disputes, not for every decision when an attorney exists.

10.q: During a late shift on an adult surgical ward, a healthcare assistant tells Ruby, the nurse in charge, that Mr Peter Grant, 70, asked for analgesia 45 minutes ago and has still not received it because both nurses in his bay are busy. What should Ruby do?
o: Complete an incident report at the end of the shift and continue with the current allocation
Record the delay in Mr Grant's notes and discuss the bay workload at the next team meeting
Arrange for Mr Grant's analgesia to be given now and escalate the red flag on staffing
Ask the healthcare assistant to tell Mr Grant that a nurse will come once the bay is quieter
10.w: NICE SG1 Safe staffing for nursing in adult inpatient wards (2014) lists a delay of more than 30 minutes in providing pain relief as a nursing red flag. A red flag should prompt an immediate escalation response by the registered nurse in charge, for example allocating additional staff (rec 1.4.3, Box 2). Mr Grant's pain is dealt with first.

n.0: Reporting is useful but does not relieve his pain or address the staffing problem now.
n.1: Documenting and deferring discussion does not meet the immediate escalation response that SG1 requires.
n.3: This prolongs his pain and treats a recognised red flag as routine.

10.q: Bea, 29, is autistic and has a learning disability. She attends the emergency department with a wrist injury and is rocking and covering her ears in the busy waiting area. The triage nurse estimates a three-hour wait. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Move her ahead of other patients so she is seen straight away
Give her ear defenders and ask her to stay in the waiting area
Ask her carer to take her home and return when the department is quieter
Move her to a quieter area while she keeps her place in the queue
10.w: A quiet space is a reasonable adjustment that removes the sensory disadvantage while clinical priority is still decided by triage (Equality Act 2010 s20; NICE CG142 1.1.8 on adjusting noise and the environment for autistic adults).

n.0: Priority should follow clinical need; the adjustment is to the environment, not to the triage order.
n.1: Ear defenders may help a little, but keeping her in the busy area leaves the main barrier in place.
n.2: Sending her home delays treatment of an injury.

10.q: A student nurse on a learning disability placement asks why the team spends weeks on a functional assessment before writing a behaviour support plan for Ayesha, 27. What is the best explanation?
o: It shows why the behaviour happens so support can target that need
It gives evidence that the behaviour is severe enough for admission
It identifies which staff members are causing the behaviour to happen
It is needed so that a referral for medication can be accepted
10.w: NICE NG11 1.5.6 recommends a written formulation of what led to the behaviour and the function it serves; this understanding is the basis for a support plan that meets the need, rather than simply suppressing the behaviour.

n.1: NG11 aims to support people in the least restrictive setting close to home, not to build a case for admission.
n.2: Staff interactions are one possible influence, but the assessment is not designed to find fault with individuals.
n.3: Medication is not the purpose of functional assessment; NG11 puts psychological and environmental approaches first.

10.q: Wearing non-sterile gloves and an apron, Sam has just emptied the stoma bag of Kofi, 47. Sam now needs to give Kofi mouth care before leaving the bed space. What should Sam do before starting the mouth care?
o: Pull a second pair of gloves over the first pair and continue
Keep the same gloves, as both tasks are for the same patient
Remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene and put on new gloves
Apply alcohol handrub over the gloves, then continue with mouth care
10.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves must be changed after completing a procedure or task even on the same patient, and hand hygiene must be performed between glove changes. Gloves must not be decontaminated with handrub.

n.0: Double gloving is not recommended for routine care and still leaves the contaminated outer layer touching the mouth.
n.1: Gloves are changed between tasks on the same patient, so contamination from the stoma is not carried to the mouth.
n.3: NIPCM states gloves are not decontaminated with handrub or soap and water between uses.

10.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
10.q: Tara, 17, has a profound learning disability. Her family are worried that her care package will stop at 18. Which duty under the Care Act 2014 helps plan for this?
o: A transition assessment before she turns 18
A continuing healthcare checklist at age 21
A carer's assessment once she turns 18
A safeguarding enquiry under section 42
10.w: The Care Act 2014 requires local authorities to carry out transition assessments for children likely to have needs for care and support after turning 18 where it would be of significant benefit (ss58-66), so that support continues without a gap.

n.1: Continuing healthcare is a different NHS process and is not triggered at 21.
n.2: A carer's assessment is for her family's needs and does not replace planning for Tara's own care.
n.3: Section 42 enquiries concern abuse or neglect, not transition planning.

10.q: Simone, 37, has Down syndrome and attends her annual health check with her support worker. She has no new symptoms. Alongside the standard check, which additional test should be offered every year?
o: An X-ray of the cervical spine
A resting electrocardiogram
A cervical screening test
A thyroid function blood test
10.w: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and the risk rises with age, so thyroid function should be tested every year throughout life (DSMIG thyroid guideline; Down's Syndrome Association).

n.0: Routine X-ray screening of the neck is not recommended in adults without symptoms.
n.1: Heart problems are common from birth, but an annual ECG is not part of routine surveillance in an adult without symptoms.
n.2: Cervical screening follows the national recall schedule of several years between tests, not an annual test.

10.q: Mr Novak, 48, starts telling the nurse about his worries about returning to work after a heart attack, then stops mid-sentence and looks down. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Use a gentle prompt such as "Go on" and wait
Change the subject to his discharge medicines
Summarise what he has said and close the conversation
Reassure him that everything will be fine at work
10.w: Annexe A 1.2: use prompts and positive verbal and non-verbal reinforcement. Minimal prompts and silence encourage the person to continue (Annexe A 1.1 active listening).

n.1: Moving on closes the conversation just as he is opening up.
n.2: Summarising can help, but closing now prevents him finishing his thought.
n.3: This is false reassurance that dismisses his concern.

10.q: Eileen, 78, is admitted to a medical ward with a chest infection. Under NICE CG32, when should she be screened for malnutrition while she is an inpatient?
o: Weekly, starting on day 7 of her stay
On admission and at discharge
On admission and weekly thereafter
On admission and when she loses weight
10.w: NICE CG32 (updated 2017): screen all hospital inpatients on admission and weekly thereafter; outpatients at their first clinic appointment; care home residents on admission and when there is clinical concern.

n.0: Waiting until day 7 delays identifying those already malnourished.
n.1: Screening only at admission and discharge misses deterioration during the stay.
n.3: Waiting for weight loss means malnutrition is found late.

10.q: Mrs Dean, 49, has just eaten an orange and asks the nurse to check her blood glucose. The nurse plans to use the side of her fingertip. What should the nurse do before taking the sample?
o: Squeeze the finger firmly to produce a large drop
Ask her to wash and dry her hands
Clean her finger with an alcohol wipe and test while still wet
Use the first drop from the centre of the fingertip pad
10.w: Sugar residue on the skin, for example from fruit, can give a falsely high capillary glucose reading. Washing and drying the hands with warm water removes residue and improves blood flow (Annexe B 2.10: measure and interpret blood glucose).

n.0: Firm squeezing dilutes the drop with tissue fluid and can give an inaccurate result.
n.2: Testing through wet alcohol can dilute the sample and alter the reading.
n.3: The pad is more painful and the problem of sugar on the skin remains.

10.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
10.q: Jamie, 41, has a learning disability and his SLT plan says IDDSI level 1 slightly thick drinks. A carer has made up his tea with a new brand of thickener. The nurse wants to check that the drink matches level 1 before it is given. Which test should she use?
o: The fork drip test
The IDDSI flow test
The fork pressure test
The spoon tilt test
10.w: The IDDSI flow test classifies drinks levels 0-3 by how much remains in a standard 10 mL slip-tip syringe after 10 seconds: under 1 mL thin, 1-4 mL slightly thick (level 1), 4-8 mL mildly thick (level 2), more than 8 mL moderately thick (IDDSI testing methods).

n.0: The fork drip test checks thicker textures (IDDSI levels 3 to 5), not whether a drink is level 1.
n.2: The fork pressure test checks how soft foods are (IDDSI levels 4 to 7), not the thickness of a drink.
n.3: The spoon tilt test checks the cohesiveness and stickiness of thick textures such as pureed food, not the flow of a slightly thick drink.

10.q: Lewis, 29, is autistic with a learning disability and needs an MRI scan. He is very sensitive to noise and has refused scans before. The scan is in six weeks. What should the learning disability nurse plan?
o: Book the scan under general anaesthetic without trying preparation
Tell Lewis about the scan on the morning so he has less time to worry
Ask the radiographer to complete the scan as quickly as possible
Graded preparation with photos, scanner sounds and a practice visit
10.w: Graded desensitisation builds familiarity with each part of the experience over time and is a reasonable adjustment that may avoid sedation or anaesthetic (Equality Act 2010 s20; least restrictive option, MCA s1(6)).

n.0: General anaesthetic carries risks; less restrictive preparation should be tried first where time allows.
n.1: Late notice removes preparation time and may increase distress.
n.2: Speed does not address his sensory sensitivity or prior refusals.

10.q: Chloe, 22, is autistic and has a moderate learning disability. She is due a blood test and has had distressing experiences with needles. Her care team is planning the test. Which approach is best?
o: Postpone the test until Chloe asks to have it done
Use gradual desensitisation and a quiet planned visit
Hold Chloe still so the test is over quickly
Take the blood while Chloe is asleep at night
10.w: Gradual desensitisation (step-by-step exposure, visual stories, practice visits) and a planned quiet appointment are reasonable adjustments that reduce anxiety and the need for restraint. Any restriction requires capacity assessment and best interests decisions (MCA 2005).

n.0: Waiting for her to ask may delay necessary care; the duty is to adjust so that the test can happen.
n.2: Holding is a restrictive intervention and a last resort; it is not the first plan for an anxious person.
n.3: A procedure on a sleeping person without consent or a best interests decision is unlawful and harmful to trust.

10.q: Joanne, 41, is on an orthopaedic ward after a fall. She has been tearful, says she feels 'a burden to everyone' and has stopped eating. The nurse is concerned about her mood. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask the GP to review her mood once she has been discharged
Avoid asking about suicide so the idea is not suggested to her
Ask her to complete a risk scale to grade her risk of suicide
Ask her directly and compassionately about thoughts of suicide
10.w: NICE NG225 (2022) rec 1.13.5 encourages professionals to use contacts to ask about thoughts of self-harm or suicide. Feeling a burden and withdrawal are warning signs; asking directly and compassionately opens the conversation and allows an appropriate response and escalation.

n.0: Deferring to the GP after discharge delays a response to warning signs present now.
n.1: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea; avoiding it leaves risk unrecognised.
n.2: NG225 recommends not using risk assessment tools and scales to predict suicide.

10.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
10.q: A community learning disability nurse explains when a local authority must make safeguarding enquiries under section 42 of the Care Act 2014. Which set of conditions triggers the duty?
o: Care and support needs; at risk of abuse or neglect; unable to protect themselves as a result
Lacks capacity for the decision; aged over 65; lives alone without daily support from family or friends
Has a learning disability; is known to services; has a family who agree to an enquiry
Is eligible for funded care; has an allocated social worker; consents to an enquiry
10.w: Care Act 2014 s42(1): the duty applies where the local authority has reasonable cause to suspect that an adult in its area (a) has needs for care and support, (b) is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and (c) as a result of those needs is unable to protect themselves.

n.1: Capacity, age and living alone are not the statutory criteria.
n.2: A diagnosis and family agreement are not the statutory criteria.
n.3: Eligibility for funding is not required; care and support needs are enough.

10.q: Kofi, 20, scored 67 on an IQ test taken during a stressful college assessment. He works part-time, travels alone by bus, cooks for himself and manages his own money. His tutor asks the nurse whether Kofi has a learning disability. What is the best response?
o: Refer him for genetic testing to identify the cause of his learning disability
The definition also needs impaired social functioning, which is not evident
Yes, because a score below 70 confirms a mild learning disability
Repeat the IQ test, because a second score below 70 would confirm it
10.w: Two steps: the definition needs impaired intelligence AND impaired social (adaptive) functioning starting before adulthood. Kofi's daily living skills show no significant impairment of social functioning, so a single IQ score cannot establish a learning disability; adaptive functioning matters as much as IQ.

n.0: Genetic testing does not decide whether the definition is met, and on these facts social functioning is not impaired.
n.2: An IQ score alone does not define a learning disability; adaptive functioning must also be impaired.
n.3: Repeating the test still ignores the adaptive functioning limb, which on these facts is not impaired.

10.q: A nurse joining a care home finds that Ada, 90, has been given her medicines covertly for 10 months. The best interests decision and management plan are filed, but there is no record of any review since. What should the nurse do?
o: Continue, as a plan is in place and signed
Ask Ada's daughter to confirm she still agrees with the plan
Stop all covert medicines until the GP's next visit
Arrange a review of the plan with the multidisciplinary team
10.w: Covert administration requires a documented management plan that is reviewed regularly (NICE SC1 1.15; RPS/RCN 2019 paras 21-23). Ada's capacity, the need for each medicine and the method should be reconsidered by the team, including the prescriber and pharmacist.

n.0: A plan without review may be out of date; review is a required safeguard.
n.1: Family views are part of the review, but the daughter cannot authorise continuation alone.
n.2: Abruptly stopping all medicines could cause harm; a prompt review is needed instead.

10.q: Jorge, 61, is prescribed potassium chloride 40 mmol in 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours. The ward has no ready-mixed bags. A colleague suggests adding concentrated potassium chloride from an ampoule to a bag of saline. What should the nurse do?
o: Run plain saline now and add the potassium when the bag is changed
Obtain a ready-mixed bag from pharmacy or another area per policy
Give the concentrated potassium chloride as a slow IV bolus instead
Add the ampoule to the bag and invert it several times to mix
10.w: Mis-selection of a strong potassium solution is a Never Event (2018 list, updated 2021); national guidance requires ready-diluted potassium infusions wherever possible, with concentrated ampoules restricted. Potassium is a high-risk medicine (P4.15).

n.0: Delaying and then adding concentrate later carries the same mis-selection risk.
n.2: Concentrated potassium must not be given as a bolus; it can cause cardiac arrest.
n.3: Ward addition of concentrated potassium risks mis-selection and poor mixing, causing fatal hyperkalaemia.

10.q: A nurse on a postnatal ward is explaining immunity to a new mother. She says her baby is born with some protection against measles because of antibodies the mother made. Which type of immunity is this?
o: Population immunity from high vaccine coverage in the community
Active immunity produced by the baby's own immune system
Innate immunity from the baby's skin and mucous membranes
Passive immunity from antibodies that crossed the placenta
10.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): passive immunity is protection from antibodies transferred from immune individuals, most commonly across the placenta; it is temporary, commonly lasting a few weeks or months, and is more effective against some infections (for example tetanus and measles) than others.

n.0: Population immunity reduces exposure; it is not antibody protection inside the baby.
n.1: The baby did not make these antibodies; they were transferred from the mother, which is passive immunity.
n.2: Innate immunity is non-specific; measles-specific antibodies from the mother are passive acquired immunity.

10.q: A healthcare assistant in a care home in England is found to have left Mr Garner, who lacks capacity, in a soiled bed without food for a whole day on purpose. The manager asks the nurse what legal status this conduct has. What should the nurse say?
o: It is an offence under the Care Act 2014 safeguarding section
It may be a criminal offence of wilful neglect under MCA s44
It is a regulatory matter for the CQC with no criminal liability
It is a disciplinary matter for the employer to deal with
10.w: MCA 2005 s44 makes it an offence for a person who has the care of someone who lacks capacity to ill-treat or wilfully neglect them; on indictment the maximum is 5 years' imprisonment. It should also be raised as a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Care Act s42 places a duty on the local authority to make enquiries; it does not create this offence.
n.2: CQC regulates the provider, but s44 creates individual criminal liability.
n.3: Employer discipline may follow, but deliberate neglect of a person lacking capacity is also a potential criminal offence.

10.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

10.q: Mr Daly, 81, on a general medical ward, has become muddled and restless since yesterday evening and is not sure where he is. His wife says he is 'not himself'. Which tool does NICE CG103 recommend the nurse uses to assess him for delirium?
o: The Abbreviated Mental Test score
The 4AT
The Mini Mental State Examination
The CAM-ICU
10.w: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.1: if indicators of delirium are identified, a competent practitioner should assess using the 4AT; in critical care or the recovery room use CAM-ICU or ICDSC instead.

n.0: The AMT is a cognitive screen, not the delirium tool recommended in CG103.
n.2: The MMSE assesses cognitive impairment and is not the CG103 delirium assessment tool.
n.3: CAM-ICU is recommended for critical care and recovery settings, not a general ward.

10.q: A supported living team plans to complete a DisDAT for Freya, 31, who has a profound learning disability. When and with whom should it ideally be completed?
o: When Freya is unwell, by the nurse who is assessing her pain
At her annual health check, by the GP using her medical record
When Freya is well, with family and staff who know her best
During an admission, by ward staff observing her for the first time
10.w: DisDAT is completed by people who know the person well, ideally when they are well, so their usual content cues are captured as a baseline. Distress cues are then recognisable when they appear.

n.0: Completing it only when unwell gives no content baseline to compare against.
n.1: The GP and records lack the day-to-day detail that close carers hold.
n.3: Ward staff who have just met Freya cannot describe her usual cues.

10.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
10.q: Jordan, 37, has a severe learning disability and cerebral palsy and lives in a residential home. His bowel chart shows Bristol type 1 stools every four or five days. He takes an anticholinergic medicine for drooling. A new support worker asks why this matters. What should the nurse explain?
o: Infrequent stools need action once he reports abdominal pain
Constipation can lead to obstruction and has contributed to deaths
Bristol type 1 stools show that his diet has enough fibre
Hard stools are expected in people with cerebral palsy
10.w: Bristol type 1 (separate hard lumps) indicates constipation. In people with a learning disability constipation is common, is worsened by immobility and anticholinergic medicines, and can cause bowel obstruction, perforation and aspiration from vomiting; LeDeR reports constipation still contributing to deaths (LeDeR 2023).

n.0: Jordan may not be able to report pain; waiting for a complaint is unsafe.
n.2: Type 1 stools suggest constipation, not adequate fibre.
n.3: Treating constipation as expected is diagnostic overshadowing; it needs active management.

10.q: Pauline, 62, a visitor, develops central crushing chest pain while in the ward waiting area. She has no known allergies and is alert. 999 has been called. What first aid should be offered?
o: Give her 400 mg ibuprofen orally
Help her chew 300 mg aspirin
Give her 75 mg aspirin to swallow
Walk her to the emergency department
10.w: RCUK first aid 2025: encourage and assist a person with cardiac-sounding chest pain to self-administer 300 mg aspirin (ideally chewable or dissolvable) as soon as possible while awaiting help, unless allergic.

n.0: Ibuprofen is not an antiplatelet treatment for suspected heart attack.
n.2: 75 mg is the long-term antiplatelet dose, not the acute first aid dose.
n.3: Exertion increases cardiac workload; she should rest and await help.

10.q: Mr Green, 66, has venous leg ulcers. NICE guidance supports compression therapy, but after a full explanation he declines it because he previously found it painful. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Discharge him from the clinic as he has declined treatment
Ask the GP to prescribe stronger analgesia and apply it anyway
Apply the compression, as NICE guidance must be followed
Explore his concerns, discuss alternatives and record his choice
10.w: NICE guidance ('Your responsibility' statement, as in NG253) is not mandatory; professionals take it fully into account alongside individual needs and preferences. Code 2.5 and 4.2; P1.8 critical evidence-informed decisions.

n.0: Declining one option does not end care; alternatives and support should be explored.
n.1: Applying compression he has refused would breach his right to refuse (Code 2.5).
n.2: NICE guidance is not mandatory; it must be applied alongside the person's needs and preferences.

10.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
10.q: In a supported living service, staff are asked what 'soft signs' of deterioration might look like in Lena, 33, who has a profound learning disability and no speech. Which example best fits?
o: A new oxygen saturation of 88% on air
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
A systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg
Eating less and sleeping more than usual
10.w: Soft signs are subtle changes from the person's baseline (eating, drinking, sleeping, mobility, mood, behaviour) that may precede changes in vital signs. Recognising them depends on knowing the person's usual presentation.

n.0: Saturation of 88% on air is a measured abnormality, not a soft sign.
n.1: A respiratory rate of 30 is a hard, measured sign that scores highly on NEWS2.
n.2: Systolic BP of 85 is a measured red-flag sign, not a soft sign.

10.q: Becca, a care home nurse, receives Mr Ian Moss, 79, back from hospital. The discharge letter says his furosemide was stopped, but the boxes sent with him and the care home's medicines record still include it. The GP practice is open. What should Becca do?
o: Contact the hospital or GP to reconcile the medicines and report the gap
Stop the furosemide, as the discharge letter is the most recent document
Continue the furosemide until the next routine GP visit
Ask Mr Moss which tablets he has been taking and follow his answer
10.w: Transitions between settings are a common point of medicines error. Discrepancies are resolved by medicines reconciliation with the prescriber and the information gap is reported for learning (P7.6 complexities of care across integrated settings; NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation; Code 18).

n.1: Acting on one document without clarifying a conflict risks error if the letter itself is wrong.
n.2: Continuing a possibly stopped diuretic for days risks harm while the discrepancy is unresolved.
n.3: Mr Moss's account is useful information but does not replace clarification with the prescriber.

10.q: Siobhan, a registered nurse, is charged by the police with a drink-driving offence on a day off. She has not yet been to court and her line manager is unaware. According to the Code, what should Siobhan do?
o: Declare the charge at her next revalidation application
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell her employer, who will then notify the NMC for her
Tell the NMC if the court convicts her of the offence
10.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and your employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, or if you have received a conditional discharge or been found guilty of a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction). A charge is reportable before any conviction.

n.0: Revalidation is every 3 years and includes a health and character declaration, but Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as possible, not at the next renewal.
n.2: The duty is personal to the registrant and covers both the NMC and the employer; passing it to the employer does not meet it.
n.3: Code 23.2 applies at the point of charge; waiting for a conviction delays a report that is already due.

10.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
10.q: Ruth, 41, has a learning disability and needs a double-length appointment and an easy read explanation for a hospital procedure. The clinic manager asks whether Ruth's care provider should pay the extra cost. What is the correct answer?
o: No, a disabled person cannot be required to pay for a reasonable adjustment
Yes, if the cost goes beyond what the clinic normally spends per patient
No, the extra cost should be shared equally between the clinic and the provider
Yes, as the adjustment benefits Ruth personally rather than the clinic
10.w: Equality Act 2010 s20(7): a person who is subject to the duty is not entitled to require a disabled person to pay the costs of complying with the duty. The NHS service bears the cost of reasonable adjustments.

n.1: There is no threshold above which the disabled person must pay.
n.2: Passing part of the cost to Ruth's provider still charges her for the adjustment.
n.3: The duty falls on the service provider, which must meet the cost.

10.q: Arthur, 88, is dying on a medical ward. His breathing has become noisy with a rattling sound. He is unconscious and appears settled. His daughter is upset and asks whether he is 'drowning'. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Explain that a medicine will be given now to stop the noise completely
Start oxygen through a face mask to make his breathing feel more comfortable
Explain that the noise means fluid on his lungs that needs a diuretic injection
Explain the noise is unlikely to be causing him discomfort, and reposition him
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.29 and 1.5.30: assess the cause of noisy respiratory secretions and the impact on the person and those important to them; reassure them that although the noise can be distressing it is unlikely to cause discomfort; consider non-drug measures such as repositioning.

n.0: Medicines are considered if secretions distress the dying person (rec 1.5.31), and they may not stop the noise completely.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen; offer it for known or suspected symptomatic hypoxaemia.
n.2: Noisy secretions in the last days are not treated as pulmonary oedema; the guidance is reassurance and non-drug measures first.

10.q: Mr Nowak, 70, has expressive aphasia after a stroke and cannot speak clearly. A decision is needed about moving him to a rehabilitation unit. Before anyone concludes he lacks capacity, what should the nurse do?
o: Wait for his speech to recover fully before discussing the move
Record that he lacks capacity because he cannot speak clearly
Ask his wife to make the decision as she knows his wishes best
Arrange communication aids or speech and language therapy input
10.w: MCA 2005 s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. s3(1)(d) allows communication by any means, so aids and specialist input should be tried.

n.0: Delaying indefinitely is not required; the duty is to take practicable steps to support his decision now.
n.1: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; s3(1)(d) covers any means.
n.2: His wife cannot decide for him unless she holds a relevant LPA; the first step is to support him to decide.

10.q: At a team meeting, a district nursing team leader explains the integrated care partnership (ICP) in her area. Which statement about the ICP is correct?
o: It inspects and rates the quality of local health services
It is the NHS body that commissions hospital and GP services
It is a joint committee that develops the integrated care strategy
It employs the community nurses who work in the local area
10.w: The ICP is a joint committee run by the NHS organisations and upper-tier local authorities in each ICS, with wider partners such as the voluntary sector. It must develop a long-term integrated care strategy to improve health, care and wellbeing (NHS England, What is integrated care?; P7.1).

n.0: Inspection and rating are carried out by the Care Quality Commission in England.
n.1: Planning NHS services and managing the budget is the role of the integrated care board.
n.3: Community nurses are employed by provider organisations, not by the ICP.

10.q: During a teaching session on health economics, a student nurse asks what a quality-adjusted life year (QALY) measures. Which answer is correct?
o: A patient's own rating of their satisfaction with care, scored from 0 to 1
Length of life adjusted for its quality, where 1 is a year in full health
The cost to the NHS of keeping one person in hospital for a year
The number of years a person lives after receiving a treatment
10.w: A QALY combines quantity and quality of life: one year in perfect health counts as 1 QALY, and years lived in poorer health are weighted below 1. NICE uses cost per QALY gained to judge cost-effectiveness (P7.3 principles of health economics; FACTS S-NICETH).

n.0: A QALY uses health-related quality of life, not satisfaction with care.
n.2: This is a cost measure; a QALY measures health benefit, not cost.
n.3: Survival alone ignores quality of life, which the QALY adjusts for.

10.q: Nadia, 34, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her carer says she eats best with familiar foods, small portions and verbal prompting. Ward staff often place her tray and leave. Her intake is now poor. What is the best action?
o: Use the carer's advice in her plan and support her at meals
Ask the carer to come in at every mealtime to feed her
Refer her for a swallowing assessment before her next meal
Start oral supplements and continue placing her tray
10.w: Annexe B 5.3 and the Equality Act 2010 s20: make reasonable adjustments and give assistance with eating. Personalising meals and providing prompting and support is the nursing team's responsibility and addresses the cause of her poor intake.

n.1: Carers may help, but meeting her nutritional needs remains the ward's responsibility.
n.2: There is no indication of a swallowing problem; the issue is support with eating.
n.3: Supplements do not address the lack of support at mealtimes.

10.q: According to NICE CG32, which finding indicates that an adult is malnourished?
o: BMI under 18.5 kg/m²
BMI between 20 and 25 kg/m²
Unintentional weight loss of 3% in 6 months
Eating normally for the past 5 days
10.w: NICE CG32 defines malnutrition as BMI under 18.5 kg/m²; or unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3-6 months; or BMI under 20 kg/m² with unintentional weight loss over 5% in 3-6 months.

n.1: BMI 20-25 is within the healthy range.
n.2: 3% weight loss is below the CG32 thresholds.
n.3: Normal intake is not a malnutrition criterion.

10.q: Ravi, 64, is prescribed his routine subcutaneous enoxaparin injection. He has intact skin at the injection site and no known infection. The nurse has prepared the syringe and checked the prescription. Which personal protective equipment approach is appropriate for giving this injection?
o: Wear non-sterile gloves and decontaminate them between patients
Wear non-sterile gloves and an apron for the injection
Perform hand hygiene; gloves are not routinely needed
Wear sterile gloves because the skin will be punctured
10.w: NIPCM ch 1.4 lists administering routine intradermal, subcutaneous and intramuscular injections among tasks where gloves should not routinely be worn because no exposure to blood or body fluids is anticipated. Hand hygiene is still required, and glove use stays a clinical risk assessment.

n.0: NIPCM states gloves must not be decontaminated with handrub or soap between uses; they are changed instead.
n.1: Gloves and apron are for anticipated exposure to blood or body fluids, which a routine SC injection does not involve.
n.3: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures such as catheter insertion, not routine SC injections.

10.q: You are alone on a quiet community visit when Sandra, 55, collapses. She is unresponsive and you have a mobile phone. According to RCUK 2025, what should you do next?
o: Give 2 minutes of CPR before calling 999
Call 999 on speaker, then assess breathing
Leave her to find a defibrillator first
Assess her breathing for one minute before calling
10.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: if alone with a phone, call 999 on speakerphone as soon as unresponsiveness is identified, before assessing breathing, so the call handler can guide CPR and locate an AED.

n.0: Delaying the call delays emergency help and AED location.
n.2: Leaving her delays both the call and CPR; the call handler can direct others to an AED.
n.3: Breathing is assessed for no more than 10 seconds, and the 2025 guideline calls 999 first if alone.

10.q: A community nursing team wants to improve the written information given to people after a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Which approach best involves people who use the service in this improvement?
o: Adapt a leaflet that a neighbouring trust has used for several years
Co-design the information with people who have recently been diagnosed
Ask the diabetes consultant to approve the content before it is printed
Ask the team's nurses to agree the content at the next team meeting
10.w: P6.9 requires nurses to work with people, their families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies. Co-design with people who have lived experience of the service makes information relevant, accessible and person-centred (Code 2.1 work in partnership).

n.0: Borrowing another organisation's leaflet may help, but it does not involve local service users in the improvement.
n.2: Clinical approval checks accuracy but does not involve people who use the service.
n.3: Staff agreement alone excludes the people the information is for.

10.q: During an in-hospital arrest, Joyce, 70, is in a non-shockable rhythm. The ALS team has IV access. When should adrenaline 1 mg IV be given according to RCUK 2025?
o: As soon as possible, then every 3-5 minutes
After 30 minutes, if no output has returned
After 10 minutes of CPR, then every 5 minutes
After the third shock, then every 3-5 minutes
10.w: RCUK 2025 ALS: in non-shockable rhythms give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as possible; for shockable rhythms give it after the third shock. Repeat every 3-5 minutes.

n.1: Adrenaline is not reserved until 30 minutes into the arrest.
n.2: Waiting 10 minutes delays adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm.
n.3: After the third shock is the timing for shockable rhythms.

10.q: Diane is the mother of Peter, 44, who has a learning disability and is on a medical ward. At visiting she tells the nurse, 'He is not himself; he usually chats to everyone and today he will not look at me.' His NEWS2 score is 1. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reassure her that his observations are stable and the team will monitor him
Ask how this differs from his usual self and repeat a full assessment now
Suggest he may be tired from the ward routine and review after he has slept
Explain that a score of 1 means his care continues with routine observations
10.w: Family and carers know the person's baseline and often notice 'soft signs' of deterioration before observations change. Their concern is clinical information: explore the change and reassess, escalating if needed (LeDeR learning; NICE NG11 and NG54 on involving people who know the person).

n.0: Stable observations do not exclude deterioration in someone whose baseline differs; this dismisses key information.
n.2: Attributing the change to tiredness without assessment is a form of overshadowing.
n.3: Relying on NEWS2 alone ignores a reported change from his usual presentation.

10.q: Dan, 24, has Prader-Willi syndrome and lives in supported living. He has taken food from housemates' cupboards and gained 6 kg in two months. Staff want to lock the kitchen. What must happen first?
o: Assess his capacity on food access and, if lacking, decide in his best interests
Lock the kitchen straight away, because hyperphagia justifies any food restriction
Lock the kitchen once his parents have agreed to it on his behalf
Leave the kitchen open and record his food choices as unwise decisions
10.w: Two steps: locking the kitchen restricts Dan and his housemates, so it needs a lawful basis. Assess his capacity for this decision (MCA s2-3); if he lacks it, make a best interests decision (s4) choosing the least restrictive option (s1(6)), and review it regularly.

n.1: Restrictions need a lawful basis and proportionality; a diagnosis does not authorise any restriction.
n.2: Parents cannot consent on behalf of an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.3: Calling his choices unwise assumes he has capacity, which has not been assessed, given the compulsive nature of hyperphagia.

10.q: Lucas, 30, has a learning disability and is on the dynamic support register, rated at high risk of admission. His behaviour has escalated over a week, and his support provider says it can no longer cope. What should the community nurse do first?
o: Tell the provider to give notice so that the council must act quickly
Arrange for Lucas to go to the emergency department for assessment
Request an urgent community C(E)TR and extra support to keep him at home
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to settle him over the weekend
10.w: For people at high risk on the DSR, the policy is a community C(E)TR and intensive support to avoid admission where possible, with the least restrictive setting close to home (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy; NICE NG11 1.1 and NG93).

n.0: Encouraging the placement to end raises the risk of admission rather than reducing it.
n.1: A busy emergency department is an unfamiliar, noisy setting for a behavioural crisis and is likely to increase distress and the risk of admission.
n.3: NG11 does not support starting an antipsychotic before psychosocial review; this may also breach STOMP.

10.q: A health visitor explains to a student nurse why she prioritises support for pregnant women and families with babies. According to Public Health England's life course guidance, which period offers an opportunity to make a difference over a person's whole lifetime?
o: The first year after retirement from work
The teenage years from age 13 to age 18
The first year of secondary school education
The first 1,000 days of a child's life
10.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): there is growing evidence that intervening in the first 1,000 days of a child's life can make a difference over their whole lifetime. NMC P2.6: understand the importance of early years and childhood experiences on later health.

n.0: Retirement is a later transition; the guidance highlights the first 1,000 days.
n.1: Adolescence is an important stage, but it is not the period the guidance singles out here.
n.2: School transitions matter, but the guidance highlights the first 1,000 days as having lifelong impact.

10.q: Rania, 33, has a severe learning disability. Staff think her rocking and grimacing may be due to period pain, and she is given prescribed paracetamol. How should the nurse evaluate whether this has worked?
o: Reassess her using the same distress cues after a suitable interval
Assume it has worked if she does not ask for more
Ask Rania whether she feels better using a yes or no question
Check her temperature to see whether it has fallen
10.w: Evaluation uses the same individual cues as the assessment: if her distress cues settle after a suitable interval for paracetamol, pain was a likely cause; if not, other causes must be explored (Annexe B 3.1; DisDAT).

n.1: Not asking for more is not evidence of relief in someone who cannot easily ask.
n.2: Yes or no questions are unreliable for Rania because of acquiescence and limited understanding.
n.3: Temperature is not a measure of pain relief.

10.q: Nurse Holly has been asked to support a doctor who will tell Mr Pearce, 61, that his biopsy shows cancer. Which preparation is most appropriate?
o: Tell Mr Pearce the result first so the doctor can focus on treatment
Arrange a private room and hand her bleep to a colleague
Ask a relative to break the news before the doctor arrives
Use the bay with curtains drawn to save time
10.w: Annexe A 2.9: engage in difficult conversations including breaking bad news. Code 1.1 dignity, 5.1 privacy and 2.6 respond compassionately to distress.

n.0: Delivering the diagnosis outside the planned conversation risks giving it without support.
n.2: Results should be given by the clinical team, with the patient's consent to involve others.
n.3: Curtains do not give privacy; a private room protects dignity and confidentiality.

10.q: Kai, 34, is on an intensive care unit, and the team have decided to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. The bedside nurse thinks organ donation may be possible and Kai's parents are at the bedside. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Raise donation with Kai's parents yourself at the bedside straight away
Contact the specialist nurse for organ donation to lead the approach
Wait to see whether Kai's parents ask about organ donation
Ask Kai's GP to discuss donation with his parents by phone
10.w: NHS Blood and Transplant / British Transplantation Society best practice: the specialist nurse for organ donation is the main professional who makes the family approach, in collaboration with the hospital team, after checking the NHS Organ Donor Register for a recorded decision or nominated representative. Families are always approached if donation is possible.

n.0: The family approach is planned jointly and led by the specialist nurse, who checks the Organ Donor Register first.
n.2: Families are approached whenever donation is possible; waiting may lose the chance to honour Kai's decision.
n.3: The GP is not part of the donation pathway; the specialist nurse for organ donation leads it.

10.q: Bernard, 77, is unconscious and nil by mouth. When you give mouth care, you see white patches on his tongue that can be wiped off to leave a red base. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Brush the patches off firmly with a toothbrush at each mouth care
Rinse his mouth with a large volume of water to clear the patches
Report the probable oral thrush so that treatment can be prescribed
Apply petroleum jelly inside his mouth to soothe the area
10.w: White plaques that wipe off leaving a red base suggest oral candidiasis (thrush), which needs assessment and antifungal treatment. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during oral care.

n.0: Firm brushing traumatises the mucosa and does not treat the infection.
n.1: Large-volume rinsing in an unconscious person risks aspiration.
n.3: Petroleum jelly does not treat infection and is not applied inside the mouth.

10.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
10.q: Rina, 40, has a learning disability and does not use speech. She communicates with Makaton signs and eye pointing to pictures. Staff are satisfied she understands and weighs the choice of having a flu vaccine. How should her decision be treated?
o: As not valid, because she cannot state her decision in spoken words
As valid once a family member has confirmed what she meant
As not valid until she has confirmed it in writing with a witness
As valid, because she can communicate it by signs or eye pointing
10.w: MCA s3(1)(d): a person is unable to make a decision if they cannot communicate it 'by talking, using sign language or any other means'. Rina can communicate by signs and eye pointing, so she meets this part of the test.

n.0: The Act accepts any means of communication, not only speech.
n.1: Her decision is her own; a relative's confirmation is not required for validity.
n.2: There is no requirement for written confirmation of consent to a vaccine.

10.q: Liam, 26, has no learning disability. He tells his GP practice nurse that he struggles with social situations and has rigid routines, and asks whether he could be autistic. Which approach is in line with NICE CG142?
o: Use the AQ-10 and record a diagnosis of autism if he scores 6 or above
Request genetic testing before deciding whether to assess for autism
Consider the AQ-10 and offer full assessment if he scores 6 or above
Arrange an MRI brain scan to look for structural signs of autism
10.w: NICE CG142 1.2.3: for adults with possible autism who do not have a moderate or severe learning disability, consider the AQ-10; a score of 6 or above, or clinical suspicion, should lead to an offer of comprehensive assessment.

n.0: The AQ-10 is a screening tool; it identifies who needs a comprehensive assessment and does not make a diagnosis.
n.1: Genetic tests are not used routinely to diagnose autism.
n.3: CG142 advises against routine neuroimaging for diagnosing autism.

10.q: Mr Bailey, 66, has pneumonia and is breathing air. His observations are: respiratory rate 22, SpO2 95%, systolic BP 104, pulse 96, alert, temperature 38.3°C. What is his NEWS2 score and the minimum response?
o: 6; inform the medical team at once and observe at least hourly
6; continue observations every 4-6 hours and reassess the score
5; inform the nurse in charge and observe every 4 hours
7; request an emergency review by the critical care team
10.w: NEWS2 Chart 1: RR 21-24 = 2; SpO2 94-95 = 1; systolic 101-110 = 1; pulse 91-110 = 1; alert = 0; temperature 38.1-39.0 = 1; air = 0. Total 6 (medium). Chart 4: 5 or more needs at least hourly monitoring and the RN must immediately inform the medical team and request urgent assessment by a clinician competent in acute illness.

n.1: A score of 5-6 is the key threshold for an urgent response; 4-6 hourly monitoring is for scores 1-4.
n.2: The total is 6, not 5, and a score of 5 or more requires hourly observation and medical review, not 4-hourly.
n.3: The total is 6, not 7, so a critical care emergency response is not yet the minimum required.

10.q: Marion, 85, lives in a care home and has had diarrhoea for 3 days. Staff say she has been drinking very little and seems more tired than usual. You are assessing her hydration status on admission. Which combination of findings most suggests dehydration?
o: Ankle oedema, crackles in the lungs and weight gain
Dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output and tachycardia
Moist mouth, pale dilute urine and normal skin turgor
Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and polyuria
10.w: Dehydration commonly presents with dry mucous membranes, thirst, reduced and concentrated urine, tachycardia and postural hypotension (Annexe B 5.4). CG174 indicators of fluid need include HR over 90 and systolic under 100.

n.0: Oedema, crackles and weight gain suggest fluid overload.
n.2: A moist mouth and pale dilute urine suggest adequate hydration.
n.3: Raised BP and bounding pulse do not indicate dehydration.

10.q: The laboratory reports a potassium of 6.4 mmol/L for Ms Lane, 35, with a note that the sample was haemolysed. She is well, with normal observations, and her potassium yesterday was normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Disregard the result and record it as laboratory error
Wait until tomorrow's routine bloods to see the trend
Treat it as genuine hyperkalaemia and start a cardiac arrest alert
Inform the doctor and arrange a repeat sample
10.w: Haemolysis releases potassium from red cells and can falsely raise the result. The finding should still be reported to the doctor and a repeat sample taken promptly to confirm or exclude true hyperkalaemia (P3.12).

n.0: A haemolysed result is unreliable but cannot simply be dismissed without repeating it.
n.1: Waiting until tomorrow could leave true hyperkalaemia unrecognised.
n.2: She is well and has no arrest; a haemolysed result needs urgent confirmation, not an emergency call.

10.q: Malik, 50, has suspected sepsis with a NEWS2 of 5. How often should his NEWS2 be recalculated under NICE NG253 (2025)?
o: Hourly
Every 4-6 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 30 minutes
10.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.6.5: recalculate NEWS2 every 30 minutes for high risk, hourly for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6), every 4-6 hours for low risk.

n.1: 4-6 hourly is for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.2: 12-hourly is the general NEWS2 minimum for a score of 0, not for suspected sepsis at 5.
n.3: Every 30 minutes is for high risk (NEWS2 7 or more).

10.q: Joe, 35, has a severe learning disability. His carers notice that he becomes very distressed when routines change, avoids eye contact and lines up objects. His GP asks how to begin assessing for possible autism. What does NICE CG142 recommend?
o: Use the AQ-10 and refer for full assessment if he scores 6 or above
Arrange neuroimaging to separate autism from his learning disability
Do not assess, as autism cannot be diagnosed alongside a severe learning disability
Consider a brief assessment of autism-related difficulties instead of the AQ-10
10.w: Two steps: recognise that the AQ-10 is for adults without a moderate or severe learning disability; for adults with a moderate or severe learning disability, CG142 1.2.4 advises a brief assessment (asking about social interaction, communication and stereotyped behaviour), leading to comprehensive assessment if indicated.

n.0: The AQ-10 is not used for adults with a moderate or severe learning disability.
n.1: Neuroimaging is not routinely used to diagnose autism.
n.2: Autism can be diagnosed in people with any level of learning disability.

10.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
10.q: Daisy, 44, has a severe learning disability and cerebral palsy. Her carers report she coughs during drinks, her voice sounds 'gurgly' after meals and she has had two chest infections this year. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer Daisy to speech and language therapy for assessment
Switch Daisy to a soft diet and review it after a month
Thicken all of her drinks to IDDSI level 4 from today
Ask her GP to prescribe antibiotics to keep at home
10.w: Coughing on drinks, a wet voice after eating and recurrent chest infections are signs of dysphagia and possible aspiration. The person should be referred to speech and language therapy for assessment and an individual eating and drinking plan (LeDeR pneumonia report; NHS England RightCare aspiration pneumonia scenario).

n.1: Changing texture without assessment may not address the risk and may be inappropriate.
n.2: Thickening levels must be set by SLT assessment; guessing a level can cause dehydration or still be unsafe.
n.3: Rescue antibiotics do not address the cause, which is unassessed dysphagia.

10.q: A train derails near a town and the local acute trust is told to expect over 40 casualties, more than the emergency department can manage with normal arrangements. Under NHS emergency preparedness guidance, how is this event best classified?
o: A business continuity incident
A serious incident
A major incident
A critical incident
10.w: NHS England EPRR guidance classes incidents as business continuity, critical or major. A major incident is an event with serious consequences that requires special arrangements by one or more emergency responder agencies; in the NHS this includes casualties in numbers or types that require special arrangements (JESIP/Cabinet Office definition used by NHS England; P6.12).

n.0: A business continuity incident disrupts an organisation's normal service delivery, for example an IT failure; it is not defined by a surge of casualties needing a multi-agency response.
n.1: 'Serious incident' was a patient safety category under the former Serious Incident Framework, not an emergency preparedness classification.
n.3: A critical incident is a localised, principally internal escalation where an organisation loses the ability to deliver critical services; an external mass casualty event needing multi-agency arrangements is a major incident.

10.q: Priti, a registered nurse, delegates a simple wound dressing to Dean, a registered nursing associate who is competent in this task. Dean applies the wrong dressing type. Who is accountable for what?
o: Priti for the decision to delegate; Dean for how he carried out the dressing
Priti is accountable for the dressing, as Dean was working under her direction
The ward manager is accountable, as the allocation of staff was set by her each shift
Dean is accountable for all aspects, as he is a registered professional in his own right
10.w: The Code (standard 11) makes the registrant accountable for decisions to delegate and for confirming outcomes. Nursing associates are NMC registrants bound by the Code, so Dean is accountable for his own practice in carrying out the task (P5.4; FACTS S-CODE).

n.1: Dean is a registrant accountable for his own actions in carrying out the dressing; Priti's accountability is for the decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome.
n.2: The manager is accountable for her own decisions, but this does not remove Priti's or Dean's accountability.
n.3: Priti remains accountable for her decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome (Code 11.3).

10.q: Mr Hale has made a formal complaint about Nurse Ivy's attitude. He is still on her ward and allocated to her care today. What does the Code require of Ivy?
o: Discuss the complaint with him to resolve it today
Continue to give him the same standard of care
Avoid speaking to him beyond essential care tasks
Ask to be moved from his care until the complaint is closed
10.w: Code 24.1: never allow someone's complaint to affect the care that is provided to them. Code 24.2: use complaints as feedback for reflection and learning.

n.0: Handling the complaint is for the complaints process; her duty is to keep caring for him fairly.
n.2: Limiting communication lets the complaint affect his care.
n.3: Moving may be considered locally, but the Code requirement is that the complaint must not affect his care.

10.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
10.q: A LeDeR review finds that Ahmed, 52, who had a learning disability, died after signs of pneumonia were attributed to his 'usual behaviour' and treatment was delayed for days. Which Human Rights Act article places a positive duty on the NHS in this context?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial
Article 3, the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 2, the right to life
10.w: Article 2 protects the right to life and places positive obligations on public authorities such as the NHS to protect life, including through proper systems of care; avoidable deaths linked to diagnostic overshadowing engage it.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings, not clinical care.
n.1: Article 3 concerns ill-treatment; the central issue in an avoidable death is the right to life.
n.2: Article 9 concerns belief and religion, not the delay in treatment.

10.q: Which is the correct order of the phases of wound healing?
o: Inflammation, haemostasis, maturation, proliferation
Proliferation, haemostasis, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, proliferation, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation
10.w: Wounds heal through overlapping phases: haemostasis (clotting), inflammation (clearing debris and bacteria), proliferation (granulation tissue and epithelialisation) and maturation or remodelling (collagen reorganisation, which can last months).

n.0: Haemostasis comes first, and proliferation precedes maturation.
n.1: Proliferation follows inflammation; it does not begin the process.
n.2: Inflammation precedes proliferation, not the other way round.

10.q: Agnieszka, 52, uses an insulin pen at home and has brought it into hospital. Her lunchtime dose is due, but the ward has run out of pen needles. A colleague suggests drawing the dose out of the pen cartridge with an insulin syringe. What should the nurse do?
o: Obtain pen needles from pharmacy or another ward and give it
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using an insulin syringe
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using a 1 mL syringe
Omit the dose until pen needles are delivered tomorrow
10.w: An NHS England patient safety alert (2016) warned of severe harm and death from withdrawing insulin from pen devices, as cartridges are not designed for this and dosing errors result. Insulin is a high-risk medicine (P4.14); the correct device should be obtained promptly so the dose is not omitted.

n.1: Withdrawing insulin from a pen cartridge is unsafe whichever syringe is used.
n.2: A standard 1 mL syringe adds a further risk of unit-to-mL confusion and overdose.
n.3: Omitting insulin for a day risks hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis when needles can be sourced.

10.q: Ahmed, 50, has a learning disability and has taken haloperidol for 15 years. He has never had psychotic symptoms. His behaviour has been settled for several years. What should the nurse recommend at his medication review?
o: Switch him to a newer antipsychotic that has fewer side effects
Continue the dose because his behaviour is now stable
Consider a gradual, monitored reduction with specialist support
Stop the haloperidol today because it is not indicated
10.w: Two-step reasoning: there is no psychosis, so the indication is behaviour; stable behaviour makes a reduction worth considering. NICE NG54 1.9.7: for people taking antipsychotics without psychotic symptoms, consider reducing or discontinuing long-term prescriptions, review after reduction, consider specialist referral and document reasons annually if continued. Withdrawal should be gradual.

n.0: Switching continues antipsychotic use without addressing whether any is needed.
n.1: Stability is a reason to review, not to continue indefinitely; NG54 asks for reduction to be considered.
n.3: Abrupt withdrawal after 15 years risks withdrawal effects and relapse; reduction should be gradual.

10.q: A ward manager asks a learning disability nurse what the national Building the Right Support programme set out to achieve for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Which answer is correct?
o: To increase specialist inpatient beds so that people are treated near home
To reduce reliance on inpatient care by developing community support
To make Care and Treatment Reviews a requirement under the Care Act 2014
To transfer all learning disability services to local authority control
10.w: Building the Right Support (2015) and its 2022 action plan aim to reduce the number of people with a learning disability and autistic people in mental health inpatient settings by developing community services; the action plan target was to halve inpatient numbers from 2015 levels by March 2024, which was missed (BRS; Commons Library SN07058).

n.0: The aim was to reduce, not increase, reliance on inpatient beds.
n.2: C(E)TRs are NHS England policy; the Care Act 2014 did not make them statutory.
n.3: The programme involves NHS and local government jointly; it did not transfer services to councils.

10.q: A student nurse is about to auscultate the chest of Mrs Hall, 68, who has a productive cough. Which technique should the supervising nurse advise?
o: Listen at one point on each side for a few seconds
Listen over her clothing to protect her dignity
Listen at the front of the chest, which is enough for a review
Sit her upright and compare each side at matching points
10.w: Chest auscultation (Annexe B 2.8) is done with the person upright where possible, the stethoscope on bare skin, comparing left with right at matching points front and back so that differences in air entry and added sounds can be detected.

n.0: A single point per side cannot detect localised changes such as basal crackles.
n.1: Clothing muffles and distorts breath sounds; dignity is maintained in other ways.
n.2: The bases are best heard from the back, so front-only listening misses findings.

10.q: Femi, 34, is autistic. During admission he tells the nurse that he prefers to be called 'an autistic person' rather than 'a person with autism'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Use the term he prefers and record his preference in his notes
Use the term 'suffers from autism', as it is the clinical wording
Explain that person-first language is the required NHS style
Remove any reference to autism from his care plan to respect him
10.w: Person-centred practice (NMC Code 1 and 2) means respecting how someone describes their own identity; many autistic people prefer identity-first language, and NICE's 2021 surveillance updated its own wording to 'autistic people'. Recording the preference helps all staff use it.

n.1: 'Suffers from' is a deficit-based phrase and is not what he asked for.
n.2: There is no NHS rule overriding a person's preferred description of their identity.
n.3: Autism is relevant to his care and reasonable adjustments, so it should stay in his plan.

11.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse finds a printed handover sheet listing patients' names, diagnoses and resuscitation status left on a table in the staff canteen. Which UK GDPR principle has most directly been breached?
o: Accuracy (keeping data up to date)
Storage limitation (retention periods)
Purpose limitation (use for stated purposes)
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
11.w: UK GDPR Article 5 requires personal data to be processed securely, protecting against unauthorised access (integrity and confidentiality). Code 10.5 also requires records to be kept securely.

n.0: Nothing suggests the content is inaccurate; the problem is security.
n.1: Storage limitation concerns keeping data no longer than necessary, not leaving it unsecured.
n.2: Purpose limitation concerns using data for the purpose it was collected; handover is a legitimate purpose.

11.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
11.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

11.q: Kofi, 20, scored 67 on an IQ test taken during a stressful college assessment. He works part-time, travels alone by bus, cooks for himself and manages his own money. His tutor asks the nurse whether Kofi has a learning disability. What is the best response?
o: Refer him for genetic testing to identify the cause of his learning disability
The definition also needs impaired social functioning, which is not evident
Yes, because a score below 70 confirms a mild learning disability
Repeat the IQ test, because a second score below 70 would confirm it
11.w: Two steps: the definition needs impaired intelligence AND impaired social (adaptive) functioning starting before adulthood. Kofi's daily living skills show no significant impairment of social functioning, so a single IQ score cannot establish a learning disability; adaptive functioning matters as much as IQ.

n.0: Genetic testing does not decide whether the definition is met, and on these facts social functioning is not impaired.
n.2: An IQ score alone does not define a learning disability; adaptive functioning must also be impaired.
n.3: Repeating the test still ignores the adaptive functioning limb, which on these facts is not impaired.

11.q: A laboratory scientist phones the ward with a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L for Mr Shaw. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to take this result?
o: Ask the laboratory to email the result to the doctor directly
Remember it and tell the doctor at the next ward round
Write it on the handover sheet for the night team to act on
Write it down, read it back, then tell the doctor at once
11.w: Annexe A 1.9 and 1.11: share verbal information clearly. Writing a telephoned result down and reading it back confirms it was heard correctly, and a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L needs the doctor told at once (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.0: Email may not be seen promptly; the nurse must act on it now.
n.1: Relying on memory risks error, and waiting delays urgent treatment.
n.2: A critical result needs immediate action, not handover.

11.q: Tyler, 20, is autistic and has a learning disability. He is admitted to a busy medical ward with a chest infection. He covers his ears, rocks and shouts when the bay is noisy. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Explain firmly that shouting disturbs other patients in the bay
Ask the doctor to prescribe PRN lorazepam to help him settle
Move Tyler to a quieter side room and reduce noise and lighting
Ask his family to go home so that he has fewer people around him
11.w: Tyler is showing signs of sensory overload. NICE CG142 1.1.8 advises adjusting the environment for autistic adults (noise, lighting, personal space) as a reasonable adjustment; a quieter room addresses the cause and is the least restrictive response.

n.0: Firm verbal correction does not reduce sensory overload and may increase distress.
n.1: Medication would be chemical restraint for a distress response the environment can address, contrary to STOMP.
n.3: Familiar people usually reduce anxiety; sending them away removes his main support.

11.q: At 07:30 the ward medicines refrigerator display reads 11°C and the overnight maximum recorded is 13°C. It contains insulin pens and influenza vaccines. Yesterday's readings were within range. What should the nurse do?
o: Quarantine the contents, report it, and seek pharmacy advice before use
Move the items to another fridge and use them as normal
