Discard all the contents immediately into the pharmaceutical waste bin
Turn the thermostat down and recheck the temperature tomorrow
11.w: Medicines such as insulin and vaccines are stored at 2-8°C (Green Book ch 3 cold chain). After a temperature excursion, the stock is quarantined in a working fridge and not used until pharmacy (or the vaccine manufacturer via pharmacy) advises; the excursion is reported and recorded (AnnexB.11.11).

n.1: Using stock after an excursion without advice risks giving ineffective vaccines or insulin.
n.2: Some stock may be usable after assessment; discarding everything without advice wastes medicines.
n.3: Adjusting the dial does not address whether the exposed stock is still safe.

11.q: Which factor is most likely to give a falsely reassuring pulse oximetry reading?
o: A fever of 38.2°C on admission
Mild iron-deficiency anaemia
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Mild dehydration after vomiting
11.w: Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so carbon monoxide poisoning can show normal or high SpO2 despite severe hypoxia. Other pitfalls include poor perfusion, nail varnish, movement and reduced accuracy in people with darker skin tones.

n.0: Fever does not directly cause oximeters to over-read.
n.1: Mild anaemia does not by itself produce a falsely high SpO2.
n.3: Mild dehydration is not a recognised cause of falsely high oximeter readings.

11.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
11.q: At a residential service for people with learning disabilities, a nurse notices that everyone is woken at 6am, clothing is shared from a communal store, and visitors may come only on Sundays. Which category of abuse is most likely?
o: Organisational abuse
Discriminatory abuse
Domestic abuse
Self-neglect
11.w: Organisational (institutional) abuse includes neglect and poor practice within a service, such as rigid routines, lack of personal possessions and restricted visiting that suit the service rather than individuals (Care and Support Statutory Guidance ch.14).

n.1: Discriminatory abuse targets a protected characteristic; here the pattern comes from the service's regime.
n.2: Domestic abuse occurs within family or intimate relationships.
n.3: Self-neglect concerns a person's own care of themselves.

11.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
11.q: Amira, 50, has a profound learning disability. Her NEWS2 score has risen from 2 to 5 over four hours, and her mother reports she is 'very different'. What is the correct escalation?
o: Change her observations to every 12 hours overnight
Repeat her observations again in four hours
Urgent review by a clinician skilled in acute illness
Inform the nurse in charge at the next handover
11.w: A NEWS2 aggregate of 5 or more triggers an urgent response: urgent review by a clinician with competence in assessing acute illness and at least hourly observations (RCP NEWS2). Her mother's concern adds weight to escalation.

n.0: Twelve-hourly observations are for scores of 0.
n.1: Four-hourly observations are too infrequent for a score of 5.
n.3: Waiting for handover delays an urgent response.

11.q: Mr Haddad, 60, speaks Arabic. For a routine review he asks that his adult son interpret rather than a professional interpreter. What should the nurse do?
o: Agree straight away, as patients may choose their interpreter
Use the son and ask him to sign the record as interpreter
Confirm his choice privately via a professional interpreter
Refuse, as family members cannot act as interpreters
11.w: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): if a patient expressly wants a family member to interpret, seek informed consent in their own language independently of the family member and note it in the record.

n.0: Guidance requires informed consent obtained independently of the family member before relying on them.
n.1: The son's signature does not show the patient gave informed consent in his own language.
n.3: Patients may choose a family member if they give informed consent independently of that person.

11.q: Charlie, a mental health nurse in England, asks in October 2026 whether the Mental Health Act 2025 has replaced the 1983 Act for detentions on his ward. Which statement is correct?
o: The 2025 Act received Royal Assent, but most provisions are not yet in force
The 2025 Act applies to new detentions; the 1983 Act applies to existing ones
The 2025 Act is still a Bill and has not yet completed its parliamentary stages
The 2025 Act is fully in force and has replaced the 1983 Act in England
11.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions (including changes to sections 3 and 4) were not in force at October 2026. The Mental Health Act 1983 as amended remains the current law for detention (BUILD-PLAN unsettled law note; P7.4 implications of current and future health policy).

n.1: There is no rule of this kind; detentions continue under the 1983 Act as amended until provisions are commenced.
n.2: The Act completed its passage and received Royal Assent in December 2025.
n.3: Most provisions of the 2025 Act await commencement, so the 1983 Act as amended still applies.

11.q: During a team discussion, a student learning disability nurse is asked to summarise the social model of disability. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Disability arises from the medical diagnosis recorded for each person
Disability is created by barriers in society that can be identified and removed
Disability is a deficit within the person that services should treat or reduce
Disability is a personal misfortune best met by charitable support
11.w: The social model locates disability in attitudinal, environmental and system barriers that society creates and can remove, rather than in the person's impairment. The medical model locates the problem in the impairment to be treated.

n.0: Linking disability to a diagnosis is a medical model framing.
n.2: This is the medical model, which locates disability in the person's impairment.
n.3: The charity or tragedy view is a deficit model, not the social model.

11.q: Mr Ortiz, 66, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. He is being admitted for elective surgery at an English NHS hospital. Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should the nurse do as part of the admission assessment?
o: Use written notes with him, as these work for all deaf people
Identify, record and flag his communication needs and arrange support
Ask his daughter to interpret during his stay to save time
Note his deafness in the record so staff know to speak more loudly
11.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet information and communication needs related to disability or sensory loss. For a BSL user this means arranging a qualified interpreter and flagging the need.

n.0: BSL is a distinct language; written English may not meet his needs.
n.2: Relying on a relative does not meet his needs and compromises confidentiality and accuracy.
n.3: Speaking louder does not help a profoundly deaf BSL user and does not meet the Standard.

11.q: Kerry, 19, has Prader-Willi syndrome and is attending her annual health check. Which health problem is most important to screen for because of her syndrome?
o: Breathing irregularities while awake, by an overnight study
Congenital heart disease, by arranging an echocardiogram
Type 2 diabetes, linked to weight gain from hyperphagia
Early-onset Alzheimer's disease, by a memory assessment
11.w: Hyperphagia in Prader-Willi syndrome leads to overeating and obesity, with a raised risk of type 2 diabetes (MedlinePlus Genetics). Weight, diet support and diabetes screening are priorities at health checks.

n.0: Breathing irregularities while awake are a feature of Rett syndrome.
n.1: Congenital heart disease is strongly associated with Down syndrome, not Prader-Willi.
n.3: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease is associated with Down syndrome.

11.q: While giving a subcutaneous injection to Peter, 61, who has hepatitis C, nurse Hana sustains a needlestick injury to her finger through her glove. The needle has been used. What should Hana do immediately?
o: Let it bleed without squeezing, wash with soap and running water, then report
Squeeze the wound firmly to express blood, then apply an alcohol wipe
Suck the wound, cover it with a plaster and report it after the drug round
Scrub the wound with a nail brush and chlorhexidine, then apply a dressing
11.w: NIPCM appendix 10: allow the area to bleed but do not squeeze, do not suck, and wash with warm running water and non-antimicrobial soap. The incident is then reported urgently so that occupational health or A&E can assess the need for post-exposure management; the Sharps Regulations 2013 require all sharps injuries to be reported.

n.1: Squeezing can push contaminated material deeper into tissue; NIPCM says allow bleeding without squeezing.
n.2: Sucking the wound is specifically advised against, and reporting must be prompt so treatment is not delayed.
n.3: Scrubbing damages tissue and may increase uptake; gentle washing under running water is advised.

11.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
11.q: Dora, 54, has a learning disability and terminal cancer. She has said in pictures that she wants to die in her own bed in her supported living home. Staff worry they cannot manage. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange a hospice place because staff feel unsure
Ask her family to decide where she should die
Admit her to hospital when she becomes more unwell at home
Plan with the palliative care team to support her at home
11.w: Preferred place of death should be respected where possible; reasonable adjustments include training staff, district nursing and specialist palliative care in-reach, anticipatory medicines and equipment (NICE NG142; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: A hospice may be right for some, but staff uncertainty is not a reason to override her wishes without trying support.
n.1: Dora has expressed her own wish; her family should be involved but not replace her choice.
n.2: Planned hospital admission ignores her stated preference.

11.q: Jasmine, 22, has a tonic-clonic seizure in a clinic waiting area. She is on the floor near a chair. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Restrain her limbs to prevent injury during the jerking
Give her sips of water as the jerking slows down
Place a padded object between her teeth to protect her tongue
Move objects away, cushion her head and time the seizure
11.w: Seizure first aid: keep the person safe by moving hazards, cushion the head, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, and place in the recovery position when the jerking stops. Seek emergency help for a prolonged seizure (RCUK special circumstances: treat with benzodiazepines).

n.0: Restraining limbs can cause injury to the person and the helper.
n.1: Oral fluids risk aspiration while consciousness is impaired.
n.2: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or obstruct the airway.

11.q: Femi, 34, is autistic. During admission he tells the nurse that he prefers to be called 'an autistic person' rather than 'a person with autism'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Use the term he prefers and record his preference in his notes
Use the term 'suffers from autism', as it is the clinical wording
Explain that person-first language is the required NHS style
Remove any reference to autism from his care plan to respect him
11.w: Person-centred practice (NMC Code 1 and 2) means respecting how someone describes their own identity; many autistic people prefer identity-first language, and NICE's 2021 surveillance updated its own wording to 'autistic people'. Recording the preference helps all staff use it.

n.1: 'Suffers from' is a deficit-based phrase and is not what he asked for.
n.2: There is no NHS rule overriding a person's preferred description of their identity.
n.3: Autism is relevant to his care and reasonable adjustments, so it should stay in his plan.

11.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
11.q: A care home holds a list of residents with a learning disability marked 'not for CPR', made during an outbreak without individual assessment. What should the learning disability nurse do?
o: Keep the list but review it after the outbreak
Escalate it as an unlawful blanket decision
Ask each resident to sign the list
Accept it, as decisions during outbreaks differ
11.w: Blanket DNACPR decisions applied to groups are unlawful and discriminatory; each decision must be individual and made with the person or in consultation with those close to them (NHS England C1146 letter; CQC review of DNACPR decisions; Human Rights Act Article 2 and 14). This should be escalated as a safeguarding and governance concern.

n.0: Keeping an unlawful list puts residents at risk now.
n.2: Signatures do not make a blanket policy lawful or individual.
n.3: Outbreaks do not make blanket decisions lawful.

11.q: Liam, 22, attends an emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high using a scoring tool, and says 'low' scores can be discharged without referral. According to NICE NG225, how should the nurse approach this?
o: Not use the score to predict risk or decide on discharge
Complete the score and refer him to liaison psychiatry if it is high
Repeat the score each hour until he is discharged
Use the score to decide whether to refer him to liaison psychiatry
11.w: NICE NG225 (2022) recs 1.6.1-1.6.3: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged; do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification.

n.1: Restricting referral to high scores is risk stratification, which NG225 advises against.
n.2: Repeating a tool does not make it a valid predictor; NG225 advises against using it for this purpose.
n.3: NG225 says tools must not decide who is offered treatment; liaison psychiatry referral should be offered after self-harm.

11.q: A genetics nurse explains to a student that two children each have the same deletion at 15q11-q13, yet one has Prader-Willi syndrome and the other Angelman syndrome. What determines which syndrome develops?
o: Whether the child also has an extra chromosome 21 present
Which parent the deleted chromosome 15 came from
How many CGG repeats the child carries in FMR1
Whether the child is male or female at birth
11.w: This is genomic imprinting: genes in 15q11-q13 are expressed from one parent's copy only. A deletion on the paternal chromosome 15 causes Prader-Willi syndrome; on the maternal chromosome 15 it causes Angelman syndrome (loss of maternal UBE3A).

n.0: An extra chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome and does not determine these syndromes.
n.2: CGG repeats in FMR1 relate to fragile X syndrome, not chromosome 15.
n.3: Both syndromes affect males and females; sex does not decide which occurs.

11.q: A learning disability nurse is supporting Ben, 25, who has Down syndrome, at his annual health check. NICE NG54 recommends a particular assessment for all adults with Down syndrome to help detect later decline. Which is it?
o: Genetic testing for the APP gene
A yearly brain MRI from the age of 25
A baseline memory clinic referral at age 25
A baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour
11.w: NICE NG54 1.7.13: complete a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour with all adults with Down's syndrome, so that later changes in skills can be measured against it.

n.0: Genetic testing does not establish a functional baseline and is not recommended for this purpose.
n.1: Routine imaging is not recommended for screening.
n.2: Memory clinic referral is for suspected dementia, not a routine baseline.

11.q: Staff have used intensive interaction with Nell, 37, who has a profound learning disability, for three months. The team wants to know whether she is making progress. What is the best way to evaluate this?
o: Repeat her IQ assessment to measure cognitive change
Record observations of her eye contact and turn-taking over time
Ask Nell's family whether she seems happier than she was before
Count how many tasks she completes each day
11.w: Progress in intensive interaction is shown by changes in the fundamentals of communication (attention, eye contact, turn-taking, length of shared interaction), so regular recorded observations, sometimes with video, are used.

n.0: IQ testing does not measure the fundamentals of communication.
n.2: Family views help but are not a structured record of communication progress.
n.3: Task completion measures compliance, not communication.

11.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
11.q: Ethan, 35, has a learning disability and an SLT plan for level 2 mildly thick drinks. At a family party his brother gives him a glass of fizzy lemonade, saying 'just this once'. Ethan has capacity to make this decision and understands the risks. What should the nurse do?
o: Add thickener to the lemonade before handing it to him
Respect his choice and support him to drink as safely as possible
Take the glass away because it breaches his eating and drinking plan
Ask the brother to leave because he has put Ethan at risk
11.w: Two-step reasoning: Ethan has capacity for this decision, so under the MCA 2005 s1(4) he may make an unwise choice. The nurse supports him to reduce risk (upright, small sips, supervision) and records it; many services use a risk feeding (eating and drinking with acknowledged risks) plan agreed with SLT.

n.0: Thickening his drink overrides the choice he has made with capacity about what to drink.
n.2: Overriding a capacitous decision is unlawful; the plan supports him, it does not bind him.
n.3: Excluding his brother is disproportionate and harms Ethan's relationships.

11.q: Mia, 6, is due her annual flu vaccine at school. Her parents tell the school nurse they decline the nasal spray vaccine because it contains porcine gelatine, which conflicts with their beliefs, but they want her protected. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that children under 9 must have the nasal vaccine to be protected
Give the nasal vaccine, explaining that gelatine is an inactive ingredient
Discuss the injected inactivated flu vaccine as an alternative for Mia
Advise them that Mia can have a flu vaccine once she reaches adulthood
11.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: the live attenuated influenza vaccine (Fluenz, nasal) contains porcine gelatine; if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used (Green Book chapter 19). UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): consent must be given freely by an appropriately informed person.

n.0: The schedule states that if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used.
n.1: Giving it against the parents' refusal would be without valid consent (Green Book chapter 2).
n.3: An inactivated alternative is available now, so she need not go unprotected.

11.q: Derek, 59, has a history of alcohol misuse. He has eaten almost nothing for 7 days and his BMI is 17.8 kg/m². Nutrition support is planned. Using NICE CG32 criteria, what is his refeeding risk and the appropriate starting approach?
o: High risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
Low risk: start at full requirements of 25-35 kcal/kg/day
Moderate risk: start at 50% of requirements without thiamin
No risk: offer normal ward meals without any monitoring
11.w: NICE CG32: high refeeding risk includes two or more of BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little or no intake for over 5 days, or alcohol misuse. Derek has three. Start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing slowly, and give thiamin and vitamin B before and during the first 10 days, with electrolyte monitoring.

n.1: Full requirements in a high-risk person can precipitate refeeding syndrome.
n.2: He meets the high-risk criteria, and thiamin is needed.
n.3: Unmonitored feeding ignores his high refeeding risk.

11.q: At 21:00 Yusuf arrives to take charge of a 24-bed ward for the night. One registered nurse has phoned in sick and no replacement has been found, leaving Yusuf as the only registered nurse with three healthcare assistants. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the shift and complete an incident report at the end of the night describing it
Start the shift and allocate the medicines round to the most senior healthcare assistant
Escalate immediately to the site manager, as fewer than two registered nurses is a red flag
Ask the day staff to stay until midnight and then manage the remainder of the shift himself
11.w: NICE SG1 Box 2 lists fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift as a nursing red flag, which requires an immediate escalation response. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt action on risks to safety and effective management of staff and resources.

n.0: Reporting after the shift leaves the risk unmanaged throughout the night.
n.1: Healthcare assistants cannot be delegated tasks outside their competence, such as a full registered nurse medicines round (Code 11.1).
n.3: A short extension by tired day staff does not solve the shortfall for most of the night and bypasses escalation.

11.q: Isla's parents are told that she has Rett syndrome caused by a MECP2 variant. Neither parent has symptoms. They ask about the chance of a future child being affected. What is the most accurate response?
o: Each future daughter has a 50% risk because the condition is X-linked dominant
Future sons have a higher risk than future daughters of being affected
The risk is 25%, as both parents must carry the variant
Most cases are new variants, so the risk is low; genetic counselling is advised
11.w: More than 99% of Rett syndrome cases arise from a new (de novo) MECP2 variant not present in either parent (MedlinePlus Genetics), so recurrence risk is low, but families should be offered genetic counselling to discuss their individual situation.

n.0: A 50% risk would apply if a parent carried the variant; in nearly all families the variant is new.
n.1: Rett syndrome affects almost exclusively girls.
n.2: Rett is not autosomal recessive, so the 25% figure does not apply.

11.q: Eric, 72, has a new ileostomy. He is preparing for discharge and asks how to fit his appliance. Which advice is correct?
o: Clean the skin with alcohol wipes before each change
Cut the flange well larger than the stoma to avoid rubbing
Measure the stoma and cut the flange slightly larger than it
Leave the appliance on for a week to protect the skin
11.w: The aperture should be cut just larger than the measured stoma (usually 2-3 mm) so that effluent does not contact the skin, re-measuring as post-operative swelling settles. Ileostomy output is corrosive, so a close fit protects skin (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: Alcohol dries and stings the skin; warm water is used.
n.1: A large gap exposes skin to corrosive effluent and causes excoriation.
n.3: Ileostomy appliances are emptied and changed regularly, not left for a week.

11.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
11.q: Shona, 35, has a moderate learning disability and her friend at the day centre has died. Staff want to help her understand. Which approach is best?
o: Say her friend has 'gone to sleep' to soften it
Use clear words such as 'died' with pictures
Avoid mentioning the friend so she does not get upset
Tell her the friend has moved to another day centre
11.w: Clear, concrete language ('died', 'dead') with pictures or easy read is easier to understand than euphemisms. 'Gone to sleep' can cause confusion and fear about sleeping; honesty supports grieving.

n.0: Euphemisms are confusing and may cause fear of sleep.
n.2: Avoiding the subject leaves her confused and unsupported.
n.3: Lying undermines trust and prevents her from grieving.

11.q: Yusuf, 27, has a mild learning disability and is due to have a dental extraction. The dentist gives him an easy read leaflet and asks him to sign the consent form at his next visit. What should the nurse supporting Yusuf do?
o: Ask his father to sign the form, as the leaflet explains it to the family
Go through the leaflet with him, check his understanding and give time to decide
Ask Yusuf to sign the consent form now, as he has the easy read leaflet
Arrange a best interests meeting, since he needed an easy read leaflet
11.w: Easy read supports, but does not replace, the consent discussion. Taking all practicable steps (MCA s1(3)) means explaining, checking understanding in his own words and giving time. Needing accessible information does not mean he lacks capacity.

n.0: An adult with capacity gives his own consent; a family member cannot consent for him.
n.2: Having a leaflet does not show understanding; consent needs discussion first.
n.3: Needing accessible information does not indicate a lack of capacity, so best interests does not apply.

11.q: Bryony, 39, is nil by mouth after surgery. Her observations are stable and her prescription is for 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours via a volumetric infusion pump. The nurse is setting up the infusion and will ask a colleague to check it. At what rate should the pump be set?
o: 166 mL/h on the volumetric pump
125 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.5 mL/h on the volumetric pump
80 mL/h on the volumetric pump
11.w: Rate (mL/h) = volume / time = 1,000 mL / 8 h = 125 mL/h. Accurate dosage calculation is a patient safety proficiency (P4.14) and the setting should be checked against the prescription.

n.0: 166 mL/h corresponds to 6 hours, not 8.
n.2: 12.5 mL/h is a decimal place error, a tenfold underinfusion.
n.3: 80 mL/h would deliver 1,000 mL over 12.5 hours.

11.q: What is the standard UK in-hospital telephone number for calling the cardiac arrest team?
11.w: RCUK 2025 in-hospital resuscitation: 2222 is the standard UK internal number for cardiac arrest and medical emergency calls.

n.0: 3333 is not the standardised UK cardiac arrest number.
n.1: 999 is the external emergency number, used out of hospital.
n.3: 111 is the NHS non-emergency advice line.

11.q: A community nursing team wants to improve the written information given to people after a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Which approach best involves people who use the service in this improvement?
o: Adapt a leaflet that a neighbouring trust has used for several years
Co-design the information with people who have recently been diagnosed
Ask the diabetes consultant to approve the content before it is printed
Ask the team's nurses to agree the content at the next team meeting
11.w: P6.9 requires nurses to work with people, their families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies. Co-design with people who have lived experience of the service makes information relevant, accessible and person-centred (Code 2.1 work in partnership).

n.0: Borrowing another organisation's leaflet may help, but it does not involve local service users in the improvement.
n.2: Clinical approval checks accuracy but does not involve people who use the service.
n.3: Staff agreement alone excludes the people the information is for.

11.q: Callum, 29, has suspected sepsis and is high risk. He has received a 250 mL bolus. Ten minutes later his BP is still 86/50 mmHg and his chest is clear. What is the most appropriate next step under NICE NG253 (2025)?
o: Wait an hour for the first bolus to take effect before reassessing
Give a 1,000 mL bolus over 15 minutes to restore his blood pressure
Stop fluids and start oxygen at 15 L/min via a reservoir mask
Reassess him and give a further 250 mL bolus as prescribed
11.w: NG253 rec 1.8.5-1.8.9: reassess after each 250 mL bolus and, if still hypotensive without signs of overload, give further 250 mL boluses up to 1,000 mL in total, seeking senior advice if no improvement after 1,000 mL.

n.0: NG253 requires reassessment after each bolus, not a fixed wait of an hour.
n.1: NG253 uses incremental 250 mL boluses rather than a single 1,000 mL bolus.
n.2: Stopping fluids leaves hypotension untreated, and oxygen is titrated to a target of 94-98%.

11.q: Ayesha, 19, attended an emergency department after taking an overdose. Her blood results are awaited. Before the liaison psychiatry assessment she says she is going home and stands up to leave. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess her immediate safety and mental state before she leaves
Give her a crisis line number as she walks out
Let her leave, as an adult has the right to discharge herself
Ask security to stop her leaving the department
11.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.5.14: if a person who has self-harmed wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment, assess their safety and any mental health problems before they leave. Capacity, consent and duty of care also need consideration (rec 1.7.1).

n.1: A phone number alone does not assess her safety or the medical risk of the overdose.
n.2: She may be free to leave, but NG225 requires an assessment of safety and mental state first; her overdose may also affect capacity.
n.3: Restraining her is not the first step; it may be considered only if she lacks capacity and is at serious risk.

11.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
11.q: Lucy, 22, has a learning disability and uses Makaton. During personal care she becomes very distressed, signs 'hurt' and points between her legs, and then signs the name of a male support worker. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask Lucy detailed questions to establish exactly what happened to her
Wait to see whether Lucy repeats the signs on another day
Record what she signed, keep her safe and raise a concern now
Speak to the named support worker to hear his explanation
11.w: A possible disclosure of sexual abuse must be taken seriously: ensure Lucy's immediate safety and medical needs, record her signs and words exactly, preserve evidence and raise a safeguarding concern immediately, with police involvement. People who use alternative communication are at higher risk of not being heard.

n.0: Detailed questioning can contaminate evidence; investigation is for the police and safeguarding team.
n.1: Waiting leaves her at risk and ignores a clear communication.
n.3: Approaching the alleged abuser may put Lucy at risk and compromise evidence.

11.q: Ben, a theatre nurse, has developed persistent back pain that is making patient transfers difficult. He has not told anyone. Which action best reflects his professional responsibility for his own health?
o: Wait until his annual appraisal to mention the problem
Seek occupational health advice and discuss adjustments
Take regular painkillers and keep doing transfers as before
Avoid transfers by swapping tasks with colleagues informally
11.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need to carry out your professional role. Proficiency P1.6: take responsibility for a healthy lifestyle to maintain fitness for practice; Code 19.4 personal precautions.

n.0: Waiting delays support; Code 20.9 requires maintaining the health needed for the role now.
n.2: Masking symptoms risks harm to himself and patients and does not address fitness for his role.
n.3: Informal swaps hide the problem and may leave the team short of safe handlers.

11.q: Sana, a staff nurse, believes that Ivy, 50, who has a learning disability, has abdominal pain: Ivy keeps rocking and holding her stomach, which her carers say is new. The registrar says, 'She does that; it is her learning disability,' and declines to review her. What should Sana do?
o: Accept the decision and document the registrar's view in the notes
Give simple analgesia and monitor the rocking over the next shift
Restate the change from baseline using SBAR and escalate further
Ask Ivy's carers to raise the concern with the registrar themselves
11.w: Carers report a new change from baseline. The Code requires nurses to act as an advocate for the vulnerable, challenging poor practice (3.4), and to raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns (16.1). Using structured communication (SBAR) with the evidence, and escalating to a senior doctor if still declined, challenges diagnostic overshadowing.

n.0: Accepting the decision leaves possible abdominal pathology unassessed despite clear evidence of change.
n.1: Analgesia without diagnosis may mask a surgical cause and does not address the refusal to review.
n.3: The nurse holds the professional duty to escalate; passing it to carers is inappropriate.

11.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
11.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

11.q: A practice nurse is updating records under the Accessible Information Standard for Kevin, 33, who has a learning disability. Which entry best meets the standard?
o: 'Requires easy read letters; support worker Jo reads them with him.'
'Learning disability: needs extra help with any letters we send.'
'Vulnerable adult: discuss all information with his carers first.'
'Unable to read: send all his letters to his mother instead.'
11.w: The Accessible Information Standard requires a person's specific information and communication needs (format and support) to be recorded, flagged and met, not just a diagnosis or vague label (DAPB1605).

n.1: A diagnosis plus vague help does not tell staff what format or support to provide.
n.2: 'Vulnerable adult' is not a communication need and does not tell staff what to do.
n.3: Routing all letters to his mother is not his recorded preference and may breach confidentiality.

11.q: Mr Doyle, 55, tells his community mental health nurse that he has been saving his prescribed tablets and has a large supply at home, as he 'might need them one day'. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Remove the tablets from his home while he is out of the room
Tell his GP to reduce his prescription at the next medication review
Note his comment in the record and review it at the next visit
Discuss removing the tablets with him and agree a plan to keep him safe
11.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.7.1: establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them with therapeutic collaboration or negotiation to keep the person safe. A stockpile with this comment is an immediate safety concern needing collaborative action and escalation.

n.0: Covert removal undermines trust; NG225 describes collaborative negotiation, not unilateral action.
n.1: Waiting for a future review leaves the means available now.
n.2: Delaying to the next visit fails to act on an immediate safety concern.

11.q: A student nurse asks how to tell delirium from dementia when an older person on the ward is confused. Which feature points most strongly to delirium?
o: A long history of difficulty with word-finding
Acute onset over hours or days with fluctuation
Confusion that is stable from day to day
Gradual memory decline over several years
11.w: NICE CG103 describes delirium indicators as recent changes or fluctuations, over hours or days, in cognition, perception, physical function or social behaviour. Dementia typically develops gradually over months to years.

n.0: Longstanding word-finding difficulty suggests an established condition rather than an acute change.
n.2: Stable confusion does not show the fluctuation characteristic of delirium.
n.3: Gradual decline over years is typical of dementia, not delirium.

11.q: A practice nurse is reviewing which patients might be contacted for lung cancer screening, available in some parts of England. Which person meets the age and smoking criteria?
o: Susan, 50, who currently smokes 15 cigarettes a day
Thomas, 78, who stopped smoking 30 years ago
Raj, 60, who smoked for 20 years and stopped 10 years ago
Ann, 65, a lifelong non-smoker who lives with a smoker
11.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked may be contacted by their GP or a local NHS service to take part in lung cancer screening.

n.0: Lung cancer screening is for people aged 55 to 74; Susan is under 55.
n.1: Thomas is over 74, above the age range for lung cancer screening.
n.3: Screening is for people who have ever smoked; Ann has never smoked.

11.q: Poppy, 24, has a moderate learning disability and autism. She is having a blood test, a weight check and then a chat with the doctor at clinic. She copes better when she knows what is coming next. Which tool will best help during the appointment?
o: A verbal explanation of the whole appointment at the start
A visual schedule showing each step in order with pictures
A leaflet describing the conditions the clinic treats
A written list of the clinic's opening times and staff names
11.w: A visual schedule (for example a 'now and next' board) shows steps in order with pictures, making the sequence predictable and reducing anxiety for autistic people and people with a learning disability (NICE CG142 1.1.8 visual supports for autistic adults).

n.0: A single spoken explanation is hard to retain and gives no ongoing reference.
n.2: Information on conditions does not prepare her for the steps of her visit.
n.3: Opening times and staff names do not show her what will happen next.

11.q: Four patients on an elderly care ward have laboratory-confirmed norovirus. All single rooms are occupied. The IPC team agrees a cohort bay. Which plan for the cohort is most appropriate?
o: Place them together in one bay with the door closed and dedicated equipment
Place them together with a neutropenic patient who also has diarrhoea
Place them with two patients who have diarrhoea that is not yet confirmed
Keep each in their current bay with curtains drawn and contact precautions
11.w: NIPCM ch 2.1-2.2: cohorting is considered when single rooms are short and two or more patients have the same confirmed infection; doors stay closed and reusable equipment is dedicated to the cohort area. Immunosuppressed patients and those with different or unconfirmed infections must not be mixed in.

n.1: NIPCM states patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes, such as those who are immunosuppressed, must not be cohorted with others.
n.2: Unconfirmed diarrhoea may be a different infection; cohorts are formed from patients with the same confirmed infection.
n.3: Leaving infected patients in mixed bays exposes susceptible patients; curtains do not contain norovirus.

11.q: On a ward, an AED is attached to Kevin, 63, during CPR. The AED announces it is analysing the rhythm. What should the team do?
o: Stop compressions and ensure nobody touches him
Continue compressions during the rhythm analysis
Check his carotid pulse while it analyses
Give two rescue breaths while it analyses
11.w: RCUK 2025: follow AED prompts; nobody should touch the person during rhythm analysis, as movement interferes with analysis. Resume compressions immediately after the shock or no-shock prompt.

n.1: Compressions during analysis cause artefact and can delay or prevent a shock.
n.2: Pulse checks involve touching him and delay the AED's decision.
n.3: Breaths involve touching him and interfere with analysis.

11.q: Arthur, 88, is dying on a medical ward. His breathing has become noisy with a rattling sound. He is unconscious and appears settled. His daughter is upset and asks whether he is 'drowning'. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Explain that a medicine will be given now to stop the noise completely
Start oxygen through a face mask to make his breathing feel more comfortable
Explain that the noise means fluid on his lungs that needs a diuretic injection
Explain the noise is unlikely to be causing him discomfort, and reposition him
11.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.29 and 1.5.30: assess the cause of noisy respiratory secretions and the impact on the person and those important to them; reassure them that although the noise can be distressing it is unlikely to cause discomfort; consider non-drug measures such as repositioning.

n.0: Medicines are considered if secretions distress the dying person (rec 1.5.31), and they may not stop the noise completely.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen; offer it for known or suspected symptomatic hypoxaemia.
n.2: Noisy secretions in the last days are not treated as pulmonary oedema; the guidance is reassurance and non-drug measures first.

11.q: Kim, 32, has a mild learning disability. She has missed several GP appointments because the surgery books appointments through an app she finds confusing. Which response best reflects the social model of disability?
o: Offer Kim a telephone or face-to-face way to book appointments
Ask Kim's support worker to book every appointment on her behalf
Teach Kim to use the app before she next needs an appointment
Refer Kim for a review of her learning disability and support needs
11.w: The social model asks what barrier the system creates. Changing how the practice offers booking removes the barrier for Kim and others, and is also a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010 s20.

n.1: Doing it for her reduces her independence and leaves the barrier in place.
n.2: Teaching Kim places the burden on her to fit the system rather than changing the barrier.
n.3: Reviewing her learning disability treats the problem as being within Kim.

11.q: Nora, 67, has a nasogastric tube. You cannot obtain an aspirate after trying the recommended measures, such as turning her onto her side and waiting before retrying. What should you do next?
o: Give the feed slowly while watching her closely for distress
Push the tube a further 10 cm and attempt aspiration again
Follow local protocol and seek a decision on X-ray confirmation
Inject air and listen over the stomach with a stethoscope
11.w: If no aspirate can be obtained, the tube must not be used until position is confirmed. CG32 rec 1.7.17 says position is confirmed by aspiration and pH paper with X-ray if necessary, and local protocols must cover failure to aspirate.

n.0: Feeding without confirming position risks pulmonary feeding.
n.1: Advancing the tube blindly without confirmation risks misplacement.
n.3: Air auscultation is unreliable and not a safe check.

11.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
11.q: Ruth, 41, has a learning disability and needs a double-length appointment and an easy read explanation for a hospital procedure. The clinic manager asks whether Ruth's care provider should pay the extra cost. What is the correct answer?
o: No, a disabled person cannot be required to pay for a reasonable adjustment
Yes, if the cost goes beyond what the clinic normally spends per patient
No, the extra cost should be shared equally between the clinic and the provider
Yes, as the adjustment benefits Ruth personally rather than the clinic
11.w: Equality Act 2010 s20(7): a person who is subject to the duty is not entitled to require a disabled person to pay the costs of complying with the duty. The NHS service bears the cost of reasonable adjustments.

n.1: There is no threshold above which the disabled person must pay.
n.2: Passing part of the cost to Ruth's provider still charges her for the adjustment.
n.3: The duty falls on the service provider, which must meet the cost.

11.q: Ellie, 35, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to an orthopaedic ward with a fractured wrist. Her support worker hands the nurse Ellie's hospital passport. What should the admitting nurse do with it?
o: Complete the trust admission assessment first and read the passport later
Photocopy it and give the original back for the support worker to take home
File it in the medical notes so it is available if questions arise
Read it, use it to plan care and keep it with Ellie for all staff to use
11.w: The passport is only useful if staff read and act on it. It should inform the care plan from admission and stay with the person, at the bedside, so every member of staff can see how to communicate with and support Ellie.

n.0: Leaving it until later means the admission assessment misses key information about communication, pain and allergies.
n.1: Sending the original home removes it from the person; a photocopy filed away is unlikely to be read by all staff.
n.2: Filed in the notes, the passport is easily missed by staff who need it at the bedside.

11.q: Asif, 32, has a moderate learning disability. His sister reports he has been talking to someone who is not there, and he is frightened in his room at night. Staff say he has always talked to himself. What is the best next step for the learning disability nurse?
o: Move him to a different bedroom and see whether his fear settles over a week
Compare with his known baseline and arrange a mental health assessment
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to help him sleep at night
Record that this is his usual self-talk and close the concern
11.w: Two-step reasoning: self-talk can be normal for some people with a learning disability, so the nurse first compares with the person's baseline; a change in content (frightened, responding to voices) suggests possible psychosis and needs a specialist mental health assessment (NICE NG54 1.1.2 differences in presentation; 1.6.5 refer suspected serious mental illness to a psychiatrist with expertise in learning disabilities).

n.0: Changing rooms may help comfort but does not assess a possible mental illness.
n.2: Medication before assessment is not appropriate and conflicts with STOMP.
n.3: Dismissing the change as usual self-talk is diagnostic overshadowing; the sister describes something new.

11.q: Nora, 80, is dying from heart failure in a nursing home. Tonight she has become restless, keeps pulling at her sheets and is groaning. She last passed urine 10 hours ago and her lower abdomen looks swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe an antipsychotic for terminal delirium
Ask a relative to sit with her and see whether she settles overnight
Give the prescribed 'as required' midazolam to settle her agitation
Assess her for urinary retention and pain before giving sedation
11.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.11 and 1.5.23: agitation in isolation is sometimes associated with unrelieved pain or a full bladder or rectum; treat reversible causes of pain such as urinary retention before considering benzodiazepines or antipsychotics.

n.0: An antipsychotic is considered for delirium only after reversible causes such as urinary retention are explored (recs 1.5.25 and 1.5.27).
n.1: Company can help, but it leaves a likely full bladder untreated; reversible causes should be assessed first.
n.2: Sedation first would mask a reversible cause; NG31 rec 1.5.23 says agitation may reflect a full bladder or unrelieved pain.

11.q: A new community nursing team has been formed by merging two teams. In the first few weeks there are disagreements about who covers which visits and how handovers should run. What should the team leader, Fiona, do first?
o: Allocate the visits herself and ask the team to follow the new system
Meet the whole team to clarify roles and agree ways of working together
Wait for the team to settle, as early disagreement usually fades with time
Ask the two former team leaders to decide the arrangements between them
11.w: In newly formed groups, uncertainty about roles commonly causes conflict. Leaders help by bringing the team together to clarify roles and agree shared ways of working, which builds cohesion and safe handovers (P5.1 group dynamics; AnnexA.4.2.2 active listening to team concerns).

n.0: Imposing a system without involving the team misses their knowledge and may prolong conflict.
n.2: Leaving role confusion unresolved risks missed visits and unsafe handovers.
n.3: Delegating to the former leaders may entrench the two old teams rather than build one team.

11.q: Marta, a registered nurse, asks Lewis, a healthcare assistant who is trained and assessed in clinical observations, to record observations on three stable patients in her bay. What must Marta do to delegate this task appropriately?
o: Tell Lewis which patients to observe and leave the escalation decisions to him
Explain what to report and when, check he understands and review the results
Ask Lewis to record the observations and to calculate the NEWS2 for each patient
Ask Lewis to observe the patients if he feels confident and has time this morning
11.w: Code 11.1-11.3: delegate only within the other person's competence, make sure they understand the instructions and are supervised and supported, and confirm the outcome meets the required standard. AnnexA.4.1.2 requires clear instructions and checking understanding when delegating. Marta remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for reviewing findings.

n.0: Escalation decisions require registered nurse assessment; leaving them to Lewis passes on responsibility Marta cannot delegate in this way.
n.2: Recording a score without clear thresholds for reporting and review does not meet Code 11.2-11.3.
n.3: Delegation must be clear and planned; leaving it to his confidence and time does not ensure the care is done.

11.q: Nadia is redressing a deep cavity wound on the sacrum of Ruth, 80. She is wearing non-sterile gloves and using ANTT, but realises she will need to touch the wound bed with her fingers to place the packing. What should she do?
o: Change to sterile gloves, as the Key-Site will be touched directly
Moisten the non-sterile gloves with sterile saline before packing
Rub alcohol handrub onto the gloves before touching the wound
Continue with the non-sterile gloves, as she cleaned her hands first
11.w: Under ANTT, if a Key-Site or Key-Part must be touched directly, sterile gloves are needed so that the hands do not contaminate it (a Surgical-ANTT approach). NIPCM ch 1.4 also requires sterile gloves for contact with a sterile site or body cavity.

n.1: Saline does not sterilise gloves; the gloves would still contaminate the wound bed.
n.2: Gloves are not decontaminated with handrub, and this does not make them sterile.
n.3: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable when Key-Sites are not touched; here she must touch the wound bed directly.

11.q: Hilda, 83, has end-stage pulmonary fibrosis and is in the last days of life. She says she feels breathless at rest. Her oxygen saturation is 95% on air and her chest is unchanged on examination. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
o: Use a fan and positioning, and check whether an opioid is prescribed
Arrange an arterial blood gas sample to guide oxygen therapy
Start oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula to ease her breathing
Give the 'as required' hyoscine butylbromide from her anticipatory box
11.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.16 and 1.5.17: consider non-pharmacological management of breathlessness (for example a fan), do not routinely start oxygen unless symptomatic hypoxaemia is known or suspected, and consider an opioid, a benzodiazepine or both.

n.1: An invasive test unlikely to change care should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.1.4).
n.2: With saturation of 95% she is not hypoxaemic; NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen for breathlessness.
n.3: Hyoscine butylbromide is used for secretions or bowel obstruction, not for breathlessness.

11.q: Agnes, 70, admitted for a planned hip replacement, asks to keep her own inhalers and eye drops in her bedside locker and use them herself, as she does at home. What should the nurse do?
o: Allow it once her daughter agrees to supervise her doses
Complete a self-administration risk assessment and record it
Decline, as nurses give all medicines on a hospital ward
Allow it, as they are her own supply brought in from home
11.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-5: organisations have a self-administration policy; a risk assessment considers risks, the person's ability and consent, decides the level of self-administration, and the outcome and the person's agreement are recorded and reassessed as necessary.

n.0: A relative's agreement does not replace the documented professional risk assessment.
n.2: RPS/RCN guidance expects patients to keep responsibility for their medicines unless a risk assessment indicates otherwise.
n.3: Ownership does not replace the risk assessment that decides whether self-administration is safe.

11.q: Mrs Cole, 76, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. She tells the nurse that her main wish is to be able to get to the bathroom by herself before she goes home. Which care plan goal best reflects a person-centred, evaluable plan?
o: She will walk to the bathroom with her frame and one helper by Friday
Staff will encourage Mrs Cole to mobilise as much as possible
Mrs Cole's mobility will be improved during her stay on the stroke unit
Mrs Cole will be independent in all activities before discharge
11.w: NMC proficiency P3.5 requires person-centred, evidence-based plans with agreed goals. A good goal is centred on the person's own priority, specific, measurable and time-bound, so progress can be evaluated (P3.15).

n.1: This describes a staff action, not an outcome for Mrs Cole.
n.2: 'Improved mobility' is vague, with no measure or timescale to evaluate against.
n.3: Full independence in all activities is not her stated goal and is unlikely to be realistic or measurable.

11.q: During a governance meeting, Marcus, a learning disability nurse consultant, explains that one CIPOLD recommendation led to a permanent national programme in England. Which change followed from that recommendation?
o: A national programme reviewing the deaths of people with a learning disability
A legal duty to offer annual health checks to people on GP registers
A statutory right to an independent mental capacity advocate
Statutory learning disability and autism training for CQC-registered providers
11.w: CIPOLD recommended a national learning disability mortality review body; this became the LeDeR programme, which now reviews the deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people (CIPOLD 2013; LeDeR).

n.1: Annual health checks are an NHS contractual scheme that predates CIPOLD; they are not a legal duty created by it.
n.2: IMCAs were created by the Mental Capacity Act 2005, before CIPOLD reported.
n.3: Statutory training came from section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 after Oliver McGowan's death, not from CIPOLD.

11.q: Nina, 33, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name and her pain score is 9 while she is using her phone. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
o: Accept her report of pain and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Delay analgesia until her behaviour matches her pain score
Offer paracetamol until the doctor has assessed her pain
Ask her to stop using her phone before reassessing her pain
11.w: Pain is what the person says it is; self-report is the most reliable measure. People with long-term painful conditions often know which analgesia works and may cope with distraction. Prompt analgesia is essential, and judgement based on stereotypes breaches Code 20.2 and 1.1.

n.1: Behaviour is a poor guide to pain in people with recurrent pain, and delay causes harm.
n.2: Withholding effective prescribed analgesia leaves severe pain undertreated.
n.3: Distraction is a coping strategy and does not invalidate her pain score.

11.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
11.q: Ruby, 38, has a profound learning disability and has been sitting in her wheelchair for six hours at a day centre. Her postural care plan says she should change position every two hours. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask her family to reposition her when she gets home
Leave Ruby in her chair as she seems content
Tilt the wheelchair back for the rest of the day
Reposition Ruby out of her chair as her plan sets out
11.w: Prolonged sitting in one position increases pressure damage and body shape distortion. The plan's schedule should be followed, using supported lying or standing as set out (24-hour postural care principles).

n.0: Delaying repositioning until she goes home breaches the plan and risks harm.
n.1: Appearing content does not mean her body is protected from prolonged sitting.
n.2: Tilting changes pressure but she has already exceeded the planned time in her chair.

11.q: Mr Bello, 30, gave verbal consent for a urinary catheter to be inserted. Partway through, he becomes distressed and says, 'Stop, I don't want this any more.' The nurse is concerned that his bladder is still full. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the procedure, then discuss his concerns and the options
Finish quickly because stopping now would cause more discomfort
Continue, because consent was obtained before the procedure began
Pause, then restart once a colleague is present to reassure him
11.w: Consent is ongoing and a person with capacity may withdraw it at any point (Code 2.5 and 4.2). The nurse should stop, explore his worries, explain the risks of not proceeding and agree a plan with him, then document the discussion.

n.1: Completing a procedure after consent is withdrawn is treatment without consent, however brief.
n.2: Earlier consent does not continue once it has been withdrawn by a person with capacity.
n.3: Restarting without fresh consent overrides his refusal; a colleague's presence does not supply consent.

11.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
11.q: Jamie, 41, has a learning disability and his SLT plan says IDDSI level 1 slightly thick drinks. A carer has made up his tea with a new brand of thickener. The nurse wants to check that the drink matches level 1 before it is given. Which test should she use?
o: The fork drip test
The IDDSI flow test
The fork pressure test
The spoon tilt test
11.w: The IDDSI flow test classifies drinks levels 0-3 by how much remains in a standard 10 mL slip-tip syringe after 10 seconds: under 1 mL thin, 1-4 mL slightly thick (level 1), 4-8 mL mildly thick (level 2), more than 8 mL moderately thick (IDDSI testing methods).

n.0: The fork drip test checks thicker textures (IDDSI levels 3 to 5), not whether a drink is level 1.
n.2: The fork pressure test checks how soft foods are (IDDSI levels 4 to 7), not the thickness of a drink.
n.3: The spoon tilt test checks the cohesiveness and stickiness of thick textures such as pureed food, not the flow of a slightly thick drink.

11.q: A newly qualified nurse is learning which ward medicines must be entered in the controlled drugs register. Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, which of these medicines is a Schedule 2 controlled drug?
o: Diazepam 5 mg tablets
Oxycodone 5 mg in 5 mL oral solution
Tramadol 50 mg capsules
Midazolam injection 10 mg in 2 mL
11.w: Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 (Home Office controlled drugs list), oxycodone is in Schedule 2, alongside morphine, diamorphine and fentanyl, and needs a CD register entry (NICE NG46). Midazolam and tramadol are Schedule 3; diazepam is Schedule 4 Part 1.

n.0: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 Part 1 benzodiazepine.
n.2: Tramadol is in Schedule 3.
n.3: Midazolam is a Schedule 3 controlled drug, although many hospitals record it in the register by local policy.

11.q: Phyllis, 85, on a medical ward, has had three episodes of loose, watery stool (Bristol type 7) since this morning with no obvious cause. She started antibiotics 5 days ago. What is the priority action?
o: Wait for two more episodes before sending a sample
Give her prescribed loperamide and continue to monitor her
Move her nearer the toilet in the shared bay
Isolate her in a single room and send a stool sample
11.w: Unexplained diarrhoea, especially after antibiotics, may be infective (for example C. difficile). Isolate promptly in a single room with contact precautions, send a stool sample, and use soap and water for hand hygiene (NIPCM; Annexe B 6.4).

n.0: Delay increases the risk of spread and delays diagnosis.
n.1: Antidiarrhoeals can be harmful in suspected C. difficile and do not reduce spread.
n.2: Staying in a shared bay risks transmission to other patients.

11.q: Mrs Lowe, 88, who has dementia, seems not to respond during the nurse's admission assessment. Her daughter mentions she normally wears hearing aids, which are in her bag. What should the nurse do first?
o: Complete the assessment by asking her daughter the questions
Refer her to audiology for a review of her hearing
Record that she is unable to answer the assessment questions
Check the hearing aids are working and help her put them in
11.w: Annexe A 2.4: support and manage the use of personal communication aids. Code 7.2: take reasonable steps to meet people's communication needs.

n.0: Her daughter can contribute, but Mrs Lowe should first be helped to take part herself.
n.1: A referral may be useful later, but her own aids should be fitted now.
n.2: Recording her as unable to communicate before fitting her aids would be inaccurate.

11.q: Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool (MITT), Lucy is triaging casualties after an explosion at a shopping centre. A man with cuts to his face and arms is walking around asking for help, with no catastrophic bleeding. Which category should she assign?
o: P2
P3
P1
Dead
11.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) first checks for catastrophic bleeding (P1); if absent, anyone who is walking is categorised P3 (minor) before further physiological assessment (P6.12).

n.0: P2 is reached after the walking, breathing, voice and respiratory rate steps in a casualty who cannot walk.
n.2: P1 is for catastrophic bleeding or abnormal findings later in the algorithm; a walking casualty without catastrophic bleeding is not P1.
n.3: The man is walking and talking; 'dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened.

11.q: Colin, 49, is found on a hospital corridor floor. He is breathing normally but responds to pain only. There is no suggestion of injury. Help is on its way. How should he be positioned?
o: Sitting upright against the wall
In the lateral recovery position
Flat on his back with legs raised
Prone with his head to one side
11.w: RCUK first aid 2025: place a person with decreased responsiveness who does not meet the criteria for CPR in a lateral (side-lying) recovery position. Do not use it if breathing is agonal or there is trauma.

n.0: Sitting a person with reduced responsiveness upright risks airway compromise and falls.
n.2: Supine positioning risks airway obstruction from the tongue or vomit.
n.3: Prone positioning impedes airway assessment and breathing.

11.q: A practice nurse is checking her understanding of vaccine types before a childhood immunisation clinic. Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
o: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23)
Inactivated poliomyelitis vaccine (IPV)
Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine
Tetanus vaccine containing inactivated toxin
11.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): live attenuated vaccines include yellow fever, measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) and BCG; the weakened organism replicates in the recipient. IPV contains inactivated virus, tetanus and diphtheria vaccines contain toxoids, and pneumococcal vaccine contains capsular polysaccharide.

n.0: PPV23 contains capsular polysaccharide, not a live organism.
n.1: IPV contains inactivated virus, which cannot cause the disease.
n.3: Tetanus vaccine contains an inactivated toxin (toxoid), not a live organism.

11.q: Marta works as an NHS ward nurse and plans to start offering cosmetic injections at a private clinic at weekends. Her NHS employer's indemnity covers her NHS work. What does the Code require before she starts the private work?
o: Confirmation from the clinic that her NHS indemnity extends to it
An appropriate indemnity arrangement that covers the private practice
Written approval of the private work from her NHS ward manager
A note of the private work in her next revalidation application
11.w: Code 12.1: make sure you have an appropriate indemnity arrangement in place relevant to your scope of practice. Professional indemnity is also a revalidation declaration.

n.0: Her NHS indemnity covers NHS work; the clinic cannot extend it, so she needs separate appropriate cover.
n.2: Employer approval may be needed under her contract, but the Code requirement is indemnity cover relevant to her scope of practice.
n.3: Recording it later does not meet Code 12.1, which requires cover to be in place before she practises.

11.q: Kieran, 26, has a learning disability and takes risperidone prescribed for behaviour that challenges. His learning disability nurse is helping the GP practice prepare his annual health check. According to NICE NG11, which area should the check specifically review?
o: A full functional assessment of his behaviour by a clinical psychologist
His medicines and side effects, and links between behaviour and physical health
A capacity assessment covering each of his major life decisions
A repeat IQ test to confirm the severity of his learning disability
11.w: NICE NG11 (1.2.1) says the annual health check should include reviewing behaviour that challenges and any links with physical health, and reviewing medication including side effects.

n.0: Functional assessment is a specialist process when behaviour is a concern, not a routine element of the GP check.
n.2: Capacity is decision-specific and assessed when a decision arises, not as a blanket review at the health check.
n.3: Re-testing IQ is not part of the annual health check and does not change his care.

11.q: Joan, 74, has lower back pain after a fall at home and is being cared for on a frailty unit. Her care plan lists several pain-relieving interventions. Which of these is a non-pharmacological intervention?
o: A rectal paracetamol suppository
A topical lidocaine plaster
Patient-controlled analgesia pump
Repositioning using pillows
11.w: Non-pharmacological measures include repositioning, heat or cold where appropriate, distraction, relaxation, reassurance and explanation. NICE NG31 gives repositioning as an example (Annexe B 3.5).

n.0: A suppository is a route for giving a drug.
n.1: A lidocaine plaster delivers a drug and is pharmacological.
n.2: PCA delivers opioid medicine and is pharmacological.

11.q: At the start of an early shift, Nina, a staff nurse, is allocated four patients on a medical ward. Which patient should she see first?
o: Mr Ali, 66, whose insulin is due with breakfast in 45 minutes
Mrs Dunn, 74, whose respiratory rate is 28/min, SpO2 89% and who is newly confused
Ms Reid, 52, who reports post-operative pain of 5/10, last analgesia 3 hours ago
Mr Shaw, 59, who is to be discharged today and needs his discharge letter
11.w: Prioritisation uses an ABCDE approach and early warning scores: Mrs Dunn has a respiratory rate of 28 (scores 3), SpO2 89% (scores 3) and new confusion (scores 3) on NEWS2 (RCP 2017), indicating possible life-threatening deterioration needing immediate assessment and escalation (P5.5 lead and manage care of a group of people with prioritisation).

n.0: Time-critical insulin matters, but there are 45 minutes before it is due and he is not unwell.
n.2: Her pain needs prompt attention, possibly by another team member, but is not life-threatening.
n.3: Discharge paperwork can safely wait while a deteriorating patient is assessed.

11.q: Daniel, 27, has a learning disability and epilepsy. His psychiatrist plans to start an antipsychotic for psychosis. Which consideration does NICE NG54 specifically highlight before starting?
o: His anti-seizure medicine should be stopped while the antipsychotic is started
Antipsychotics may lower the seizure threshold, so consult the epilepsy team
Antipsychotics are contraindicated in people who have epilepsy
He should be admitted to hospital for the first week of treatment
11.w: NICE NG54 1.9.3: before starting medication, take account of interactions and effects on other conditions, consulting specialists when necessary, for example neurologists providing epilepsy care when prescribing antipsychotics that may lower the seizure threshold.

n.0: Stopping anti-seizure medication would risk seizures and status epilepticus.
n.2: Epilepsy is a reason for caution and consultation, not an absolute bar to antipsychotics for psychosis.
n.3: Admission is not routinely required to start an antipsychotic.

11.q: Marcus Bell, 66, is on a surgical ward. His observations are: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on air, BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, alert, temperature 37.2°C. His NEWS2 total is 3. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Increase observations to at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat the observations in 4 hours and escalate if the total rises
Continue 4 to 6 hourly observations as the total score is below 5
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
11.w: A respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3 in a single parameter (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Chart 1). A score of 3 in any one parameter triggers a low-medium clinical risk response: minimum 1-hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team, who decide whether escalation is needed (Chart 4). Two steps: calculate the parameter score, then apply the single-parameter rule.

n.1: Four-hourly review delays recognition of deterioration when a single parameter is already scoring 3.
n.2: The aggregate of 3 is low, but a single red score of 3 overrides this and requires at least hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.3: Emergency critical care assessment is the response to an aggregate of 7 or more; this is an urgent ward-based response.

11.q: Leon, 39, stopped smoking three months ago with support. He tells the nurse he is worried he will start again at a family wedding next month, where many guests smoke. What is the most appropriate support?
o: Help him make an 'if-then' plan for moments when he is tempted
Advise him to avoid weddings and other social events for a year
Close his episode of care, as his quit attempt is now complete
Reassure him that relapse is rare once three months have passed
11.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) recs 6 and 10: interventions should address relapse and recognise that it is common; help people maintain change by giving them well-rehearsed action plans such as 'if-then' plans, social support and feedback and monitoring for at least 1 year.

n.1: Avoiding all social contact is unrealistic and removes social support that helps people maintain change.
n.2: PH49 rec 10 recommends feedback and monitoring for at least a year to help maintain change.
n.3: PH49 recognises that relapse is common and asks for interventions to address it.

11.q: Nurse Kemi is asked by a colleague to countersign the controlled drugs register for a dose of subcutaneous morphine that the colleague prepared and gave while Kemi was on her break. Trust policy requires a witness for CD administration. What should Kemi do?
o: Sign it and add a note that she did not see the dose given
Sign it, as she trusts her colleague's practice and experience
Sign the stock balance but leave the witness column blank for now
Decline, and offer to witness the next dose from preparation onwards
11.w: NICE NG46 and RPS/RCN guidance: the CD administration record includes the person administering and any witness, and witnessing means observing the process. Signing for something not seen is a false record (NMC Code 10.3, records accurate). Kemi should decline and the colleague should report the gap per policy.

n.0: A witness signature with a disclaimer still misrepresents the record and breaches the witness policy.
n.1: Trust does not make a signature truthful; she did not witness the dose.
n.2: Countersigning the balance still implies checking a transaction she did not see.

11.q: Mrs Taylor cares for her husband, 79, who has capacity and is being discharged after a stroke. She says nobody has involved her in his care planning. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her to the GP to discuss her husband's care plan
Ask if he wants her involved, then involve her and offer a carer's assessment
Involve her fully, as she will be the one providing his care at home
Explain that his care plan is confidential and cannot be shared with her
11.w: Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows; Code 2.1 partnership. Care Act 2014 s10: carers have a right to a carer's assessment. Proficiency P1.13 relationships with carers.

n.0: Passing her elsewhere does not involve her in his discharge planning.
n.2: His consent is needed before sharing his information and involving her.
n.3: If he agrees, she can be involved; refusing outright ignores her role.

11.q: Bridget, 58, is due to have her first red cell transfusion before surgery. She asks the nurse what she should know about it. According to NICE NG24, which information should the nurse include?
o: That she will be able to give blood herself once she has recovered
That she will no longer be eligible to donate blood after a transfusion
That she cannot refuse once the transfusion has been prescribed
That a transfusion has no risks if the bedside checks are completed
11.w: NICE NG24 rec 1.14.2: give verbal and written information on the reason for transfusion, risks and benefits, the process, alternatives, that the person is no longer eligible to donate blood, and encourage questions; document the discussion (1.14.3).

n.0: NG24 states people who have had a transfusion are no longer eligible to donate blood.
n.2: A person with capacity may refuse a transfusion; consent remains her decision.
n.3: Transfusion carries risks that must be explained even with correct checks.

11.q: The Department of Health and Social Care opens a public consultation on changes to nurse education funding. Mariam, a staff nurse, has concerns about the effect on recruitment to her mental health service. What is the most appropriate way for her to influence the policy?
o: Post her views on social media, naming her employer and the vacancies
Respond to the consultation with evidence, directly or through her union
Ask her manager to raise it with the patients' families at visiting
Write to the NMC and ask it to block the proposed funding changes
11.w: P5.12 and P7.13 ask nurses to understand mechanisms for influencing public policy and to use political awareness. Responding to consultations with evidence, individually or through professional bodies and unions, is a legitimate and effective route, consistent with Code 20 (professionalism).

n.0: Naming her employer and service on social media risks breaching Code 20.10 and confidentiality, and is not a formal route of influence.
n.2: Involving visiting families is inappropriate and does not feed into the consultation.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not control government education funding.

11.q: On a surgical ward, Femi asks the ward manager about the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 because a new bariatric care pathway is being written. Which step do the regulations require the employer to take first?
o: Set a maximum weight that any member of staff may lift on the ward
Reduce the risk of injury to the lowest level by providing equipment
Avoid hazardous manual handling so far as is reasonably practicable
Assess the risk of injury from every manual handling task on the ward
11.w: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 set out a hierarchy for employers: avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable; assess the risk of injury from any hazardous operations that cannot be avoided; and reduce that risk to as low as reasonably practicable (HSE, Manual handling at work).

n.0: The HSE states that the law does not set specific weight limits; weight is one factor in the risk assessment.
n.1: Reducing risk is the third step, after avoidance and assessment.
n.3: Assessment is the second step and applies to hazardous handling that cannot be avoided, not to every task.

11.q: Which contemporary tool is most widely used in UK adult care settings to screen for malnutrition?
o: The Braden scale for predicting risk
The 4AT rapid assessment test
The Waterlow risk assessment score
The 'MUST' screening tool
11.w: 'MUST' (BAPEN) combines BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect to give a low, medium or high risk of malnutrition, with a management plan for each (Annexe B 5.2).

n.0: Braden assesses pressure ulcer risk.
n.1: The 4AT screens for delirium.
n.2: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

11.q: A ward nurse is referring Mr Kaur, 70, to the community dietitian after finding he has lost 8% of his body weight in 3 months. Which action best supports a safe referral?
o: Ask his GP to make the referral so that it is from a doctor
Send the referral and let the dietitian explain it when they contact him
Send his entire hospital record so that the dietitian has all details
Explain the referral to him and include the reason, urgency and key findings
11.w: P3.16: know when and how to refer safely. The person should understand and agree to the referral (Code 4.2), and the referral should give the reason, urgency and relevant findings, sharing the minimum necessary information (Caldicott principle 3).

n.0: Nurses can refer directly to a dietitian; routing via the GP adds delay.
n.1: He should know about and agree to the referral before it is sent.
n.2: Sending the whole record exceeds the minimum necessary information for the purpose.

11.q: A patient's family was told in person, with an apology, about a notifiable safety incident on the day it was identified. Under regulation 20, what must the provider do next?
o: Follow it with a written notification and keep a copy
Arrange a further meeting within 28 days to repeat the apology
Report the incident to the NMC for each nurse involved
Wait for the investigation to finish before any further contact
11.w: Reg 20(3)-(4): notification must be given in person, include an apology and be followed by a written notification; the provider must keep a copy and written records.

n.1: Reg 20 requires a written notification after the in-person one; a repeat meeting is not the specified step.
n.2: Reg 20 is about notifying the relevant person; NMC referral relates to fitness to practise concerns, not candour steps.
n.3: The written notification follows the in-person notification and gives what is known so far; it does not wait for the investigation to finish.

11.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
11.q: Bill, 54, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about his care. He lives in a care home and has started trying to leave in the afternoons, saying he wants to 'go to work'. Staff suggest locking the front door and giving PRN sedation. What should be considered first?
o: Less restrictive ways to meet his need, such as accompanied walks
PRN sedation in the afternoons to reduce his attempts to leave the home
