A locked front door as a blanket rule applied to all residents
His family's consent to the door being locked and the sedation
11.w: MCA s1(6): before acting, regard must be had to whether the purpose can be achieved in a way that is less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom. Understanding the meaning of his behaviour and offering accompanied walks or meaningful activity may meet the need without restriction (STOMP; NICE NG11).

n.1: Sedation to control behaviour is a chemical restraint and contrary to STOMP as a first response.
n.2: Blanket restrictions affect everyone and are not individually justified.
n.3: Family cannot consent to restrictions for an adult without legal authority.

11.q: A student nurse asks what a Care and Treatment Review (CTR) is for an adult with a learning disability at risk of admission. Which answer is best?
o: A formal complaint process for families who are unhappy with care
An independent review of whether care is safe and community options are used
A Care Act needs assessment completed by a local authority social worker
A review of whether the person meets the criteria for detention
11.w: C(E)TRs bring an independent panel to look at whether the person's care, (education) and treatment are safe and effective, whether community alternatives to admission have been used and what is needed to avoid admission or speed discharge (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy).

n.0: Complaints have their own process; a CTR reviews care and treatment, not complaints.
n.2: A Care Act assessment determines eligible care and support needs; a CTR is a different, NHS-led review.
n.3: Detention criteria are decided under the Mental Health Act by AMHPs and doctors, not by a CTR.

11.q: Mrs Rita Holmes, 87, lived alone before a fall and is now medically fit for discharge but still slow and unsteady. At the board round, a doctor suggests arranging a permanent nursing home place directly from the ward. What does current discharge guidance in England advise?
o: Discharge her home with no support and review her needs if she falls
Arrange the permanent place now, as hospital is the best place to assess needs
Discharge her for a period of recovery, then assess her long-term needs
Keep Mrs Holmes in hospital until she has fully recovered her mobility
11.w: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, not in hospital. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without an opportunity to recover first (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P4.18). Two steps: recognise she is medically fit, then apply discharge to assess.

n.0: She has clear new needs; discharge without support is unsafe.
n.1: Assessing long-term needs in hospital, before recovery, tends to overestimate need; the guidance advises against it.
n.3: Staying in hospital once medically fit risks deconditioning and delays recovery.

11.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation, Lucy, a staff nurse, is tearful in the clean utility room. She is due to start the next medicines round in ten minutes. What is the most appropriate response from her colleague?
o: Tell her to go home and let the nurse in charge know later
Reassure her that she will get used to deaths over time
Advise her to take a few minutes and then start the round on time
Offer support, ask how she feels and help arrange cover if needed
11.w: Code 8.7: be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems without compromising safety. Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risk.

n.0: Sending her home without discussion or escalation leaves the ward uncovered and her unsupported.
n.1: This dismisses her distress and offers no practical support.
n.2: This overlooks whether she is safe to give medicines right now.

11.q: Owen, a learning disability liaison nurse, is presenting CIPOLD data to hospital consultants. He wants to compare the proportion of deaths from causes amenable to good-quality healthcare in people with and without a learning disability. Which comparison is correct?
o: 20% in people with a learning disability compared with 13% in the general population
50% in people with a learning disability compared with 25% in the general population
37% in people with a learning disability compared with 13% in the general population
13% in people with a learning disability compared with 37% in the general population
11.w: CIPOLD (2013) found 37% of deaths of people with a learning disability were from causes amenable to good-quality healthcare, compared with 13% in the general population.

n.0: 20% understates the CIPOLD figure of 37% for people with a learning disability.
n.1: These are not the CIPOLD figures; 37% and 13% were reported.
n.3: The figures are reversed; people with a learning disability had the higher proportion.

11.q: Mr Hussain, 69, has died on a medical ward after an expected death. The death is not being referred to the coroner. His family tell the nurse that their faith requires family members to wash his body and that they would like to do this themselves. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that hospital policy requires staff to wash all deceased patients
Leave the washing to the family and support them with the rest of his care
Ask the mortuary staff to wash him before he is released to the family
Wash him before the family arrive so that they are spared any distress
11.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): wash the deceased unless requested not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons, or the death is being referred to the coroner; key contacts may wish to assist and should be supported. NMC Code 1.3 and 1.5: recognise diversity and individual choice, and respect and uphold people's human rights.

n.0: Care after death guidance says wash the deceased unless asked not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons.
n.2: Washing by mortuary staff would also override the family's wish to carry out the washing themselves.
n.3: This disregards the family's stated religious wishes, which the guidance says must be respected.

11.q: A district nurse visits Mr Shaw, 68, whose wife died recently. He has given his dog to a neighbour, written letters to his children and says calmly that 'everything is sorted now'. He denies any physical symptoms. How should the nurse interpret these signs?
o: They are warning signs of suicidal intent needing direct enquiry
They suggest early dementia, so a memory screen is the priority
They show he is adjusting well and needs routine follow-up
They suggest normal grief, so a bereavement leaflet is enough
11.w: Giving away possessions, putting affairs in order and sudden calm after loss can signal suicidal intent (NMC Annexe B 1.1.6: recognise signs of self-harm and suicidal ideation). NICE NG225 supports asking about suicidal thoughts and acting on immediate safety concerns.

n.1: Nothing suggests cognitive decline; the behaviour points to risk of suicide.
n.2: Settling affairs after recent bereavement with sudden calm is a recognised warning sign, not evidence of adjustment.
n.3: A leaflet does not address possible suicidal intent, which needs direct enquiry.

11.q: Mr Hughes, 70, tells Ama, a Black staff nurse, that he does not want 'someone like her' looking after him. Ama is upset. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse in charge?
o: Reassign Ama quietly to avoid any further conflict
Challenge the remark, support Ama and report the incident
Ask Ama to carry on and to disregard the remark
Tell Mr Hughes he must leave the ward for his behaviour
11.w: Code 3.4: challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour; Code 20.2: treat people fairly without discrimination, bullying or harassment. Proficiency P1.4: understand and challenge discriminatory behaviour; report through local policy.

n.0: Reassigning without challenge colludes with the discrimination; Code 3.4 and 20.2 require it to be challenged.
n.2: This leaves the racist behaviour unchallenged and fails to support the colleague.
n.3: Withdrawing care is disproportionate; the behaviour should be challenged while care continues safely.

11.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
11.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

11.q: Ms Fry, 45, is on a surgical ward after an appendicectomy. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 26, SpO2 97%, systolic BP 124, pulse 88, alert, temperature 37.2°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Repeat the observations in 4-6 hours as her total is 3
Record the observations and recheck them in 12 hours
Observe at least hourly and inform the medical team
Call the critical care outreach team as an emergency
11.w: Respiratory rate 25 or more scores 3; all other parameters score 0, giving a total of 3. NEWS2 Charts 2 and 4: a score of 3 in any single parameter is low-medium risk and requires an urgent ward-based response, at least hourly monitoring, and the RN informing the medical team.

n.0: Although the total is low, a single parameter scoring 3 triggers hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.1: 12-hourly observation applies to a total of 0, not to a score of 3 in one parameter.
n.3: An emergency critical care response is required at an aggregate of 7 or more.

11.q: Ibrahim, 38, has a severe learning disability. For three weeks he has been more agitated, slapping his face and refusing food. Staff ask for a referral to the mental health team for 'challenging behaviour'. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase his PRN medication until the referral is seen
Ask staff to reduce his activities to lower his stress
Make the referral now and start an ABC chart while waiting to be seen
Arrange a physical check to exclude pain, constipation or infection
11.w: NICE NG54 and NG11 advise excluding physical health problems, including pain, that may cause or worsen changes in behaviour or mental state. Face slapping and food refusal could indicate dental or ear pain, constipation or infection; physical assessment first prevents overshadowing.

n.0: Increasing PRN masks distress and is a restrictive response contrary to STOMP.
n.1: Reducing activities lowers quality of life and does not find the cause.
n.2: Referral may be needed later, but a physical cause should be excluded first.

11.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
11.q: Phil, 66, has a learning disability and developed delirium from a urinary tract infection. On day 3 of treatment he cannot discuss whether to move into a care home after discharge, which is planned in about ten days. What should the nurse advise first?
o: Consider whether he will regain capacity and, if so, delay the decision
Instruct an IMCA straight away to make the care home placement decision
Ask his brother to decide, as he is the closest relative
Make the best interests decision now, as he lacks capacity today
11.w: Two steps: recognise that delirium is often temporary; then apply MCA s4(3): the decision-maker must consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. If the decision can wait, it should, so Phil can decide himself.

n.1: An IMCA does not make decisions, and the first step is to consider whether he will regain capacity.
n.2: Relatives are consulted but do not make the decision without legal authority.
n.3: Deciding now ignores the likelihood that he will regain capacity soon.

11.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
11.q: Katie, 17, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to her care at a residential college, where the team agrees the arrangements need authorising as a deprivation of liberty. Her parents say they are happy to consent. What is the correct approach?
o: Ask the local authority for a standard DoLS authorisation
Rely on her parents' consent, as she is under 18
Apply to the Court of Protection, as DoLS apply from age 18
Use section 2 of the Mental Health Act to authorise the arrangements
11.w: DoLS apply from 18. For 16 and 17 year olds who lack capacity, a deprivation of liberty must be authorised by the court (Court of Protection). The Supreme Court in Re D [2019] UKSC 42 held that parents cannot consent to the deprivation of liberty of a 16 or 17 year old.

n.0: Standard DoLS authorisations are for people aged 18 and over.
n.1: Parents cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for a 16 or 17 year old (Re D 2019).
n.3: Section 2 is for assessment of mental disorder in hospital, not authorising care at a college.

12.q: Sophie, a student nurse on an acute medical ward, hears that Callum, 27, who has a learning disability, has brought his hospital passport. She asks her mentor what a hospital passport is. Which description is correct?
o: A legal record of his best interests decisions, signed by his consultant
A trust form completed by the admitting nurse that replaces the nursing assessment
A person-held document telling staff what they must know about him and how to support him
A GP summary of diagnoses and medicines sent with the referral letter
12.w: A hospital (health) passport is held by the person and travels with them. It records things staff must know (allergies, medicines, communication, how the person shows pain, capacity and consent information), things that are important to them, and likes and dislikes.

n.0: Best interests decisions are recorded in the clinical record under the Mental Capacity Act; the passport is not a legal decision record.
n.1: The passport is the person's own document and supports, not replaces, the nursing assessment.
n.3: A GP summary is a clinical referral document; the passport is person-held and describes how to support the person.

12.q: In theatre, Callum, a newly registered scrub nurse, sees the surgeon pick up the scalpel before the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist time out has been done. The team seems not to have noticed. What should Callum do?
o: Complete an incident report after the operation so the omission is recorded
Note the omission and raise it at the team debrief at the end of the list
Quietly tell the anaesthetist so that the surgeon is not challenged openly
Say clearly that the time out has not been done and ask the team to pause
12.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 (preserve safety) require nurses to intervene. Checklists work only if anyone can stop the process; speaking up clearly and directly at the moment of risk is the safest action, whatever the speaker's seniority (P6.6; P5.2).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate later, but the immediate risk must be addressed before the incision.
n.1: Raising it afterwards allows the operation to proceed without the safety check that prevents wrong site and wrong patient surgery.
n.2: An indirect approach delays action and may not stop the procedure in time.

12.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
12.q: In a supported living service, staff are asked what 'soft signs' of deterioration might look like in Lena, 33, who has a profound learning disability and no speech. Which example best fits?
o: A new oxygen saturation of 88% on air
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
A systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg
Eating less and sleeping more than usual
12.w: Soft signs are subtle changes from the person's baseline (eating, drinking, sleeping, mobility, mood, behaviour) that may precede changes in vital signs. Recognising them depends on knowing the person's usual presentation.

n.0: Saturation of 88% on air is a measured abnormality, not a soft sign.
n.1: A respiratory rate of 30 is a hard, measured sign that scores highly on NEWS2.
n.2: Systolic BP of 85 is a measured red-flag sign, not a soft sign.

12.q: Kezia, a second-year adult nursing student, is ending her placement on a surgical ward. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment (SSSA), who conducts the assessment that confirms her achievement of proficiencies for this placement?
o: Her practice assessor, informed by feedback from her supervisors
Her practice supervisor, who has worked most shifts with her
Her academic assessor, who visits the ward at the end of placement
The ward manager, who signs off all students on the ward
12.w: Under the SSSA (NMC 2018), practice supervisors support and supervise and contribute feedback; the practice assessor conducts the assessment and confirms achievement of practice proficiencies, drawing on that feedback; the academic assessor works with the practice assessor on progression decisions (P5.8).

n.1: Practice supervisors contribute to assessment through feedback but do not confirm achievement of proficiencies.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement for progression with the practice assessor, but does not assess practice on the ward.
n.3: SSSA roles are defined by function, not by management position; the ward manager has no automatic assessment role.

12.q: Emma, 28, has Down syndrome. Her mother has read about dementia and asks the learning disability nurse when they should talk about it. Which approach follows NICE NG96?
o: Raise the topic once Emma reaches 60, when dementia usually starts
Explain the link early to Emma and her family, and plan a baseline assessment
Discuss it with her mother and not with Emma, to avoid upsetting her
Avoid raising dementia until symptoms appear, to prevent needless worry
12.w: NICE NG96 (1.5.36) advises explaining early to people with learning disabilities, particularly those with Down syndrome, and their families about the link with dementia. A baseline of skills and abilities in adulthood helps later change to be measured.

n.0: Dementia in Down syndrome usually starts much earlier than 60.
n.2: Emma has a right to accessible information about her own health; excluding her is not person-centred.
n.3: Waiting for symptoms means there is no baseline and no early planning.

12.q: A community nursing team wants to improve the written information given to people after a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Which approach best involves people who use the service in this improvement?
o: Adapt a leaflet that a neighbouring trust has used for several years
Co-design the information with people who have recently been diagnosed
Ask the diabetes consultant to approve the content before it is printed
Ask the team's nurses to agree the content at the next team meeting
12.w: P6.9 requires nurses to work with people, their families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies. Co-design with people who have lived experience of the service makes information relevant, accessible and person-centred (Code 2.1 work in partnership).

n.0: Borrowing another organisation's leaflet may help, but it does not involve local service users in the improvement.
n.2: Clinical approval checks accuracy but does not involve people who use the service.
n.3: Staff agreement alone excludes the people the information is for.

12.q: Nurse Adebayo nearly gives insulin to the wrong patient but notices at the bedside check, so no dose is given. A colleague says there is no need to report it because nothing happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discuss it at the next team meeting without making a report
Make a note in her own reflective log for revalidation
Tell the patient about the near miss and make no further record
Report the near miss through the local incident reporting system
12.w: The NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (refreshed December 2024) covers openness within organisations, including reporting adverse incidents and near misses. Code 19.1 requires action to reduce the likelihood of mistakes and near misses.

n.0: Discussion helps learning, but candour guidance expects near misses to be reported formally so the system can learn.
n.1: Personal reflection is useful but does not replace organisational reporting of the near miss.
n.2: Telling the patient is not enough; the near miss must still be documented and reported (Code 14.3, 19.1).

12.q: Gladys, 88, died at home this morning and her death has been verified. Her daughter, Pam, wants to help the community nurse with washing her. As they turn Gladys, there is a sighing sound from her mouth. Pam becomes frightened and asks whether her mother is still alive. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Explain gently that air can escape from the body when it is moved
Recheck Gladys's pulse and breathing and then call 999 for help
Call the GP to come and verify the death a second time
Ask Pam to leave the room while the nurse completes the washing
12.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): when moving the deceased, air can be released and this should not be mistaken for breathing; share this sensitively with the key contact or carer assisting. Prepare key contacts sensitively for changes to the body after death.

n.1: Death has been verified; the guidance says released air should not be mistaken for breathing.
n.2: The death was properly verified; a sound from released air is expected and is not a reason to re-verify.
n.3: Pam wishes to take part; the guidance is to prepare and support key contacts, not exclude them.

12.q: Tariq, 26, has a mild learning disability and capacity to decide about blood tests. He has a strong fear of needles and pulled away at his last two attempts. He needs regular blood tests to monitor his lithium. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Record that he has refused blood tests and inform the prescriber
Arrange a graded desensitisation programme with numbing cream
Ask the GP to prescribe a sedative before the next attempt
Ask two staff to hold his arm still for a quick test
12.w: Tariq has capacity, so holding him would be unlawful restraint. A reasonable adjustment such as gradual desensitisation over several visits, with a familiar person and topical anaesthetic, supports him to have the test he needs (MCA 2005 s1; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: His fear is a barrier that adjustments can address; recording refusal without trying them risks unsafe lithium monitoring.
n.2: Sedation is a restrictive option to consider only after less restrictive adjustments have been tried, and needs his consent.
n.3: Holding a person with capacity against his will is assault and not a reasonable adjustment.

12.q: Ruth is running late at the end of a shift and plans to email herself her patients' details so she can finish the care plans at home on her personal laptop. What should she do?
o: Print the details and complete the plans at home that night
Email the details to herself and delete them afterwards
Finish the care plans on the trust system before leaving
Email the details to herself with the names removed
12.w: Code 10.5: take all steps to make sure records are kept securely; Caldicott principle 6 comply with the law; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality principle. Annexe A 1.10 share digital information safely.

n.0: Taking paper records home risks loss and breaches confidentiality (Code 5, 10.5).
n.1: Sending patient data to personal email breaches secure storage requirements, even if later deleted.
n.3: Pseudonymised clinical details on a personal device remain a security risk and are not trust records (Code 10.5).

12.q: Valerie, 58, is choking in a hospital café. She cannot cough, speak or breathe but remains conscious. Help has been called. What should you do first?
o: Perform a blind finger sweep
Give up to 5 back blows
Start chest compressions
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts
12.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): for severe obstruction in a conscious person, give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat until relieved.

n.0: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in and are not part of the algorithm.
n.2: Chest compressions start once she becomes unconscious.
n.3: Abdominal thrusts come after 5 back blows.

12.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is concerned that a planned reduction in local district nursing posts will affect housebound patients. He wants to use his professional knowledge to influence the decision. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Refuse to accept new referrals until the reduction in posts is withdrawn
Share named patients' stories with a local newspaper to raise awareness
Write to his MP with anonymised evidence about the impact on care
Tell his patients during home visits that they should vote against the council
12.w: Political awareness and influence are part of the nurse's role (P7.13; P5.12). Engaging with elected representatives using anonymised evidence is legitimate, while the Code requires confidentiality (Code 5) and that personal political views are not expressed inappropriately to people in his care (Code 20.7).

n.0: Refusing referrals puts patients at risk and is not a professional way to influence policy.
n.1: Sharing identifiable patient information breaches confidentiality (Code 5).
n.3: Expressing personal political views to patients during care breaches Code 20.7.

12.q: A school nurse is teaching staff about adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), using the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh ACE study. Which experience is counted as an ACE in that study?
o: Living with a household member who served a prison sentence
Being born early and spending time in a neonatal unit
Moving house and changing school during the primary years
Having a parent who regularly worked night shifts
12.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): the nine ACEs were verbal, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up in a household with parental separation, domestic violence, mental illness, alcohol abuse, drug use or incarceration.

n.1: Prematurity is not one of the nine ACEs measured.
n.2: Moving house is not one of the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh study.
n.3: Parental shift work is not one of the nine ACEs measured.

12.q: Lily, 83, wears full upper and lower dentures. She asks what she should do with them at night while in hospital. What is the best advice?
o: Keep them in overnight so that her gums keep their shape
Soak them in boiling water overnight to sterilise them
Remove, clean and store them in a labelled pot overnight
Wrap them in a tissue on her bedside table overnight
12.w: Dentures should be removed and cleaned daily and generally left out overnight to rest the gums, stored in a labelled, named denture pot to prevent loss or damage (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wearing dentures overnight increases the risk of denture stomatitis and infection.
n.1: Boiling water can warp acrylic dentures.
n.3: Tissue-wrapped dentures are easily thrown away by mistake.

12.q: On a dementia ward, Mr Payne, 81, lacks capacity and needed to be briefly held by two trained staff to stop him hitting another patient. He is now calm. Besides checking him for injury, what should the nurse record about the incident?
o: The details in the incident system, rather than his care record
A brief note that restraint was needed, to avoid labelling him
The reasons for the hold, technique used, duration and his response
That he was held in his best interests, with the names of staff
12.w: Code 10.1-10.4 requires accurate, timely records that attribute, date and time entries. Any restraint must be justified as necessary and proportionate (MCA s6), so the record should show why it was used, how, for how long and its effect, supporting review and learning.

n.0: Incident reporting is appropriate, but the care record must also document what happened to him.
n.1: A minimal note fails Code 10 and prevents review of whether the restraint was justified.
n.3: Stating 'best interests' without reasons, technique and duration does not show the hold was necessary and proportionate.

12.q: Hilda, 83, has end-stage pulmonary fibrosis and is in the last days of life. She says she feels breathless at rest. Her oxygen saturation is 95% on air and her chest is unchanged on examination. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
o: Use a fan and positioning, and check whether an opioid is prescribed
Arrange an arterial blood gas sample to guide oxygen therapy
Start oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula to ease her breathing
Give the 'as required' hyoscine butylbromide from her anticipatory box
12.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.16 and 1.5.17: consider non-pharmacological management of breathlessness (for example a fan), do not routinely start oxygen unless symptomatic hypoxaemia is known or suspected, and consider an opioid, a benzodiazepine or both.

n.1: An invasive test unlikely to change care should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.1.4).
n.2: With saturation of 95% she is not hypoxaemic; NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen for breathlessness.
n.3: Hyoscine butylbromide is used for secretions or bowel obstruction, not for breathlessness.

12.q: Lillian, 89, has dementia and gets out of bed at night. Her son asks for bed rails to be put up to stop her falling. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Assess the risks first, as rails can harm her if she climbs
Put the rails up and add a lap belt in her chair by day
Refuse the request because bed rails are not allowed
Put the rails up straight away, as her son has asked
12.w: Annexe B 7.4: use safety devices appropriately. Bed rails must be individually risk-assessed; for a person with dementia who mobilises, they may cause entrapment or a higher fall from climbing over. Alternatives include a low bed, crash mat or sensor alarm, discussed with her and her family.

n.1: A lap belt is a restriction needing capacity and best-interests consideration, not a routine add-on.
n.2: Bed rails can be used after individual assessment.
n.3: A relative's request does not replace an individual risk assessment.

12.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
12.q: A student nurse asks when a learning disability, on its own, can count as a mental disorder for detention for treatment under section 3 of the Mental Health Act 1983. What does section 1(2A) require?
o: Association with a serious and continuing risk of self-neglect or exploitation
Association with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct
Assessment of the learning disability as severe or profound
A coexisting diagnosis of autism or of a personality disorder of any kind
12.w: MHA 1983 s1(2A)-(2B): for section 3, guardianship, CTOs and most Part 3 provisions, a person with a learning disability is not considered to have a mental disorder by reason of that disability unless it is associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.

n.0: Self-neglect or exploitation is not the statutory qualifier.
n.2: The qualifier concerns conduct, not the severity of the learning disability.
n.3: A second diagnosis is not what the qualifier requires.

12.q: Joan, 70, has suspected sepsis and a NEWS2 of 7. The doctor prescribes an initial intravenous fluid bolus. Under NICE NG253 (2025), what is the recommended initial bolus?
o: 20 mL/kg of 5% glucose over 30 minutes
250 mL isotonic crystalloid over 10-15 minutes
500 mL isotonic crystalloid over 10-15 minutes
1,000 mL isotonic crystalloid over 1 hour
12.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.5-1.8.9: give an initial bolus of 250 mL isotonic crystalloid ideally over 10-15 minutes, reassess after each bolus, and repeat up to 1,000 mL in total.

n.0: 5% glucose is not an isotonic resuscitation fluid and 20 mL/kg is not the adult sepsis bolus.
n.2: 500 mL in under 15 minutes is the general CG174 resuscitation bolus, not the NG253 sepsis bolus.
n.3: 1,000 mL is the cumulative ceiling before seeking senior advice, not the first bolus.

12.q: Ms Hunt, 55, has had the same leg ulcer care plan for three weeks. Measurements show the wound has not reduced in size, and she says the dressing leaks and stops her going out. What should the nurse do?
o: Reassess the wound with her and revise the plan, referring if needed
Ask her to stay at home more until the leaking settles down
Continue the plan, as wounds can take several months to heal
Change to a more absorbent dressing without discussing it with her
12.w: P3.15: work in partnership to monitor, evaluate and reassess care plans, readjusting goals and documenting progress. Lack of progress and a poor experience for the person mean the plan should be reviewed with her, with referral (for example to tissue viability) if needed (P3.16).

n.1: Restricting her life to suit the dressing is not person-centred and does not address the problem.
n.2: Continuing an unchanged plan ignores evidence that it is not working.
n.3: Changing the plan without her involvement is not partnership working.

12.q: Miss Patel, 45, has a learning disability and has substantial difficulty understanding the safeguarding process. Her only relative is the person suspected of abusing her. The local authority is starting a section 42 enquiry. What should happen?
o: The local authority arranges an independent advocate for her
Her relative supports her, as her closest family member
The enquiry continues without her views, to avoid distress
The nurse acts as her advocate throughout the enquiry
12.w: Care Act 2014 s68 and statutory guidance para 7.3: the local authority must arrange an independent advocate for a safeguarding enquiry where the adult has substantial difficulty being involved and there is no appropriate person to support them. The suspected abuser cannot be that person.

n.1: A relative suspected of abuse is not an appropriate person to support her.
n.2: Excluding her views contradicts Making Safeguarding Personal and the advocacy duty.
n.3: The nurse is not an independent advocate under the Care Act and has a different role.

12.q: Mr Day, 77, has type 2 diabetes and an infection. He is drowsy and his glucose meter displays 'HI' instead of a number. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the reading as normal and recheck it before the next meal
Assume the meter is faulty and replace it next week
Repeat the test in 4 hours with a different finger
Inform the doctor and send a venous sample for laboratory glucose
12.w: A 'HI' result means the glucose is above the meter's measurable range. In a drowsy person this needs urgent escalation and a laboratory glucose to establish the true value (Annexe B 2.10 and 2.5: manage and interpret blood glucose monitors).

n.0: 'HI' indicates a very high reading, not a normal one.
n.1: Assuming a fault without confirming the glucose risks missing a hyperglycaemic emergency.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours is unsafe in a drowsy person with a possible very high glucose.

12.q: Patience Okoro, 61, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab is left in her abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital in England. Under regulation 20 (statutory duty of candour), what must the provider do?
o: Notify her in person as soon as reasonably practicable, with an apology
Send her a written notification within 28 days of the incident
Notify her if she asks the surgical team whether anything went wrong
Notify her in writing once the incident investigation is completed
12.w: An unplanned return to surgery is moderate harm, so this is a notifiable safety incident. Regulation 20 (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014) requires notification in person as soon as reasonably practicable, including an apology, followed by a written notification, with records kept. Two steps: classify the harm, then apply the duty.

n.1: Regulation 20 requires notification as soon as reasonably practicable and in person first; 28 days is the duration test for prolonged pain or psychological harm.
n.2: Candour is proactive; the provider must notify without waiting to be asked.
n.3: The duty is not deferred until an investigation ends; further information is shared as enquiries progress.

12.q: Tom, 34, attends an acute medical unit with a urinary tract infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and sepsis is suspected. Under NICE NG253 (2025), within what time should broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics be given?
o: Within 3 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 6 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 4 hours of arrival in the department
12.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.3: for people at high risk (NEWS2 7 or more), give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score.

n.0: Up to 3 hours is the deferral window a clinician may use for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6).
n.2: Up to 6 hours is the deferral window for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.3: A 4-hour arrival target is not a sepsis treatment standard.

12.q: Bill, 85, has advanced dementia and cannot describe his pain. After a fall he grimaces, groans and guards his left hip when moved. Which assessment is most appropriate?
o: A visual analogue scale explained slowly to him
A behavioural pain tool such as the Abbey pain scale
A 0-10 numerical rating scale completed by Bill himself
His daughter's estimate of his pain on a 0-10 scale
12.w: Where a person cannot reliably self-report, for example because of dementia or a learning disability, use a validated behavioural or observational pain assessment tool such as the Abbey pain scale or PAINAD (NICE NG31 principle; Annexe B 3.1).

n.0: A visual analogue scale still needs him to self-report, which he cannot reliably do.
n.2: Numerical self-report relies on abilities Bill no longer has.
n.3: Family insight is valuable, but a proxy number is not a validated assessment.

12.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
12.q: Shona, 35, has a moderate learning disability and her friend at the day centre has died. Staff want to help her understand. Which approach is best?
o: Say her friend has 'gone to sleep' to soften it
Use clear words such as 'died' with pictures
Avoid mentioning the friend so she does not get upset
Tell her the friend has moved to another day centre
12.w: Clear, concrete language ('died', 'dead') with pictures or easy read is easier to understand than euphemisms. 'Gone to sleep' can cause confusion and fear about sleeping; honesty supports grieving.

n.0: Euphemisms are confusing and may cause fear of sleep.
n.2: Avoiding the subject leaves her confused and unsupported.
n.3: Lying undermines trust and prevents her from grieving.

12.q: Nadia, 49, has Down syndrome and lives in supported living. Over six months she has started needing prompts to wash and dress, and has become forgetful and withdrawn. Staff wonder if she has dementia. Which should the nurse ask the GP to check first?
o: Her IQ score compared with childhood
Her serum cholesterol and lipid profile
An urgent CT head scan
Thyroid function, hearing and vision
12.w: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and can mimic dementia or depression; hearing and vision loss also cause apparent cognitive decline. These treatable causes should be excluded before a dementia diagnosis (DSMIG/DSA thyroid guidance; NICE NG54 1.7.4 review physical health).

n.0: IQ tests do not measure change reliably and do not exclude treatable causes; adaptive behaviour compared with a baseline is used instead.
n.1: Lipids are part of general health checks but do not explain new loss of skills.
n.2: Neuroimaging is not the first step; reversible causes such as thyroid and sensory problems are checked first.

12.q: Bryony, 39, is nil by mouth after surgery. Her observations are stable and her prescription is for 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours via a volumetric infusion pump. The nurse is setting up the infusion and will ask a colleague to check it. At what rate should the pump be set?
o: 166 mL/h on the volumetric pump
125 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.5 mL/h on the volumetric pump
80 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.w: Rate (mL/h) = volume / time = 1,000 mL / 8 h = 125 mL/h. Accurate dosage calculation is a patient safety proficiency (P4.14) and the setting should be checked against the prescription.

n.0: 166 mL/h corresponds to 6 hours, not 8.
n.2: 12.5 mL/h is a decimal place error, a tenfold underinfusion.
n.3: 80 mL/h would deliver 1,000 mL over 12.5 hours.

12.q: You are alone on a quiet community visit when Sandra, 55, collapses. She is unresponsive and you have a mobile phone. According to RCUK 2025, what should you do next?
o: Give 2 minutes of CPR before calling 999
Call 999 on speaker, then assess breathing
Leave her to find a defibrillator first
Assess her breathing for one minute before calling
12.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: if alone with a phone, call 999 on speakerphone as soon as unresponsiveness is identified, before assessing breathing, so the call handler can guide CPR and locate an AED.

n.0: Delaying the call delays emergency help and AED location.
n.2: Leaving her delays both the call and CPR; the call handler can direct others to an AED.
n.3: Breathing is assessed for no more than 10 seconds, and the 2025 guideline calls 999 first if alone.

12.q: After inserting a peripheral cannula into the hand of Agnes, 88, the nurse needs to secure and cover the site. Which type of dressing is recommended so that the site can be inspected?
o: A sterile hydrocolloid dressing over the hub
A sterile gauze dressing and crepe bandage
Non-sterile adhesive tape over a gauze square
A sterile transparent semipermeable dressing
12.w: Vascular access device care (NICE CG139 and the IPC facts sheet) uses a sterile, transparent, semipermeable membrane dressing so the insertion site can be observed for signs of infection or phlebitis without removing it.

n.0: Hydrocolloid dressings are for wounds; they are opaque and not designed for cannula sites.
n.1: A bandage over gauze prevents regular inspection of the insertion site.
n.2: Non-sterile tape and gauze hide the site and are not a sterile covering for a Key-Site.

12.q: A student nurse on placement in a day centre reads that several people there have 'profound and multiple learning disabilities' (PMLD). Which description best fits PMLD?
o: A profound learning disability with physical or sensory impairments and complex health needs
A mild learning disability occurring together with autism, an anxiety disorder and sensory sensitivities
A learning disability acquired after a severe brain injury sustained in adult life
A moderate learning disability with behaviour that challenges and repeated placement breakdowns
12.w: PMLD means a profound learning disability together with additional physical and/or sensory impairments and complex health needs, usually with very limited or no verbal communication.

n.1: Autism and anxiety can coexist with any level of learning disability, but this does not describe PMLD.
n.2: An impairment starting in adult life is not a learning disability, whatever its severity.
n.3: Behaviour that challenges is not a defining feature of PMLD, and the learning disability is profound, not moderate.

12.q: During an incident, Harvey, 22, who has a learning disability, falls to the floor face down while staff are holding him. One staff member suggests keeping him there until he calms. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep him face down and count his breathing rate every five minutes
Help him into a seated or side position and monitor his breathing
Keep him face down with weight across his shoulders until he is calm
Leave him face down and ask all staff to step back and observe
12.w: Prone (face down) restraint carries a serious risk of positional asphyxia; Department of Health 'Positive and Proactive Care' (2014) says people must not be deliberately held face down. Staff should release or move to a safer position as soon as possible and monitor airway, breathing and wellbeing throughout (NICE NG10/NG11 principles).

n.0: Monitoring every five minutes does not remove the danger of continuing to hold him face down.
n.2: Pressure on the back or shoulders in the prone position greatly increases the risk of asphyxia.
n.3: Stepping back without helping him change position leaves him in an unsafe position and unmonitored at close range.

12.q: Mr Gordon Bailey, 79, is recovering from a hip fracture repair. He is not yet safe at home but the team expects he will be able to return home after a few weeks of rehabilitation in a community hospital bed. Which discharge pathway is this?
o: Pathway 3
Pathway 2
Pathway 1
Pathway 0
12.w: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based setting with dedicated recovery support, where short-term care helps the person recover before living independently or receiving longer-term care (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.2: Pathway 1 is discharge home with new support; Mr Bailey is not yet ready to go home.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new needs.

12.q: A student nurse asks Priti why she called the outreach team for a patient whose NEWS2 is 4, when the escalation chart only requires a ward review. Priti had noticed new subtle confusion. Which response best shows sound professional judgement?
o: Explain that her clinical concern justified the escalation
Explain that students should not question escalation decisions
Explain that the score required outreach review at that level
Explain that she prefers to escalate every patient to be safe
12.w: Proficiency P1.10: demonstrate resilience and emotional intelligence and explain the rationale for judgements and decisions. NEWS2 (RCP 2017): clinical concern can prompt escalation beyond the aggregate score; new confusion scores 3.

n.1: This shuts down learning; Code 9.4 requires her to support students' learning.
n.2: Under NEWS2 (RCP 2017) an aggregate of 4 calls for a ward-based response, urgent review by the ward medical team if one parameter scores 3, not outreach; her call rested on clinical concern.
n.3: Blanket escalation is not a reasoned judgement; P1.10 requires the rationale to be explained.

12.q: Before giving the first dose of oral amoxicillin to Stanley, 67, the nurse notices he is wearing a red allergy wristband labelled 'penicillin'. The allergy section of his drug chart is blank and the prescriber has gone home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose with an antihistamine to cover any possible reaction
Withhold it, clarify the allergy with Stanley and contact a prescriber
Give the dose, as the drug chart has no allergy recorded
Give half the dose and observe Stanley closely for any reaction
12.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 requires the person administering to check allergies or previous adverse drug reactions, and to raise ambiguities with the prescriber or pharmacy without delay. Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so the dose is withheld, the reaction history clarified, the chart updated and an alternative sought.

n.0: An antihistamine would not prevent anaphylaxis and the nurse cannot add a medicine.
n.2: The wristband is a warning that must be resolved; a blank chart is an omission, not evidence of no allergy.
n.3: Altering the prescribed dose is not within the nurse's role, and any dose risks anaphylaxis.

12.q: Nora, 80, is dying from heart failure in a nursing home. Tonight she has become restless, keeps pulling at her sheets and is groaning. She last passed urine 10 hours ago and her lower abdomen looks swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe an antipsychotic for terminal delirium
Ask a relative to sit with her and see whether she settles overnight
Give the prescribed 'as required' midazolam to settle her agitation
Assess her for urinary retention and pain before giving sedation
12.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.11 and 1.5.23: agitation in isolation is sometimes associated with unrelieved pain or a full bladder or rectum; treat reversible causes of pain such as urinary retention before considering benzodiazepines or antipsychotics.

n.0: An antipsychotic is considered for delirium only after reversible causes such as urinary retention are explored (recs 1.5.25 and 1.5.27).
n.1: Company can help, but it leaves a likely full bladder untreated; reversible causes should be assessed first.
n.2: Sedation first would mask a reversible cause; NG31 rec 1.5.23 says agitation may reflect a full bladder or unrelieved pain.

12.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
12.q: Kelly, 39, has a moderate learning disability and lacks capacity to manage her finances. A neighbour has started collecting her benefits and keeps most of the money, giving Kelly a small allowance. Kelly says she likes the neighbour and is happy. What should the community nurse do?
o: Raise a safeguarding concern, as Kelly meets the section 42 criteria
Respect Kelly's wishes, as she is happy with the arrangement
Ask the neighbour to keep receipts for everything that is spent
Apply to become Kelly's benefits appointee to control the money
12.w: Two steps: Kelly has care and support needs, is at risk of financial abuse and, lacking capacity about money, cannot protect herself (Care Act s42); so raise a safeguarding concern. Her wishes are important but do not remove the duty to protect.

n.1: Her wishes matter but she lacks capacity about finances and is at risk.
n.2: Receipts do not stop the neighbour keeping her money and do not address the abuse.
n.3: A nurse becoming her appointee creates a conflict of interest and bypasses safeguarding.

12.q: Chloe, 22, has a profound learning disability. Her DisDAT records that she makes loud moaning sounds when she is happy and goes silent and still when distressed. On admission a new nurse hears her moaning and plans to give PRN analgesia. What should the nurse do first?
o: Check her DisDAT and look for her other cues before deciding
Ask the doctor to prescribe regular analgesia in case of pain
Calculate a pain score using a numerical rating scale
Give the analgesia, since moaning is a common sign of pain
12.w: Cues are individual. Chloe's DisDAT shows moaning is a content cue, so the nurse should compare her presentation with the baseline and other cues before deciding she is in pain (DisDAT; Annexe B 3.1).

n.1: Prescribing regular analgesia without evidence of pain is not person-centred.
n.2: A numerical scale requires self-report, which Chloe cannot give.
n.3: General assumptions about pain signs can be wrong for an individual; her own cues must guide the decision.

12.q: Ollie, 21, has a moderate learning disability and is learning to brush his teeth independently. His nurse breaks the task into steps. Which approach to reinforcement is most likely to help him learn?
o: Correct each mistake as it happens and praise the finished task
Praise him straight after each step he completes
Praise him at the end of the week if he has brushed every day
Offer a reward once he can complete all steps without help
12.w: Immediate positive reinforcement of each step, with repetition, helps people with a learning disability learn new skills (Annexe A, repetition and positive reinforcement).

n.0: Focusing on correction with praise only at the end gives little reinforcement for each step learned.
n.2: Delayed praise is weakly linked to the behaviour and is less effective.
n.3: Waiting until full independence means no reinforcement during learning.

12.q: Roger, 61, is on an oncology ward having chemotherapy. He says he feels nauseated before each meal and has been leaving most of his food. He has a prescription for a regular antiemetic. Which nursing action is most appropriate first?
o: Encourage large meals to settle his stomach
Withhold all food until the nausea fully resolves
Give the prescribed antiemetic before meals and review it
Offer strong-smelling hot food to stimulate appetite
12.w: Annexe B 5.5: identify and manage nausea and vomiting. Give prescribed antiemetics at a time that covers meals, assess the response, and use measures such as small frequent meals and reducing food odours.

n.0: Large meals worsen nausea; small frequent meals are better tolerated.
n.1: Withholding all food risks malnutrition.
n.3: Strong food smells often worsen nausea.

12.q: Patricia, 73, lives in England and has had regular breast screening. She asks the practice nurse why she has not received an invitation since she turned 71. Which response is accurate?
o: Invitations stop after 70, but she can refer herself for screening
Women over 70 are invited every 5 years instead of every 3 years
Breast screening ends at 70 because no benefit remains after that age
She needs a GP referral to a breast clinic to be screened
12.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): breast screening is offered to women aged 50 to 70; women over 70 can self-refer.

n.1: Routine invitations are for women aged 50 to 70; after 70 screening is by self-referral.
n.2: Women over 70 can still self-refer; screening is available to them on request.
n.3: A breast clinic referral is for symptoms; screening after 70 is by self-referral.

12.q: Mr Tanaka, 82, has severe hearing loss and lip-reads. The nurse needs to explain his discharge plan. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Stand beside him and speak loudly into his better ear
Face him in good light and speak clearly at a normal pace
Give the information to his daughter to pass on later
Speak very slowly with exaggerated mouth movements
12.w: Annexe A 2.3: recognise and accommodate sensory impairments. Code 7.2-7.3: meet people's communication needs using a range of methods.

n.0: He lip-reads, so he needs to see the speaker's face; shouting distorts lip patterns.
n.2: This excludes him from his own care when he can communicate with adjustments.
n.3: Exaggeration distorts lip shapes and makes lip-reading harder.

12.q: A patient's family was told in person, with an apology, about a notifiable safety incident on the day it was identified. Under regulation 20, what must the provider do next?
o: Follow it with a written notification and keep a copy
Arrange a further meeting within 28 days to repeat the apology
Report the incident to the NMC for each nurse involved
Wait for the investigation to finish before any further contact
12.w: Reg 20(3)-(4): notification must be given in person, include an apology and be followed by a written notification; the provider must keep a copy and written records.

n.1: Reg 20 requires a written notification after the in-person one; a repeat meeting is not the specified step.
n.2: Reg 20 is about notifying the relevant person; NMC referral relates to fitness to practise concerns, not candour steps.
n.3: The written notification follows the in-person notification and gives what is known so far; it does not wait for the investigation to finish.

12.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
12.q: Sarah, 40, has a learning disability. Her father is dying in a hospice. Staff in her supported living home think she should not visit or go to the funeral because she 'won't understand'. What should the nurse advise?
o: Decide for her once her father has died
Support Sarah to choose whether to visit and attend
Agree that she should stay at home to avoid distress
Let her attend the funeral but not visit the hospice
12.w: Including people with a learning disability in saying goodbye and in rituals such as funerals supports healthy grieving. Assumptions that a person 'won't understand' are discriminatory; Sarah should be prepared accessibly and supported to make her own choice.

n.0: Delaying the decision removes her chance to see her father.
n.2: Excluding her denies her the chance to say goodbye and can complicate grief.
n.3: Restricting her to the funeral is a choice made for her, not by her.

12.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
12.q: Ruby, 38, has a profound learning disability and has been sitting in her wheelchair for six hours at a day centre. Her postural care plan says she should change position every two hours. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask her family to reposition her when she gets home
Leave Ruby in her chair as she seems content
Tilt the wheelchair back for the rest of the day
Reposition Ruby out of her chair as her plan sets out
12.w: Prolonged sitting in one position increases pressure damage and body shape distortion. The plan's schedule should be followed, using supported lying or standing as set out (24-hour postural care principles).

n.0: Delaying repositioning until she goes home breaches the plan and risks harm.
n.1: Appearing content does not mean her body is protected from prolonged sitting.
n.2: Tilting changes pressure but she has already exceeded the planned time in her chair.

12.q: Mr Daly, 81, on a general medical ward, has become muddled and restless since yesterday evening and is not sure where he is. His wife says he is 'not himself'. Which tool does NICE CG103 recommend the nurse uses to assess him for delirium?
o: The Abbreviated Mental Test score
The 4AT
The Mini Mental State Examination
The CAM-ICU
12.w: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.1: if indicators of delirium are identified, a competent practitioner should assess using the 4AT; in critical care or the recovery room use CAM-ICU or ICDSC instead.

n.0: The AMT is a cognitive screen, not the delirium tool recommended in CG103.
n.2: The MMSE assesses cognitive impairment and is not the CG103 delirium assessment tool.
n.3: CAM-ICU is recommended for critical care and recovery settings, not a general ward.

12.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
12.q: Phil, 48, has a learning disability and lives in supported living, where staff help him manage his money. Which finding is most suggestive of financial abuse?
o: Phil asking staff to help him check his bank statement at the end of each month
Phil choosing to spend a large amount on a football season ticket
Unexplained cash withdrawals and no money for food despite benefits
A planned increase in Phil's rent agreed at his tenancy review
12.w: Unexplained withdrawals and a lack of money for basics when income is adequate are recognised indicators of financial abuse and need a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Seeking help to check statements is a protective habit, not a sign of abuse.
n.1: A person's own spending choice, even if large, is not abuse.
n.3: An agreed rent increase is an expected, transparent cost.

12.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
12.q: Following an SLT assessment last month, Tom, 37, who has a learning disability and dysphagia, has a new drinks chart. A support worker in his supported living service asks the nurse what IDDSI level 2 on the chart means. Which description is correct?
o: Slightly thick
Extremely thick
Mildly thick
Moderately thick
12.w: IDDSI drinks levels: 0 thin, 1 slightly thick, 2 mildly thick, 3 moderately thick, 4 extremely thick (IDDSI framework).

n.0: Slightly thick is level 1.
n.1: Extremely thick is level 4.
n.3: Moderately thick is level 3.

12.q: Asif, a staff nurse, is explaining risk to a group of student nurses. Which statement best describes the difference between risk management and risk aversion?
o: Risk management weighs harms and benefits with the person; risk aversion avoids any activity with risk
Risk management is the manager's task; risk aversion is the approach expected of each nurse
Risk management is completed on admission; risk aversion is used once a person has been harmed
Risk management removes every activity that could cause harm; risk aversion accepts all risk
12.w: Risk management identifies hazards, weighs harms against benefits with the person and puts in proportionate controls so that valued activity can continue. Risk aversion avoids activity to prevent any chance of harm, often at the cost of independence and wellbeing (P6.10). Positive risk-taking is part of person-centred care.

n.1: Every registrant manages risk (Code 16, 19 and 25.1); risk management is not confined to managers.
n.2: Risk management is continuous and is reviewed when circumstances change, not a single admission task.
n.3: This describes avoiding harm at all costs, which is risk aversion, and misdescribes risk aversion as accepting all risk.

12.q: Jordan, 28, has a mild learning disability and is about to sign a consent form for a hernia repair. He speaks fluently and says 'yes, that's fine' to everything the surgeon explains. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
o: Check what he has understood, as fluent speech can mask poor comprehension
Accept his signature, as a mild learning disability rarely affects consent
Ask his mother, who attends with him, to sign the form on his behalf
Request a formal capacity assessment by a psychiatrist before surgery
12.w: People with a mild learning disability may have expressive language that exceeds their understanding and may agree to please. Asking Jordan to explain the procedure in his own words, with accessible information, checks understanding before consent is relied on (MCA s1(3): all practicable steps).

n.1: Capacity is presumed, but agreement alone does not show that Jordan has understood the information.
n.2: Another adult cannot consent for Jordan; a parent has no legal authority to sign for an adult.
n.3: There is no reason yet to doubt capacity formally; the first step is to check and support understanding, which any clinician can do.

12.q: Ruby, 7, is autistic and uses PECS. She now walks across the room to her communication book and hands a single picture to adults to request items. Her teacher asks what the next PECS phase will teach. Which answer is correct?
o: Answering 'What do you want?' using a sentence strip
Commenting on things she sees, such as 'I see a dog'
Building a sentence strip with 'I want' and an item picture
Choosing the correct picture from two or more pictures
12.w: Ruby has achieved Phase 2 (distance and persistence). Phase 3 is picture discrimination: choosing the right picture from several. Phase 4 then adds sentence structure (PECS).

n.0: Responding to 'What do you want?' is Phase 5.
n.1: Commenting is Phase 6, the final phase.
n.2: Sentence structure is Phase 4, after discrimination in Phase 3.

12.q: Mrs Oyelaran, 79, is being discharged to a care home. Her son repeatedly tells staff in front of her that she 'has to go' and answers questions for her. When asked, Mrs Oyelaran looks at her son and says, 'I suppose so.' What should the nurse do first?
o: Refer her for an assessment of her mental capacity
Ask her son to sign the agreement on his mother's behalf
Record that she has agreed to the move to the care home
Speak with Mrs Oyelaran alone to explore her own wishes
12.w: Valid consent must be given voluntarily, free from pressure by others. The nurse should first speak with Mrs Oyelaran privately to establish her own view. Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)), so concern about influence is not a reason to question capacity.

n.0: There is nothing to suggest an impairment of mind or brain; pressure from a relative raises a question of voluntariness, not capacity.
n.1: A son has no authority to consent for an adult unless he holds a relevant LPA or deputyship; nothing suggests this.
n.2: Her hesitant answer under pressure may not be voluntary; recording it as agreement could be invalid.

12.q: Mrs Anita Rao, 68, is admitted for elective surgery. She is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. Her 12-year-old grandson has come with her and offers to interpret. What should the admitting nurse do?
o: Record and flag her need for a BSL interpreter and arrange one to attend
Rely on lip reading by facing Mrs Rao and speaking slowly and clearly
Accept the grandson's offer, as Mrs Rao is comfortable with him interpreting
Use written notes for the admission, as she can read English well
12.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs arising from disability or sensory loss. A qualified BSL interpreter ensures accurate information and valid consent; children should not be used to interpret clinical information (Code 7.2; P7.9).

n.1: Lip reading is unreliable for complex clinical information and is not her preferred communication method.
n.2: A child interpreter may mistranslate clinical information and is placed in an inappropriate role, risking invalid consent.
n.3: Written English may not be fully accessible to a first-language BSL user, and the standard requires her preferred format.

12.q: While giving a subcutaneous injection to Peter, 61, who has hepatitis C, nurse Hana sustains a needlestick injury to her finger through her glove. The needle has been used. What should Hana do immediately?
o: Let it bleed without squeezing, wash with soap and running water, then report
Squeeze the wound firmly to express blood, then apply an alcohol wipe
Suck the wound, cover it with a plaster and report it after the drug round
Scrub the wound with a nail brush and chlorhexidine, then apply a dressing
12.w: NIPCM appendix 10: allow the area to bleed but do not squeeze, do not suck, and wash with warm running water and non-antimicrobial soap. The incident is then reported urgently so that occupational health or A&E can assess the need for post-exposure management; the Sharps Regulations 2013 require all sharps injuries to be reported.

n.1: Squeezing can push contaminated material deeper into tissue; NIPCM says allow bleeding without squeezing.
n.2: Sucking the wound is specifically advised against, and reporting must be prompt so treatment is not delayed.
n.3: Scrubbing damages tissue and may increase uptake; gentle washing under running water is advised.

12.q: A practice nurse is reviewing which patients might be contacted for lung cancer screening, available in some parts of England. Which person meets the age and smoking criteria?
o: Susan, 50, who currently smokes 15 cigarettes a day
Thomas, 78, who stopped smoking 30 years ago
Raj, 60, who smoked for 20 years and stopped 10 years ago
Ann, 65, a lifelong non-smoker who lives with a smoker
12.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked may be contacted by their GP or a local NHS service to take part in lung cancer screening.

n.0: Lung cancer screening is for people aged 55 to 74; Susan is under 55.
n.1: Thomas is over 74, above the age range for lung cancer screening.
n.3: Screening is for people who have ever smoked; Ann has never smoked.

12.q: Ken, 72, had severe delirium with sepsis and lacked capacity, so a covert plan was agreed for his antibiotics. Five days later his delirium has resolved, and an assessment shows he now has capacity to decide about his medicines. What should happen next?
o: Stop all his antibiotics, as the covert plan no longer applies
Stop covert administration and discuss his medicines with him
Continue covertly until the antibiotic course is complete
Continue covertly, as the plan states it runs for 14 days
12.w: Covert administration is lawful only while the person lacks capacity and refuses (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21). Once Ken regains capacity, the plan ends; his medicines are discussed openly and his informed decision respected (MCA 2005 s1).

n.0: The covert method ends, not the treatment; he can be offered the antibiotics openly.
n.2: Continuing covertly once he has capacity overrides his right to decide.
n.3: A plan's stated duration does not authorise covert use once capacity returns.

12.q: Kyle, a staff nurse, notices that Bev, a healthcare assistant, has become quiet and withdrawn since a relative criticised her in front of colleagues. Bev's care remains of a good standard. What is the most appropriate way for Kyle to support and motivate her?
o: Give Bev lighter tasks for the next few shifts so that she can recover
Speak with Bev privately, acknowledge her good care and ask how she is
Report Bev's change in mood to the ward manager for a formal welfare review
Tell Bev that complaints are part of the job and she should not take it personally
12.w: Leaders guide, support and motivate others (P5.6) and the Code asks registrants to work cooperatively and support the staff they are responsible for (Code 8, 25.2). Specific recognition and a private, supportive conversation help restore confidence and show that her work is valued.

n.0: Changing her work without discussion may suggest a lack of confidence in her.
n.2: Escalating to a formal process before talking with her is disproportionate.
n.3: Dismissing her feelings is unsupportive and unlikely to restore motivation.

12.q: Arthur, 88, is dying on a medical ward. His breathing has become noisy with a rattling sound. He is unconscious and appears settled. His daughter is upset and asks whether he is 'drowning'. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Explain that a medicine will be given now to stop the noise completely
Start oxygen through a face mask to make his breathing feel more comfortable
Explain that the noise means fluid on his lungs that needs a diuretic injection
Explain the noise is unlikely to be causing him discomfort, and reposition him
12.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.29 and 1.5.30: assess the cause of noisy respiratory secretions and the impact on the person and those important to them; reassure them that although the noise can be distressing it is unlikely to cause discomfort; consider non-drug measures such as repositioning.

n.0: Medicines are considered if secretions distress the dying person (rec 1.5.31), and they may not stop the noise completely.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen; offer it for known or suspected symptomatic hypoxaemia.
n.2: Noisy secretions in the last days are not treated as pulmonary oedema; the guidance is reassurance and non-drug measures first.

12.q: Over two months, Zara has noticed her usually cheerful colleague has become withdrawn, irritable with patients and has had several short-term absences. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Speak to her privately, voice concern and signpost support
Avoid raising it in case it causes her more stress
Suggest she takes annual leave to recover from stress
Report her absence pattern to the ward manager at once
12.w: Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risks to health. Code 8.7 support colleagues; escalate if patient safety becomes affected.

n.1: Avoiding the issue fails to support a colleague showing signs of vulnerability (P1.5).
n.2: Advising leave without understanding the problem may not meet her needs.
n.3: Raising it with the manager may follow, but a supportive conversation is the appropriate first step when there is no immediate safety risk.

12.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation attempt on a medical ward, Sofia, the nurse in charge, arranges a short team debrief once the immediate tasks are complete. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: Identify which member of staff made an error so that it can be dealt with formally
Reflect together on what went well and what could improve, and support staff
Complete the incident report and the statutory notification to the regulator
Decide as a team what information the family should and should not be given
12.w: Team reflection and debriefing support staff wellbeing and turn experience into learning for future practice (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; Code 8 work cooperatively; human factors and just culture principles).

n.0: A debrief is a supportive learning discussion, not a disciplinary process; a blame focus discourages openness.
n.2: Reporting is a separate governance step and is not the purpose of a team debrief.
n.3: Communication with the family is guided by candour and the person's wishes, not by a team agreement to withhold information.

12.q: Callum, 24, has a severe learning disability. Staff record that he screams and pushes his plate away at most mealtimes. The learning disability nurse starts an ABC chart. What should staff write in the 'A' column?
o: Staff members' views on why Callum behaves this way at meals
How staff responded and what happened straight afterwards
What happened just before Callum screamed and pushed his plate
Exactly what Callum did and how long the screaming lasted
12.w: ABC recording captures the Antecedent (what happened immediately before, the trigger), the Behaviour (a clear description of what the person did) and the Consequence (what happened afterwards). Antecedents point to triggers and setting events (NICE NG11 1.5.9-1.5.10).

n.0: Opinions about cause are not part of ABC data; the record should be objective observation.
n.1: Staff responses and what followed are recorded in the 'C' (consequence) column.
n.3: A description of what he did and its duration belongs in the 'B' (behaviour) column.

12.q: Jas, a learning disability nurse, is writing a Social Story for Riley, 15, who is autistic and is having a blood test. Which sentence fits the Social Story approach best?
o: The nurse will put a band on my arm. It will feel tight for a short time.
If I do not keep still, the nurse will have to try again.
Most young people are brave and do not cry when they have blood taken.
The needle is tiny, so it will not hurt me when it goes in.
12.w: Social Stories use descriptive, accurate and reassuring sentences, often in the first person, that explain what will happen and how it may feel. They avoid threats, comparisons and false promises (Carol Gray).

n.1: This frames the story as a warning, which can increase anxiety.
n.2: Comparisons and pressure to be 'brave' are not descriptive and can cause shame.
n.3: Promising it will not hurt is inaccurate and can damage trust.

12.q: Daniel, 52, is on a surgical ward breathing room air. His observations are: RR 18, SpO2 97%, BP 124/78, pulse 86, alert, temperature 37.4°C. His NEWS2 is 0. What is the minimum frequency of his observations under NEWS2?
o: Hourly
12-hourly
Every 30 minutes
4-6 hourly
12.w: RCP NEWS2 (2017) chart 4: an aggregate score of 0 requires a minimum of 12-hourly monitoring.

n.0: Hourly is the minimum for a single parameter scoring 3 or a total of 5 or more.
n.2: Every 30 minutes is not a NEWS2 chart 4 frequency; it is the NG253 recalculation interval for high sepsis risk.
n.3: 4-6 hourly is the minimum for a total score of 1-4.

12.q: At a team meeting, a district nursing team leader explains the integrated care partnership (ICP) in her area. Which statement about the ICP is correct?
o: It inspects and rates the quality of local health services
It is the NHS body that commissions hospital and GP services
It is a joint committee that develops the integrated care strategy
It employs the community nurses who work in the local area
12.w: The ICP is a joint committee run by the NHS organisations and upper-tier local authorities in each ICS, with wider partners such as the voluntary sector. It must develop a long-term integrated care strategy to improve health, care and wellbeing (NHS England, What is integrated care?; P7.1).

n.0: Inspection and rating are carried out by the Care Quality Commission in England.
n.1: Planning NHS services and managing the budget is the role of the integrated care board.
n.3: Community nurses are employed by provider organisations, not by the ICP.

12.q: Grace, 68, is admitted to a surgical ward. Three months ago she was an inpatient in a hospital abroad after a car accident. She has no symptoms of infection. What is the most appropriate placement while admission screening is arranged?
o: A single room with contact precautions while screening for CPE
A bay with other patients recently treated abroad, pending results
An open bay, after starting prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
An open bay, with screening repeated if she develops a fever
12.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 lists patients who have been inpatients in any hospital in the UK or abroad as a possible cross-infection risk for multidrug-resistant organisms such as carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE). She should be placed in a single room with contact precautions pending screening, and the decision documented.

n.1: Cohorting is for patients with the same confirmed infection; unscreened patients may carry different organisms.
n.2: Prophylactic antibiotics do not clear carriage and drive resistance, contrary to NICE NG15 stewardship.
n.3: CPE carriage is usually symptomless, so waiting for a fever leaves the bay exposed.

12.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
12.q: Priya, 18, has a learning disability and has just moved from children's to adult services. Her mother is used to making all health decisions for her. At her first adult appointment, how should the nurse approach decision-making?
o: Wait until Priya's mother arrives before any decision
Assume Priya lacks capacity because of her disability
Ask her mother to sign consent as she did before
Presume Priya has capacity and support her to decide
12.w: Adults (and young people aged 16+ under the MCA) are presumed to have capacity (MCA 2005 s1(2)) and must be given all practicable support to decide (s1(3)). Parental responsibility ends at 18, so a parent cannot consent on behalf of an adult; if Priya lacks capacity for a decision, a best interests process applies.

n.0: Her mother's views matter, but Priya should be supported to decide for herself.
n.1: A learning disability does not by itself mean lack of capacity.
n.2: A parent has no legal power to consent for an adult unless appointed as a deputy or attorney.

12.q: Reviewing the night's charts, Nurse Hana sees that a healthcare assistant recorded hourly observations for a patient who was off the ward in theatre for three of those hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Mention it informally to the healthcare assistant next week
Amend the entries herself so the chart is accurate
Leave it, as the patient has now returned safely
Escalate it to the nurse in charge straight away
12.w: Code 10.3: complete records without falsification, taking immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to these requirements. Code 16.1 escalate concerns.

n.0: Falsified observations are a safety concern; Code 10.3 requires immediate action.
n.1: Altering another person's entries is itself inappropriate; the concern must be escalated.
n.2: The patient's safety now does not remove the falsification; it must be acted upon.

12.q: Evie, 37, has a profound learning disability and pulls out her gastrostomy tube. Staff suggest arm splints at all times. The nurse wants the least restrictive option. Which plan is best?
o: Use arm splints at night and remove them for meals during the day
Ask the GP to prescribe sedation so that she does not pull the tube
Fit splints day and night and review them at the next annual review
Use a tube cover and abdominal binder, agreed in a best interests review
