12.w: MCA 2005 s1(6) requires the less restrictive option to be considered. A tube cover or binder protects the gastrostomy with far less restriction of movement than splints, and any restriction must be agreed through a best interests decision and reviewed (NICE NG11 1.9.5).

n.0: Night-time splints still restrict her movement for long periods when a less restrictive device could protect the tube.
n.1: Sedation is chemical restraint and is more restrictive than protecting the tube directly.
n.2: Continuous splints are highly restrictive, and waiting a year to review breaches the duty to minimise restriction.

12.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
12.q: Keith, 58, has a severe learning disability and has been assessed as lacking capacity to decide about chemotherapy for bowel cancer. He has no family or friends, and lives in a care home where paid staff have supported him for years. What should happen?
o: Consult the care home manager, who can act as his advocate for this decision
Let the oncology team make the decision, as there is no family to involve in it
Apply for a deputy to be appointed before any treatment decision
Instruct an IMCA, as this is serious treatment and no one is appropriate to consult
12.w: MCA 2005 s37: an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate must be instructed when serious medical treatment is proposed by the NHS for a person who lacks capacity and there is no one, other than paid carers, whom it would be appropriate to consult.

n.0: Paid care staff are not 'appropriate to consult' for IMCA purposes, so they cannot replace an IMCA.
n.1: A best interests decision without family still requires an IMCA for serious medical treatment.
n.2: A deputy is not needed; the IMCA route is the statutory safeguard and a deputy application would cause delay.

12.q: Dev, 27, has a moderate learning disability and enjoys cooking. His support team is planning his week. Which plan best reflects social role valorisation?
o: Support Dev into a paid job at a local café, a socially valued role
Plan for Dev to do colouring books in the evenings to help him relax
Book Dev into a hospital-based day unit where staff can supervise him
Arrange for Dev to attend a day centre for people with learning disabilities
12.w: Social role valorisation (Wolfensberger) holds that people who are devalued gain respect and a better life by being supported into socially valued roles, such as worker, neighbour or student, in ordinary community settings.

n.1: Children's activities for an adult reinforce a devalued, childlike image.
n.2: A hospital setting reinforces the sick role and segregation.
n.3: A segregated service does not create a valued role in the wider community.

12.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
12.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

12.q: Daniel, 24, has a learning disability and becomes agitated in a busy emergency department. He is shouting and pacing but has not hurt anyone. His support worker says loud noise upsets him. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the doctor to prescribe rapid tranquillisation
Tell him he must sit down or he will be removed
Move him somewhere quieter and use calm de-escalation
Call security to hold him until he is calmer
12.w: Restraint and restrictive interventions are a last resort. The first response to distress is to identify and reduce triggers and use de-escalation, applying the least restrictive option (MCA s1(6)) and person-centred information from those who know him.

n.0: Rapid tranquillisation is a restrictive intervention considered after other measures have been tried.
n.1: Threats are likely to escalate distress and are not person-centred de-escalation.
n.3: Physical holding is a last resort when there is risk of harm and de-escalation has failed; he has not harmed anyone.

12.q: Ivy, 85, has confirmed norovirus and her bed linen is soiled with diarrhoea. The healthcare support worker strips the bed. How should the soiled linen be handled?
o: Roll it up and seal it in a water-soluble bag inside an impermeable bag
Shake it out over the bin, then put it in a red-tagged bag at the bedside
Rinse off the faeces in the sluice, then place it in the used linen bag
Place it on the chair while remaking the bed, then bag it as used linen
12.w: NIPCM ch 1.7: infectious linen is not sorted or rinsed but rolled together and sealed in a water-soluble (alginate) bag, then placed in an impermeable bag immediately on removal, secured and tagged before leaving the area.

n.1: Shaking linen disperses organisms into the environment.
n.2: NIPCM says used linen must not be rinsed, and linen from an infectious patient is infectious, not used, linen.
n.3: Used linen must not be placed on floors or other surfaces such as chairs.

12.q: A community mental health nurse asks Leon, 27, "Think of a day recently when things were a little better. What was different about that day?" Which approach is the nurse using?
o: Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Motivational interviewing
Reminiscence therapy
12.w: Annexe A 3.2: solution-focused therapies. Asking about exceptions, when the problem was less present, builds on existing strengths.

n.0: CBT works on links between thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
n.2: MI explores ambivalence about change.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories to support wellbeing, mainly in older adults.

12.q: Mrs Harper, 58, is choosing between two treatment options for her knee. She asks the nurse what she would do. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to decide by tomorrow morning
Tell her which of the two options the nurse would personally choose
Advise her to follow whatever the consultant recommends
Explore what matters to her and each option's risks and benefits
12.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire [2015] UKSC 11: patients must be made aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions; P4.2 shared decision making.

n.0: Written information alone, with a deadline, does not support shared decision making.
n.1: Personal preference replaces her own values and undermines shared decision making.
n.2: This removes her from the decision instead of supporting an informed choice.

12.q: Lucas, 30, has a learning disability and is on the dynamic support register, rated at high risk of admission. His behaviour has escalated over a week, and his support provider says it can no longer cope. What should the community nurse do first?
o: Tell the provider to give notice so that the council must act quickly
Arrange for Lucas to go to the emergency department for assessment
Request an urgent community C(E)TR and extra support to keep him at home
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to settle him over the weekend
12.w: For people at high risk on the DSR, the policy is a community C(E)TR and intensive support to avoid admission where possible, with the least restrictive setting close to home (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy; NICE NG11 1.1 and NG93).

n.0: Encouraging the placement to end raises the risk of admission rather than reducing it.
n.1: A busy emergency department is an unfamiliar, noisy setting for a behavioural crisis and is likely to increase distress and the risk of admission.
n.3: NG11 does not support starting an antipsychotic before psychosocial review; this may also breach STOMP.

12.q: Amira, 29, is admitted to a gynaecology ward. Her notes record a history of sexual assault. When the nurse reaches to hold her hand during an examination, Amira flinches. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop, ask whether touch is acceptable and explain each step first
Ask a colleague to hold her hand in place of the nurse
Continue gently, as touch is a recognised comforting technique
Stop all communication until the examination is finished
12.w: Annexe A 1.3: use appropriate non-verbal communication, including touch, eye contact and personal space. Code 1.1 and 4.2: treat with respect and gain consent before any action.

n.1: Changing who touches her does not address whether she wants touch at all.
n.2: Comforting touch is only therapeutic when welcome; her reaction shows it is not.
n.3: Withdrawing communication leaves her anxious and unsupported.

12.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
12.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

12.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
12.q: Ella, 17, has a learning disability and is due to move to adult services next month, the same month her family moves house and she starts a new college. What does NICE NG43 advise about the timing of transfer?
o: Transfer at a time of relative stability, not on a rigid age
Transfer on her 18th birthday whatever else is happening
Transfer as planned, as delay will cause confusion
Transfer after she has settled in adult services
12.w: Two-step reasoning: several big changes coincide, so the timing of transfer should be reconsidered. NICE NG43 1.2.3: the point of transfer should not be based on a rigid age threshold and should take place at a time of relative stability for the young person.

n.1: NG43 says transfer should not be tied to a rigid age.
n.2: Proceeding during multiple changes ignores NG43's advice on stability.
n.3: She cannot settle in adult services before she has been transferred.

12.q: Bethan, a ward manager, asks her learning disability liaison nurse which theme runs through Death by Indifference, CIPOLD and the LeDeR reports, so that staff training can target it. Which theme should the liaison nurse identify?
o: A shortage of specialist learning disability inpatient beds nationally
Too many early referrals to specialist palliative care services
Over-reliance on community nurses in place of GP review
Delayed diagnosis and treatment, with family concerns not acted on
12.w: All three identify delays in recognising and treating illness, failures to make reasonable adjustments, diagnostic overshadowing and not listening to families and carers who know the person (Death by Indifference 2007; CIPOLD 2013; LeDeR 2023).

n.0: National policy aims to reduce reliance on inpatient beds; the reports did not identify bed shortages as the cause of avoidable deaths.
n.1: The reports raised concerns about end-of-life decisions, but early palliative referral was not a recurring cause of avoidable death.
n.2: The reports did not attribute deaths to community nurses replacing GP review.

12.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
12.q: A LeDeR review finds that Ahmed, 52, who had a learning disability, died after signs of pneumonia were attributed to his 'usual behaviour' and treatment was delayed for days. Which Human Rights Act article places a positive duty on the NHS in this context?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial
Article 3, the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 2, the right to life
12.w: Article 2 protects the right to life and places positive obligations on public authorities such as the NHS to protect life, including through proper systems of care; avoidable deaths linked to diagnostic overshadowing engage it.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings, not clinical care.
n.1: Article 3 concerns ill-treatment; the central issue in an avoidable death is the right to life.
n.2: Article 9 concerns belief and religion, not the delay in treatment.

12.q: Ellie, 35, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to an orthopaedic ward with a fractured wrist. Her support worker hands the nurse Ellie's hospital passport. What should the admitting nurse do with it?
o: Complete the trust admission assessment first and read the passport later
Photocopy it and give the original back for the support worker to take home
File it in the medical notes so it is available if questions arise
Read it, use it to plan care and keep it with Ellie for all staff to use
12.w: The passport is only useful if staff read and act on it. It should inform the care plan from admission and stay with the person, at the bedside, so every member of staff can see how to communicate with and support Ellie.

n.0: Leaving it until later means the admission assessment misses key information about communication, pain and allergies.
n.1: Sending the original home removes it from the person; a photocopy filed away is unlikely to be read by all staff.
n.2: Filed in the notes, the passport is easily missed by staff who need it at the bedside.

12.q: Liam, 26, has no learning disability. He tells his GP practice nurse that he struggles with social situations and has rigid routines, and asks whether he could be autistic. Which approach is in line with NICE CG142?
o: Use the AQ-10 and record a diagnosis of autism if he scores 6 or above
Request genetic testing before deciding whether to assess for autism
Consider the AQ-10 and offer full assessment if he scores 6 or above
Arrange an MRI brain scan to look for structural signs of autism
12.w: NICE CG142 1.2.3: for adults with possible autism who do not have a moderate or severe learning disability, consider the AQ-10; a score of 6 or above, or clinical suspicion, should lead to an offer of comprehensive assessment.

n.0: The AQ-10 is a screening tool; it identifies who needs a comprehensive assessment and does not make a diagnosis.
n.1: Genetic tests are not used routinely to diagnose autism.
n.3: CG142 advises against routine neuroimaging for diagnosing autism.

12.q: Sam, 22, has cerebral palsy with severe dysarthria and uses a communication aid. He does not have a learning disability. On admission, a nurse begins asking his mother questions about his symptoms. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Use simplified language and pictures, as for a person with a learning disability
Speak to Sam directly and allow time for him to use his aid
Continue with his mother, as she understands his speech more quickly
Ask closed yes or no questions throughout to save him effort
12.w: Cerebral palsy does not imply a learning disability. Sam should be addressed directly as the patient, with time to use his communication aid (Accessible Information Standard; NMC Code 7.1-7.3). His mother may help only if he wishes.

n.0: He does not have a learning disability, so simplifying language assumes a need he does not have.
n.2: Directing questions to his mother bypasses Sam and his right to speak for himself.
n.3: Closed questions may help at times, but limiting him to them throughout restricts what he can tell staff.

12.q: During lunch, the nurse notices that Mr Jacobs, 83, who had a stroke last week, coughs and splutters each time he drinks water, and his voice sounds wet afterwards. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop oral intake per local policy and refer him to speech and language therapy
Record the coughing and review at the next weekly team meeting
Give him thickened fluids of the nurse's choosing and continue his meal
Ask his family to bring in his favourite soft foods to help him eat
12.w: Coughing and a wet voice when drinking suggest unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk. Code 13.2 requires a timely referral to another practitioner when action, care or treatment is required, and P3.16 requires knowing when and how to refer safely: the speech and language therapist assesses swallowing, with intake managed per local dysphagia policy meanwhile.

n.1: Waiting a week leaves him at risk of aspiration pneumonia.
n.2: Choosing a fluid thickness without specialist assessment may still be unsafe.
n.3: Soft foods brought from home do not address the aspiration risk and may be unsafe.

12.q: A covert administration plan for Sidney, 88, states that his dispersible aspirin and liquid antibiotic may be mixed with food on pharmacist advice. The nurse plans to stir them into his full bowl of porridge, which he often leaves half-eaten. What is the best approach?
o: Mix them into the whole bowl so they are well disguised
Mix them into the porridge and give the rest with lunch
Mix them into a small amount of the advised food first
Mix them into his tea, which he usually finishes
12.w: The covert plan details how each medicine is given, with pharmacist advice (RPS/RCN 2019; NICE SC1). Using a small amount of the advised food, offered first, makes it more likely that the full dose is taken; mixing into a large portion risks a partial dose.

n.0: If he leaves half the bowl he receives only part of the dose.
n.1: Splitting a dose across meals is not in the plan and makes the dose taken uncertain.
n.3: Changing the vehicle to tea departs from the agreed plan and pharmacist advice on compatibility.

12.q: Ted, 67, has a PCA pump after bowel surgery. He is very drowsy, difficult to rouse, with RR 8 per minute and pinpoint pupils. His wife says he has been pressing the button for him while he slept. What is the priority?
o: Stop the PCA, support his breathing and call for urgent help
Explain to his wife that Ted must press the PCA button himself
Encourage him to take deep breaths and press the button less
Reduce the PCA bolus dose and recheck his observations in 1 hour
12.w: RR 8 scores 3 on NEWS2 and drowsiness scores 3: this is opioid toxicity. Stop the infusion, open and support the airway, give oxygen and get urgent help so that naloxone can be given as prescribed (P4.15). The PCA safety principle is that the person alone presses the button; this is addressed after the emergency.

n.1: Education is needed, but only after treating life-threatening respiratory depression.
n.2: He cannot respond reliably and needs emergency treatment, not encouragement.
n.3: Altering the dose and waiting an hour leaves respiratory depression untreated.

12.q: A nurse on a postnatal ward is explaining immunity to a new mother. She says her baby is born with some protection against measles because of antibodies the mother made. Which type of immunity is this?
o: Population immunity from high vaccine coverage in the community
Active immunity produced by the baby's own immune system
Innate immunity from the baby's skin and mucous membranes
Passive immunity from antibodies that crossed the placenta
12.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): passive immunity is protection from antibodies transferred from immune individuals, most commonly across the placenta; it is temporary, commonly lasting a few weeks or months, and is more effective against some infections (for example tetanus and measles) than others.

n.0: Population immunity reduces exposure; it is not antibody protection inside the baby.
n.1: The baby did not make these antibodies; they were transferred from the mother, which is passive immunity.
n.2: Innate immunity is non-specific; measles-specific antibodies from the mother are passive acquired immunity.

12.q: A nurse preparing a presentation on Building the Right Support checks progress on reducing inpatient numbers for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Which statement is accurate?
o: Inpatient numbers had not changed since the 2015 baseline
The halving target was met on time in March 2024
Numbers fell by about 29% by February 2025, missing the target
Inpatient numbers had fallen by about 75% by February 2025, beating it
12.w: In February 2025 there were 2,055 inpatients, down 29% from 2,905 in March 2015, so the target to halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 was missed (House of Commons Library SN07058).

n.0: Numbers did fall, from 2,905 to 2,055.
n.1: The target was not met; numbers fell by under a third.
n.3: The fall was about 29%, not 75%.

12.q: Edith, 90, is frail, weighs 45 kg and has chronic kidney disease. Routine IV maintenance fluids are prescribed at 30 mL/kg/day. What should the nurse do?
o: Double the rate to protect her kidneys from dehydration
Give the fluids as prescribed, as this is the standard rate
Query the prescription, as a lower rate may be needed
Change her to oral fluids without consulting the prescriber
12.w: NICE CG174: consider prescribing less fluid (for example 20-25 mL/kg/day) for people who are older or frail, or who have renal or cardiac impairment. Raising a concern about a prescription supports safe practice (Code 18, RPS/RCN 2019).

n.0: Doubling the rate risks serious fluid overload.
n.1: Standard rates may cause overload in frail people with renal impairment.
n.3: Changing the route without the prescriber is outside a nurse's authority.

12.q: Mrs Dawson, 84, has a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and is on a ward in England. She tells the nurse she wants to go home today rather than wait for physiotherapy. A junior doctor says, 'She has dementia, so she can't make that decision.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: She can go home, because a person with dementia keeps all their rights
A best interests meeting should be arranged before any assessment
Her capacity for this decision must be assessed, not assumed from diagnosis
Her daughter should be asked to decide, as she is her next of kin
12.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it. s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's condition. Capacity must be assessed for this decision at this time.

n.0: Whether she can safely go home depends on whether she has capacity for this decision; that has not yet been assessed.
n.1: Best interests decisions (s4) follow a finding that the person lacks capacity; the assessment comes first.
n.3: Next of kin has no legal power to make decisions for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.

12.q: Raymond, 74, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He usually wet shaves with a blade razor and asks for help to shave while in hospital. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply pressure to any cuts for 30 seconds afterwards
Use an electric razor to reduce the risk of bleeding
Postpone shaving until his anticoagulant is stopped
Use a new disposable blade razor and press gently
12.w: Annexe B 4.3: when assisting with shaving, consider risks such as anticoagulation. An electric razor reduces the risk of cuts and bleeding in people taking anticoagulants such as apixaban.

n.0: This responds to cuts rather than preventing them.
n.2: His anticoagulant is needed for stroke prevention and shaving is part of his personal care.
n.3: A blade razor still risks cuts that bleed more with anticoagulation.

12.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
12.q: A learning disability nurse is preparing a teaching session on international policy. Which statement about the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) is accurate?
o: It is a UK Act of Parliament that can be enforced directly in any UK court
It is a NICE guideline setting national quality standards for disability services
It is a European directive that replaced the Equality Act 2010 in the UK
It is an international treaty including the right to live independently in the community
12.w: The UNCRPD is a United Nations human rights treaty ratified by the UK. It sets out the rights of disabled people, including Article 19, living independently and being included in the community, and Article 12, equal recognition before the law.

n.0: It is an international treaty, not a UK statute directly enforceable in the courts.
n.1: It is not a NICE guideline.
n.2: It is a UN convention, and the Equality Act 2010 remains in force.

12.q: A family carer asks a learning disability nurse what STOMP is. Her son Liam, 30, has a learning disability and takes risperidone for behaviour that challenges. Which description is correct?
o: A medicines review that pharmacists complete when a person turns 18
A scheme that pays GPs to prescribe fewer antidepressants
A rule that people with a learning disability must not take antipsychotics
A national programme to stop the overuse of psychotropic medicines
12.w: STOMP (stopping over medication of people with a learning disability, autistic people or both) is an NHS England programme launched in 2016. It aims to stop inappropriate use of psychotropic medicines and to ensure the right medicine for the right reason, with regular review and non-drug alternatives; it is not anti-medication (NHS England STOMP).

n.0: STOMP is not tied to an age-18 review; STAMP covers children and young people.
n.1: STOMP is a health and care improvement programme, not a GP payment scheme for antidepressants.
n.2: STOMP supports appropriate use; antipsychotics remain right for some people, for example those with psychosis.

12.q: Jordan, 29, has a learning disability and has just had his annual health check. The practice nurse found raised blood pressure and that he has not seen a dentist for three years. Where should the agreed actions be recorded so Jordan and his supporters can follow them?
o: In his hospital passport held by the ward
In a behaviour support plan written by the team
In a health action plan agreed with Jordan
In a care and support plan from the local authority
12.w: Actions from the annual health check are written into a health action plan, which sets out what will be done, by whom and when, in a format the person can use (NHS.uk, Annual health checks).

n.0: A hospital passport tells hospital staff about the person on admission; it is not where annual health check actions are tracked.
n.1: A behaviour support plan addresses behaviour that challenges, not general health actions such as blood pressure and dental care.
n.3: A Care Act care and support plan covers social care needs; health actions belong in the health action plan.

12.q: A ward manager in an English hospital is updating staff training on people who lack capacity and whose care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. A nurse asks which legal scheme is currently in force to authorise such arrangements in hospitals and care homes. What should the manager say?
o: The nurse's holding power under the Mental Health Act 1983
The Liberty Protection Safeguards under the 2019 Amendment Act
The community treatment order scheme under the Mental Health Act
The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards under the MCA 2005
12.w: DoLS (MCA 2005 Schedules A1 and 1A) remain the scheme in force in England and Wales for hospitals and care homes. The Liberty Protection Safeguards in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 have not been implemented.

n.0: The nurse's holding power under MHA s5(4) briefly detains an informal inpatient with mental disorder; it does not authorise care arrangements under the MCA.
n.1: The LPS have not been brought into force; DoLS remain the live scheme.
n.2: Community treatment orders apply to certain detained patients leaving hospital, not to people lacking capacity in hospitals or care homes.

12.q: Dorothy, 86, has advanced dementia. For three days she has spat out her anticonvulsant and pushed staff away at medicine rounds. Her son suggests hiding it in her tea. What is the nurse's most appropriate first step?
o: Assess her capacity to make this specific decision about the medicine
Arrange for the medicine to be given by injection instead
Hide the medicine in her tea, as she has a diagnosis of dementia
Stop the anticonvulsant, as she is repeatedly refusing it
12.w: The MCA 2005 (ss1-3) requires a capacity assessment that is decision-specific and time-specific; a diagnosis of dementia alone does not establish incapacity. Only if she lacks capacity can a best interests decision about covert administration follow (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21).

n.1: Changing the route needs a prescriber and does not address capacity or consent.
n.2: A diagnosis does not prove lack of capacity (MCA s2(3)); covert use also needs a best interests process.
n.3: Stopping an anticonvulsant risks seizures; the refusal needs assessment, not unilateral cessation.

12.q: At the end of a shift, the nurse is evaluating Mrs Dunn's care plan for pain after a hip fracture. Which entry best documents her progress?
o: Pain management ongoing; patient seems a lot more comfortable this afternoon.
Patient complained of pain all morning but is settled now.
14:30 Pain 7/10 moving at 12:00; 3/10 at 13:00 after oxycodone. Plan continued.
Analgesia given as prescribed. Continue current plan as per care plan.
12.w: Code 10.1-10.4: complete records accurately at the time, attributing, dating and timing entries without speculation. P3.15 requires documenting progress against goals; a timed, measured pain score before and after the intervention shows whether the plan is working.

n.0: 'Seems more comfortable' gives no measurement and is open to interpretation.
n.1: 'Complained' is judgemental, and the entry gives no times, scores or interventions.
n.3: This records an action but not its effect, so progress cannot be evaluated.

12.q: Ama is due to revalidate next month. Her CPD log shows 35 hours: 18 hours at a study day and team workshops, and 17 hours reading journal articles on her own. What is the position on her CPD requirement?
o: She needs five more hours of any type of CPD
She needs two more hours of participatory learning
She needs fifteen more hours of participatory learning
She meets it, as she has 35 hours in total
12.w: NMC revalidation CPD requirement (updated 08/09/2021): 35 hours of CPD in three years, of which at least 20 must include participatory learning. 20 - 18 = 2 participatory hours still needed.

n.0: Her total of 35 is already met; the shortfall is in participatory hours, not overall hours.
n.2: She needs 20 participatory hours in total; with 18 already logged, the gap is two hours.
n.3: The total is met, but at least 20 of the 35 hours must be participatory; she has 18.
